title: A Design Science Research Methodology for Information Systems Research
authors: Ken Peffers; Tuure Tuunanen; Marcus A. Rothenberger; Samir Chatterjee
venue: Journal of Management Information Systems
domain: Information Systems and Computer Science Research Methodology
problem_statement: The lack of a widely accepted, standardized methodology for conducting and evaluating design science research in Information Systems, leading to uncertainty in research execution and evaluation.
theoretical_framework: Design Science Research (DSR) paradigm and Systems Development Methodology
methodology: Development of a six-stage sequential process model synthesized from prior design science literature and validated through four case study applications across different research entry points.
evaluation: Qualitative evaluation of the methodology across four distinct case studies demonstrating problem-centered, objective-centered, design-and-development-centered, and client-initiated research trajectories.
key_findings: Established a six-step nominal process model for Design Science Research: Problem Identification, Objectives Definition, Design and Development, Demonstration, Evaluation, and Communication.; Demonstrated that DSR can initiate from multiple entry points depending on whether the research originates from an observed problem, an objective opportunity, a technical artifact innovation, or a client need.; Provided a standard structure for rigorous evaluation of computational artifacts against explicit quantitative and qualitative solution objectives.
scope_and_delimitations: Focuses on design-oriented information systems and computational artifact research, excluding purely behavioral survey methods.
limitations_summary: The methodology is presented as a nominal linear sequence but inherently requires iterative cycles in practical implementation.
limitations_verbatim: The process model presented here is not intended to suggest that DSR should always proceed in a rigid, linear fashion. Research processes are often iterative and may cycle through steps.
generalizability_gap: Primarily illustrated in information systems research; requires adaptation for specialized deep learning and optimization engineering workflows.
methodological_gap: Does not prescribe domain-specific statistical significance testing protocols for machine learning benchmarks.
future_work: Application and refinement of DSRM across specialized computational, artificial intelligence, and software engineering domains.
local_dir: A Design Science Research Methodology for Information Systems Research

title: A Joint Many-Task Model: Growing a Neural Network for Multiple NLP Tasks
authors: Kazuma Hashimoto; Caiming Xiong; Yoshimasa Tsuruoka; Richard Socher
venue: Proceedings of the 2017 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2017)
domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Multi-Task Learning, Linguistic Hierarchy Modeling, Deep Neural Networks, Sequence Tagging, Syntactic Parsing, Sentence Semantics
problem_statement: How to jointly train a single deep neural network across multiple increasingly complex NLP tasks across morphological, syntactic, and semantic levels by reflecting linguistic hierarchies in network depth, sharing low-level predictions with higher layers, and preventing catastrophic forgetting or catastrophic interference across tasks.
theoretical_framework: Linguistic hierarchy principles in NLP (morphology to syntax to semantics, e.g. POS tags -> chunk tags -> syntactic dependencies -> semantic relatedness -> textual entailment); multi-task learning with deep neural networks (Caruana, 1997; Collobert et al., 2011; Søgaard and Goldberg, 2016) where lower-level tasks are supervised at lower layers; continual learning without catastrophic forgetting (Li and Hoiem, 2016; Rusu et al., 2016); Skip-gram word and character n-gram distributional semantics (Mikolov et al., 2013; Bojanowski et al., 2017); bidirectional LSTMs (Graves & Schmidhuber, 2005; Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997); greedy dependency parsing as head selection (Zhang et al., 2017; Dozat & Manning, 2017; Eisner, 1996); and sentence-pair semantic representation via element-wise operations and Maxout networks (Tai et al., 2015; Goodfellow et al., 2013).
methodology: The Joint Many-Task (JMT) model implements a five-layer bidirectional LSTM architecture where depth successively grows to solve five NLP tasks ordered by linguistic hierarchy: (1) POS tagging on layer 1 with a ReLU softmax classifier; (2) chunking on layer 2 taking layer 1 hidden states, shared word/character embeddings, and weighted POS label embeddings; (3) dependency parsing on layer 3 taking layer 2 hidden states, shared embeddings, and POS + chunking label embeddings, scoring candidate parents via a matching function and applying Eisner's algorithm when non-projective cycles occur; (4) semantic relatedness on layer 4 using max-pooling over token hidden states, element-wise difference and product operations between sentence representations, and a Maxout softmax classifier trained via KL-divergence loss; and (5) textual entailment on layer 5 using max-pooling, asymmetric sentence subtraction and multiplication, and weighted relatedness label embeddings fed into three Maxout hidden layers with cross-entropy loss. All layers use shortcut connections feeding the shared input embeddings (Skip-gram word + averaged unique character n-gram embeddings). Training follows a sequential dataset iteration per epoch with growing gradient clipping (min(3.0, depth)), L2-norm regularization, dropout, and a successive regularization term δ||θ_{task} - θ'_{task}||^2 that penalizes divergence from parameters trained at the previous task/epoch to prevent catastrophic interference.
datasets: Penn Treebank (WSJ): POS tagging (Sections 0-18 train / 19-21 dev / 22-24 test; 39,832 train sentences); CoNLL-2000 Shared Task (WSJ): Chunking (Sections 15-18 train / 19 dev / 20 test; IOBES tagging scheme); Penn Treebank (WSJ) with Stanford Dependencies (v3.3.0): Dependency parsing (Sections 2-21 train / 22 dev / 23 test; UAS and LAS metrics excluding punctuation); SICK (Sentences Involving Compositional Knowledge): Semantic relatedness (4,500 train / 500 dev / 4,927 test sentence pairs; real-valued relatedness score 1-5); SICK (Sentences Involving Compositional Knowledge): Textual entailment (4,500 train / 500 dev / 4,927 test sentence pairs; 3 classes: entailment, contradiction, neutral)
evaluation: {'metrics': ['POS tagging: Word-level accuracy (%)', 'Chunking: F1 score (%) under IOBES scheme', 'Dependency parsing: Unlabeled Attachment Score (UAS %) and Labeled Attachment Score (LAS %) excluding punctuation', "Semantic relatedness: Mean Squared Error (MSE), Pearson's r, Spearman's rho", 'Textual entailment: 3-class classification accuracy (%)'], 'benchmark_results': {'POS_Tagging_WSJ_Accuracy': {'Single_Task': 97.1, 'JMTall': 97.55, 'Ling_et_al_2015_SOTA': 97.78}, 'Chunking_CoNLL2000_F1': {'Single_Task': 95.05, 'JMTAB': 95.77, 'Sogaard_and_Goldberg_2016': 95.56, 'Suzuki_and_Isozaki_2008_SOTA': 95.15}, 'Dependency_Parsing_WSJ_UAS_LAS': {'Single_Task_UAS': 93.35, 'Single_Task_LAS': 91.21, 'JMTall_UAS': 94.71, 'JMTall_LAS': 93.0, 'Andor_et_al_2016_UAS': 94.61, 'Dozat_and_Manning_2017_SOTA_UAS': 95.74}, 'Semantic_Relatedness_SICK_MSE': {'Single_Task': 0.26, 'JMTDE': 0.24, 'JMTall': 0.233, 'Tai_et_al_2015_SOTA': 0.253, 'Zhou_et_al_2016_SOTA': 0.243}, 'Textual_Entailment_SICK_Accuracy': {'Single_Task': 83.1, 'JMTDE': 85.8, 'JMTall': 86.2, 'Yin_et_al_2016_SOTA': 86.2}}}
key_findings: Stacking NLP tasks at successively deeper layers according to linguistic hierarchy (POS tagging -> chunking -> dependency parsing -> semantic relatedness -> textual entailment) significantly outperforms predicting tasks at the same depth or handling tasks separately.; Joint multi-task training in the JMT model improves performance across all five tasks compared to their single-task baselines, demonstrating that joint learning benefits both higher-level semantic tasks and lower-level syntactic/tagging tasks.; Shortcut connections that directly feed shared word and character n-gram representations into all deeper BiLSTM layers are critical for performance, particularly for semantic tasks in higher layers.; Explicitly passing predicted output label embeddings from lower layers to higher layers provides substantial improvements over solely sharing internal hidden states (vertical connections).; Successive regularization prevents catastrophic interference across tasks, yielding notable performance gains on tasks with smaller dataset sizes (such as chunking).; Training tasks in order from lower-level to higher-level within each epoch outperforms random task shuffling or mixed mini-batching.; Pre-trained character n-gram embeddings combined with word embeddings provide essential morphological features that improve POS tagging, chunking, and parsing accuracy without requiring complex character LSTM encoders.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Evaluated exclusively on English-language text benchmarks spanning five specific tasks across the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) Penn Treebank and SICK datasets, without testing on non-English languages, multilingual transfer, machine translation, or dialogue systems.', "Constrained model architecture to five stacked bidirectional LSTM layers with hidden state and embedding dimensionality of 100, using greedy head-selection parsing backed by Eisner's algorithm and max-pooling sentence representations.", 'Limited shared input representations to Skip-gram word embeddings and averaged unique character n-gram embeddings (n=1,2,3) without transformer-based contextual language models.', 'Delimited training optimization to sequential iteration over full datasets per epoch with gradient clipping capped at min(3.0, depth) and joint parameter regularization.']
limitations_summary: The JMT model lacks an optimal stopping and scheduling mechanism across tasks with highly imbalanced dataset sizes, forcing all tasks to share identical training epochs and learning rate decay schedules despite semantic tasks reaching peak performance earlier than data-heavy syntactic parsing tasks. In addition, the model does not explicitly exploit predicted dependency tree structures for downstream semantic tasks, uses simple greedy parsing requiring post-hoc tree corrections, and relies on fixed-dimensional static embeddings.
limitations_verbatim: In our JMT model, it is not obvious when to stop the training while trying to maximize the scores of all the five tasks. We focused on maximizing the accuracy of dependency parsing on the development data in our experiments. However, the sizes of the training data are different across the different tasks; for example, the semantic tasks include only 4,500 sentence pairs, and the dependency parsing dataset includes 39,832 sentences with word-level annotations. Thus, in general, dependency parsing requires more training epochs than the semantic tasks, but currently, our model trains all of the tasks for the same training epochs. The same strategy for decreasing the learning rate is also shared across all the different tasks, although our growing gradient clipping method described in Section 5.2 helps improve the results. Indeed, we observed that better scores of the semantic tasks can be achieved before the accuracy of dependency parsing reaches the best score. Developing a method for achieving the best scores for all of the tasks at the same time is important future work.
generalizability_gap: The JMT architecture was evaluated exclusively on English language corpora across a limited set of five standardized tasks (WSJ Penn Treebank and SICK); the authors did not test generalization to non-English languages, morphologically rich languages, cross-lingual transfer, cross-domain adaptation, long-document understanding, or generative sequence-to-sequence tasks.
methodological_gap: The model trains all tasks for a uniform number of epochs with a uniform learning rate schedule despite large disparities in dataset sizes and convergence rates; it does not dynamically balance task losses or optimize task-specific early stopping; the higher-level semantic layers use simple max-pooling and do not explicitly consume the parse trees or structural outputs generated by the dependency parsing layer; and dependency parsing relies on greedy head selection requiring post-hoc Eisner algorithm projection rather than global biaffine attention or transition-based search.
future_work: Developing a method for achieving the best scores for all of the tasks at the same time by addressing task-specific training epochs and learning rate scheduling.; Incorporating more complex tasks into the JMT model, such as entity detection, relation extraction, and language modeling.; Training each task across multiple domains to enhance domain adaptation capabilities.; Efficiently utilizing large unlabeled text corpora to improve the entire hierarchical multi-task representation beyond initial word and character embedding pre-training.; Explicitly incorporating learned syntactic dependency structures into higher-level semantic reasoning layers.; Learning low-level tasks via task-oriented optimization of high-level objectives, such as latent graph parsing driven by neural machine translation.

title: A Model of Inductive Bias Learning
authors: Jonathan Baxter
venue: Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research (JAIR)
domain: Theoretical Machine Learning, Statistical Learning Theory, and Inductive Transfer
problem_statement: Providing a formal theoretical model and sample complexity bounds for how learning multiple related tasks simultaneously allows a machine learning system to learn an effective inductive bias and improve generalization.
theoretical_framework: Statistical Learning Theory, VC Dimension, Covering Numbers, and Inductive Bias Learning
methodology: Formal mathematical proof of generalization bounds and sample complexity in multi-task learning environments using uniform convergence and covering numbers over representation spaces.
evaluation: Rigorous mathematical proofs establishing upper bounds on generalization error and sample complexity for multi-task representation learning.
key_findings: Formulated the foundational statistical learning theory of multi-task learning as bias learning over an environment of tasks.; Proved that joint multi-task representation learning reduces the sample complexity required per task by a factor of 1/K for shared representation capacity.; Demonstrated mathematically that sharing representations across related tasks restricts hypothesis space capacity, preventing overfitting and improving generalization on low-resource tasks.
scope_and_delimitations: Theoretical mathematical analysis of inductive bias learning across families of hypothesis spaces.
limitations_summary: Assumes tasks share an underlying environment distribution; incompatible tasks can induce negative transfer.
limitations_verbatim: The bounds assume that tasks are sampled independently from a stationary task distribution. If tasks in the multi-task set are fundamentally incompatible or unrelated, the shared bias may hinder rather than help learning.
generalizability_gap: Pre-dates deep neural networks and modern Transformer architectures.
methodological_gap: Does not address gradient dynamics, directional gradient conflicts, or dynamic loss weighting in non-convex neural optimization.
future_work: Extending statistical learning theory bounds to non-linear deep neural network feature spaces and gradient-based optimization algorithms.
local_dir: A Model of Inductive Bias Learning

title: A Survey of Code-switching: Linguistic and Social Perspectives for Language Technologies
authors: A. Seza Doğruöz; Sunayana Sitaram; Barbara E. Bullock; Almeida Jacqueline Toribio
venue: Proceedings of the 59th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 11th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (ACL-IJCNLP 2021)
domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Computational Linguistics, Sociolinguistics, Multilingualism, Code-Switching (C-S) in European and Indian multilingual contact contexts
problem_statement: Computational linguistics and natural language processing research on code-switching predominantly focuses on algorithmic and computational improvements while ignoring rich linguistic, structural, cognitive, and sociolinguistic theories from linguistics literature, resulting in massive multilingual models that fail to capture diverse code-switching types, lack adequate training data and benchmarks, and omit sociolinguistic dynamics in user-facing applications.
theoretical_framework: Theoretical linguistic and sociolinguistic frameworks of code-switching, including the Matrix Language Frame (MLF) model (Myers-Scotton; Joshi), Equivalence Constraint (Poplack), Government Constraint (DiSciullo et al.), Functional Head Constraint (Belazi et al.), Constraint-free models (Mahootian & Santorini; MacSwan), Auer's continuum of bilingual speech (prototypical code-switching, language mixing, mixed languages), Politeness theory and face-saving (Lavric), Clyne's eight-factor interactional model, and socio-indexical identity marking/backflagging (Muysken; Poplack; Gumperz; Zentella; Finnis).
methodology: Cross-disciplinary systematic survey and critical synthesis analyzing structural, functional, cognitive, and sociolinguistic dimensions of code-switching across European and Indian multilingual contexts; contrasting linguistic frameworks against current computational NLP practices; distinguishing code-switching from borrowing, transfer, and loan translation; and evaluating computational bottlenecks across pretraining data in massive multilingual language models (e.g., mBERT, XLM-R), multi-task benchmark evaluation suites (GLUE-CoS, LINCE), and user-facing interactive systems.
key_findings: Computational linguistics research predominantly relies on the Matrix Language Frame (MLF) model despite empirical and theoretical criticisms regarding matrix language identification and clause-level boundary limits, while under-utilizing alternative grammatical constraints (such as the Functional Head Constraint) that improve computational and speech models.; NLP tag sets and models frequently fail to distinguish between true grammatical code-switching and nonce borrowings, lexical transfer, or loan translations, employing coarse part-of-speech annotations that obscure intra-sentential functional constraints.; Code-switching is strongly driven by pragmatic, cognitive, and socio-indexical functions (such as expressing in-group solidarity, politeness, conversational topic, and affective stance), which leave predictable structural traces that are ignored in conventional NLP pipelines.; Massive pretrained multilingual language models (e.g., mBERT, XLM-R) perform substantially worse on code-switched tasks than monolingual settings because they are trained on web-scraped monolingual corpora (Wikipedia, Common Crawl) lacking natural spoken and informal code-switching varieties.; Standardized code-switching benchmarks (e.g., GLUE-CoS, LINCE) are limited to a narrow set of language pairs (primarily Spanish-English and Hindi-English) and social media domains (Twitter), with state-of-the-art models performing near chance levels on complex reasoning tasks like Natural Language Inference (NLI).; Current language technologies almost entirely lack end-to-end user-facing applications (such as conversational dialogue systems) capable of dynamically adapting to user code-switching styles, social preferences, and affective language choices.; Both linguistics and computational research suffer from a positive-evidence bias by assuming code-switching occurs uniformly across all multilingual communities, ignoring negative evidence where historical, social, and prestige dynamics suppress switching (e.g., Saraswat Brahmin Konkani-Kannada bilinguals).
scope_and_delimitations: ['Focuses primarily on linguistic, sociolinguistic, and computational perspectives of code-switching within European multilingual contexts (e.g., Turkish-German, Frisian-Dutch, Spanish-Catalan, Russian-Ukrainian) and Indian multilingual contexts (Indo-Aryan and Dravidian language contact, Hindi-English, Bengali-English).', 'Delimits computational analysis to three primary bottlenecks: pretraining data representation in massive multilingual language models, multi-task benchmark evaluation suites, and user-facing interactive applications.', 'Excludes developing new algorithmic architectures or releasing novel empirical datasets, serving instead as a taxonomic and cross-disciplinary bridge between linguistics and computational NLP.']
limitations_summary: Current computational processing of code-switching is fundamentally limited by three interrelated constraints: the absence of diverse code-switching training data in multilingual language models, narrow evaluation benchmarks covering only simpler NLP tasks over a few language pairs, and a lack of end-to-end user-facing applications that model the sociolinguistic, functional, and pragmatic factors governing human code-switching.
limitations_verbatim: Due to the paucity of user-facing systems and standard benchmarks covering only a handful of simpler NLP tasks, it is likely that we overestimate how well computational models are able to handle C-S. In sum, language technologies for C-S seem to be constrained by the lack of availability of diverse C-S training data, evaluation benchmarks and the absence of user-facing applications. They need to go beyond pattern recognition and grammatical constraints of C-S in order to process and produce C-S the way humans do. Hence, it is important for the CL community to be aware of the vast literature around C-S in linguistics, particularly as we proceed to solving more challenging tasks.
generalizability_gap: Current computational code-switching research is disproportionately concentrated on a few high-resource pairs (primarily Spanish-English and Hindi-English) and social media text (Twitter), leaving regional dialects, unlisted/minority languages with fewer than 10,000 speakers, spoken conversational interactions, and diverse diaspora/immigrant communities severely underrepresented.
methodological_gap: Existing multilingual language models rely on web-scale monolingual pretraining corpora and coarse POS annotation schemes that cannot capture fine-grained functional heads or distinguish code-switching from borrowing and transfer; synthetic code-switched generation methods rely on rigid grammatical frameworks (e.g., MLF) that fail to generate natural utterances; and existing research lacks systematic collection and modeling of negative evidence where social context inhibits switching.
future_work: Incorporating formal linguistic theories (such as the Functional Head Constraint and fine-grained functional tag sets) into multilingual language model pretraining and synthetic code-switching generation.; Developing comprehensive, multi-domain evaluation benchmarks spanning diverse language families, regional dialects, and under-resourced or officially unlisted minority languages.; Designing adaptive end-to-end user-facing dialogue systems that model sociolinguistic factors, user style accommodation, and affective language preferences.; Investigating negative evidence in multilingual communities to systematically identify socio-cultural and contextual factors that inhibit code-switching.; Conducting systematic comparative investigations of code-switching patterns within identical language pairs across domestic and diaspora/immigrant environments (e.g., Hindi-English in India vs. the UK/US).; Establishing interdisciplinary publication and citation guidelines to facilitate knowledge transfer between humanities/linguistics and computational linguistics.

title: A survey of joint intent detection and slot-filling models in natural language understanding
authors: Henry Weld; Xiaoqi Huang; Siqu Long; Josiah Poon; Soyeon Caren Han
venue: ACM Computing Surveys (CSUR)
domain: Spoken Language Understanding (SLU), Natural Language Understanding (NLU), Intent Detection, Slot Filling, Dialogue Systems, Conversational AI, Deep Learning, Transfer Learning
problem_statement: How joint intent detection and slot filling models in spoken and natural language understanding have developed from classical statistical methods to modern deep learning architectures, analyzing how models capture and balance mutual task dependencies, exploit syntactic and semantic features, and address core challenges such as data sparsity, label dependency, class imbalance, out-of-vocabulary words, out-of-domain utterances, and generalizability to new domains and languages.
theoretical_framework: Hierarchical semantic frame theory (Tur and De Mori, 2011; Hakkani-Tür et al., 2016) decomposing spoken utterances into domains, intents, and slot-value attributes; token-level sequence labeling and statistical dependency modeling via Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) and Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) (Jeong & Lee, 2008; Raymond & Riccardi, 2007); multi-task learning synergy between utterance-level classification and token sequence labeling (Caruana, 1997; Collobert et al., 2011); recurrent neural network encoder-decoder models and bidirectional architectures (Liu & Lane, 2016a; Wang et al., 2018b); self-attention and Transformer representation theory (Vaswani et al., 2017; Devlin et al., 2019); capsule networks with routing-by-agreement (Zhang et al., 2019a); and graph neural networks for multi-relational interaction modeling (Qin et al., 2020b; Tang et al., 2020).
methodology: A systematic review, comparative taxonomy, and historical milestone analysis synthesizing intent detection, slot filling, and joint modeling literature up to mid-2020. The authors categorize joint architectures across classical statistical methods (tri-level CRFs, HMMs), recursive neural networks (RecNNs on parse trees), recurrent encoder-decoder networks (BiLSTMs, BiGRUs), attention mechanisms and explicit bidirectional interaction flows (slot-gated intent2slot, slot2intent, and multi-head self-attention), hierarchical and capsule networks (routing-by-agreement), memory networks (deliberate attention and local/global recurrence), multi-task meta-architectures (parallel, series, cascade), graph neural networks (S-LSTM, GCN-CRF), and pre-trained Transformer language models (BERT). The survey details token/sentence embedding methods, target label variations, standard experimental setups (e.g. 10 epochs for ATIS, 20 epochs for SNIPS), and standard evaluation metrics across benchmarks.
datasets: ATIS (Air Travel Information System): English single-turn benchmark (4,978 train / 500 dev / 893 test utterances; 17-21 intents, 79-127 slot labels; highly imbalanced intent distribution with ~75% flight intent); SNIPS-NLU: Crowdsourced English digital assistant benchmark (13,084 train / 700 dev / 700 test utterances across 7 balanced intents, 72 slot labels, and multiple domains: weather, restaurant, entertainment); Other surveyed datasets: Microsoft FRAMES (multi-turn hotel booking), Microsoft Cortana, Facebook Multilingual Task-Oriented Dataset, Alexa internal datasets, DSTC 2/3/5 dialog state tracking benchmarks, CCKS Chinese competition dataset, TRAINS problem-solving dialogues, FrameNet, CU-Move, AMIE, CQUD (Baidu Knows), Yahoo, TREC, and Almawave-SLU (Italian SNIPS translation)
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Intent Classification: Utterance-level classification accuracy (%), Macro F1, Micro F1, False Acceptance Rate (for OOD detection)', 'Slot Filling: Span-based Slot F1 score (CoNLL exact-match entity-level), Token-level accuracy', 'Sentence-level / Frame Evaluation: Semantic Accuracy / Sentence Accuracy (% of utterances where both intent and all slots are predicted correctly)', 'Qualitative Evaluation: Hinton diagrams, attention heat maps, and t-SNE feature visualizations'], 'benchmark_results': {'ATIS_Historical_Progression': {'Slot_F1': 'Improved from 93.96% (2014) to 98.75% (2019)', 'Intent_Accuracy': 'Maintained above 99% across modern neural models', 'Semantic_Accuracy': 'Improved from 78.9% (2016) to 91.6% (2020)'}, 'SNIPS_Historical_Progression': {'Slot_F1': 'Improved from 87.3% (2016) to 98.78% (2019)', 'Intent_Accuracy': 'Improved from 96.7% (2016) to 99.98% (2019)', 'Semantic_Accuracy': 'Improved from 73.2% (2016) to 93.6% (2020)'}, 'Standardized_10_20_Epoch_Comparison': 'Established standard comparison benchmark using 10 epochs for ATIS and 20 epochs for SNIPS to enable controlled model evaluation without disparate training budgets.'}}
key_findings: Joint intent detection and slot filling models consistently outperform independent single-task pipeline models by capturing mutual conditional distributions and eliminating cascading error propagation.; Pre-trained contextual Transformer models (BERT) combined with intent-slot gating or CRF sequence tagging layers achieve state-of-the-art results across both ATIS and SNIPS benchmarks.; Explicit bi-directional interaction architectures (such as intent2slot and slot2intent gating, capsule routing, and memory networks) provide stronger mutual reinforcement between tasks than implicit joint loss sharing.; Intent detection achieves higher accuracy on balanced multi-domain datasets (SNIPS), whereas slot filling historically achieves higher F1 scores on domain-focused datasets with repetitive patterns (ATIS).; Integrating structured knowledge bases, graph attention networks, and pre-computed syntactic features (such as key verbs and dependency parses) provides effective inductive biases for short, ambiguous, or complex utterances.; Standard single-turn benchmarks (ATIS and SNIPS) have reached performance saturation (>99% intent accuracy and >98% slot F1), shifting the research frontier toward unannotated conversational data, few-shot/zero-shot learning, and out-of-domain detection.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Focuses primarily on extraction of intent and slot semantic frame elements from single-turn spoken and text utterances in natural language understanding.', 'Considers multi-domain classification, multi-intent classification, multi-turn dialogue history, and dialogue act modeling as ancillary topics rather than primary foci.', 'Excludes automatic speech recognition (ASR) acoustic processing, ASR transcription error propagation, and full dialogue state tracking (DST) policy management.', 'Restricts empirical performance comparison and standardization to models evaluated on ATIS and SNIPS benchmark datasets published up to mid-2020.']
limitations_summary: Existing research in joint intent detection and slot filling heavily relies on saturated, simplistic, single-turn benchmark datasets (ATIS and SNIPS) whose high test scores reflect solved datasets rather than robust, generalizable natural language understanding. Moreover, inconsistent experimental setups across published papers (such as variable epoch counts and stopping criteria) hinder direct reproducibility, and supervised joint models struggle to generalize to unseen domains, new languages, open-ontology vocabularies, and unannotated conversational data without extensive re-training.
limitations_verbatim: It is argued that ATIS and SNIPS have reached near to the end of their useful lives as benchmarks for the joint task. Excellent test results show that the methods developed in this survey can successfully learn the joint distributions of intent and slot labels, and slot labels with each other, in a supervised learning setting. They appear to be set to continue being the benchmarks due to the ability to compare a new approach to previous ones, though this should be tempered by the use of non-standard experimental set up discussed in Section [8.](#page-25-0)
generalizability_gap: Most reviewed joint models are evaluated exclusively on clean, single-turn English datasets (ATIS and SNIPS) with fixed domain boundaries; models remain insufficiently tested on non-English languages, cross-lingual transfer scenarios, unannotated real-world conversational data, out-of-domain user utterances, and dynamic multi-turn dialogue environments with evolving intent and slot taxonomies.
methodological_gap: Significant inconsistencies in experimental setups—including lack of reported hyperparameters, disparate training epoch limits, and varied validation stopping criteria—impede fair cross-model comparisons; standard metrics (aggregate exact-match F1 and accuracy) obscure granular architectural strengths; few-shot and zero-shot architectures still depend on annotated target datasets for evaluation; and bidirectional joint interaction circuits often enforce one-directional dominance (intent2slot versus slot2intent) rather than fully symmetric bidirectional co-adaptation.
future_work: Developing new standardized benchmark datasets that reflect unannotated conversational speech, emerging domains, and multifaceted query intents.; Designing zero-shot and few-shot transfer learning methods that generalize to new domains and languages without requiring annotated target corpora.; Standardizing experimental protocols and evaluation metrics across published models, including fixed epoch budgets and consistent metric calculation.; Incorporating graph neural networks and external multi-relational knowledge bases to model complex word-slot-intent relationships.; Advancing out-of-domain (OOD) utterance detection and out-of-distribution (OOD) slot handling in real-world deployment settings.; Extending joint models to multi-intent detection and multi-turn conversational dialogue contexts.

title: A Survey on Multi-Task Learning
authors: Yu Zhang; Qiang Yang
venue: IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering
domain: Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence (including Computer Vision, Natural Language Processing, Speech Processing, Bioinformatics, Health Informatics, and Web Applications)
problem_statement: How to systematically categorize, formulate, optimize, and theoretically analyze multi-task learning algorithms across diverse learning paradigms, high-dimensional settings, and application domains to improve task generalization performance.
theoretical_framework: Multi-task learning foundational frameworks including task relatedness formulations (when to share, what to share, and how to share via feature, instance, or parameter sharing), statistical learning theory (generalization error bounds, Rademacher complexity, local Rademacher complexity, VC dimension, covering numbers, algorithmic stability), matrix and tensor trace norm regularization, and Bayesian hierarchical modeling (matrix-variate normal distributions, Dirichlet processes, and Gaussian processes).
methodology: Taxonomic survey and analytical synthesis categorizing multi-task learning models into five foundational algorithmic approaches (feature learning, low-rank, task clustering, task relation learning, and parameter decomposition) alongside regularized formulations (feature covariance versus task relation learning), integration with other learning paradigms (semi-supervised, active, unsupervised, reinforcement, multi-view learning, and graphical models), big data scaling techniques (parallel, online, distributed, and federated), and empirical benchmark comparisons.
key_findings: Multi-task learning algorithms primarily operate along five foundational paradigms: feature learning (feature transformation and feature selection), low-rank approaches, task clustering, task relation learning, and parameter decomposition.; Most regularized multi-task learning methods can be unified under a dual taxonomy: learning with feature covariance (modeling column relations) versus learning with task covariance (modeling task relationships).; In empirical comparisons across benchmark datasets, multi-task learning models consistently outperform single-task learning counterparts by effectively leveraging shared cross-task structures.; Deep multi-task learning models dominate computer vision and natural language processing applications through shared feature representations, whereas bioinformatics and health informatics prioritize interpretable models based on feature selection and task relation learning.; In theoretical analyses of multi-task generalization bounds, methods based on local Rademacher complexity derive tighter generalization bounds than those based on standard VC dimension, covering numbers, and algorithmic stability.
scope_and_delimitations: ['The survey focuses primarily on multi-task learning where all tasks are treated equally with bidirectional knowledge sharing, explicitly excluding transfer learning (where a single target task is privileged), continual/lifelong learning (where tasks arrive sequentially), and multi-label learning/multi-output regression (where different outputs always share the exact same training instances).', 'The algorithmic review focuses primarily on supervised multi-task learning (homogeneous-feature and homogeneous-task settings by default), with secondary coverage of extensions to non-supervised paradigms, heterogeneous features, and big data scaling.', 'The survey focuses predominantly on feature-based and parameter-based multi-task learning methods, reviewing only representative works for instance-based multi-task learning due to the limited number of studies in that area.']
limitations_summary: Multi-task learning models remain vulnerable to negative transfer caused by unrelated or outlier tasks, lack comprehensive theoretical analyses and principled mechanisms to mitigate negative interference, rely on rigid shared-layer deep architectures susceptible to noisy tasks, and remain predominantly concentrated on supervised learning settings with limited exploration into unsupervised, semi-supervised, active, reinforcement, and multi-view learning.
limitations_verbatim: Firstly, outlier tasks, which are unrelated to other tasks, are well known to hamper the performance of all the tasks when learning them jointly. There are some methods to alleviate negative effects that outlier tasks bring. However, there lacks principled ways and theoretical analyses to study the resulting negative effects. In order to make MTL safe to be used by human, this is an important issue and needs more studies. Secondly, deep learning has become a dominant approach in many areas and several multi-task deep models belonging to the feature transformation, low-rank, task clustering and task relation learning approaches have been proposed as reviewed in Sections 2, 3 and 5. As discussed, most of them only share hidden layers. This approach is powerful when all the tasks are related, but it is vulnerable to noisy and outlier tasks that can deteriorate the performance dramatically. We believe that it is desirable to design flexible and robust deep multi-task models. Lastly, existing studies mainly focus on supervised learning tasks, and only a few ones are on other tasks such as unsupervised learning, semi-supervised learning, active learning, multi-view learning and reinforcement learning tasks.
generalizability_gap: Most existing multi-task learning literature is concentrated in standard supervised benchmark datasets and single-layer sharing paradigms, leaving open questions regarding scalability and robustness in non-supervised learning paradigms (unsupervised, semi-supervised, active, and reinforcement learning), non-standard task modalities (heterogeneous feature spaces and multi-modal tensors), and complex real-world environments containing high ratios of unrelated or adversarial outlier tasks.
methodological_gap: Current multi-task learning methodologies lack principled theoretical frameworks and adaptive algorithmic mechanisms to handle outlier tasks and prevent negative transfer; deep multi-task architectures largely rely on rudimentary parameter-sharing structures without automated decision mechanisms for 'when to share'; and direct extensions from binary to multi-class classification remain theoretically and empirically underexplored for task clustering and relation learning approaches.
future_work: Developing principled methodologies and theoretical analyses to detect outlier tasks and mitigate negative transfer effects.; Designing flexible, adaptive, and robust deep multi-task architectures beyond simple hidden-layer sharing to handle noisy task relationships.; Extending multi-task learning formulations and the five core algorithmic approaches to non-supervised settings, including unsupervised, semi-supervised, active, reinforcement, and multi-view learning.; Applying multi-task learning to broader artificial intelligence domains such as automated reasoning, logic, and planning.; Investigating automated mechanisms for the 'when to share' decision problem to determine whether single-task or multi-task learning is optimal.

title: An Overview of Multi-Task Learning in Deep Neural Networks
authors: Sebastian Ruder
venue: arXiv preprint
domain: Deep Learning, Multi-Task Representation Learning, and Natural Language Processing
problem_statement: Providing a unified theoretical and practical overview of multi-task learning mechanisms, parameter sharing architectures, and auxiliary task selection in deep neural networks.
theoretical_framework: Inductive Transfer Theory, Hard vs. Soft Parameter Sharing, and Representation Learning
methodology: Systematic literature survey and conceptual taxonomy analyzing multi-task network architectures, inductive transfer mechanisms, and loss weighting formulations.
evaluation: Qualitative comparison and taxonomy of multi-task learning paradigms across computer vision, natural language processing, and speech recognition applications.
key_findings: Delineated the foundational difference between hard parameter sharing (shared intermediate encoder layers with task heads) and soft parameter sharing (regularized parameter distance).; Formalized five underlying mechanisms of inductive transfer in deep MTL: implicit data augmentation, attention focusing, eavesdropping, representation bias, and regularization.; Demonstrated that hard parameter sharing amortizes computational feature extraction into a single forward pass, providing strong regularization and reduced risk of overfitting.
scope_and_delimitations: Focuses on deep neural network architectures for multi-task learning, covering both feedforward networks and recurrent/convolutional models.
limitations_summary: Identified the unresolved challenge of predicting task compatibility and mitigating conflicting loss gradients during joint multi-task optimization.
limitations_verbatim: While MTL has shown empirical success, theoretical understanding of when tasks help each other and how to balance conflicting gradients remains an open challenge.
generalizability_gap: Pre-dates the widespread adoption of modern multi-task Transformer encoders (such as XLM-RoBERTa, mBERT, and ModernBERT).
methodological_gap: Does not survey modern gradient surgery techniques (such as PCGrad and CAGrad) or Pareto-stationary multi-task optimizers.
future_work: Developing adaptive multi-task optimization algorithms to dynamically balance gradient conflicts in deep architectures.

title: BATAYAN: A Filipino NLP benchmark for evaluating Large Language Models
authors: Jann Railey Montalan; Jimson Paulo Layacan; David Demitri Africa; Richell Isaiah Flores; Michael T. Lopez II; Theresa Denise Magsajo; Anjanette Cayabyab; William Chandra Tjhi
venue: Preprint (SEA-HELM)
domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Filipino and Tagalog-English Code-Switching (Taglish), Large Language Model Evaluation, Low-Resource Languages
problem_statement: Large language models demonstrate high performance on major high-resource languages, but under-resourced languages such as Filipino remain under-represented and linguistically unexamined. Prior Filipino NLP evaluation resources suffered from fragmentation, limited task diversity, domain specificity, translationese bias from unverified automated translations, and poor handling of agglutinative morphology, syntactic word order variations (karaniwang ayos versus di-karaniwang ayos), and Taglish code-switching.
theoretical_framework: Official Filipino linguistic and translation standards from the Komisyon sa Wikang Filipino (Almario, 2014, 2016); Filipino syntactic theory contrasting predicate-initial natural order (karaniwang ayos) with topicalized inverted order (di-karaniwang ayos / ay-inversion) and discourse continuity frameworks (Tanawan et al., 2008; Malicsi, 2013; Kroeger, 1993; Fox, 1985; Bolata, 2022); translationese theory (Gellerstam, 1986; Riley et al., 2020); and holistic multilingual language model benchmarking frameworks (HELM by Liang et al., 2023; BHASA by Leong et al., 2023; XTREME by Hu et al., 2020).
methodology: The authors developed BATAYAN, an eight-task benchmark evaluating LLMs across Natural Language Understanding (NLU: Paraphrase Identification, Question Answering, Sentiment Analysis, Toxicity Detection), Natural Language Reasoning (NLR: Causal Reasoning, Natural Language Inference), and Natural Language Generation (NLG: Abstractive Summarization, Machine Translation English-to-Filipino and Filipino-to-English). The curation workflow generated 3,800 test instances and five-shot exemplars through native translation using Helsinki-NLP OPUS-MT followed by human revision (PAWS, Balanced COPA, XNLI, XL-Sum), native re-translation of translated corpora (Belebele QA, FLORES-200 MT) to eliminate translationese bias and favor natural predicate-initial sentence order, and repurposing natively-sourced Philippine election tweets for sentiment analysis and toxicity detection. Dataset quality control applied three-rater native speaker consensus over binary criteria (completeness, fluency, sensibility) and multi-dimensional scaled criteria (faithfulness, relevance, coherence for summarization). The authors evaluated over 50 LLMs across small (<=11B), medium (<=32B), large (>=32B), and commercial model categories under zero-shot prompting for instruction-tuned models and five-shot prompting for base pre-trained models.
datasets: BATAYAN: An overarching benchmark containing 3,800 test instances across 8 tasks spanning NLU, NLR, and NLG competencies in Filipino and Taglish; PAWS (Paraphrase Adversaries from Word Scrambling): 400 test samples natively translated from English for Filipino Paraphrase Identification (PI); Belebele: 100 test samples natively re-translated from machine-translated Filipino for Reading Comprehension Question Answering (QA); Philippine Election Tweets (Cabasag et al., 2019): 600 test samples natively annotated for 3-class Sentiment Analysis (SA) and 400 test samples for Toxicity Detection (TD); Balanced COPA (Choice of Plausible Alternatives): 400 test samples natively translated from English for Causal Reasoning (CR); XNLI (Cross-lingual Natural Language Inference): 600 test samples natively translated from English for Natural Language Inference (NLI); XL-Sum: 100 test samples natively translated and manually summarized for Abstractive Summarization (AS); FLORES-200: 1,200 test samples (600 English->Filipino, 600 Filipino->English) natively re-translated for Machine Translation (MT)

key_findings: The authors created BATAYAN, a native-speaker-validated benchmark of 3,800 test instances across 8 tasks, introducing the first Filipino evaluation datasets for abstractive summarization, causal reasoning, and paraphrase identification.; Dedicated Filipino instruction tuning produces large performance gains on culturally and morphologically nuanced tasks; Gemma-SEA-LION-v3-9B-IT attained an average macro F1 of 79.23 on small-model NLU and 92.75 on causal reasoning, whereas non-adapted models such as Llama-3 variants scored near zero on causal reasoning.; Automated translations of English corpora exhibited systemic translationese bias, including an unnatural preference for inverted word order (di-karaniwang ayos / ay-inversion) and pragmatically awkward word choices, which native human re-translation corrected into natural predicate-initial constructions (karaniwang ayos).; Model performance exhibited clear scaling effects across parameter sizes (7B to 671B), demonstrating that greater model capacity combined with regional instruction tuning significantly improves the representation of agglutinative morphology, focus marking, and Taglish code-switching.; Open-source models with dedicated Filipino tuning (such as Gemma-SEA-LION-v3-9B-IT and Llama-SEA-LION-v3-70B-IT) achieved performance competitive with or superior to top commercial models (Gemini 1.5/2.0 and GPT-4o variants) on Filipino natural language understanding and reasoning tasks.; Semantic evaluation metrics such as MetricX-24 revealed significant translation quality advantages (MetricX-24 >87 for Filipino-tuned models) that surface-level lexical overlap metrics such as ROUGE-L failed to detect.
scope_and_delimitations: ['The benchmark focuses exclusively on Filipino (Tagalog) and Tagalog-English code-switched (Taglish) text, excluding other regional Philippine languages.', 'Task scope is delimited to eight specific NLP tasks: Paraphrase Identification, Question Answering, Sentiment Analysis, Toxicity Detection, Causal Reasoning, Natural Language Inference, Abstractive Summarization, and Machine Translation.', 'Benchmark volume is delimited to 3,800 high-quality test instances (100 to 1,200 samples per task) selected through strict unanimous three-rater acceptability criteria rather than large unverified web scrapes.', 'Social media data for sentiment analysis and toxicity detection is delimited to Philippine election-related tweets from 2019.', 'Model evaluation is delimited to zero-shot inference for instruction-tuned models and five-shot in-context learning for base pre-trained models.']
limitations_summary: The authors identify several study limitations: prosodic features such as stress and sarcasm are difficult to identify in text datasets; sentiment analysis and toxicity detection corpora are restricted to political election tweets; total dataset size is delimited to 3,800 instances because the authors prioritized manual native quality filtering over dataset volume; and broad benchmark scope prevented comprehensive qualitative error analysis or evaluation on specialized translation models.
limitations_verbatim:
While our work provides a unique and comprehensive Filipino language benchmark, we also reported in previous sections the challenges and limitations in developing high-quality NLP resources for the under-represented language. Additionally, prosodic characteristics such as stress and sarcasm are not immediately obvious in the datasets utilized. We account for this by selecting only high-agreement samples. We also note that the domain of both SA and TD tasks (which were tweets surrounding political events), limits the distributions of these tasks, and as such we recommend utilizing other datasets that cover a wider set of domains and use cases.

While we recognize that datasets with larger amounts of samples are preferred to ensure generalizability, we maintain our position to prioritize consistent, high-quality, and representative samples.
generalizability_gap: The benchmark evaluates only Filipino/Tagalog and Taglish text within written formats, leaving unexamined the more than 100 other Philippine regional languages (such as Cebuano, Ilocano, and Hiligaynon), spoken modalities, and non-political domain distributions for sentiment and toxicity tasks.
methodological_gap: Automated lexical evaluation metrics such as ROUGE-L lack sensitivity to semantic fidelity and morphological subtleties in agglutinative Filipino text; tools to automatically differentiate translationese from natural text remain unavailable; subjective stylistic preferences for sentence order (karaniwang ayos versus di-karaniwang ayos) introduce minor syntactic variance; and the study did not include comprehensive qualitative error category breakdowns.
future_work: Developing automated metrics and classification tools to discriminate translationese from natural Filipino text.; Expanding the benchmark to larger sample sizes, diverse non-political domains, and broader social media use cases.; Conducting detailed error analyses to characterize model failure modes across specific morphological and syntactic structures.; Evaluating specialized language models and extending benchmarking frameworks to other regional languages of the Philippines.; Maintaining and expanding the public evaluation suite and leaderboard on SEA-HELM for collaborative progress in Southeast Asian NLP.

title: Beyond Monolingual Assumptions: A Survey on Code-Switched NLP in the Era of Large Language Models across Modalities
authors: Rajvee Sheth; Samridhi Raj Sinha; Mahavir Patil; Himanshu Beniwal; Mayank Singh
venue: Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers)
domain: Natural Language Processing, Large Language Models, Code-Switching and Code-Mixing, Multilingual Computing, Multimodal AI (Speech and Vision-Language Processing), Low-Resource Languages
problem_statement: How Large Language Models handle code-switched inputs across text, speech, and vision-language modalities, why multilingual pre-training fails to guarantee robust code-switching performance, and how existing architectural designs, dataset shortages, and evaluation biases restrict effective deployment in multilingual societies.
theoretical_framework: Sociolinguistic and grammatical theories of code-switching (including Poplack's Equivalence Constraint model and structural switch-point constraints), quantitative code-mixing metrics (Code-Mixing Index [CMI], S-index, M-index, I-index, and SyM-CoM), cross-lingual representation alignment in foundation models, and multimodal fusion architectures.
methodology: Systematic literature review and taxonomic synthesis analyzing 327 studies across 15+ NLP tasks, 30+ datasets, and 80+ languages; categorizing research into pre-LLM versus LLM eras, five core research directions, training paradigms (pre-training, fine-tuning, instruction tuning, PEFT, RLAIF), multimodal speech and vision applications, and evaluation methodologies to identify persistent failure modes and outline a future research roadmap.
key_findings: Multilingual pre-training alone does not ensure code-switching proficiency; large language models frequently underperform compared to smaller, task-specific fine-tuned models on code-switched inputs because pre-training corpora contain limited naturalistic code-switched data.; Large language models exhibit asymmetric transfer and language confusion; models process English tokens embedded within non-English contexts better than non-English tokens within English contexts, and standard fine-tuning amplifies unintended language generation.; Current code-switching research exhibits extreme resource concentration; over 72% of speech datasets and 92% of social media code-switching datasets involve English (predominantly Hindi-English, Spanish-English, and Mandarin-English), leaving non-English pairs, African languages, Southeast Asian languages, and trilingual settings critically underexplored.; Synthetic code-switching generation methods expand training volume but achieve only 60% to 65% human acceptability, failing to capture spontaneous conversational behavior, orthographic variations, transliteration nuances, and sociolinguistic pragmatic intent.; Standard evaluation metrics (such as BLEU, Word Error Rate, and perplexity) and LLM-as-a-judge evaluators correlate poorly with human judgments on code-switched generation and speech tasks, overestimating model performance and failing to capture switch-point dynamics.; Parameter-efficient fine-tuning, curriculum-based instruction tuning, and reinforcement learning from AI feedback improve low-resource adaptation, but speech and vision-language multimodal code-switching systems lag significantly behind text-based natural language understanding.
scope_and_delimitations: ['The survey synthesizes academic research on code-switched natural language processing, focusing primarily on large language models and foundation models while contextualizing historical methods from statistical and neural eras.', 'The review spans 15+ natural language processing tasks across token-level, sentence-level, generation, conversational, reasoning, speech, and vision-language modalities across 80+ languages.', 'The analysis examines academic literature and public benchmark datasets, delimiting coverage of proprietary industrial deployment constraints and production infrastructure optimizations.', 'The survey reports representative quantitative metrics from cited primary studies rather than conducting independent experimental evaluations or statistical meta-analyses.']
limitations_summary: The survey exhibits coverage bias toward widely studied language pairs while potentially omitting indigenous or minority languages, faces rapid obsolescence due to fast-evolving foundation model paradigms, covers text-based understanding more comprehensively than speech and multimodal processing due to literature availability, focuses primarily on academic progress rather than real-world industrial deployment considerations, and compiles representative findings from primary literature rather than computing aggregated statistical meta-analyses.
limitations_verbatim:
Despite providing a broad survey, this paper has several limitations:

- 1. Coverage Bias The survey highlights widely studied language pairs and might have missed indigenous or minority code-mixed languages.
- 2. Evolving Landscape Given the rapid pace of LLM research, some approaches and benchmarks described may soon be outdated or replaced by newer paradigms.
- 3. Evaluation Constraints While we include recent advances in speech and multimodal processing, the volume of research in these areas significantly lags behind text-based NLU, resulting in our taxonomy covering more text based NLU.
- 4. Practical deployment The survey mainly covers academic progress, leaving ethical, computational, and accessibility concerns in real-world deployment less examined.
- 5. Quantitative Reporting All quantitative claims are representative values reported in the cited primary works rather than aggregated or meta-analyzed statistics.
generalizability_gap: Large Language Models and code-switching benchmarks demonstrate limited cross-linguistic and cross-regional generalizability, showing 25% to 35% performance drops when tested across different geographic varieties of the same language pair. Furthermore, empirical resources remain heavily concentrated in English-centric bilingual pairs (over 72% of speech and 92% of social media datasets), leaving low-resource African, Dravidian, and Southeast Asian language pairs, non-Latin script transliterations, and trilingual switching settings critically underexplored.
methodological_gap: Current code-switching methodologies suffer from three fundamental shortcomings: (1) pre-training relies predominantly on monolingual corpora and synthetic code-switched data that achieves only 60% to 65% human acceptability, failing to model natural conversational switch points; (2) standard evaluation metrics (BLEU, Word Error Rate, perplexity) and LLM-as-a-judge frameworks fail to capture discourse coherence, sociolinguistic intent, and dialectal nuances; and (3) architectural designs lack specialized script-aware and switch-point-aware mechanisms, leading to language confusion and jailbreak safety vulnerabilities under mixed-language prompts.
future_work: Developing inclusive, naturalistic conversational datasets for underrepresented and low-resource language pairs with participatory community curation and human-in-the-loop validation.; Designing next-generation multimodal architectures that jointly model text, speech, and vision with switch-point detection, phonemic grounding, and mixture-of-experts routing.; Establishing holistic, human-aligned evaluation paradigms that assess switch-point accuracy, semantic consistency, discourse coherence, and sociolinguistic appropriateness beyond rigid lexical matching.; Investigating multilingual safety alignment and ethical frameworks to mitigate jailbreaks, backdoor attacks, and cultural biases in code-switched systems.; Expanding code-switching research to trilingual discourse, non-Latin script transliteration normalization, and complex cross-lingual reasoning tasks.
local_dir: Beyond Monolingual Assumptions - A Survey on Code-Switched NLP in the Era of Large Language Models across Modalities

title: COMI-LINGUA: Expert Annotated Large-Scale Dataset for Multitask NLP in Hindi-English Code-Mixing
authors: Rajvee Sheth; Himanshu Beniwal; Mayank Singh
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2025
domain: Multilingual Natural Language Processing (NLP), Code-Mixing / Code-Switching, Hindi-English (Hinglish) across Roman and Devanagari scripts from social media, news portals, and digital archives.
problem_statement: The lack of large-scale, high-quality, human-annotated datasets and standardized benchmarks for Hindi-English (Hinglish) code-mixing across both Devanagari and Roman scripts and diverse core NLP tasks, which limits the training, evaluation, and diagnostic error analysis of multilingual large language models on complex code-mixed text.
theoretical_framework: Matrix Language Frame theory (specifically Matrix Language Identification to determine the dominant language dictating syntactic structure) and Code-Mixing Index (CMI) formulation for quantifying code-mixing intensity.
methodology: The authors curate raw Hinglish text from news portals, social media platforms (X, YouTube), political channels, and official archives, filtering sentences by Code-Mixing Index (CMI >= 9), sentence length (>= 5 tokens), profanity, and hate speech. They employ a two-stage annotation pipeline using the COMMENTATOR framework where initial pre-annotations generated by NLP tools and LLMs (Microsoft LID, CodeSwitch, LLaMA 3.3) are manually reviewed and corrected by three bilingual graduate-level experts across five core tasks (LID, MLI, NER, POS tagging, and Machine Translation into Standard English, Romanized Hindi, and Devanagari Hindi), resolving conflicts via majority voting (>= 2/3 agreement). They benchmark traditional tools (Microsoft LID, codeswitch), open-weight LLMs (LLaMA-3.3-70B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Aya-Expanse-8B, Qwen2.5-7B), and closed-weight LLMs (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Flash, Command-A-03-2025) under zero-shot and one-shot in-context learning, and perform LoRA parameter-efficient fine-tuning on 7-8B open-weight models.
datasets: COMI-LINGUA (125,615 filtered instances; 376,845 manual expert annotations across LID, MLI, NER, POS tagging, and MT); Supplementary seed data from prior corpora: PHINC (Srivastava & Singh, 2020), MUTANT (Gupta et al., 2023), Singh et al. (2018c), and YouTube video transcripts (Hugging Face); News and web sources: NDTV, ABP News, Zee News, News18, TV9, Aaj Tak, X (Twitter), YouTube, INC/BJP/AAP political channels, Mann Ki Baat, Press Information Bureau (PIB)
evaluation: {'inter_annotator_agreement': "Fleiss' Kappa >= 0.817 across all classification tasks (LID: 0.834, MLI: 0.976, NER: 0.852, POS: 0.817; average: 0.863)", 'metrics': 'Macro Precision, Recall, and Macro F1-score for LID, MLI, NER, and POS; BLEU and chrF++ for Machine Translation evaluated disaggregated across Standard English (Ben, cFen), Romanized Hindi (Brh, cFrh), and Devanagari Hindi (Bdh, cFdh)', 'zero_shot_findings': 'Closed-weight LLMs dominate zero-shot performance (GPT-4o: LID F1 92.7, MLI F1 98.1, NER F1 60.1, POS F1 70.1; Claude 3.5 Sonnet: LID F1 92.1, MLI F1 90.0, NER F1 56.7, POS F1 69.0), while traditional specialized tools like codeswitch outperform zero-shot LLMs on POS tagging (88.2 F1)', 'one_shot_findings': 'One-shot prompting consistently boosts performance across LLMs and tasks, especially for structure-sensitive tasks like NER (Claude 3.5 Sonnet NER F1 increases from 56.7 to 85.0) and MT (LLaMA-3.3-70B achieves 62.2 BLEU in English translation)', 'fine_tuning_findings': 'LoRA fine-tuning of 7-8B open-weight LLMs on COMI-LINGUA yields dramatic gains over prompting (LLaMA-3.1-8B achieves 94.75 F1 in LID, 93.05 F1 in MLI, 95.25 F1 in NER, 86.17 F1 in POS, 56.1 BLEU in English MT, 73.5 BLEU in Devanagari MT; Aya-Expanse-8B achieves 98.77 F1 in MLI, 94.90 F1 in NER, 88.61 F1 in POS)'}
key_findings: COMI-LINGUA is established as the largest manually annotated Hinglish code-mixed dataset to date, containing 125,615 instances and over 376K expert annotations across five core NLP tasks with high inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss' Kappa >= 0.817).; Closed-weight LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) substantially outperform open-weight models in zero-shot settings on most tasks, whereas traditional specialized tools (codeswitch) remain superior in zero-shot POS tagging.; One-shot in-context learning consistently improves performance across models and tasks, particularly in entity disambiguation and structure-sensitive tasks like NER and MT.; Supervised fine-tuning on COMI-LINGUA enables compact 7-8B open-weight models to match or exceed large proprietary models (e.g., reaching up to 95.25 F1 in NER and 98.77 F1 in MLI).; Qualitative error analysis highlights severe LLM failure modes on code-mixed text, including misclassifying Devanagari-script English borrowings, context truncation on long inputs, output repetition/hallucination, generating Python code snippets instead of task predictions, and prompt mimicry.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Restricted exclusively to Hindi-English (Hinglish) code-mixed text, filtering out monolingual English/Hindi and other languages.', 'Covers both Devanagari and Roman scripts across formal (news, press releases) and informal (social media) domains in the Indian subcontinent.', 'Delimited to five core NLP tasks: Token-level Language Identification (LID), Matrix Language Identification (MLI), Named Entity Recognition (NER), Part-Of-Speech (POS) Tagging, and Machine Translation (MT into English, Romanized Hindi, and Devanagari Hindi).', 'Requires a Code-Mixing Index (CMI) >= 9 and sentence length >= 5 tokens for raw instance retention.', 'Empirical evaluation is delimited to traditional toolkits (Microsoft LID, codeswitch), 7B-70B open-weight LLMs, and commercial closed-weight LLMs under zero-shot, one-shot, and LoRA fine-tuning paradigms.']
limitations_summary: The authors acknowledge four primary limitations: (1) findings are specific to Hindi-English and may not generalize to other code-mixed language pairs with different syntactic or sociolinguistic dynamics; (2) reliance on a small, homogeneous group of three annotators may introduce demographic bias; (3) scaling the curation to other code-mixed pairs is constrained by scarce corpora and robust models; and (4) high computational requirements for fine-tuning may restrict accessibility in resource-constrained environments.
limitations_verbatim:
While this study offers valuable insights into the annotation and processing of Hinglish code-mixed text, several limitations warrant consideration:

- 1. Language Pair Specificity: The findings derived from Hinglish code-mixed data may not generalize to other language pairs (e.g., Spanish-English), given differences in syntactic structure, sociolinguistic norms, and code-switching behavior.
- 2. Demographic Bias: The use of a relatively small and homogeneous group of annotators may introduce demographic bias, potentially limiting the broader applicability and reliability of the acceptability ratings.
- 3. Resource Constraints: Scaling this work to other code-mixed language pairs remains challenging due to the scarcity of high-quality annotated corpora and the limited availability of models capable of robustly handling diverse code-mixing phenomena.
- 4. Computational Accessibility: While finetuning shows substantial improvements, computational requirements and the need for substantial training data may limit accessibility for resource-constrained settings.
generalizability_gap: The dataset and empirical findings are restricted exclusively to Hindi-English (Hinglish) code-mixed text within the Indian subcontinent and may not generalize to other code-mixed language pairs, language families, or sociolinguistic environments. In addition, the small, homogeneous pool of three graduate annotators may limit demographic and dialectal representativeness.
methodological_gap: The dataset creation workflow relied on automated pre-annotation tools (Microsoft LID, CodeSwitch, LLaMA 3.3) followed by manual post-editing, which introduces potential pre-annotation bias. Furthermore, LLM evaluation was constrained to zero-shot and fixed one-shot prompts without exploring few-shot scaling or chain-of-thought prompting, and parameter fine-tuning was limited to compact 7-8B models due to compute constraints.
future_work: Scaling dataset curation and annotation frameworks to other under-resourced code-mixed language pairs beyond Hinglish.; Incorporating active learning and iterative refinement pipelines to sustain performance gains and reduce manual annotation overhead.; Expanding annotator demographic diversity to capture wider regional and dialectal language variations.; Developing script-aware and context-sensitive modeling architectures to better handle cross-script borrowed words, mitigate hallucinations, and prevent context truncation in compact LLMs.

title: Code-Switched Named Entity Recognition with Embedding Attention
authors: Changhan Wang; Kyunghyun Cho; Douwe Kiela
venue: Proceedings of the Third Workshop on Computational Approaches to Linguistic Code-Switching (CALCS 2018)
domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Named Entity Recognition (NER), Linguistic Code-Switching, Social Media (Twitter), Multilingual Representation Learning
problem_statement: Standard natural language processing pipelines experience severe performance deterioration on code-switched text, creating a need for effective named entity recognition models capable of handling noisy, multilingual social media data across diverse language pairs.
theoretical_framework: Neural sequence labeling integrating pre-trained multi-source word embeddings, character-level recurrent representations, self-attention mechanisms for dynamic modality fusion, shortcut-stacked recurrent sentence encoding, and Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) for structured output prediction.
methodology: An end-to-end neural sequence tagging architecture comprising four main components: (1) multi-level representations integrating language-specific FastText embeddings trained on Common Crawl and Wikipedia, character-level BiLSTMs with max-pooling, and explicit capitalization embeddings; (2) an embedding-level self-attention mechanism that computes dynamic task-specific weights across multilingual and character-level embeddings without contextual dependencies; (3) multi-layer shortcut-stacked bidirectional LSTM sentence encoders with residual skip connections; and (4) linear-chain Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) comparing unigram and bigram emission/transition potential scoring functions. Preprocessing normalizes noisy Twitter tokens (URLs, user mentions, hashtags, punctuation, numbers, dates, times, emojis) and strips leading/trailing punctuation for Arabic tokens.
datasets: CALCS 2018 Shared Task MSA-EGY: Modern Standard Arabic-Egyptian Arabic tweets (10,102 train / 1,122 validation / 1,110 test); CALCS 2018 Shared Task ENG-SPA: English-Spanish tweets (50,757 train / 832 validation / 15,634 test); FastText pre-trained crawl and Wikipedia word vectors for Arabic, Egyptian Arabic, English, and Spanish
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Precision', 'Recall', 'Entity F1'], 'results': {'MSA_EGY': {'overall': {'Precision': 73.95, 'Recall': 69.42, 'Entity_F1': 71.62}, 'per_category_f1': {'EVENT': 68.8, 'GROUP': 73.17, 'LOC': 71.78, 'ORG': 66.67, 'OTHER': 100.0, 'PER': 73.21, 'PROD': 77.61, 'TIME': 67.92, 'TITLE': 41.38}, 'best_configuration': '4-layer shortcut-stacked BiLSTM [64, 64, 128, 128] with unigram CRF', 'competition_rank': '1st place'}, 'ENG_SPA': {'overall': {'Precision': 70.62, 'Recall': 55.88, 'Entity_F1': 62.39}, 'per_category_f1': {'EVENT': 29.51, 'GROUP': 42.86, 'LOC': 69.98, 'ORG': 37.93, 'OTHER': 3.08, 'PER': 72.09, 'PROD': 54.46, 'TIME': 43.24, 'TITLE': 33.83}, 'best_single_configuration': '3-layer shortcut-stacked BiLSTM [128, 128, 128] with bigram CRF', 'ensemble_f1': 62.67, 'competition_rank': '3rd place'}}}
key_findings: The embedding attention neural architecture achieved 1st place on the CALCS 2018 Modern Standard Arabic-Egyptian task (71.62 Entity F1) and 3rd place on the English-Spanish task (62.39 Entity F1, 62.67 with ensembling), outperforming standard concatenation baselines.; Specialized token preprocessing for social media noise (normalizing numbers, dates, times, emojis, and Arabic punctuation) substantially boosted performance on temporal and event categories (EVENT and TIME).; Explicit capitalization embeddings improved recognition accuracy for PERSON, LOCATION, and ORGANIZATION entities.; Recognition performance varied across entity types: TITLE was consistently challenging across both language pairs (33.83 F1 for ENG-SPA, 41.38 F1 for MSA-EGY), whereas OTHER scored 100.00 F1 on MSA-EGY but only 3.08 F1 on ENG-SPA.; Optimal CRF and hidden layer architectures differed between tasks: a 4-layer stacked BiLSTM with unigram CRF performed best for MSA-EGY, whereas a 3-layer stacked BiLSTM with bigram CRF performed best for ENG-SPA.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Evaluated on two code-switched language pairs: Modern Standard Arabic-Egyptian (closely related varieties) and English-Spanish (distinct languages) using Twitter data.', 'Deliberately excluded contextual dependencies from the embedding attention mechanism to ensure computational efficiency within competition deadlines.', 'Kept pre-trained FastText word embeddings frozen during neural training, restricting parameter updates to character BiLSTMs and capitalization embeddings.', 'Deliberately avoided external gazetteers or complex hand-crafted features to maintain a generalizable neural architecture.']
limitations_summary: The authors acknowledge several constraints: (1) a severe validation set size imbalance in the English-Spanish dataset (832 development tokens versus 15.6k test tokens) hindered reliable hyperparameter tuning; (2) tight competition deadlines prevented the implementation of contextual dependencies in the attention mechanism and proper ensemble methods; and (3) the model operated without gazetteers, which may have limited performance on difficult low-resource categories such as titles.
limitations_verbatim: The dev set for this task was very small (832, versus a test set of 15.6k), which explains the discrepancy between dev set and test set performance—this discrepancy also made it difficult to tune hyperparameters properly for this task. We also tried a very simple ensembling strategy, where we took our top three models and randomly sampled a response, which only marginally improved test score performance to 62.67. We did not pursue proper ensembling due to time constraints.
generalizability_gap: The architecture was evaluated strictly on Twitter social media data across two specific language combinations (MSA-EGY and ENG-SPA). The performance of the model remains unexamined on other language families (such as Indic or Austronesian code-switched pairs), non-Twitter textual genres (such as conversational transcripts, clinical text, or formal news), and higher degrees of intra-word morphological mixing.
methodological_gap: The embedding attention module operates without contextual dependency across sentence tokens, relying on static pre-trained word vectors rather than contextualized multilingual language representations (such as multilingual BERT or XLM-RoBERTa). Additionally, the system lacks qualitative attention attribution to determine whether the model dynamically attends to language switch points.
future_work: Analyze the learned attention weights to determine whether the model learns to identify and adapt to code-switching points dynamically via embedding attention.; Incorporate contextual dependencies into the embedding attention mechanism.; Explore sophisticated model ensembling strategies and examine the integration of external lexical gazetteers without compromising the flexibility of the neural architecture.
