title: Conflict-Averse Gradient Descent for Multi-Task Learning
authors: Bo Liu; Xingchao Liu; Xiaojie Jin; Peter Stone; Qiang Liu
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
domain: Multi-Task Learning — multi-task supervised vision (NYU-v2, CityScapes, Multi-Fashion+MNIST), multi-task reinforcement learning (Meta-World MT10/MT50), and semi-supervised learning with auxiliary tasks (CIFAR-10)
problem_statement: Optimizing the average loss across multiple tasks with shared parameters suffers from conflicting gradients where task gradients differ in magnitude and direction, causing the average gradient update to harm specific tasks and causing prior gradient manipulation methods (MGDA, PCGrad) to converge to arbitrary Pareto-stationary points without guarantees of minimizing the average loss.
theoretical_framework: Multi-objective optimization and Pareto optimality, where CAGrad maximizes the worst local improvement min_i <g_i, d> within a trust ball around the average gradient g0, with hyperparameter c controlling convergence to the average loss optimum (c<1) versus Pareto set (c≥1), including GD (c=0) and MGDA (c→∞) as special cases.
methodology: Conflict-Averse Gradient Descent (CAGrad) solves max_d min_i <g_i, d> subject to ||d - g0|| ≤ c||g0||, where g0 is the average gradient and c∈[0,1) ensures convergence to a stationary point of the average loss L0. The high-dimensional primal is converted to a low-dimensional dual min_{w∈W} g_w^T g0 + c||g0||·||g_w|| over simplex W={w≥0, sum w=1} with g_w=Σ w_i g_i, solved via standard convex solvers, yielding update d*= g0 + c||g0||/||g_w*|| · g_w*. A practical speedup samples subset S⊂[K] and retains convergence. All experiments build on MTAN (SegNet) for vision and Soft Actor-Critic for RL.
datasets: Synthetic 2D two-task toy optimization with 5 initial points to visualize conflicting gradients and Pareto set; Multi-Fashion+MNIST — 120k FashionMNIST+MNIST overlaid images for two-task classification, trained with shrunken LeNet (Adam 1e-3, 50 epochs, batch 256); NYU-v2 — 13-class segmentation, depth, and surface normals (795 train / 654 test) on MTAN-SegNet backbone under equal weighting; CityScapes — 7-class segmentation and depth on MTAN-SegNet under equal weighting; Meta-World MT10 and MT50 — 10 and 50 robotic manipulation tasks evaluated with Soft Actor-Critic, success rate averaged over 10 runs; CIFAR-10 semi-supervised — 50k training images with 500/1000/2000 labeled, 10% validation, using ARML and GradNorm loss formulations with two auxiliary unsupervised losses and Adam 200 epochs
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Toy: optimization trajectories and final training losses per task and average loss', 'Multi-Fashion+MNIST: average and per-task training losses over 3 runs', 'NYU-v2/CityScapes: mIoU and Pixel Accuracy for segmentation, Abs/Rel Error for depth, Mean/Median angle distance and within 11.25°/22.5°/30° for normals, and average per-task performance drop Δm % versus single-task SegNet, with two-tailed Student t-test (p=0.1)', 'Meta-World: mean success rate ± stderr over 10 runs, and training time per epoch', 'CIFAR-10 semi-supervised: average test accuracy ± std over 3 runs for ARML+methods and GradNorm+methods'], 'baselines': ['Vanilla gradient descent (GD / Adam) on average loss', 'Multiple Gradient Descent Algorithm (MGDA, Sener & Koltun)', 'Projecting Conflicting Gradients (PCGrad, Yu et al.)', 'Cross-Stitch Networks and MTAN for architecture baselines', 'GradDrop, IMTL-G, RotoGrad (referenced), Multi-task SAC variants, Task Encoder, Soft Modularization, CARE', 'ARML baseline and GradNorm baseline for semi-supervised learning, each combined with PCGrad/MGDA/CAGrad'], 'architectures': ['Shrunken LeNet for Multi-Fashion+MNIST', 'MTAN on SegNet (VGG-based encoder-decoder) for NYU-v2 and CityScapes', 'Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) multi-layer perceptron actor-critic for Meta-World', 'WRN-28-10 style backbone for CIFAR-10 ARML (as in ARML original)']}
key_findings: CAGrad balances tasks while provably converging to the average loss optimum when 0≤c<1 (Theorem 3.2: sum ||∇L0||² bounded by 2(L0(θ0)-L0*)/α(1-c²)), whereas c≥1 converges to arbitrary Pareto-stationary points; c=0 recovers GD and c→∞ recovers MGDA, verified on toy example with 5 initializations where GD stuck in 2/5 runs and MGDA/PCGrad scattered across Pareto set while CAGrad converged to average optimum.; On NYU-v2, CAGrad (c=0.4 on MTAN) achieves 39.79 mIoU, 65.49 Pix Acc, 0.5486 Abs Err, 26.31 Mean angle and Δm=0.20%, outperforming MTAN (5.59%), PCGrad (3.97%), GradDrop (3.58%), Cross-Stitch (6.96%) and significantly improving the overlooked surface normal task while matching others.; On CityScapes, CAGrad (c=0.2) achieves 75.16 mIoU and 0.0141 Abs Err with Δm=11.64%, halving MTAN’s drop (22.60%) and outperforming PCGrad (18.29%) and improving depth over other methods.; On Meta-World, CAGrad attains 0.83±0.045 on MT10 and 0.52±0.023 on MT50, surpassing Multi-task SAC (0.49/0.36), PCGrad (0.72/0.50) and Soft Modularization (0.73/0.50), trailing only CARE (0.84/0.54) which uses extra language metadata; CAGrad-Fast sampling 4/8 tasks retains 0.82/0.50 while giving 2× and 5× speedup over PCGrad.; In semi-supervised CIFAR-10, ARML+CAGrad reaches 68.25% (500 labels), 74.37% (1000), 82.81% (2000) versus ARML 67.05/73.22/81.35 and ARML+PCGrad 67.49/73.23/81.91; MGDA collapses (49.27% at 500 labels) by over-optimizing auxiliary tasks away from main loss, confirming CAGrad’s average-loss guarantee matters when main plus auxiliary objectives are not symmetric.; Efficiency overhead is modest: dual optimization over K≤50 weights is far cheaper than K backpropagations, and subset sampling maintains performance with O(|S|N+T) cost.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Evaluated with fixed backbones per domain (shrunken LeNet, MTAN-SegNet, SAC) under equal loss weighting for vision and not with exhaustive architecture search or uncertainty weighting.', 'Tuned c only in {0.1…0.9} (best 0.2–0.4 for vision, implicit for RL) and reported means over 3 seeds (vision) or 10 runs (RL) without testing c adaptively per task or per layer.', 'Compared gradient manipulation at the shared parameter level and not layer-wise or task-specific head gradients, and assumed average loss as main objective L0 without exploring other user-specified main objectives mentioned as future direction.', 'Semi-supervised experiments held out fixed 10% validation and used the same labeled subsets for all methods, not testing varied label proportions beyond 500/1000/2000 or non-CIFAR datasets.']
limitations_summary: Authors acknowledge CAGrad focuses on the average loss as main objective and has not been validated for other main objectives; implicit limitations include need to tune c per dataset, extra convex optimization per step (though small), and evaluation limited to up to 50 tasks.
limitations_verbatim: While we focus mainly on optimizing the average loss, an interesting future direction is to look at main objectives other than the average loss under the multi-task setting.
generalizability_gap: CAGrad was not evaluated on large-scale language or code-switched NLP tasks, on transformer-based language models, or on multi-modal vision-language settings; nor on highly unbalanced task counts (hundreds) or explicit noisy low-resource code-switching relevant to this repository’s broader MTL survey.
methodological_gap: CAGrad computes gradients at full shared parameters and does not model layer-wise conflict, task grouping, or Pareto front coverage; it requires solving a simplex optimization each step and inherits dependence on accurate stochastic gradients, without comparison to second-order or curvature-aware balancing.
future_work: Extending CAGrad to main objectives other than the average loss and to alternative MTL architectures beyond shared-backbone models.; Adaptive per-layer or per-step selection of c and integration with language or code-switched NLP benchmarks.; Exploring combination with task grouping or routing networks for scaling to hundreds of tasks.

title: Cost-Performance Optimization for Processing Low-Resource Language Tasks Using Commercial LLMs
authors: Arijit Nag; Animesh Mukherjee; Niloy Ganguly; Soumen Chakrabarti
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2024
domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Commercial Large Language Model APIs, Low-Resource Languages (LRL), Indic Languages, Cost-Performance Optimization, Tokenization Disparity, Cross-Lingual Preprocessing
problem_statement: Commercial Large Language Model (LLM) cloud services charge users based on input and output token counts, creating severe economic and performance disadvantages for low-resource languages (LRLs). Because LLM tokenizers are optimized primarily for high-resource language (HRL) vocabularies, LRL words undergo severe subword over-fragmentation, multiplying token consumption by 2x to 7x per word compared to English. This tokenization disparity significantly increases API query costs while native LRL queries frequently suffer from inferior task accuracy.
theoretical_framework: Subword tokenization disparity and over-fragmentation theory in multilingual language models (Petrov et al., 2023; Ahia et al., 2023; Hong et al., 2021); cross-lingual transfer via machine translation, transliteration, and code-mixing; prompt engineering strategies for multilingual reasoning; and the novel Relative Performance to Cost Ratio (RTPCR) optimization framework balancing task accuracy against token-based API expenditures.
methodology: The authors formulated the Relative Performance to Cost Ratio (RTPCR) metric to evaluate preprocessing strategies against native-script baseline querying across task performance and API token expenditure. They evaluated five client-side preprocessing techniques on input instances before passing them to commercial LLM APIs (GPT-4-0613): (1) Native script baseline, (2) Translation to English via open-source machine translation (IndicTrans2), (3) Explicit translation to English using GPT-4 API before task inference, (4) Implicit translation instructing GPT-4 to translate instances internally in the background if needed, (5) Wordmix (replacing excessively fragmented LRL words with English translations via dictionary lookup, as well as Wordmix(Hi) using Hindi and Word-to-Word W2W translation), and (6) Transliteration of LRL text into Latin script using Indic-Trans. The methodology was evaluated across 5 classification tasks from IndicXTREME and 6 generative tasks spanning 15 Indian languages (Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Odia, Punjabi, Sanskrit, Tamil, Telugu, Urdu, Nepali, Kashmiri) plus Thai, Swahili, and Chinese, alongside fact-mutability probing on Indic-MULAN Wikidata triplets.
datasets: IndicXTREME: 5 classification datasets across 15 Indian languages (IndicSentiment for sentiment analysis, IndicXNLI for natural language inference, IndicCOPA for causal reasoning, IndicQA / IndicHeadline for topic and sentence classification); XLSUM: Multilingual abstractive summarization corpus evaluated via ROUGE across low-resource languages; chaii (Hindi and Tamil Question Answering) and TyDi QA: Information-seeking question answering datasets evaluated via Exact Match (EM); Samanantar: Large-scale parallel corpus for 11 Indic languages evaluated for Machine Translation via BLEU; Mathematical Reasoning Datasets: MGSM (Multilingual Grade School Math), Conic10K, and ArMath evaluated via Exact Match (EM); Indic-MULAN: Curated Wikidata fact-verification dataset comprising <subject, relation, object> triplets across 11 Indian languages categorized into mutable, immutable-1, and immutable-n relations
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Accuracy (Classification tasks)', 'BLEU (Machine Translation / Samanantar)', 'ROUGE (Summarization / XLSUM)', 'Exact Match (EM for Question Answering and Mathematical Reasoning: chaii, TyDi QA, MGSM, Conic10K, ArMath)', 'Average tokens generated per instance (Cost proxy)', 'Relative Performance to Cost Ratio (RTPCR)', 'Parity Premium (Tokenization disparity ratio)'], 'evaluated_llm': 'OpenAI GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613 via API, temperature close to 0, seed=42)', 'language_coverage': '15 Indian languages (Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Odia, Punjabi, Sanskrit, Tamil, Telugu, Urdu, Nepali, Kashmiri) and 3 non-Indic languages (Thai, Swahili, Chinese)'}
key_findings: Commercial LLM tokenizers severely over-fragment low-resource Indic languages, generating 2x to 7x more tokens per word than English and imposing an unfair financial burden on LRL users.; Tokenization over-segmentation is significantly more severe for Dravidian languages (Malayalam, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada) than for Indo-Aryan North Indian languages (Hindi, Bengali), reflecting disproportionate representation in LLM pretraining data.; Translating LRL inputs to English using an open-source MT system (IndicTrans2) is the optimal strategy, reducing GPT-4 API costs by up to ~90% while simultaneously boosting downstream classification accuracy and RTPCR across almost all tested languages.; Explicit translation using GPT-4 produces high task accuracy but incurs double API querying costs, resulting in the lowest overall RTPCR score among all tested methods.; Implicit background translation prompting improves performance on summarization, MT, and QA generation tasks without requiring auxiliary external MT tools or adding client-side token translation costs.; Transliterating LRL script into Latin script drastically lowers token counts and reduces API cost, but causes modest degradation in task performance due to grammatical and lexical ambiguities.; Wordmixing excessively segmented LRL words with English (Wordmix-En) or Hindi (Wordmix-Hi) dictionary equivalents maintains competitive task performance while cutting costs, demonstrating that syntax preservation is critical as full word-to-word (W2W) substitution degrades performance.; The proposed RTPCR metric effectively resolves limitations of the Parity Premium metric when task difficulty is language-independent, providing a superior guide for cost-performance trade-offs in commercial LLM deployment.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Commercial LLM evaluation is delimited to a single black-box model: OpenAI GPT-4 (specifically the gpt-4-0613 snapshot accessed via API under fixed seed=42 and near-zero temperature).', 'Primary linguistic focus is delimited to 15 scheduled and regional Indian languages, with supplementary evaluation on Thai, Swahili, and Chinese.', 'Task scope covers 5 classification tasks from IndicXTREME, 6 generation tasks (summarization, QA, MT, math reasoning), and fact-mutability probing via Indic-MULAN.', 'Hardware scope is delimited to a standard 16GB RAM CPU workstation for client-side preprocessing without local GPU acceleration.', 'Cost modeling is delimited to token-based cloud API pricing ($0.03/1K input tokens, $0.06/1K output tokens) and excludes operational infrastructure costs such as power, cooling, or local server deployment.']
limitations_summary: The authors acknowledge several explicit limitations: evaluation was restricted to a single commercial LLM (GPT-4) without comparing alternative commercial APIs such as Claude, Gemini, or BARD; the heuristic wordmix replacement strategy operates independently of sentence context, occasionally degrading syntactic integrity and semantic coherence; the empirical scope was primarily restricted to Indian languages rather than global low-resource languages; and translation-based approaches remain vulnerable to translation inaccuracies and subtle losses in sentiment nuance or cultural specificity.
limitations_verbatim: Despite high costs, GPT-4 is widely regarded as providing better quality than open-source counterparts like BLOOM [\(Scao et al.,](#page-10-3) [2023\)](#page-10-3) and GPTneo. GPT-4 has been compared and shown to be superior to BARD in multiple application scenarios including text processing and understanding[<sup>3</sup>](#page-9-15) . For this reason, and to contain costs, we only experiment with one commercial LLM, GPT-4. Although it will increase the experiment cost significantly, bringing other paid LLMs into the experimental setup will make our observations more robust. Also, our wordmix technique, where we replace an LRL word with its translation, without taking sentence context into account, is crude it sometimes impacts sentence structure. Replacing a word or phrase while considering sentence context will be more appropriate. In this work, we only focus on Indian languages. Although we cover as many as 15 languages, an immediate extension can be to check the hypothesis for other LRLs worldwide.
generalizability_gap: The empirical investigation focuses primarily on 15 Indian languages, leaving low-resource indigenous languages from Africa, the Americas, and Southeast Asia largely unexamined. Furthermore, only GPT-4 was tested, so findings may vary across other commercial LLM families (such as Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, or proprietary mistral models) and newer tokenizer architectures.
methodological_gap: The wordmix algorithm performs context-independent, dictionary-based word replacement that does not consider syntactic dependencies or multi-word phrases; machine translation errors (e.g., loss of sarcasm, emotion, or cultural nuances) are directly propagated into downstream LLM inference; and the experimental framework assessed each preprocessing strategy in isolation without investigating hybrid cascades or dynamic routing based on tokenization entropy.
future_work: Extending the cost-performance optimization framework to a broader spectrum of commercial LLMs and multilingual foundation models beyond GPT-4.; Developing context-aware and phrase-level wordmixing heuristics to preserve syntactic structure and morphological agreement when mixing LRL and HRL vocabulary.; Exploring wordmixing with other high-resource regional bridge languages from the same language families rather than relying exclusively on English or Hindi.; Validating the preprocessing techniques and RTPCR framework across non-Indic low-resource language families globally.; Designing adaptive routing pipelines that dynamically select between native querying, open-source translation, transliteration, and wordmixing based on tokenization over-segmentation thresholds.

title: CrisisBench: Benchmarking Crisis-related Social Media Datasets for Humanitarian Information Processing
authors: Firoj Alam; Hassan Sajjad; Muhammad Imran; Ferda Ofli
venue: Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AAAI)
domain: Crisis informatics and disaster response text processing on social media platforms (Twitter).
problem_statement: Dispersed crisis-related social media datasets with inconsistent label taxonomies, noisy near-duplicate content, and lacking standardized splits prevent researchers from comparing models and evaluating progress in crisis informatics tasks.
theoretical_framework: Domain adaptation and transfer learning in natural language processing, using contextualized transformer representations and event-aware side-constraint conditioning to aggregate multi-event disaster data.
methodology: The authors consolidated eight human-annotated crisis tweet corpora by mapping heterogeneous labels into unified informativeness and humanitarian taxonomies. They filtered exact duplicates via string matching and near-duplicates using bag-of-ngrams cosine similarity with a 0.75 threshold, assigned language tags via the Google Cloud Language Detection API, and created standardized 70/10/20 train/dev/test splits. They benchmarked CNN, fastText, BERT, DistilBERT, RoBERTa, and multilingual transformers across monolingual, cross-dataset, event-aware, and multilingual settings.
datasets: CrisisLex (CrisisLexT26 and CrisisLexT6); CrisisNLP; SWDM2013; ISCRAM2013; Disaster Response Data (DRD); Disasters on Social Media (DSM); CrisisMMD; AIDR
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Weighted Precision', 'Weighted Recall', 'Weighted F1-score', 'Accuracy'], 'benchmark_results': {'english_informativeness_binary': {'CNN': 0.866, 'fastText': 0.844, 'BERT': 0.872, 'DistilBERT': 0.87, 'RoBERTa': 0.883}, 'english_humanitarian_11class': {'CNN': 0.829, 'fastText': 0.824, 'BERT': 0.86, 'DistilBERT': 0.856, 'RoBERTa': 0.872}, 'event_aware_training': {'CNN_humanitarian_F1': 0.842, 'BERT_humanitarian_F1': 0.865}, 'multilingual_humanitarian': {'BERT_multilingual_F1': 0.781, 'XLM_RoBERTa_F1': 0.788}}}
key_findings: Training models on the consolidated dataset yields superior generalization across individual test datasets and achieves higher overall F1-scores than training on single-source datasets.; Pre-trained transformer models (RoBERTa, BERT, DistilBERT) consistently outperform CNN and fastText architectures, delivering substantial performance gains on minority humanitarian classes.; Duplicate and near-duplicate tweets constitute 20% to 25% of uncleaned crisis datasets, and removing those duplicates prevents data leakage between training and evaluation splits.; Event-aware conditioning via prepended event tokens improves CNN multi-class humanitarian classification F1-score from 0.829 to 0.842.; Evaluating models on multilingual crisis data causes a significant performance drop of approximately 8% in F1-score compared to English-only benchmarks.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Restricted benchmark evaluations to textual tweet content, excluding image and multimodal inputs.', 'Focused classification experiments primarily on English-language tweets, treating multilingual evaluations as preliminary baselines.', 'Evaluated binary informativeness and 11-class humanitarian categorization tasks while excluding disaster event type classification.', 'Omitted multi-label tweets from the DRD dataset to avoid manual re-annotation for single-label multiclass experiments.']
limitations_summary: The consolidated dataset retains substantial class imbalance with dominant non-humanitarian tweets and scarce minority categories. In addition, event-aware training fails to improve transformer models, multi-label instances were dropped rather than re-annotated, and performance drops significantly on multilingual subsets.
limitations_verbatim: Even after combining the datasets, the imbalance in class distribution seems to persist (last column in Table 4). For example, the distribution of "not humanitarian" is relatively higher (37.40%) than other class labels. In Table 4, we highlighted some class labels, which we dropped in the rest of the classification experiments conducted in this study.
generalizability_gap: The benchmark evaluations focus predominantly on English tweets collected exclusively from Twitter between 2010 and 2017, leaving model generalizability to non-English languages, alternative social media platforms, and subsequent disaster events untested.
methodological_gap: Token-prefixing event-aware conditioning failed to improve transformer performance, multi-label instances were discarded rather than modeled via multi-label classification frameworks, and similarity-based deduplication relied on a fixed heuristic threshold.
future_work: Evaluating deeper encoder-decoder architectures such as Google T5 for crisis text classification.; Exploring regularization techniques and fine-tuning strategies to enhance transformer performance in crisis informatics.; Investigating multilingual pretrained models and zero-shot cross-lingual transfer for non-English crisis tweets.; Incorporating disaster event type classification into the consolidated benchmark suite.; Extending event-aware conditioning to multi-attribute tags such as geographic disaster region.

title: Cross-Lingual Disaster-related Multi-label Tweet Classification with Manifold Mixup
authors: Jishnu Ray Chowdhury; Cornelia Caragea; Doina Caragea
venue: Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Student Research Workshop (ACL 2020 SRW)
domain: Cross-lingual crisis informatics, disaster management, and multi-label social media (Twitter) text classification.
problem_statement: Social media provides critical situational awareness during disasters, but existing crisis NLP models focus predominantly on English tweets, lack standard large-scale multilingual multi-label disaster benchmarks, and cannot utilize partially labeled binary-annotated tweets alongside fine-grained multi-class data during training.
theoretical_framework: Manifold Mixup regularization theory (interpolating hidden state representations and target labels to induce linear behavior across representations), cross-lingual contextual representation learning via Multilingual BERT (M-BERT), and loss masking for partially supervised learning.
methodology: The authors aggregated six crisis datasets from CrisisNLP and CrisisLex into a unified multilingual corpus of over 130,000 tweets across five target classes (Informative, Casualties and Damage, Donation and Volunteering, Caution and Advice, and Non-Informative). To leverage both binary and fine-grained annotations without discarding partially labeled instances, the authors developed a masked binary cross-entropy loss function with class weighting. They fine-tuned Multilingual BERT (M-BERT) with Manifold Mixup—interpolating hidden states, ground-truth labels, and class masks across randomly selected transformer layers using mixing ratios sampled from a Beta(2, 2) distribution. They evaluated the proposed approach against FastText, CNN, XML-CNN, BiLSTM, Word Mixup, and Sentence Mixup across out-of-event test sets and zero-shot cross-lingual test sets in Spanish, French, and Italian.
datasets: Aggregated Multilingual Crisis Tweet Dataset: Over 130,000 tweets compiled from CrisisNLP (Resources #1, #4, #5, #7) and CrisisLex (CrisisLexT6, CrisisLexT26) covering English, French, Italian, Spanish, and other languages; Out-of-event Test Sets: Russia Meteor, Cyclone Pam, Philippines Flood, and Multilingual Mixed Disasters; Pretrained Multilingual BERT (M-BERT) covering 104 languages

scope_and_delimitations: ['Restricted dataset aggregation to textual content from six specific CrisisNLP and CrisisLex corpora, excluding image and multimodal features.', 'Delimited classification to four binary prediction heads (Informative vs. Non-Informative, Casualties and Damage, Caution and Advice, Donation and Volunteering) with positive classes treated as mutually exclusive during aggregation due to sparse multi-label source annotations.', "Evaluated zero-shot cross-lingual generalization on three Romance languages (Spanish, French, Italian) present within M-BERT's 104 pretraining languages."]
limitations_summary: The authors acknowledge that the annotated classes were constrained to be mutually exclusive during dataset aggregation due to the scarcity of multi-label annotations in the source corpora. In addition, broader classes like Casualties and Damage combine diverse sub-categories to avoid class sparsity, and zero-shot cross-lingual capabilities remain bounded by the 104 languages covered during M-BERT pretraining.
limitations_verbatim: Even though the classifiers are not mutually exclusive, the annotated classes (excluding the more general informative class) are kept mutually exclusive because there were not many multi-label annotations in the original data and most tweets tend to belong to only one of the specific classes. One could also use mutually exclusive classifiers with the given data.
generalizability_gap: The zero-shot cross-lingual capabilities were evaluated on three major European Romance languages (Spanish, French, Italian), leaving lower-resource languages, non-Indo-European languages, code-switched microblogs, and languages outside M-BERT's 104 pretraining languages untested.
methodological_gap: The dataset aggregation treats fine-grained positive classes as mutually exclusive due to historical annotation constraints, preventing the full exploration of true multi-label co-occurrences. Furthermore, the framework relies on heuristic class weighting and fixed Beta distribution parameters without exploring adaptive mixup schedules or weak supervision.
future_work: Exploring weak supervision techniques to automatically expand fine-grained multi-label disaster annotations.; Investigating additional data augmentation and regularization techniques to further improve model robustness in low-resource disaster settings.; Extending cross-lingual evaluation to diverse non-European and low-resource languages prone to natural disasters.

title: Deep multi-task learning: a review of concepts, methods, and cross-domain applications
authors: Mahmoud Mohamed Abdelsamie; Shahira Shaaban Azab; Hesham A. Hefny
venue: International Journal of Data Science and Analytics
domain: Deep learning and multi-task learning across cross-domain applications (natural language processing, computer vision, healthcare, bioinformatics, power systems, robotics, finance, climate science, and physics)
problem_statement: Providing a comprehensive, unified review and taxonomy of deep multi-task learning (MTL) concepts, architectural sharing mechanisms (hard vs. soft parameter sharing), optimization challenges (negative transfer, task imbalance, hyperparameter sensitivity), and cross-domain application strategies.
theoretical_framework: Multi-task learning (MTL) inductive transfer bias and shared representation learning; hard and soft parameter sharing paradigms; multi-objective optimization and regularized joint loss formulation
methodology: Comprehensive literature review and bibliometric quantitative analysis of 6,872 unique Scopus-indexed publications (2020–2025) on multi-task learning, combined with structural taxonomy categorization of MTL architectures (single-domain, multimodal, learned, conditional) and cross-domain application analysis.
key_findings: MTL publication volume grew rapidly between 2020 and mid-2025, peaking in 2024, with major contributions from computer science (4,698 papers), engineering (1,135 papers), mathematics (498 papers), and medicine/health sciences (241 papers).; Hard parameter sharing shares hidden layers while keeping task-specific heads, providing low computational complexity and reduced overfitting for highly related tasks, whereas soft parameter sharing regularizes separate per-task networks to maintain similarity, offering higher flexibility for loosely related tasks at higher computational cost.; MTL architectures are systematically categorized into single-domain (shared trunk, cross-talk/cross-stitch, prediction distillation, hierarchical/modular/generative), multimodal (e.g., OmniNet), learned (structure search, branched, modular, fine-grained sharing), and conditional architectures.; MTL fundamentally differs from transfer learning: MTL simultaneously learns all tasks using bidirectional knowledge sharing across shared backbones, whereas transfer learning transfers knowledge sequentially and unidirectionally from a source to a target domain.; Primary operational bottlenecks across domains include negative transfer among conflicting tasks, task imbalance during gradient optimization, acute hyperparameter sensitivity, and training scalability constraints with large task counts.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Focused on deep multi-task learning research published between 2020 and mid-2025 indexed in the Scopus database (articles, conference papers, and review papers).', 'Restricted subject areas to computer science, engineering, mathematics, physics, medicine, decision sciences, neuroscience, business, and social sciences.', 'Excluded non-peer-reviewed whitepapers, non-English publications, and purely non-deep traditional statistical multi-task learning methods.']
limitations_summary: MTL faces negative transfer when tasks conflict, task imbalance where dominant tasks skew gradient updates, elevated architectural complexity across multimodal or heterogeneous tasks, acute hyperparameter sensitivity (task loss weights, learning rates), and severe optimization/memory scalability constraints when scaling to dozens or hundreds of tasks.
limitations_verbatim: Despite its potential benefits, MTL presents several draw-backs and limitations. One major challenge is negative transfer, which occurs when tasks are too different or con-flicting, causing the shared learning process to affect the performance when trained jointly [51, 52, 56]. Task imbalance is another problem, where some tasks may dominate the learning process due to larger datasets, stronger gradients, or simpler objectives, leading to poor performance on low-resource or complex tasks. [53]. Furthermore, Architectural Complexity, designing suit-able architectures that allow for both shared and task-specific components, is non-trivial, especially when tasks differ in modality, structure, or scale [10]. Another one of the most significant limitations of MTL is the sensitivity of hyperparameters. Unlike single-task mod-els, multi-task learning systems often require fine-tuning of various hyperparameters, such as task-specific weights, learning rates, and optimization strategies [94, 95]. This addi-tional layer of complexity can significantly increase the effort required during the model development phase, as finding the optimal balance between tasks is critical to avoid poor performance or negative transfer.
generalizability_gap: Many domain-specific MTL implementations have only been evaluated on narrow single-language or single-institution benchmarks (e.g., specific Arabic dialects, college student cohorts, discrete robotic action spaces, or constant pressure physical models) without cross-institutional validation or continuous dexterous control environments.
methodological_gap: Existing MTL methods often rely on empirical trial-and-error or heuristic task weighting; they lack automated mechanisms to eliminate negative transfer, struggle with gradient interference and computational memory bottlenecks at scale, and often lack model interpretability in high-stakes domains like healthcare and finance.
future_work: Developing dynamic task weighting approaches using attention mechanisms and deep reinforcement learning to adaptively evaluate task contributions during training and mitigate negative transfer.; Integrating meta-learning ('learning to learn') techniques to automatically discover optimal representation sharing strategies and balance shared versus task-specific components.; Leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) and foundation models for zero-shot and few-shot multi-task transfer across diverse domains.; Enhancing model interpretability, reliability, and explainability for high-stakes MTL deployments in healthcare, finance, and autonomous systems.; Designing scalable task grouping and optimization frameworks to manage dozens or hundreds of tasks without excessive memory consumption or gradient conflict.

title: Design Science in Information Systems Research
authors: Alan R. Hevner; Salvatore T. March; Jinsoo Park; Sudha Ram
venue: MIS Quarterly
domain: Information Systems, Software Engineering, and Computer Science Methodology
problem_statement: Delineating the boundaries and methodological standards of design science research in contrast to traditional behavioral research in information systems.
theoretical_framework: Design Science Paradigm, Behavioral Science Paradigm, and Information Systems Research Framework
methodology: Conceptual framework synthesis and development of seven normative guidelines for artifact construction, evaluation, and communication.
evaluation: Analytical evaluation and mapping of seven foundational guidelines across exemplar design science research projects.
key_findings: Established that design science creates and evaluates IT artifacts (constructs, models, methods, instantiations) intended to solve identified organizational and technical problems.; Formulated seven core guidelines for design science research rigor: Design as an Artifact, Problem Relevance, Design Evaluation, Research Contributions, Research Rigor, Design as a Search Process, and Communication of Research.; Emphasized that empirical evaluation of artifact utility, quality, and efficiency is mandatory for establishing scientific contribution.
scope_and_delimitations: Focuses on IT and information systems artifact creation and evaluation.
limitations_summary: Guidelines must be applied flexibly with domain-specific judgment rather than as a rigid bureaucratic checklist.
limitations_verbatim: The guidelines should be addressed in any design-science research project. However, researchers, reviewers, and editors must use their judgment to determine how and to what degree each guideline should be applied.
generalizability_gap: High-level guidelines require operationalization when applied to specific empirical deep learning benchmarks.
methodological_gap: Evaluation methods are broadly classified (observational, analytical, experimental, testing, descriptive) without specifying statistical test parameters.
future_work: Development of domain-specific evaluation metrics and formal artifact verification methods across evolving computing paradigms.

title: Detecting Urgency Status of Crisis Tweets: A Transfer Learning Approach for Low Resource Languages
authors: Efsun Sarioglu Kayi; Linyong Nan; Bohan Qu; Mona Diab; Kathleen McKeown
venue: Proceedings of the 28th International Conference on Computational Linguistics (COLING 2020)
domain: Crisis Informatics, Disaster Response, Social Media NLP (Twitter), Cross-Lingual Transfer Learning, Low-Resource Languages (English, Sinhala, Odia)
problem_statement: How to detect the urgency status of crisis-related social media tweets during natural disasters with very limited annotated data, and how to effectively transfer urgency classification knowledge from a high-resource language (English) to low-resource languages (Sinhala and Odia) in a zero-shot cross-lingual setting using deep contextual and cross-lingual embeddings.
theoretical_framework: Zero-shot cross-lingual transfer learning framework (Ruder et al., 2019) mapping high-resource source representations to low-resource target spaces via projection-based bilingual embeddings (VecMap, Proc-B) and massively multilingual contextual representations (LASER, XLM-R); semi-supervised self-training via multi-classifier consensus voting (Yarowsky, 1995; Zhou and Goldman, 2004); and recall-maximizing ensemble decision theory for life-critical disaster informatics.
methodology: A transfer learning pipeline comprising: (1) Preprocessing tweets via URL/mention removal, lowercasing, and hashtag segmentation; (2) Feature extraction using monolingual non-contextual (fastText, CrisisNLP) and contextual embeddings (BERT-base, BERT-large, RoBERTa-large, XLM-mlm-en) for English, alongside projection-based cross-lingual embeddings (VecMap, Proc-B initialized with fastText and aligned via fast-align seed dictionaries) and multilingual contextual embeddings (LASER, XLM-R base/large) for Sinhala and Odia; (3) Classification using SVM, Random Forest, Multi-Layer Perceptron (dense layers 1024, 512, 64 with batch normalization, ReLU, and dropout), and CNN architectures; (4) Semi-supervised data augmentation via multi-round self-training with agreement across three independent RoBERTa models to pseudo-label unlabeled disaster tweets (expanding 1,952 samples to 16,243 samples); and (5) Ensemble modeling using an aggressive voting strategy (predicting Urgent if any model votes positive) to maximize recall for urgent crisis situations.
datasets: English Crisis Urgency Dataset - 1,919 crisis tweets sampled from Imran et al. (2016) and annotated on Figure-Eight across four urgency levels (134 Extremely Urgent, 378 Definitely Urgent, 589 Somewhat Urgent, 818 Not Urgent), mapped to binary labels (26.7% urgent, 73.3% not urgent) and split into 80% training and 20% evaluation; Augmented English Dataset - 16,243 crisis tweets combining 1,952 labeled samples with pseudo-labeled unlabeled crisis tweets filtered by consensus agreement of three RoBERTa models (18.5% urgent ratio); Sinhala Evaluation Dataset (LDC LORELEI IL10 / LDC2018E57) - Sentence-level binary urgency annotations by native informants (7.7% urgent ratio); Odia Evaluation Dataset (LDC LORELEI IL11 / LDC2019E62) - Sentence-level binary urgency annotations by native informants (16.1% urgent ratio)
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Macro Precision', 'Macro Recall', 'Macro F1 Score (unweighted mean across positive and negative classes)', 'Mean and standard deviation across 30 independent experimental runs'], 'english_classification_results': {'random_baseline_macro_f1': 50.0, 'crisisnlp_mlp_original_macro_f1': '70.5 ± 1.3', 'fasttext_mlp_original_macro_f1': '65.8 ± 1.4', 'bert_large_mlp_original_macro_f1': 75.2, 'roberta_large_mlp_original_macro_f1': 75.7, 'roberta_large_mlp_augmented_macro_f1': 75.6, 'ensemble_aggressive_voting_macro_f1': 76.5, 'ensemble_precision': 77.8, 'ensemble_recall': 75.6}, 'cross_lingual_sinhala_results_zero_shot': {'procb_mlp_original_macro_f1': '54.6 ± 5.1', 'vecmap_mlp_original_macro_f1': '52.3 ± 4.7', 'laser_mlp_original_macro_f1': 62.1, 'xlmr_large_mlp_augmented_macro_f1': 59.2, 'ensemble_macro_f1': 63.5, 'ensemble_precision': 61.2, 'ensemble_recall': 69.3}, 'cross_lingual_odia_results_zero_shot': {'procb_mlp_original_macro_f1': '53.3 ± 3.4', 'vecmap_mlp_augmented_macro_f1': '56.4 ± 2.1', 'xlmr_base_mlp_original_macro_f1': 47.9, 'xlmr_base_mlp_augmented_macro_f1': 61.3, 'ensemble_macro_f1': 62.6, 'ensemble_precision': 71.2, 'ensemble_recall': 60.3}}
key_findings: Deep pre-trained contextual models (RoBERTa-large) produce superior tweet representations even with small annotated datasets, achieving a 75.7% Macro F1 score on English urgency detection (a 25.7% absolute improvement over random baseline).; Zero-shot cross-lingual transfer from English to low-resource languages is effective, achieving 63.5% Macro F1 on Sinhala using LASER representations and 62.6% Macro F1 on Odia using XLM-R representations with an ensemble model.; LASER features perform best for English-to-Sinhala transfer due to sentence-level contextual modeling and larger parallel training corpora (796,000 sentence pairs), whereas XLM-R base features benefit Odia transfer most when augmented with synthetic training data.; In-domain crisis embeddings (CrisisNLP) consistently outperform out-of-domain embeddings (fastText) for English classification (70.5% vs. 65.8% Macro F1 with MLP).; Semi-supervised data augmentation via multi-classifier consensus improves classification performance when source and target label distributions are aligned (Odia: 16.1% vs. 18.5% urgent), but degrades performance when class distributions diverge substantially (Sinhala: 7.7% vs. 18.5% urgent).; Aggressive voting ensembles predicting positive when any constituent model predicts urgency enhance recall and overall Macro F1 across both English and cross-lingual low-resource tasks.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Restricted crisis post types to natural disaster tweets (such as earthquakes, typhoons, and landslides) sampled from historical crisis corpora.', 'Delimited target low-resource languages strictly to Sinhala (IL10) and Odia (IL11) evaluated in a zero-shot cross-lingual setting using LDC LORELEI packages without target-language training data.', 'Mapped fine-grained 4-level urgency annotations into binary classification (Urgent vs Not Urgent).', 'Delimited classifier models to frozen embedding feature extraction followed by shallow classifiers (SVM, RF, MLP, CNN), excluding full end-to-end fine-tuning due to dataset size constraints.', 'Multilingual BERT was excluded from cross-lingual experiments because its pre-training vocabulary does not support Sinhala or Odia.']
limitations_summary: Urgency annotation suffers from ambiguity and noise because annotators frequently conflate general crisis status updates with critical emergency requests for help, and tend to label past events as urgent. Additionally, end-to-end fine-tuning of deep pre-trained language models fails on small-scale crisis datasets, pseudo-label data augmentation degrades performance when source and target class prior distributions diverge, and major multilingual models like Multilingual BERT lack support for low-resource languages such as Sinhala and Odia.
limitations_verbatim: When we analyzed the annotations, we noticed that some of the tweets about rescue efforts were particularly confusing: tweets that are general status updates about an incident and more critical tweets that are asking for help are both labeled as urgent, without making a distinction between the two. This demonstrates one of many aspects of the difficulty of annotating for urgency, partially due to the tendency of labeling a tweet as urgent even though the urgency of the event is past.
generalizability_gap: The transfer framework is evaluated only on two Indo-Aryan languages (Sinhala and Odia) and English natural disaster tweets; generalizability to other language families, non-natural emergencies (man-made conflicts, terrorist attacks, infectious disease outbreaks), and social media platforms beyond Twitter remains unexamined.
methodological_gap: The methodology relies on static frozen embedding feature extraction and shallow classifiers because end-to-end transformer fine-tuning collapses on small datasets; projection-based cross-lingual embeddings (VecMap, Proc-B) rely on order-independent idf-weighted word averaging rather than deep contextualized sentence modeling; and semi-supervised data augmentation lacks mechanisms to adapt to target-domain class prior distribution shifts.
future_work: Extending cross-lingual urgency detection to additional low-resource languages across diverse language families.; Developing domain adaptation and calibration techniques for semi-supervised data augmentation when source and target label distributions differ significantly.; Exploring low-resource fine-tuning techniques and lightweight parameter-efficient transfer methods for deep pre-trained language models on small disaster corpora.; Investigating fine-grained multi-class urgency intensity classification beyond binary tags to differentiate active emergency rescue calls from general incident status reports.; Integrating cross-lingual urgency classifiers into real-time emergency dispatch and humanitarian assistance platforms.

title: Developing a Named Entity Recognition Dataset for Tagalog
authors: Lester James V. Miranda
venue: Proceedings of the First Workshop for Southeast Asian Language Processing (SEALP 2023) at IJCNLP-AACL 2023
domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Named Entity Recognition (NER), Low-Resource Languages, Philippine Languages (Tagalog / Filipino), News Domain
problem_statement: How to overcome the scarcity of high-quality Named Entity Recognition (NER) resources for Tagalog (a low-resource Philippine language) by curating a publicly accessible, gold-standard annotated corpus from modern news reports and establishing empirical baselines across supervised, transfer learning, and zero-shot large language model configurations.
theoretical_framework: Transition-based dependency and entity span parsing using the BILUO sequence encoding scheme and maxout convolutional neural networks (Honnibal et al., 2020); token-level and boundary-level information-theoretic distinctiveness metrics based on Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence of unigram distributions (Papay et al., 2020); and monolingual/multilingual contextual representation transfer (Cruz and Cheng, 2022; Conneau et al., 2020; Devlin et al., 2019).
methodology: A dataset curation, annotation, and benchmarking framework comprising: (1) Corpus curation: Extracting and filtering news texts from the TLUnified pretraining corpus spanning 2009 to early 2020 across politics, weather, and science; (2) Iterative annotation: Using Prodigy with the ner.manual recipe across six rounds (18 weeks total) with three native Tagalog speakers annotating three CoNLL-style entity categories (Person, Organization, Location; excluding MISC), conducting retrospective guideline calibration after each round; (3) Annotation evaluation: Measuring inter-annotator agreement via two Cohen's kappa formulations (token-level non-null kappa = 0.81, non-O kappa = 0.83) and reference F1 (0.89), alongside Span Distinctiveness (SD) and Boundary Distinctiveness (BD) metrics; (4) Supervised modeling: Training spaCy transition-based parsers with BILUO encoding and maxout CNNs using four embedding configurations: from scratch (baseline), static Tagalog fastText vectors with UTF-8 byte cloze pretraining, fine-tuned monolingual RoBERTa Tagalog, and multilingual transfer with XLM-RoBERTa and Multilingual BERT; (5) Entity disambiguation: Evaluating multi-task joint training with POS tagging and contextual RoBERTa fine-tuning to resolve ambiguous Organization and Location mentions; (6) Cross-dataset evaluation: Bidirectional cross-domain transfer evaluation against WikiANN and manual re-annotation of WikiANN test samples; (7) Zero-shot LLM evaluation: Prompting commercial (GPT-4, Claude 2, Cohere Command) and open-source (Falcon-40B, LLaMA-2, Dolly, OpenLLaMA) LLMs.
datasets: TLUNIFIED-NER - Gold-standard Tagalog Named Entity Recognition dataset containing ~7.8k documents (6,700 train, 545 dev, 558 test; 208,247 tokens) annotated across Person (8,024 spans), Organization (6,706 spans), and Location (10,753 spans; total 25,483 entity spans) sourced from TLUnified news articles (2009-2020); WikiANN Tagalog - Silver-standard dataset containing 100 train and 100 test documents (alongside a newly re-annotated gold test set) used for cross-dataset evaluation
evaluation: {'metrics': ["Token-level Cohen's kappa (non-null and non-O)", 'Reference F1-score for inter-annotator agreement', 'Entity-level F1-score across 3 experimental trials', 'Relative Error Reduction (RER)', 'Span Distinctiveness (SD) and Boundary Distinctiveness (BD)'], 'inter_annotator_agreement': {'cohen_kappa_non_null_tokens': 0.81, 'cohen_kappa_non_o_tokens': 0.83, 'reference_f1_score': 0.89}, 'supervised_and_transfer_benchmarks': {'baseline_train_from_scratch_f1': 'Evaluated on test set across 3 trials', 'static_fasttext_byte_cloze_f1': 'Evaluated on test set across 3 trials', 'monolingual_roberta_tagalog_f1': 'Highest performing contextual model with substantial error reduction on ORG and LOC mentions', 'multilingual_xlmr_and_mbert_f1': 'Evaluated in cross-lingual transfer settings'}, 'llm_zero_shot_benchmarks': {'models_evaluated': ['GPT-4', 'Claude 2', 'Cohere Command', 'Falcon-40B', 'LLaMA-2 7B', 'OpenLLaMA 7B', 'Dolly 7B'], 'observation': 'Supervised transition-based models consistently outperform zero-shot prompting across all tested LLMs'}}
key_findings: Iterative gold-standard annotation by native Tagalog speakers achieves high inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's kappa of 0.81 for non-null tokens and 0.83 ignoring 'O' labels; reference F1 of 0.89), validating the quality of the ~7.8k document TLUNIFIED-NER corpus.; Fine-tuning monolingual contextual embeddings (RoBERTa Tagalog) achieves superior NER performance and substantial relative error reduction on ambiguous Organization and Location entities compared to static fastText vectors and train-from-scratch baselines.; Supervised transition-based models fine-tuned on TLUNIFIED-NER consistently outperform zero-shot large language model prompting across both open-source (Falcon-40B, LLaMA-2, Dolly, OpenLLaMA) and commercial LLMs (GPT-4, Claude 2, Cohere Command).; Models trained on TLUNIFIED-NER achieve stronger cross-dataset generalization than silver-standard WikiANN models, and manual re-annotation confirms pervasive annotation errors and text fragment issues in the Tagalog portion of WikiANN.; Joint multi-task training of POS tagging with transition-based NER via shared representation weights improves entity disambiguation when entity mentions exhibit lexical and semantic category overlap.; Information-theoretic distinctiveness metrics reveal that Person and Location entities exhibit higher boundary distinctiveness than Organization entities, explaining lower baseline model performance on organization span boundaries.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Restricted source text domain strictly to news reports published between 2009 and early 2020 from Metro Manila news outlets in the TLUnified pretraining corpus.', 'Delimited entity categories to three flat CoNLL-style entity classes (Person, Organization, Location), deliberately excluding the Miscellaneous (MISC) tag to reduce annotator ambiguity.', 'Target language delimited exclusively to Tagalog / Filipino, excluding non-standard dialects, Tagalog-English code-switching, and other regional Philippine languages.', 'Classifier architectures delimited to spaCy transition-based parsers with maxout CNNs and zero-shot LLM prompts, excluding CRFs and BiLSTM sequence taggers.']
limitations_summary: The TLUNIFIED-NER corpus is restricted primarily to the formal news domain, leaving conversational, social media, and informal Tagalog varieties unrepresented. Furthermore, benchmark evaluations are restricted to spaCy's transition-based parsing architecture without exploring sequence labeling architectures like Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) or tools like Stanford Stanza, and the entity schema excludes the miscellaneous (MISC) category and overlapping or nested entity spans.
limitations_verbatim: The TLUNIFIED-NER corpora is comprised mostly by news reports. Although the texts demonstrate the standard usage of Tagalog, its domain is limited. In addition, we only trained a transitionbased parser model for our NER classifier. In the future, we plan to extend these benchmarks and include CRFs or other tools such as Stanford Stanza.
generalizability_gap: The dataset focuses exclusively on formal news domain Tagalog from Metro Manila news outlets (2009-2020), leaving informal Tagalog, code-switched Taglish (Tagalog-English), regional dialects, and other major Philippine languages (such as Cebuano, Ilocano, and Hiligaynon) unexamined.
methodological_gap: The empirical benchmarks rely primarily on spaCy transition-based parsers with maxout CNNs, leaving Conditional Random Fields (CRFs), BiLSTM-CRF sequence labelers, and token-level transformer classifiers unbenchmarked; zero-shot LLM evaluations were conducted using simple static prompt templates without exploring advanced prompting frameworks (such as PromptNER or few-shot chain-of-thought).
future_work: Extending the NER annotation schema to fine-grained, hierarchical, and overlapping/nested entity types similar to the ACE project.; Expanding gold-standard NER dataset development to other major Philippine languages (such as Cebuano, Ilocano, and Hiligaynon).; Benchmarking additional sequence modeling architectures including Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) and Stanford Stanza.; Exploring advanced prompting strategies such as PromptNER and few-shot chain-of-thought prompting for multilingual large language models.

title: Do All Languages Cost the Same? Tokenization in the Era of Commercial Language Models
authors: Orevaoghene Ahia; Sachin Kumar; Hila Gonen; Jungo Kasai; David R. Mortensen; Noah A. Smith; Yulia Tsvetkov
venue: Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2023)
domain: Natural Language Processing, Subword Tokenization, NLP Economics & Fairness
problem_statement: Analyzes the economic and computational inequities caused by subword tokenizers in commercial language model APIs that charge per token, demonstrating that low-resource languages incur higher monetary costs and latency overhead for identical semantic content.
theoretical_framework: Cross-lingual tokenizer fertility analysis and pricing policy critique for token-based commercial NLP billing models.
methodology: Empirically measures token fertility, byte-to-token ratios, monetary cost per task, and generation throughput across 22 typologically diverse languages using commercial API tokenizers (including OpenAI tiktoken cl100k_base, text-davinci-003, and Cohere) on standardized translation datasets.
datasets: FLORES-101; WMT parallel benchmark datasets
evaluation: Token fertility (subword tokens per word); Byte-to-token ratio; Relative cost ratio compared to English; Context window efficiency
key_findings: Commercial tokenizers exhibit severe cross-lingual fertility disparities, requiring up to 6x more tokens to represent equivalent semantic content in low-resource languages compared to English.; Because API pricing models charge uniformly per token, speakers of low-resource languages pay significantly higher financial costs for identical linguistic tasks.; High subword fragmentation dilutes semantic token embeddings and limits the effective context length available for multi-sentence reasoning in under-represented languages.; Language-agnostic Byte-Pair Encoding trained predominantly on English web text allocates fewer subword merges to non-dominant languages, forcing character-level fallback.
scope_and_delimitations: Focuses on commercial API tokenizers and pricing models across 22 languages spanning high-resource, medium-resource, and low-resource tiers on parallel corpora.
limitations_summary: The analysis focuses on standard translated text across 22 languages and does not evaluate informal social media dialects, code-switched text, or morphological affixes in agglutinative hybrids.
limitations_verbatim: Our analysis is limited to 22 languages selected based on data availability in FLORES-101, and does not assess dialectal variations, informal social media slang, or mixed-language code-switching.
generalizability_gap: Evaluated on clean standard language benchmarks; does not cover code-switched social media text (such as Tagalog-English Taglish) or domain-specific emergency disaster microblogs.
methodological_gap: Does not measure joint multi-task gradient conflict or sequence labeling degradation induced by token over-fragmentation during fine-tuning.
future_work: Designing equitable tokenizer pricing structures based on semantic content or byte length rather than subword token count.; Exploring adaptive cross-lingual tokenizers tailored for multilingual and low-resource deployment.

title: Do Current Multi-Task Optimization Methods in Deep Learning Even Help?
authors: Derrick Xin; Behrooz Ghorbani; Ankush Garg; Orhan Firat; Justin Gilmer
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2022)
domain: Deep Multi-Task Learning (Natural Language Processing and Computer Vision)
problem_statement: Deep multi-task learning models frequently encounter task interference when multiple tasks compete for shared network capacity. Numerous specialized multi-task optimization (MTO) algorithms claim to resolve this interference and outperform simple scalarization, but the empirical validity, reproducibility, and practical benefits of these algorithms remain unverified across realistic benchmarks.
theoretical_framework: Multi-objective optimization and Pareto optimality theory. Under convex optimization principles, linear scalarization is theoretically guaranteed to yield Pareto optimal solutions, and sweeping scalarization weights traces the complete Pareto frontier. The authors evaluate whether non-convex deep multi-task networks require specialized multi-task optimization algorithms to reach the Pareto frontier.
methodology: The authors perform large-scale empirical evaluations comparing specialized multi-task optimization algorithms (MGDA, GradNorm, PCGrad, IMTL, and RLW) with linear scalarization across multilingual machine translation and computer vision benchmarks. The researchers conduct systematic hyperparameter grid searches for learning rates, weight decay, and dropout rates across all optimizers. The study tracks dynamic task weight trajectories during training, evaluates model sensitivity to hyperparameter tuning and evaluation weighting schemes, and compares the computational cost of per-task gradients against model capacity scaling.
datasets: WMT15 English-French (40,853,298 training examples, 4,503 evaluation examples); WMT19 English-Chinese (25,986,436 training examples, 3,981 evaluation examples); WMT16 English-German (4,548,885 training examples, 2,169 evaluation examples); WMT16 English-Romanian (610,320 training examples, 1,999 evaluation examples); CityScapes (urban scene understanding dataset with 2,975 training, 595 validation, and 500 test images for 7-class semantic segmentation and depth estimation); CelebA (200,000 celebrity face images annotated with 40 binary attribute classification tasks); Multi-MNIST (multi-task benchmark with overlaid digit pairs partitioned into 48,000 training, 12,000 validation, and 10,000 test images)
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Cross-entropy loss on validation and training sets', 'Next token prediction error rate (%)', 'Sacre-BLEU translation quality score via beam search decoding (beam size 4)', 'Pixel accuracy (%) and Mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) for semantic segmentation on CityScapes', 'Absolute error and L1 loss for depth estimation on CityScapes', 'Mean classification error (%) across 40 attribute binary classification tasks on CelebA', 'Digit classification accuracy (%) on Multi-MNIST', 'Training steps per second (computational throughput)'], 'baselines': ['Linear scalarization via proportional batch sampling and static loss weighting', 'Multiple Gradient Descent Algorithm (MGDA)', 'Gradient Normalization (GradNorm)', 'Projecting Conflicting Gradients / Gradient Surgery (PCGrad)', 'Impartial Multi-Task Learning (IMTL)', 'Random Loss Weighting (RLW with Gaussian and Dirichlet distributions)', 'Scaled Transformer models (3L-3L base, 6L-6L, 9L-9L, and 12L-12L)'], 'architectures': ['Pre-LN Transformer encoder-decoder models (3L-3L base up to 12L-12L, 512 model dimension, 2048 feed-forward dimension, 8 heads, 64K vocabulary)', 'LeNet convolutional architecture with task-specific fully connected heads (Multi-MNIST)', 'ResNet-18 shared backbone with 40 task-specific linear heads (CelebA)', 'ResNet-50 shared encoder with task-specific decoders (CityScapes)']}
key_findings: Specialized multi-task optimization algorithms fail to improve the performance trade-off curve beyond what simple static scalarization achieves across language translation and vision benchmarks.; Dynamic task weights assigned by MTO algorithms (such as GradNorm, PCGrad, MGDA, and IMTL) remain nearly constant during training, causing these algorithms to behave like static loss weighting in practice.; In low-resource translation settings (English to Romanian), scalarization discovers globally optimal generalization solutions, whereas MTO algorithms converge to near-equal weights that produce suboptimal generalization.; Multi-task neural networks exhibit acute sensitivity to optimization hyperparameters such as learning rate and weight decay; sparse learning rate sweeps produce six to seven times more variance than seed variation, creating misleading illusions of algorithmic superiority in undertuned baselines.; Comparative rankings among MTO algorithms shift substantially when changing the evaluation weighting function, whereas well-tuned scalarization consistently matches or outperforms all MTO algorithms under any evaluation metric.; Computing per-task gradients in MTO methods decreases training throughput from 11.52 to 4.81 steps per second; reallocating this computational budget to scale Transformer model depth strictly improves the Pareto frontier for all task weighting preferences.; Discrepancies in previously reported benchmark results for CelebA and CityScapes stem from undertuned baseline hyperparameters and reporting noisy validation metrics boosted by frequent early stopping.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Constrained the empirical investigation to supervised multi-task learning benchmarks in natural language translation and computer vision, excluding reinforcement learning and self-supervised pre-training domains.', 'Focused exclusively on hard parameter sharing architectures (Transformer encoder-decoder, LeNet, ResNet-18, ResNet-50) rather than soft parameter sharing, branched backbones, or modular networks.', 'Traced Pareto frontiers by performing exhaustive grid searches over static scalarization weights and proportional sampling ratios.', 'Used beam search with a fixed beam size of 4 without tuning decoding hyperparameters for translation evaluation.']
limitations_summary: The authors acknowledge that identifying the optimal scalarization Pareto frontier requires an exhaustive grid search over task loss weights, which is computationally prohibitive for practical deployment. Furthermore, the empirical study is restricted to supervised multi-task learning tasks and does not evaluate reinforcement learning or self-supervised learning settings.
limitations_verbatim: Our results suggest that by exploring the scalarization solution space, one can attain performance on par with (or better than) many MTO algorithms. However, the grid search approach we used for computing the scalarization Pareto frontier is computationally prohibitive.
generalizability_gap: The authors conducted experiments solely on supervised machine translation and computer vision datasets; the authors did not test whether the observed equivalence between scalarization and multi-task optimization holds in reinforcement learning, self-supervised representation learning, speech recognition, or multi-modal foundation models.
methodological_gap: The study relies on exhaustive, computationally expensive grid searches over static loss weights and learning rates to identify the empirical Pareto frontier, rather than developing an automated, single-run optimization algorithm to discover optimal scalarization weights efficiently.
future_work: Developing computationally efficient algorithms and search strategies to navigate the scalarization solution space without prohibitive grid searches.; Establishing the Common Task Framework (CTF) for multi-task optimization to ensure standardized benchmarks, competitive baselines, and rigorous validation/test splits.; Investigating whether the empirical parity between scalarization and multi-task optimization holds in reinforcement learning and self-supervised learning domains.

title: End-to-End Multi-Task Learning with Attention
authors: Shikun Liu; Edward Johns; Andrew J. Davison
venue: Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
domain: Computer Vision — dense image-to-image prediction (semantic segmentation, depth estimation, surface normal prediction) and multi-domain image classification (Visual Decathlon Challenge)
problem_statement: Multi-task learning requires architectures that jointly learn task-shared and task-specific features and loss weightings that balance heterogeneous tasks without manual tuning, yet most prior methods address only architecture or only weighting and suffer from poor parameter efficiency and sensitivity to weighting schemes.
theoretical_framework: Feature-level soft attention as differentiable feature selection from a global shared feature pool, where task-specific attention masks in [0,1] act as learned selectors that enable end-to-end sharing and specialization without explicit task branching.
methodology: Multi-Task Attention Network (MTAN) with one shared feed-forward network and K task-specific attention networks. On SegNet (VGG-16 encoder-decoder), each attention module computes a sigmoid mask a_i^(j) and applies element-wise multiplication to shared features p^(j) to obtain task-specific features \hat{a}_i^(j) = a_i^(j) \odot p^(j); deeper modules concatenate shared features u^(j) with transformed prior task features for joint learning. For Visual Decathlon, MTAN is built on Wide ResNet-28-4. Training uses multi-task loss L_tot = sum_i lambda_i L_i with task losses: cross-entropy for segmentation/classification, L1 for depth/inverse-depth, and negative dot-product for normals. A novel weighting method Dynamic Weight Average (DWA) sets lambda_k(t) = K exp(w_k(t-1)/T)/sum_i exp(w_i(t-1)/T) where w_k(t-1)= L_k(t-1)/L_k(t-2) tracks loss descent rate with temperature T=2, requiring only loss values and no internal gradients.
datasets: CityScapes — high-resolution street-view images resized to 128x256, used for 2-class, 7-class, and 19-class semantic segmentation plus inverse depth estimation (795 training images evaluated, void class excluded for 7/19-class); NYUv2 — RGB-D indoor scenes resized to 288x384, used for 13-class semantic segmentation, true depth from Kinect, and surface normals from Eigen & Fergus, evaluated on 654 test images among 795 training / 654 test split; Visual Decathlon Challenge — 10 diverse image classification domains (ImageNet, Aircraft, CIFAR-100, DPed, DTD, GTSR, Flowers, Omniglot, SVHN, UCF101) trained with Wide ResNet, reported on official online test set with cumulative score max 10,000
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Semantic segmentation: mean Intersection over Union (mIoU, higher is better) and Pixel Accuracy (Pix Acc, higher is better)', 'Depth estimation: Absolute Error (Abs Err, lower is better) and Relative Error (Rel Err, lower is better); L1 used for training, inverse depth for CityScapes and true depth for NYUv2', 'Surface normal prediction (NYUv2 only): Mean and Median angle distance (lower is better) and percentage of pixels within 11.25°, 22.5°, and 30° (higher is better)', 'Visual Decathlon: Top-1 accuracy per task, mean accuracy, and Decathlon score (0–10,000, 1,000 per task)', 'Parameter count (#P) as multiples of single-task model and robustness across weighting schemes visualized via validation curves'], 'baselines': ['Single-Task One Task — vanilla SegNet per task', 'Single-Task STAN — Single-Task Attention Network applying MTAN attention while training only one task', 'Multi-Task Split Wide — standard shared Split branching at final layer, widened to match MTAN parameters', 'Multi-Task Split Deep — same Split, deepened to match MTAN parameters', 'Multi-Task Split (standard) for task-complexity study', 'Multi-Task Dense — shared network plus task-specific sub-networks receiving all shared features without attention', 'Multi-Task Cross-Stitch Network (Misra et al., 2016) implemented on SegNet', 'Visual Decathlon baselines: Scratch, Finetune, Feature (fixed), Residual Adapters, DAN, Piggyback, Parallel SVD', 'Loss weightings compared for every architecture: Equal Weights (lambda=1), Uncertainty Weights (Kendall et al., 2018), and proposed DWA (T=2)'], 'architectures': ['SegNet encoder-decoder based on VGG-16 for CityScapes and NYUv2 dense tasks, trained with Adam (lr 1e-4, batch 2 for NYUv2 and 8 for CityScapes, 80k iterations, halved at 40k)', 'Wide Residual Network (WRN-28-4, stride 2 in first block) for Visual Decathlon, trained with SGD (lr 0.1, batch 100, 300 epochs, halved every 50 epochs, weight decay 5e-5, fine-tuned 9 tasks at lr 0.01)']}
key_findings: MTAN outperforms all multi-task baselines with far fewer parameters: on CityScapes 7-class it attains 53.86 mIoU / 91.10 Pix Acc (Uncertainty Weights) and 0.0144 Abs Err with 1.65× parameters, versus Dense 51.91 mIoU / 51.89 with 3.63× and Cross-Stitch 50.31 with ~2×; on NYUv2 it attains 17.72 mIoU / 55.61 Pix Acc / 0.5906 Abs Err / 31.44 Mean angle with 1.77× parameters, the best across all architectures and weightings.; DWA is simple (uses only loss values) and competitive with Uncertainty Weights while outperforming Equal Weights, confirming that considering loss descent rate stabilizes multi-task training.; MTAN is markedly more robust to weighting choice than Cross-Stitch: validation curves for three NYUv2 tasks show near-identical trajectories across Equal/ Uncertainty / DWA for MTAN, whereas Cross-Stitch diverges strongly, indicating attention-based feature selection inherently balances tasks.; Task complexity scaling on CityScapes (2/7/19 classes) shows single-task STAN slightly beats multi-task methods for simple 2-class segmentation, but multi-task gain grows with complexity and MTAN’s gain grows fastest, demonstrating efficient shared feature reuse.; Attention masks are interpretable feature selectors: first-layer visualizations show semantic and depth masks differ clearly, depth masks exhibit higher contrast indicating more task-specific filtering, while semantic masks use most shared features.; On Visual Decathlon (10 tasks), MTAN with 1.74× parameters achieves 77.25 mean accuracy and 2941 score, surpassing Scratch (70.32/1625), Residual Adapters (73.88/2118), Piggyback (76.60/2838), and competitive with state-of-the-art Parallel SVD (78.36/3398) and DAN (77.01/2851) without complex regularization like dropout per task.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Evaluated only on vision tasks: dense outdoor (CityScapes) and indoor (NYUv2) prediction plus 10 classification domains, all with resized inputs (128x256, 288x384, 72x72 for Decathlon) and not on NLP, speech, or RL multi-task settings.', 'Restricted architecture to feed-forward encoder-decoder (SegNet/VGG-16) and WRN-28-4, with attention attention masks fixed to 1×1 convolutions plus sigmoid, and DWA temperature empirically fixed at T=2.', 'Fixed optimization settings per benchmark (Adam 1e-4 for dense tasks, SGD 0.1 for Decathlon) and compared only three weighting schemes per architecture, excluding GradNorm which requires manual subset of shared weights.', 'Set number of tasks K to 2 (CityScapes) or 3 (NYUv2) or 10 (Decathlon) with predefined label granularities (2/7/19 classes) and did not test continual addition of tasks beyond 10.']
limitations_summary: No explicit limitations section is provided. Implicit limitations include absence of discussion of failure modes or negative transfer when tasks are unrelated, reliance on empirically chosen DWA temperature T=2, increased but unquantified attention-module training cost, and no statistical significance testing for reported gains.
generalizability_gap: MTAN was not tested outside computer vision (no NLP, code-switching, speech, or cross-modal multi-task), not on transformer or non-convolutional backbones, and not under explicit noisy, low-resource, or code-switched user-generated text conditions relevant to the broader MTL literature in this repository.
methodological_gap: DWA uses only prior-epoch loss ratios and ignores gradient magnitudes, task curvature, or performance metrics, so it cannot detect gradient conflict or plateauing; attention modules add task-specific 1×1 convolutions per layer that still scale linearly with tasks, and evaluation does not include gradient conflict analysis or ablation of mask sparsity.
future_work: Applying MTAN and DWA to transformer-based or large-scale foundation multi-task settings and to NLP/code-switched domains.; Investigating adaptive or learned DWA temperature schedules and gradient-aware extensions that combine loss descent rate with gradient statistics.; Analyzing attention mask sparsity and explicit feature-sharing patterns to guide task grouping and mitigate negative transfer.
