title: Evaluating Urgency of Typhoon-Related Tweets Through Sentiment Analysis Using Artificial Neural Networks
authors: Ronnel P. Ermino; Ray Carlo A. Abacan; Nadine Gweneth C. Diamante; Kristine Marie N. Faca; Thatiana Erica D. Juntereal
venue: International Journal of Computing Sciences Research
domain: Crisis informatics and disaster management in the Philippines, focusing on social media NLP (Twitter) in English, Tagalog, and bilingual English-Tagalog (Taglish).
problem_statement: Evaluating the urgency of disaster- and typhoon-related tweets in the Philippines to rapidly identify urgent distress and rescue calls from social media data during and after natural calamities, addressing the operational gap between public social media usage and government emergency response workflows.
theoretical_framework: Supervised sentiment analysis and crisis communication modeling using a feed-forward artificial neural network to estimate tweet urgency on a continuous scale.
methodology: A supervised feed-forward artificial neural network (ANN) constructed in Python with TensorFlow. The NLP pipeline involves data collection via Tweepy/Twitter API, text preprocessing (deduplication, lowercasing, non-alphanumeric character removal, tokenization, sequence conversion, and padding to 140 words), an Embedding layer (8,000 vocabulary size, 8 embedding dimensions), a Global Average Pooling 1D layer, a Dense hidden layer (24 units with ReLU activation), and a Dense output layer (1 unit with Sigmoid activation) trained with Binary Cross-Entropy loss.
datasets: 4,020 labeled Typhoon Ulysses (Vamco) tweets (2,010 urgent, 2,010 non-urgent) collected from November 8 to November 16, 2020 in English, Tagalog, and Taglish, partitioned into 3,900 training tweets and 120 validation tweets; A separate validation dataset of 100 disaster-related tweets (43 urgent, 57 non-urgent) for confusion matrix analysis
evaluation: {'training_metrics': {'accuracy': 0.9987, 'binary_cross_entropy_loss': 0.0074}, 'simultaneous_validation_metrics': {'dataset_size': 120, 'accuracy': 0.9917, 'binary_cross_entropy_loss': 0.068}, 'confusion_matrix_validation_metrics': {'dataset_size': 100, 'true_positives': 42, 'true_negatives': 57, 'false_positives': 0, 'false_negatives': 1, 'accuracy': 0.99, 'sensitivity_recall': 0.9767, 'specificity': 1.0, 'precision_positive_predictive_value': 1.0, 'negative_predictive_value': 0.9828, 'false_positive_rate': 0.0, 'false_discovery_rate': 0.0, 'false_negative_rate': 0.0233, 'f1_score': 0.9882}}
key_findings: The feed-forward artificial neural network achieved 99.87% accuracy and 0.0074 loss on training, and 99.17% accuracy and 0.0680 loss on simultaneous validation.; Confusion matrix analysis on a separate 100-tweet validation dataset demonstrated 99% accuracy, 97.67% sensitivity, 100% specificity, 100% precision, 98.28% negative predictive value, and a 98.82% F1 score, with zero false positives and one false negative.; The lightweight architecture with an 8-dimensional embedding layer and global average pooling outperformed prior recurrent neural network baselines (86.99% for standard RNN and 87.6% for bidirectional RNN) on disaster tweet sentiment evaluation.; Continuous urgency scoring via sigmoid activation effectively differentiated high-urgency rescue requests from lower-urgency calamity posts such as donation drives.; The model was successfully exported to Protobuf (.pb), HDF5 (.h5), and JSON formats, enabling lightweight cross-platform deployment across Python and JavaScript/Node.js web applications via TensorFlow.js.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Restricted data collection exclusively to tweets regarding Typhoon Ulysses (Vamco) between November 8 and November 16, 2020.', 'Delimited languages to English, Tagalog, and bilingual Taglish.', 'Fixed maximum tweet sequence length to 140 words and vocabulary size to 8,000 words.', 'Constrained urgency evaluation to binary supervision (urgent vs. non-urgent) mapped to a continuous 0 to 1 score.', 'Delimited model architecture to a feed-forward ANN with 8-dimensional embeddings, global average pooling, and one 24-unit ReLU dense layer, excluding recurrent or transformer models.']
limitations_summary: The model utilizes a small, fixed vocabulary of 8,000 words and was trained on a dataset limited to a single typhoon event (Typhoon Ulysses) in English and Tagalog, which restricts vocabulary coverage, handling of regional Philippine dialects, and out-of-vocabulary terms in unseen disaster scenarios.
limitations_verbatim: Even though the researchers were able to reach a high accuracy using the model and the preprocessed dataset but it is still recommended for future researchers to expand the vocabulary of the embedding layer by adding more diverse data to the dataset, even more so if the model will process multilingual inputs.
generalizability_gap: The dataset and evaluation are restricted exclusively to a single typhoon event (Typhoon Ulysses) in the Philippines in November 2020 and limited to English and Tagalog text; generalizability across other natural disaster types (e.g., earthquakes, volcanic eruptions), different typhoon events, other Philippine regional languages (e.g., Cebuano, Ilocano, Waray), and international crisis settings has not been established.
methodological_gap: The study evaluated model performance on relatively small validation sets (120 simultaneous validation tweets and 100 test tweets) without k-fold cross-validation, out-of-domain testing, or ablation analysis. The model uses static 8-dimensional token embeddings and global average pooling rather than contextual language representations (e.g., RoBERTa or multilingual transformer encoders), and does not leverage metadata (timestamps, retweets, user credibility) or multimodal features (images and videos).
future_work: Expanding the embedding layer vocabulary and training dataset by collecting more diverse and multilingual disaster data.; Integrating the urgency evaluation model into live disaster incident reporting systems for government agencies and non-governmental organizations.; Implementing real-time tweet stream processing using JavaScript, Node.js, and TensorFlow.js with the exported JSON model format.; Developing Python-based emergency management and rescue applications utilizing the Protobuf (.pb) and HDF5 (.h5) model exports.

title: Examining Common Paradigms in Multi-Task Learning
authors: Cathrin Elich; Lukas Kirchdorfer; Jan M. Köhler; Lukas Schott
venue: DAGM German Conference on Pattern Recognition (GCPR 2024)
domain: Multi-Task Learning and Deep Computer Vision (Dense Prediction and Facial Attribute Recognition)
problem_statement: Despite widespread interest in multi-task learning (MTL), its underlying optimization mechanisms remain poorly understood, and complex multi-task optimization methods often fail to consistently outperform single-task learning (STL) or simple loss weighting baselines. In particular, the influence of standard optimizers (such as Adam versus SGD) and the foundational premise that gradient alignment conflicts represent a challenge unique to MTL remain insufficiently examined.
theoretical_framework: Multi-task optimization dynamics and loss-scale invariance theory. The authors mathematically prove that uncertainty weighting (UW) achieves full loss-scale invariance across all network parameters under optimal analytical sigma values, and that the Adam optimizer achieves partial loss-scale invariance for task-specific head parameters because loss scaling factors cancel out between the first and second moment updates.
methodology: The authors perform theoretical derivations and extensive empirical evaluations across three computer vision datasets (Cityscapes, NYUv2, and CelebA) using hard parameter sharing networks (SegNet, DeepLabV3+, and ResNet-18). The study compares Adam against SGD with momentum across ten initial learning rates and nine multi-task optimization methods (EW, UW, RLW, PCGrad, CAGrad, IMTL, Aligned-MTL, MTL-IO, and AdaTask); proves and empirically validates loss-scale invariance properties in controlled toy experiments; measures cosine similarity, magnitude similarity, and conflict ratios between inter-task and inter-sample gradients; and evaluates out-of-distribution robustness against 15 corruption types across five severity levels.
datasets: Cityscapes (urban street scenes dataset with 2,975 training, 595 validation, and 500 test images for 7-class semantic segmentation and depth estimation); NYUv2 (indoor scene understanding dataset with 636 training, 159 validation, and 654 test images for 13-class semantic segmentation, depth estimation, and surface normal prediction); CelebA (200,000 celebrity face images split into 162,770 training, 19,867 validation, and 19,962 test images annotated with 40 binary attribute classification tasks); Synthetic Two-Task Depth Regression Dataset (toy dataset evaluating loss-scale invariance with scaled L1 losses); Toy 2D Optimization Landscape (optimization benchmark from CAGrad)
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Delta_m metric (average relative task performance drop compared to single-task baselines)', 'Mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) and pixel accuracy (%) for semantic segmentation', 'Absolute error, relative error, and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) for depth estimation', 'Mean error, median error, and percentage of pixels within angle thresholds (<11.25 deg, <22.5 deg, <30 deg) for surface normal estimation', 'Mean classification error (%) across 40 attribute binary classification tasks on CelebA', 'Gradient cosine similarity (S_cos), gradient magnitude similarity (S_mag), and ratio of conflicting gradient parameters', 'Delta^t metric measuring relative performance drop on corrupted test data across 15 corruption types and 5 severity levels', 'Maximum iteration steps to reach the global minimum in toy optimization'], 'baselines': ['Equal Weighting (EW / Unitary Scalarization)', 'Uncertainty Weighting (UW / Kendall et al., 2018)', 'Optimal Uncertainty Weighting (UW-O / Kirchdorfer et al., 2024)', 'Random Loss Weighting (RLW)', 'Projecting Conflicting Gradients (PCGrad)', 'Conflict-Averse Gradient Descent (CAGrad)', 'Impartial Multi-Task Learning (IMTL)', 'Independent Component Alignment (Aligned-MTL)', 'Multi-Task Independent Optimizers (MTL-IO)', 'Task-Aware Adaptive Learning Rate (AdaTask)', 'Single-Task Learning (STL) baselines', 'signSGD with momentum'], 'architectures': ['SegNet encoder-decoder architecture with task-specific decoders', 'DeepLabV3+ encoder-decoder architecture with atrous separable convolutions', 'ResNet-18 shared backbone with 40 task-specific linear heads', '2-layer MLP shared backbone with 2-layer task-specific heads (toy experiments)']}
key_findings: The choice of standard optimizer is a critical confounder in multi-task learning; Adam consistently outperforms SGD with momentum across all tested datasets, network architectures, and multi-task optimization methods.; The Adam optimizer achieves partial loss-scale invariance for task-specific head parameters because loss scaling factors cancel out between the first and second moment updates, enabling head parameter updates to proceed independently of task loss scales.; Optimal uncertainty weighting (UW-O) achieves full loss-scale invariance across both the shared backbone and task heads under mild analytical assumptions.; Equal Weighting (EW) trained with Adam achieves Pareto optimal performance in three out of four vision benchmark setups and is not dominated by any specialized MTO method trained with SGD with momentum.; Angular gradient alignment conflicts (negative cosine similarity) are not unique to multi-task learning; gradient direction conflicts between different samples within a single task occur with equal or greater frequency compared to conflicts between distinct tasks.; Disparities in gradient magnitudes across tasks constitute the primary optimization challenge distinguishing MTL from STL, validating gradient magnitude balancing methods while showing that vector alignment modifications are often superfluous.; Multi-task representations do not provide universal or consistent improvements in out-of-distribution corruption robustness; robustness gains depend strongly on the specific combination of task, corruption mode, network architecture, and dataset.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Focused exclusively on supervised multi-task computer vision problems involving single-input, multi-output dense prediction and classification tasks.', 'Delimited architectural exploration to hard parameter sharing models (SegNet, DeepLabV3+, ResNet-18) without evaluating soft parameter sharing or branched networks.', 'Maintained a fixed weight decay of 10^-5 across Cityscapes and NYUv2 experiments based on initial parameter sensitivity analyses.', 'Subsampled eight random samples or tasks per training step to compute gradient similarity statistics due to computational constraints.']
limitations_summary: The authors acknowledge that the theoretical loss-scale invariance of Adam applies strictly to constant loss weightings and does not hold completely for dynamic loss weights due to the accumulation of gradient histories. Additionally, gradient comparisons between samples and tasks rely on indirect approximations from subsampled batches, and the mechanisms governing task-specific capacity allocation relative to task-specific learning rates remain insufficiently disentangled.
limitations_verbatim: We would like to note that our derivation for Adam is only valid for constant αt, e.g., measuring depth in different units or unitary weightings [\[25,](#page-14-1) [50\]](#page-15-1). In case of dynamic loss weights that are not constant (e.g., UW), the weights do not cancel out fully due to the accumulation of gradient histories within Adam.
generalizability_gap: The empirical evaluations are confined to supervised computer vision benchmarks (Cityscapes, NYUv2, and CelebA); the authors did not examine multi-task learning dynamics in natural language processing, reinforcement learning, speech recognition, or multi-modal domains.
methodological_gap: Gradient similarity metrics were evaluated by subsampling eight samples or tasks per training step rather than computing full-dataset pairwise gradient distributions; furthermore, the mathematical loss-scale invariance proof for Adam assumes a fixed backbone, leaving dynamic interactions between shared backbone parameters and adaptive moments unmodeled.
future_work: Investigating task-specific and sample-specific capacity allocation within shared backbones and disentangling the interaction between task loss weights and task-specific learning rates.; Applying gradient alignment and conflict resolution methods to intra-task sample-level gradient conflicts in single-task learning settings.; Developing computationally efficient implementations of task-specific adaptive optimizers (such as independent Adam optimizers per task) to scale across large task counts.; Exploring systematic underlying patterns and architectural factors that determine when multi-task learning representations improve out-of-distribution corruption robustness.

title: FAMO: Fast Adaptive Multitask Optimization
authors: Bo Liu; Yihao Feng; Peter Stone; Qiang Liu
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
domain: Multi-Task Learning — multi-task supervised vision (NYU-v2, CityScapes, CelebA), molecular property prediction on graph neural networks (QM-9), and multi-task reinforcement learning (Meta-World MT10)
problem_statement: Optimizing the average loss in multi-task learning frequently causes severe under-optimization of certain tasks due to generalized conflicting gradients, while existing gradient manipulation methods require storing and computing all task gradients at each step, incurring prohibitive O(k) space and time complexities for large models and many-task settings.
theoretical_framework: Multi-objective optimization and multiple gradient descent algorithm (MGDA) formulated over task log-loss improvement rates. FAMO maximizes the worst-case instantaneous task loss improvement rate max_{d_t} min_{i} (1/alpha * r_i(alpha, d_t) - 1/2 ||d_t||^2), whose dual problem minimizes 1/2 ||J_t z||^2 over the probability simplex S^k. When the optimal combination weights z* form an interior point, all tasks achieve equal instantaneous loss improvement rates. Continuous-time dynamical system analysis demonstrates that stationary points of FAMO correspond to the minima of the sum of log losses sum_{i=1}^k log l_i(theta).
methodology: Fast Adaptive Multitask Optimization (FAMO) amortizes the dual optimization across training iterations by performing a single-step gradient descent update on unconstrained task weighting logits xi_t in R^k, where combination weights follow z_t = Softmax(xi_t). The algorithm approximates the gradient of the dual objective without computing individual task gradients by utilizing temporal differences of log losses: delta_t = [nabla^T z_1(xi_t), ..., nabla^T z_k(xi_t)]^T [log l_{1,t} - log l_{1,t+1}, ..., log l_{k,t} - log l_{k,t+1}]^T. Model parameters are updated via theta_{t+1} = theta_t - alpha sum_{i=1}^k (c_t z_{i,t} / l_{i,t}) nabla l_{i,t} through a single backward pass of the weighted loss using re-normalization constant c_t = (sum_{i=1}^k z_{i,t} / l_{i,t})^{-1}. An L2 regularization decay term gamma stabilizes logit updates as an exponential moving average: xi_{t+1} = xi_t - beta (delta_t + gamma xi_t), achieving O(1) space and time complexity per iteration.
datasets: Synthetic 2D two-task optimization problem with five initial parameter points; NYU-v2 — indoor scene dataset comprising 1,449 RGBD images evaluated on 13-class semantic segmentation, depth estimation, and surface normal prediction; CityScapes — urban street-view dataset comprising 5,000 RGBD images evaluated on 7-class semantic segmentation and depth estimation; QM-9 — molecular graph dataset of over 130,000 molecules (110,000 train, 10,000 validation, 10,000 test) evaluated on 11 quantum chemical property regression tasks; CelebA — facial attribute dataset comprising 200,000 images of 10,000 celebrities evaluated on 40 binary facial attribute classification tasks; Meta-World MT10 — multi-task robotic manipulation benchmark comprising 10 distinct manipulation tasks
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Synthetic: 2D loss trajectories, runtime for 50,000 optimization steps, and Pareto front convergence', 'NYU-v2: Mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) and Pixel Accuracy for semantic segmentation; Absolute Error and Relative Error for depth estimation; Mean angle distance, Median angle distance, and percentage within 11.25°, 22.5°, and 30° thresholds for surface normals; Mean Rank (MR); average per-task performance drop Delta_m% relative to Single-Task Learning (STL)', 'QM-9: Mean Absolute Error (MAE) across 11 molecular properties (mu, alpha, HOMO, LUMO, <R^2>, ZPVE, U, U0, H, G, Cv), Mean Rank (MR), and Delta_m%', 'CityScapes: mIoU and Pixel Accuracy for semantic segmentation, Absolute Error and Relative Error for depth estimation, Mean Rank (MR), and Delta_m%', 'CelebA: Mean classification error across 40 facial attributes, Mean Rank (MR), and Delta_m%', 'Meta-World MT10: Mean task success rate ± standard error of the mean over 10 random seeds', 'Computational efficiency: Relative training time per epoch normalized to Linear Scalarization (LS)'], 'baselines': ['Single-Task Learning (STL)', 'Linear Scalarization (LS / Uniform Average Gradient)', 'Scale-Invariant Baseline (SI / Sum of Log Losses)', 'Dynamic Weight Average (DWA)', 'Uncertainty Weighting (UW)', 'Random Loss Weighting (RLW)', 'Multiple Gradient Descent Algorithm (MGDA)', 'Projecting Conflicting Gradients (PCGrad)', 'GradDrop', 'Conflict-Averse Gradient Descent (CAGrad)', 'IMTL-G', 'Nash-MTL', 'Soft Modularization (Meta-World)'], 'architectures': ['Multi-Task Attention Network (MTAN with SegNet backbone) for NYU-v2 and CityScapes', 'SchNet graph neural network for QM-9 molecular property prediction', 'ResNet-18 backbone for CelebA 40-task attribute classification', 'Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) multi-layer perceptron actor-critic network for Meta-World MT10']}
key_findings: FAMO optimizes multi-task models by decreasing task losses at approximately equal rates using only O(1) space and time per iteration, matching the computational efficiency of standard Adam on the average loss.; On the 2D synthetic benchmark, FAMO resolves conflicting gradients and reaches the Pareto front across all five initializations while training 25 times faster than Nash-MTL.; On NYU-v2 (three tasks) across three random seeds, FAMO achieves Delta_m% = -4.10% and Mean Rank 3.44, outperforming Nash-MTL (-4.04%, MR 2.11), IMTL-G (-0.76%), CAGrad (0.20%), PCGrad (3.97%), and Linear Scalarization (5.59%).; On QM-9 (11 molecular property tasks) across three random seeds, FAMO achieves the best overall Delta_m% = 58.5% and Mean Rank 3.27, outperforming Nash-MTL (62.0%, MR 2.09), IMTL-G (77.2%), Scale-Invariant baseline (77.8%), CAGrad (112.8%), and Linear Scalarization (177.6%).; On CelebA (40 tasks) across three random seeds, FAMO achieves Delta_m% = 4.72% and Mean Rank 1.21, outperforming Nash-MTL (4.97%), CAGrad (6.20%), PCGrad (6.65%), and Linear Scalarization (6.28%), while eliminating the prohibitive O(k) memory overhead of gradient manipulation methods.; On CityScapes (two tasks), FAMO achieves Delta_m% = 8.13% with gamma = 0.01, outperforming CAGrad (11.64%), PCGrad (18.29%), and Linear Scalarization (14.11%).; On the Meta-World MT10 robotic manipulation benchmark over 10 random seeds, FAMO achieves an average success rate of 0.83 ± 0.05, matching CAGrad (0.83 ± 0.05) and exceeding PCGrad (0.72 ± 0.02), Soft Modularization (0.73 ± 0.04), Uncertainty Weighting (0.77 ± 0.05), and shared-model SAC (0.49 ± 0.07).; Training runtime benchmarks demonstrate that FAMO introduces negligible time overhead relative to Linear Scalarization across all task scales, whereas existing gradient manipulation methods scale linearly with the number of tasks k.
scope_and_delimitations: ['FAMO assumes a shared-parameter multi-task setting where a single input batch allows simultaneous computation of all task losses in a single forward pass.', 'The method requires smooth non-negative task losses (l_i(theta) >= 0) bounded away from zero by adding a small constant (1e-8) or shifting by known loss lower bounds.', 'The regularization hyperparameter gamma requires selection from a discrete set {0.0001, 0.001, 0.01} based on validation performance (gamma = 0.01 for CityScapes and gamma = 0.001 for other benchmarks).', 'The empirical evaluation covers vision, molecular property graphs, and robotic control benchmarks, without evaluating natural language understanding, machine translation, or transformer-based large language models.']
limitations_summary: The authors acknowledge that FAMO depends on the regularization hyperparameter gamma to stabilize the stochastic updates of the task weighting logits, which currently requires manual hyperparameter tuning. In addition, FAMO assumes that temporal loss differences accurately approximate directional derivatives, which requires small learning rates and smooth loss functions, and can become sensitive when task losses approach zero.
limitations_verbatim: One limitation of FAMO is its dependency on the regularization parameter γ, which is introduced due to the stochastic update of the task weighting logits w. Future work can investigate a more principled way of determining γ.
generalizability_gap: The authors did not evaluate FAMO on natural language processing tasks, code-switched or multilingual NLP benchmarks, transformer language models, or multimodal foundation models; furthermore, the method was not evaluated in multi-task scenarios where tasks have unaligned data sources requiring separate forward passes.
methodological_gap: FAMO relies on a first-order Taylor approximation of temporal loss differences to approximate gradient inner products, which can introduce estimation errors under large learning rates or high-variance mini-batch stochasticity. In addition, the regularization decay coefficient gamma must be manually tuned per dataset rather than scheduled dynamically.
future_work: Developing principled and automated methods to dynamically determine or adapt the regularization hyperparameter gamma.; Evaluating FAMO on large language models, multilingual language benchmarks, and multimodal vision-language representations.; Extending FAMO to multi-task learning settings with disjoint datasets that cannot be evaluated in a single forward pass.; Designing adaptive learning rate mechanisms for task weighting logit updates.

title: GLUE: A Multi-Task Benchmark and Analysis Platform for Natural Language Understanding
authors: Alex Wang; Amanpreet Singh; Julian Michael; Felix Hill; Omer Levy; Samuel R. Bowman
venue: Proceedings of the 7th International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2019)
domain: Natural Language Understanding (NLU), Multi-Task Learning, Transfer Learning, Sentence Representation Evaluation across Diverse Linguistic Phenomena and Genres (English)
problem_statement: Most natural language understanding models above the word level are engineered for isolated tasks and struggle with out-of-domain generalization; existing evaluation platforms focus narrowly on sentence-to-vector encoders and sentiment-heavy datasets, lacking a model-agnostic multi-task benchmark with private test data and diagnostic probing tools to measure general, robust linguistic understanding.
theoretical_framework: Multi-task and transfer representation learning in NLP; sentence-level semantic compositionality; formal linguistic semantics and natural logic (factivity, intersectivity, monotonicity, quantification, and syntactic alternations for diagnostic probing).
methodology: The authors introduce the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark, consisting of: (1) A suite of nine English sentence understanding tasks spanning single-sentence classification (CoLA, SST-2), similarity/paraphrase identification (MRPC, QQP, STS-B), and natural language inference / textual entailment (MNLI, QNLI, RTE, WNLI); (2) An online evaluation platform with an automated scoring service and public leaderboard based primarily on privately-held test sets to prevent data snooping and ensure fair comparisons; (3) An expert-constructed diagnostic evaluation dataset containing 550 naturally-occurring sentence pairs (1,100 directed inference examples) tagged across four coarse categories (Lexical Semantics, Predicate-Argument Structure, Logic, and Knowledge) and over thirty fine-grained phenomena to probe model reasoning mechanisms and error modes; and (4) Baseline empirical experiments comparing multi-task models against separate single-task models and pre-trained sentence representation encoders (CBoW, Skip-Thought, InferSent, DisSent, GenSen, and ELMo/CoVe augmented BiLSTMs with and without cross-sentence attention).
datasets: CoLA (Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability): 8.5k train, 1k dev, 1k test sentences for grammatical acceptability judgments from linguistics literature.; SST-2 (Stanford Sentiment Treebank): 67k train, 872 dev, 1.8k test movie review sentences for binary positive/negative sentiment classification.; MRPC (Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus): 3.7k train, 408 dev, 1.7k test news sentence pairs for semantic equivalence.; QQP (Quora Question Pairs): 364k train, 40k dev, 391k test question pairs from Quora for semantic duplicate detection.; STS-B (Semantic Textual Similarity Benchmark): 5.7k train, 1.5k dev, 1.4k test sentence pairs drawn from news, captions, and NLI data with similarity scores from 1 to 5.; MNLI (Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference Corpus): 393k train, 20k dev, 20k test sentence pairs across 10 genres for 3-class textual entailment, augmented optionally with 550k SNLI examples.; QNLI (Question-answering NLI converted from SQuAD): 105k train, 5.5k dev, 5.5k test question-context sentence pairs for binary entailment.; RTE (Recognizing Textual Entailment): 2.5k train, 276 dev, 3k test sentence pairs combining RTE1, RTE2, RTE3, and RTE5 for binary entailment.; WNLI (Winograd NLI converted from Winograd Schema Challenge): 634 train, 71 dev, 146 test sentence pairs for pronoun coreference resolution.; Diagnostic Dataset: 550 naturally-occurring sentence pairs (1,100 directed inference examples) annotated across 4 coarse and 30+ fine-grained linguistic phenomena.
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Accuracy for SST-2, QNLI, RTE, and WNLI', 'Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) for CoLA', 'Average of Accuracy and F1 Score for MRPC and QQP', 'Average of Pearson and Spearman Correlation Coefficients for STS-B', 'Accuracy across Matched (in-domain) and Mismatched (cross-domain) test sets for MNLI', 'Macro-Average Score across all nine benchmark tasks for leaderboard ranking', 'R3 three-class correlation coefficient for the Diagnostic Dataset'], 'baseline_performance': ['Multi-task BiLSTM + ELMo + Attention achieves highest overall GLUE score (70.0 macro-average) vs. single-task counterpart (67.4).', 'Pre-trained sentence encoders achieve lower overall scores: CBoW (58.9), Skip-Thought (61.5), InferSent (65.6), DisSent (62.2), GenSen (66.5).', 'Baseline models perform poorly on WNLI (all models score at or below most-frequent class baseline of 65.1%) and RTE (best model scores 61.7%).', 'On diagnostic evaluation, best model achieves an R3 of only 0.28 (human baseline reaches 0.80 with Fleiss kappa of 0.73), exhibiting severe drops on Logic and downward monotonicity.']}
key_findings: Multi-task training across GLUE tasks consistently outperforms training separate single-task models when incorporating attention mechanisms or pre-trained ELMo representations.; Contextualized word representations from ELMo significantly improve performance over static GloVe and translation-derived CoVe embeddings, especially on single-sentence tasks.; Pre-trained sentence representation models (CBoW, Skip-Thought, InferSent, GenSen) lag behind multi-task models directly trained on the benchmark, particularly on grammatical acceptability (CoLA).; Current models struggle substantially with low-resource and complex inference tasks, failing to exceed the majority-class baseline on WNLI (65.1%) and obtaining low accuracy on RTE.; Diagnostic probing reveals that baseline NLU models exploit shallow lexical heuristics (such as quantifier keywords and subsequence overlap) rather than true compositional reasoning, failing severely on downward monotonicity, double negation, and restrictivity.; Multi-task models underperform single-task models on the diagnostic MNLI evaluation (R3 score drops), indicating destructive task interference during joint training with uniform sampling.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Benchmark tasks are strictly delimited to English single-sentence and sentence-pair understanding tasks, excluding generation, token-level sequence labeling, and multi-turn dialogue.', 'Dataset formats are recast into classification or regression, eliminating token span extraction for question answering in QNLI and candidate pronoun selection in WNLI.', 'Evaluation is confined to sentence-level semantics and inference without testing long-document contexts or multimodal inputs.', 'Diagnostic suite is curated specifically for error analysis of NLI models rather than general downstream task evaluation.']
limitations_summary: The authors highlight several key limitations of the benchmark and evaluated baselines: (1) the diagnostic evaluation set is hand-crafted and not drawn from a natural input distribution, meaning diagnostic scores reflect qualitative error patterns rather than general downstream application performance; (2) simple multi-task training regimes suffer from destructive task interference, leading multi-task models to underperform single-task models on diagnostic NLI probing; (3) baseline sentence representation and multi-task models fail on challenging reasoning tasks like WNLI (unable to beat majority-class guessing) and struggle with complex logical structures like downward monotonicity and restrictivity; and (4) recasting tasks into sentence-pair classification introduces specific artifacts, such as adversarial dev sets in WNLI.
limitations_verbatim: The diagnostic examples are hand-picked to address certain phenomena, and NLI is a task with no natural input distribution, so we do not expect performance on the diagnostic set to reflect overall performance or generalization in downstream applications. Performance on the analysis set should be compared between models but not between categories. The set is provided not as a benchmark, but as an analysis tool for error analysis, qualitative model comparison, and development of adversarial examples.
generalizability_gap: The GLUE benchmark is restricted exclusively to English-language sentence-level understanding tasks, leaving unaddressed multilingual NLU, low-resource languages, code-switched text, long-form document comprehension, generative dialogue, and multi-modal grounding tasks.
methodological_gap: The baseline models rely on basic multi-task training with proportional task sampling and uniform loss aggregation without gradient conflict resolution (e.g., PCGrad, CAGrad) or adaptive routing, leading to negative transfer; additionally, the benchmark recasts token-level span extraction (SQuAD to QNLI) and pronoun selection (Winograd to WNLI) into sentence-pair classification, altering the native task mechanics and introducing dataset-specific artifacts.
future_work: Developing improved general NLU architectures capable of deep semantic and logical reasoning beyond surface-level lexical heuristics.; Exploring advanced multi-task training and optimization regimes to mitigate destructive task interference between heterogeneous objectives.; Extending diagnostic probing suites to evaluate additional fine-grained linguistic phenomena and broader task distributions.; Investigating methods that effectively transfer knowledge to low-resource and complex inference tasks like WNLI and RTE.
local_dir: GLUE - A Multi-Task Benchmark and Analysis Platform for Natural Language Understanding

title: GLUECoS: An Evaluation Benchmark for Code-Switched NLP
authors: Simran Khanuja; Sandipan Dandapat; Anirudh Srinivasan; Sunayana Sitaram; Monojit Choudhury
venue: Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL 2020)
domain: Multilingual Natural Language Processing (NLP), Code-Switching / Code-Mixing across English-Hindi (En-Hi; Roman and Devanagari scripts) and English-Spanish (En-Es; Roman script) from social media, chat, search queries, and conversational transcripts.
problem_statement: The lack of standardized datasets and comprehensive multi-task evaluation benchmarks for code-switched natural language processing, hindering rigorous comparison across different representation methods (cross-lingual embeddings vs. pre-trained multilingual language models) on varied linguistic tasks.
theoretical_framework: Linguistic theories of grammatical code-switching (including Equivalence Constraint and Switch Point Fraction for synthetic generation) alongside quantitative code-mixing metrics (Code-Mixing Index [CMI], Switch-Point Average [SP Avg], Multilingual Index [M-index], Probability of Switching [I-index], Burstiness, Language Entropy [LE], and Span Entropy [SE]).
methodology: The authors introduce GLUECoS, a standardized evaluation benchmark spanning six NLP tasks (Language Identification, Part-of-Speech Tagging, Named Entity Recognition, Sentiment Analysis, Question Answering, and a newly curated conversational Natural Language Inference task) across English-Hindi and English-Spanish. They standardize datasets into balanced 8:1:1 train:dev:test splits and evaluate five representation paradigms: (1) baseline monolingual word embeddings, (2) cross-lingual embeddings (unsupervised and supervised MUSE, BiCVM, BiSkip), (3) synthetic code-switched skip-gram embeddings (GCM), (4) pre-trained Multilingual BERT (mBERT), and (5) Modified mBERT fine-tuned via masked language modeling on a curriculum of synthetic code-switched data (gCM) followed by real code-switched data (rCM). Tasks are evaluated using task-specific architectures including BiLSTM-CRF for word-level sequence labeling, BiLSTM for sentence classification, and BiDAF/Transformers for QA and NLI.
datasets: FIRE 2013 (FIRE LID) - English-Hindi word-level Language Identification (Devanagari script; 3,537 sentences); EMNLP 2014 - English-Spanish word-level Language Identification (14,413 sentences); UD POS (Bhat et al., 2018) - English-Hindi Universal Dependency POS tagging (Devanagari script; 1,814 sentences); FG POS (ICON 2016 / Jamatia et al., 2016) - English-Hindi fine-grained POS tagging (Roman script; 2,631 sentences); Bangor Miami Corpus (Bangor POS) - English-Spanish POS tagging (2,758 sentences); IIITH NER (Singh et al., 2018) - English-Hindi Twitter Named Entity Recognition (Roman script; 3,084 sentences); CALCS 2018 (Aguilar et al., 2019) - English-Spanish Twitter Named Entity Recognition (34,208 sentences); SAIL 2017 (Patra et al., 2018) - English-Hindi social media Sentiment Analysis (Roman script; 12,601 sentences); Vilares et al. (2016) - English-Spanish Twitter Sentiment Analysis (2,103 sentences); Chandu et al. (2018a) / DrQA - English-Hindi Question Answering (313 question-answer-context triples); Khanuja et al. (2020) - English-Hindi Conversational Natural Language Inference (Roman script; 1,300 sentence pairs); Pre-training Corpora: IIT Bombay English-Hindi parallel corpus (10M GCM / 2M gCM), Twitter English-Spanish parallel corpus (4.5M), Pratapa et al. (2018a) English-Spanish synthetic corpus (8M), Chandu et al. (2018b) En-Hi real code-mixed corpus (93k), Rijhwani et al. (2017) En-Es real code-mixed corpus (93k)
evaluation: {'metrics': 'Token-level F1 for LID, NER, and Sentiment Analysis; F1 and Accuracy for POS tagging; F1 for QA; Accuracy for NLI', 'lid_performance': 'Modified mBERT achieves top performance (FIRE En-Hi F1: 96.60 vs mBERT 95.87, Sup MUSE 94.92; EMNLP En-Es F1: 96.24 vs mBERT 95.97, Sup MUSE 93.39)', 'pos_tagging_performance': 'Modified mBERT achieves top results among embedding methods (UD En-Hi F1: 88.06 vs mBERT 87.16, SOTA 90.53; Bangor En-Es F1: 93.62 vs mBERT 93.33, SOTA 95.39; FG En-Hi F1: 63.31 vs mBERT 63.42, SOTA 80.80)', 'ner_performance': 'Modified mBERT significantly outperforms baseline and cross-lingual models (IIITH En-Hi F1: 78.21 vs mBERT 74.96, baseline 71.52; CALCS En-Es F1: 61.77 vs mBERT 59.69, baseline 47.90)', 'sentiment_analysis_performance': 'Modified mBERT reaches highest F1 scores (SAIL En-Hi F1: 59.35 vs mBERT 58.24, baseline 50.44; En-Es Sentiment F1: 69.31 vs mBERT 66.03, baseline 50.62)', 'qa_and_nli_performance': 'mBERT achieves highest score on En-Hi QA (F1: 71.96 vs Modified mBERT 68.01, BiSkip 65.56); on Conversational NLI, Modified mBERT outperforms standard mBERT but both perform only slightly above chance'}
key_findings: Pre-trained multilingual contextual language models (mBERT) significantly outperform static cross-lingual word embedding techniques (MUSE, BiCVM, BiSkip) across all evaluated code-switching tasks and language pairs.; Fine-tuning mBERT on synthetically generated code-switched data (gCM) paired with a small portion (<5%) of real code-mixed text (rCM) on masked language modeling further improves downstream performance across most tasks.; Models consistently perform better on English-Spanish than English-Hindi, reflecting syntactic similarities between English and Spanish (word order preservation), the absence of script variation noise, and higher domain alignment in training data.; Word-level tasks like Language Identification (F1 > 96%) and POS tagging are relatively tractable, whereas semantic and discourse-level reasoning tasks (QA and NLI) remain far from solved, with NLI performance hovering near chance levels.; Static cross-lingual word embeddings underperform in code-switched contexts because bilingual lexicon induction objectives fail to model the non-linear semantic and distributional shifts characteristic of mixed discourse.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Restricted to two code-switched language pairs: English-Hindi (typologically distinct language family with script variation) and English-Spanish (typologically closer pair in Roman script).', 'Delimited to six specific NLP tasks: Language Identification (LID), Part-of-Speech (POS) Tagging, Named Entity Recognition (NER), Sentiment Analysis, Question Answering (QA), and Natural Language Inference (NLI).', 'Focuses strictly on textual modalities (social media, microblogs, chats, and Wikipedia text), excluding spoken code-switching.', 'Evaluates models in individual task setups rather than a joint multi-task learning architecture.', 'Employs synthetic code-switching generation using linguistic constraints (Switch Point Fraction) for pre-training, supplemented with less than 5% real code-switched data.']
limitations_summary: The authors acknowledge several major limitations: (1) direct comparison between cross-lingual word embeddings and mBERT is confounded by large differences in training data scale and pre-training domains (social media/query logs vs. Wikipedia dump); (2) performance on English-Hindi is hindered by non-standard Romanized spelling, transliterator errors, syntactic differences in word order, and generic pre-training data; (3) evaluation is conducted on single-task pipelines rather than a multi-task learning framework; and (4) performance on complex semantic reasoning tasks like NLI and Sentiment Analysis remains low, demonstrating that current models do not yet truly understand code-switched language.
limitations_verbatim:
The results using mBERT cannot be directly compared to the cross-lingual models because of the difference in the magnitude of data involved in training. Also, due to the fact that mBERT is trained on 104 languages together, with massive amounts of data for a large number of epochs, it learns several common features better providing for a well represented common embedding space. The training data used for training the cross-lingual embeddings is restricted to Twitter and query logs, while mBERT is trained on the entire wiki dump.

Overall, the cross-lingual and mBERT models perform better for *English-Spanish* as compared to *English-Hindi*. This could be due to several reasons.

- English and Spanish are similar languages, with both mostly retaining individual word order while code-switching, which is not the case for English and Hindi.
- Romanized Hindi does not use standardized spellings, and errors made by the transliterator could have influenced the results.
- We use Twitter and social media data to train cross lingual word embeddings for *English-Spanish* which are similar in domain to the task datasets, while we use the IITB and query-based parallel corpora for *English-Hindi* which is generic in domain, constrained by the available resources at hand.

We find that accuracies vary across tasks in the GLUECoS benchmark, and except in the case of LID, code-switched NLP is far from solved. This is particularly stark in the case of Sentiment and NLI, which are three and two way classification tasks respectively. Modified mBERT performs only a little over chance, which shows that we are still in the early days of solving NLI for code-switched languages, and also indicates that our models are far from truly being able to understand code-switched language.
generalizability_gap: The benchmark is limited to only two language pairs (English-Hindi and English-Spanish) in written social media and conversational domains. It leaves unexamined other code-switched language families (e.g., non-Indo-European pairs, low-resource African or Southeast Asian languages), spoken code-switching contexts, and domains beyond social media and chat.
methodological_gap: The benchmark evaluates models on isolated tasks using standard task-specific heads rather than utilizing a unified multi-task learning architecture to facilitate cross-task transfer for data-scarce code-switched tasks. Additionally, processing Romanized Hindi relies on external off-the-shelf transliteration and language identification tools rather than end-to-end normalization.
future_work: Implementing and benchmarking models in a multi-task learning setup to allow data-scarce code-switched tasks to benefit from resource-rich tasks.; Adding more diverse tasks and language pairs to subsequent versions of the GLUECoS benchmark.; Pre-training dedicated language models from scratch on code-switched and constituent monolingual corpora rather than solely fine-tuning pre-existing multilingual models.; Releasing the new code-switched conversational Natural Language Inference (NLI) dataset for broader research community use.
local_dir: GLUECoS - An Evaluation Benchmark for Code-Switched NLP

title: GradNorm: Gradient Normalization for Adaptive Loss Balancing in Deep Multitask Networks
authors: Zhao Chen; Vijay Badrinarayanan; Chen-Yu Lee; Andrew Rabinovich
venue: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)
domain: Computer Vision and Deep Multitask Learning
problem_statement: Deep multitask neural networks frequently suffer from poor training dynamics because different tasks exhibit disparate loss scales and learning speeds, which produces severe gradient magnitude imbalances across shared parameters and causes dominant tasks to suppress the learning of other tasks.
theoretical_framework: Multi-task optimization and gradient dynamics, based on the principle that optimal multi-task representation sharing requires balancing task learning rates by scaling gradient norms proportionally to relative inverse training speeds.
methodology: GradNorm dynamically balances multitask training by tuning task loss weights w_i(t) at each step to equalize task training rates. The algorithm measures the L2 gradient norm G_W^(i)(t) of each weighted task loss at the final shared layer W, determines target gradient norms G_W(t) * [r_i(t)]^alpha based on the average gradient norm across tasks and the relative inverse training rate r_i(t) = (L_i(t)/L_i(0)) / E[L_j(t)/L_j(0)], updates weights w_i(t) via gradient descent on an L1 loss L_grad between actual and target gradient norms, and renormalizes task weights to sum to the total number of tasks T.
datasets: Synthetic Multi-Task Regression Dataset (Toy 2-task and 10-task non-linear regression problems with varied task loss scales); NYUv2+seg (NYU Depth V2 dataset with 795 training and 654 test indoor images annotated for depth, surface normals, and 13-class semantic segmentation); NYUv2+kpts (Augmented NYU Depth V2 dataset with 90,000 indoor images annotated for depth, surface normals, and 48 room keypoint types); 9-task Facial Landmark Dataset (Supplementary multi-task facial benchmark)
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Task-normalized test-time loss (sum of test loss ratios relative to initial loss)', 'Root Mean Square Error (RMS in meters) for depth estimation', '100 - Mean Intersection over Union (100 - IoU) for semantic segmentation error', 'Cosine distance (1 - cos theta) for surface normal error', 'Percentage pixel error (%) for room keypoint layout prediction', 'L2 parameter distance to optimal static weights'], 'baselines': ['Single-task networks (dedicated single-task models)', 'Equal weights baseline (static w_i = 1 for all tasks)', 'GradNorm Static (static weights set to time-averaged weights from a dynamic GradNorm run)', 'Uncertainty weighting baseline (Kendall et al., 2017)', 'Exhaustive random grid search (100 multi-task networks trained with uniformly sampled weights)'], 'architectures': ['4-layer fully connected trunk for synthetic regression', 'VGG-16 SegNet encoder-decoder (29M parameters)', 'Modified thin ResNet-50 FCN (15M parameters)']}
key_findings: GradNorm improves multi-task test performance across regression and classification tasks, outperforming single-task models, equal weights baselines, and uncertainty weighting baselines.; On NYUv2+seg with a VGG-16 backbone, GradNorm with alpha = 1.5 achieves 0.925m depth RMS error, 67.8 segmentation error, and 0.174 normals error, surpassing the equal weights baseline (0.944m, 70.1, 0.192).; On NYUv2+kpts, GradNorm reduces depth error to 0.629m, keypoint error to 7.73%, and normals error to 0.139, outperforming both single-task networks and adaptive uncertainty weighting.; GradNorm provides effective regularization by preventing fast-learning tasks from overfitting, which allows tasks such as depth estimation to achieve lower test error despite converging to higher training loss.; A single GradNorm training run identifies task weights that match or surpass the performance of 100-run exhaustive grid searches, drastically reducing hyperparameter tuning computation.; The asymmetry hyperparameter alpha controls balancing intensity, where low values (e.g., alpha = 0.12) suit symmetric tasks and higher values (e.g., alpha = 1.5) effectively stabilize highly asymmetric multi-task learning dynamics.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Applied gradient normalization specifically to the final shared layer of weights W to restrict computational overhead to approximately 5%.', 'Constrained loss weighting to linear combinations of single-task losses subject to the normalization constraint sum(w_i(t)) = T.', 'Evaluated primarily on computer vision problems comprising simultaneous dense prediction tasks (depth, normals, segmentation, and keypoint heatmaps) with fixed input resolutions of 320x320 and output resolutions of 80x80.', 'Assumed model architectures with shared trunks and task-specific heads rather than branched or cross-talk architectures.']
limitations_summary: The authors acknowledge that no general scalar metric exists to evaluate multitask performance objectively across diverse task combinations with different loss scales. Additionally, GradNorm adds gradient compute overhead (~5%), relies on stable initial loss values L_i(0), and balances gradients only at a single shared layer.
limitations_verbatim: There unfortunately exists no general single scalar which gives a meaningful measure of multitask performance in all scenarios, but our toy problem was specifically designed with tasks which are statistically identical except for their loss scales σ i .
generalizability_gap: The proposed method was evaluated exclusively on computer vision datasets (NYUv2 and facial landmarks) and synthetic multi-output regressions; the authors did not test the algorithm on other machine learning domains such as natural language processing, speech synthesis, reinforcement learning, or multi-modal foundation models.
methodological_gap: GradNorm computes gradient norms solely at the final shared layer W rather than across intermediate backbone layers, which may not resolve gradient conflicts occurring in earlier shared layers; furthermore, the method requires an empirical hyperparameter alpha and depends on stable initial loss values L_i(0) to compute relative training rates.
future_work: Extending the GradNorm gradient balancing formulation to class-imbalanced classification problems.; Applying GradNorm to sequence-to-sequence models and language processing tasks with conflicting gradient updates.; Investigating gradient manipulation algorithms in other complex architectures and non-vision multi-objective learning settings.
local_dir: GradNorm - Gradient Normalization for Adaptive Loss Balancing in Deep Multitask Networks

title: Gradient Surgery for Multi-Task Learning
authors: Tianhe Yu; Saurabh Kumar; Abhishek Gupta; Sergey Levine; Karol Hausman; Chelsea Finn
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2020)
domain: Multi-Task Supervised Learning and Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning
problem_statement: Multi-task learning frequently suffers from severe optimization failures where joint training performs worse than independent single-task training because task gradients conflict with one another under high curvature and disparate gradient magnitudes.
theoretical_framework: Multi-objective optimization and gradient dynamics under the tragic triad condition, establishing convergence for convex Lipschitz objectives and proving local loss improvement conditions for orthogonal gradient projection.
methodology: Projecting Conflicting Gradients (PCGrad) deconflicts task gradients by projecting each task gradient onto the normal plane of any conflicting task gradient with negative cosine similarity. The algorithm computes gradients for each task minibatch, iterates through all other tasks in random order, subtracts the projected component along conflicting gradients, and sums the resulting modified gradients to update shared network parameters.
datasets: MultiMNIST (multi-task digit classification dataset); Cityscapes (urban scene understanding benchmark); CelebA (200,000 celebrity face images with 40 binary attribute classification tasks); Multi-task CIFAR-100 (20 coarse-class classification tasks with 2,500 training and 500 testing instances per task); NYUv2 (indoor scene understanding dataset with 13-class semantic segmentation, depth estimation, and surface normal prediction); Meta-World MT10 (robotic manipulation benchmark with 10 distinct manipulation tasks); Meta-World MT50 (robotic manipulation benchmark with 50 distinct manipulation tasks); Goal-conditioned RL environments (2D navigation and Fetch robotic manipulation domains)
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Top-1 classification accuracy (%) for Multi-task CIFAR-100', 'Average binary classification error (%) across 40 attribute tasks for CelebA', 'Mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) and pixel accuracy for NYUv2 semantic segmentation', 'Absolute error and relative error for NYUv2 depth estimation', 'Mean angle distance, median angle distance, and percentage of pixels within 11.25°, 22.5°, and 30° thresholds for NYUv2 surface normal prediction', 'Task success rate (%) and sample efficiency (million environment steps) for Meta-World MT10 and MT50 reinforcement learning benchmarks'], 'baselines': ['Vanilla multi-task gradient descent (equal loss weights with Adam or SGD)', 'Independent single-task learning models', 'Multi-Task Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) and Multi-Head SAC', 'Cross-Stitch Networks (Misra et al., 2016)', 'Routing Networks with Weak Positive Localization (Rosenbaum et al., 2018)', 'Multi-Task Attention Network (MTAN, Liu et al., 2018)', 'Uncertainty Weighting (Kendall et al., 2018)', 'Dynamic Weight Average (DWA, Liu et al., 2018)', 'Multiple-Gradient Descent Algorithm (MGDA, Sener & Koltun, 2018)', 'GradNorm (Chen et al., 2018)', 'Cosine Similarity Regularization (Suteu & Guo, 2019)'], 'architectures': ['Convolutional neural network trunk for CelebA multi-label classification', 'Routing network architecture with fully connected modules for CIFAR-100', 'Multi-Task Attention Network (MTAN) with SegNet backbone for NYUv2', 'Multi-layer perceptron actor and critic networks in Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) for Meta-World RL']}
key_findings: PCGrad significantly improves optimization stability, data efficiency, and asymptotic performance across multi-task supervised learning and reinforcement learning domains by eliminating destructive gradient interference.; On CIFAR-100 multi-task classification, PCGrad on a single network achieves 71.0% accuracy, surpassing independent training (67.7%) and cross-stitch networks (53.0%). Combining PCGrad with routing networks achieves 77.5% accuracy, which adds a 2.8% absolute gain over routing networks alone.; On the CelebA 40-task attribute prediction benchmark, PCGrad reduces average classification error to 8.69%, outperforming the multi-objective optimization baseline by Sener and Koltun (8.95%).; On the NYUv2 multi-task benchmark, combining MTAN with PCGrad achieves superior results across 8 out of 9 evaluation metrics across semantic segmentation (20.17 mIoU), depth estimation (0.5904 absolute error), and surface normal prediction.; On Meta-World MT10, PCGrad with SAC successfully solves all 10 robotic manipulation tasks (100% success rate) while saving 2 million environment samples compared to independent SAC models, whereas vanilla multi-task SAC fails to solve half of the tasks.; On Meta-World MT50, PCGrad with SAC learns approximately 70% of the 50 manipulation tasks, matching independent training while reducing sample requirements by 15 million environment transitions.; Ablation studies confirm that altering both gradient directions and gradient magnitudes is essential because altering only gradient directions or only gradient magnitudes degrades multi-task performance substantially.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Evaluates gradient projection on shared network parameters in multi-task supervised learning, multi-task reinforcement learning, and goal-conditioned reinforcement learning.', 'Requires individual per-task gradient computations for all tasks present within each training minibatch prior to applying gradient projection.', 'Implements pairwise sequential gradient projections using a randomized task ordering rather than computing simultaneous multi-gradient quadratic programming solutions.', 'Focuses on multi-task settings where task identity metadata or task conditioning vectors are available during training.']
limitations_summary: The theoretical convergence of PCGrad can stall or yield sub-optimal parameters if task gradients exhibit exact opposite alignment (cosine similarity of -1), which causes zero gradient updates. In addition, computing separate backward passes for every task in a minibatch introduces computational and memory overhead as the task count increases.
limitations_verbatim: A sub-optimal solution occurs when the cosine similarity between the gradients of the two tasks is exactly −1, i.e. the gradients directly conflict, leading to zero gradient after applying PCGrad. However, in practice, since we are using SGD, which is a noisy estimate of the true batch gradients, the cosine similarity between the gradients of two tasks in a minibatch is unlikely to be −1, thus avoiding this scenario. Note that, in theory, convergence may be slow if cos(φ12) hovers near −1.
generalizability_gap: The authors evaluated PCGrad on computer vision image datasets and simulated robotic manipulation benchmarks; the authors did not test the algorithm on large-scale natural language processing models, real-world physical robotic platforms, generative models, or multi-agent environments.
methodological_gap: PCGrad computes task projections sequentially based on a random task order rather than solving a joint multi-task optimization problem, which introduces order-dependent variance; furthermore, computing individual backward passes for each task scales computational complexity linearly with the number of tasks in each minibatch.
future_work: Applying PCGrad to meta-learning, continual lifelong learning, multi-goal imitation learning, and natural language processing tasks.; Extending gradient surgery principles to stabilize broader machine learning settings such as two-player games and multi-agent optimization.; Designing robust and safe multi-task reinforcement learning algorithms to mitigate unsafe exploration behaviors.; Developing self-supervised and unsupervised multi-task reinforcement learning methods to overcome reward specification challenges on physical robotic systems.

title: HumAID: Human-Annotated Disaster Incidents Data from Twitter with Deep Learning Benchmarks
authors: Firoj Alam; Umair Qazi; Muhammad Imran; Ferda Ofli
venue: Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media (ICWSM 2021)
domain: Crisis Informatics, Natural Language Processing, Disaster Response and Management, Social Media Text Classification
problem_statement: Social media streams generated during disaster events provide time-critical situational information for emergency response, but raw microblog posts contain high volumes of noise, redundancy, and irrelevant content. Existing crisis informatics datasets suffer from small event scales, exact and near-duplicate messages, lack of location-based filtering for impacted zones, and absent standardized test splits, which prevents researchers from rigorously training and benchmarking modern data-hungry deep learning models for humanitarian disaster management.
theoretical_framework: Crisis informatics taxonomy and humanitarian information requirements grounded in the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (UN OCHA) Multi-Cluster/Sector Initial Rapid Assessment (MIRA) framework, situational awareness theory in emergency response, and inter-coder reliability theory (Fleiss' kappa, Krippendorff's alpha, and majority agreement metrics).
methodology: The authors created a standardized data collection, filtering, crowdsourcing, and benchmarking pipeline comprising: (1) streaming keyword and hashtag data collection through the AIDR platform across 19 major disaster events (2016–2019) capturing 24,859,155 raw tweets; (2) a multi-stage filtering pipeline incorporating event date bounding, geographic filtering (prioritizing GPS coordinates, followed by place bounding boxes, and OpenStreetMap/Nominatim user profile geocoding), English language filtering, classifier-based pre-filtering with a Random Forest model (F1 = 76.9%) to prune non-humanitarian messages, minimum token length thresholds (greater than or equal to three words or hashtags), and cosine similarity de-duplication on uni-gram and bi-gram term-frequency vectors (threshold 0.75) reducing the collection to 337,082 candidate tweets; (3) class-balanced random sampling yielding 109,612 tweets for annotation; (4) crowdsourced Amazon Mechanical Turk annotation with 10-tweet qualification tests, embedded gold standard check tweets in 30-tweet HITs (requiring at least 70% accuracy), and a 66% inter-annotator consensus threshold across 11 humanitarian categories yielding 77,196 agreed labeled tweets; and (5) supervised multiclass classification benchmarking across event-level, event-type-level, and all-combined splits (70% train, 10% development, 20% test) comparing classical algorithms (Random Forest and Support Vector Machines with TF-IDF n-gram features) against deep learning architectures (fastText, BERT, DistilBERT, RoBERTa, and XLM-RoBERTa).
datasets: HumAID: 77,196 human-annotated English tweets (76,484 tweets utilized in benchmark classification tasks across 10 humanitarian categories after pruning low-prevalence classes with fewer than 15 samples) covering 19 natural disaster events across four disaster types (earthquakes, wildfires, floods, and hurricanes/cyclones) between 2016 and 2019; AIDR 24.8M Raw Disaster Tweet Stream: 24,859,155 raw tweets collected via Twitter Streaming API across 19 disaster events; Pre-trained fastText Common Crawl Word Embeddings; Pre-trained Transformer Checkpoints: BERT (bert-base-uncased), DistilBERT (distilbert-base-uncased), RoBERTa (roberta-base), and XLM-RoBERTa (xlm-roberta-base)
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Weighted Average Precision (P)', 'Weighted Average Recall (R)', 'Weighted Average F1-Measure (F1)', "Fleiss' Kappa (κ)", "Krippendorff's Alpha (K-α)", 'Average Observed Agreement (Avg obs.)', 'Average Majority Agreement (Maj agr.)'], 'inter_annotator_agreement': {'fleiss_kappa_mean': 0.55, 'krippendorff_alpha_mean': 0.57, 'average_observed_agreement_mean': 0.64, 'average_majority_agreement_mean': 0.83, 'range_observed_agreement': '55% to 83%'}, 'benchmark_results_weighted_f1_averages': {'RoBERTa (Best Overall)': 0.781, 'XLM-RoBERTa': 0.777, 'DistilBERT': 0.769, 'BERT': 0.768, 'fastText': 0.712, 'SVM': 0.71, 'Random_Forest': 0.7}, 'benchmark_results_by_event_type_weighted_f1': {'Earthquake (9 classes)': {'Random_Forest': 0.766, 'SVM': 0.783, 'fastText': 0.789, 'BERT': 0.833, 'DistilBERT': 0.839, 'RoBERTa': 0.836, 'XLM-RoBERTa': 0.837}, 'Fire (10 classes)': {'Random_Forest': 0.685, 'SVM': 0.717, 'fastText': 0.727, 'BERT': 0.771, 'DistilBERT': 0.771, 'RoBERTa': 0.787, 'XLM-RoBERTa': 0.779}, 'Flood (10 classes)': {'Random_Forest': 0.653, 'SVM': 0.693, 'fastText': 0.704, 'BERT': 0.749, 'DistilBERT': 0.734, 'RoBERTa': 0.758, 'XLM-RoBERTa': 0.755}, 'Hurricane (10 classes)': {'Random_Forest': 0.702, 'SVM': 0.716, 'fastText': 0.73, 'BERT': 0.74, 'DistilBERT': 0.742, 'RoBERTa': 0.741, 'XLM-RoBERTa': 0.739}, 'Combined_All (10 classes)': {'Random_Forest': 0.707, 'SVM': 0.731, 'fastText': 0.744, 'BERT': 0.758, 'DistilBERT': 0.758, 'RoBERTa': 0.76, 'XLM-RoBERTa': 0.758}}}
key_findings: Transformer-based pretrained language models consistently outperform classical machine learning algorithms (Random Forest and Support Vector Machines) and fastText across individual disaster events, disaster event types, and the combined dataset.; Monolingual RoBERTa achieved the highest overall average performance with a weighted F1-score of 0.781, outperforming XLM-RoBERTa (0.777), DistilBERT (0.769), BERT (0.768), fastText (0.712), SVM (0.710), and Random Forest (0.700).; DistilBERT achieved classification performance comparable to BERT (average weighted F1 of 0.769 compared to 0.768) while operating with substantially fewer parameters and lower computational overhead, establishing DistilBERT as an effective architecture for latency-sensitive operational deployment.; Monolingual pretraining in RoBERTa yielded higher performance on English disaster tweets than multilingual pretraining in XLM-RoBERTa, although XLM-RoBERTa demonstrated strong competitive capability across all disaster categories.; Support Vector Machines outperformed Random Forest across almost all event configurations (0.710 versus 0.700 average weighted F1), demonstrating competitive performance relative to fastText (0.712 weighted F1).; The systematic filtering pipeline (date boundaries, geographic resolution, relevance pre-filtering, token length pruning, and cosine similarity de-duplication) successfully eliminated redundant noise and out-of-area chatter from 24.8 million tweets, yielding moderate to substantial inter-annotator agreement (average Fleiss' kappa of 0.55, Krippendorff's alpha of 0.57, and majority agreement of 0.83).
scope_and_delimitations: ['The corpus is delimited strictly to English-language tweets collected from the Twitter streaming API via the AIDR platform.', 'The research scope is restricted to 19 sudden-onset natural disaster events occurring between 2016 and 2019 across four disaster categories (earthquakes, wildfires, floods, and hurricanes/cyclones) that directly affected land and caused major damage.', 'The annotation framework enforces a single-label mutually exclusive classification task per tweet across 11 predefined humanitarian categories, deliberately omitting multi-label assignments to optimize crowdworker annotation budgets.', 'Benchmark classification experiments excluded low-prevalence classes containing fewer than 15 samples per event, reducing the experimental benchmark pool from 77,196 tweets to 76,484 tweets across 10 evaluable humanitarian categories.']
limitations_summary: The authors acknowledge key constraints in their research design: (1) annotation was limited strictly to English-language tweets due to budgetary restrictions, omitting non-English crisis communications; (2) tweets were assigned a single mutually exclusive category despite microblog messages frequently containing multi-faceted situational information; and (3) low-prevalence classes with fewer than 15 instances were removed from specific event evaluation benchmarks.
limitations_verbatim: We choose to only annotate English tweets due to budget limitations. Therefore, we discard all non-English tweets using the Twitter provided language metadata for a given tweet. It would be interesting to annotate tweets in other languages in future studies. Though multiple labels can be assigned to a tweet, however, we limited it to one category to reduce the annotation efforts.
generalizability_gap: The dataset and benchmark models focus exclusively on English-language Twitter messages across four types of natural disasters (earthquakes, wildfires, floods, and hurricanes/cyclones). Consequently, the empirical findings and trained models may not generalize to non-English or code-switched crisis messages, human-induced emergencies (such as industrial accidents, acts of terrorism, or armed conflicts), slow-onset crises (such as droughts or famines), or alternative social media and messaging platforms (such as Facebook, Telegram, WhatsApp, or Sina Weibo).
methodological_gap: The study employs a mutually exclusive single-label formulation that cannot capture multi-intent disaster messages containing both urgent supply requests and infrastructural damage reports. In addition, geographic filtering relies on user-provided profile metadata for the 98% of tweets lacking GPS coordinates, which introduces potential location noise and geographical selection bias. Furthermore, the pipeline utilizes an automated Random Forest pre-filter that may discard borderline humanitarian messages prior to human crowdsourcing.
future_work: Annotating disaster tweets in non-English and low-resource languages to broaden linguistic coverage in crisis informatics.; Conducting cross-event and cross-disaster-type transfer learning and domain adaptation experiments using the standardized public benchmark splits.; Developing multimodal classification architectures that jointly analyze disaster tweet text and accompanying crisis imagery.; Extending annotation taxonomies and machine learning architectures to support multi-label crisis classification.; Deploying and evaluating computationally lightweight transformer models, such as DistilBERT, within real-time streaming disaster relief pipelines.

title: Humaid-Ner: A Disaster Tweet Dataset for Joint Named Entity Recognition and Event Classification Via Uncertainty-Weighted Multitask Learning
authors: Aijaz Ali; Nazish Basir; Sarfaraz Nawaz; Danish Nazir Arain; Haris Ali
venue: The Asian Bulletin of Big Data Management
domain: Crisis Informatics, Disaster Response, Social Media NLP (Twitter/X Disaster Tweets in English), Multitask Learning, Named Entity Recognition
problem_statement: Disaster-related social media benchmarks provide document-level category annotations but lack span-level entity labels (such as location, casualties, displaced counts, or requested supplies) required for operational humanitarian response coordination. Additionally, joint multi-task training of dense token-level named entity recognition and single sentence-level event classification leads to severe gradient asymmetry and task conflict (2,688 NER token signals vs. 1 classification signal per example), causing classification macro-F1 to progressively degrade under fixed-weight multi-task learning.
theoretical_framework: Homoscedastic uncertainty-based multi-task loss weighting (Kendall et al., 2018) derived from a probabilistic log-likelihood formulation with learnable task variance parameters, coupled with the hierarchical representation learning hypothesis (Liu et al., 2019 / MT-DNN) positing that lower transformer layers capture universal linguistic representations while upper layers encode task-specific patterns.
methodology: Constructed the HUMAID-NER dataset by extending 60,000 English tweets from the HumAID benchmark across 19 disaster events into 10 operationally motivated entity types (yielding 21 BIO classes) via a three-stage hybrid auto-labelling pipeline combining a spaCy transformer backbone (en_core_web_trf), domain-specific EntityRuler patterns, and regular expressions with priority- and length-based overlap resolution. Designed a joint multitask architecture using a shared RoBERTa-large encoder (24 layers, 355M parameters) with a linear token projection head for sequence labeling and a dual-pooled classification head concatenating the [CLS] embedding and mean non-padding token representations (2,048 dimensions). Trained the model using homoscedastic uncertainty loss weighting with learnable task log-variance parameters (s_NER, s_CLS) and a two-stage training schedule: Stage 1 (epochs 1–7) jointly trains all 24 encoder layers; Stage 2 (epochs 8–15) freezes the bottom 18 layers (reducing active parameters from 355M to 47M) to specialize upper layers and task heads. Developed and deployed a real-time web dashboard for simultaneous single-forward-pass inference.
datasets: HUMAID-NER (60,000 English tweets from 19 natural disaster events between 2016 and 2019 sampled from HumAID, annotated with ~175,000 entity spans across 10 disaster-specific types in BIO format; partitioned into 72% train [43,200 tweets], 14% validation [8,400 tweets], and 14% test [8,400 tweets] stratified by 10 humanitarian categories); HumAID benchmark (77,637 English tweets from 19 natural disaster events labelled across 10 humanitarian categories)
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Entity-level span micro-F1 via seqeval (exact entity type and span boundary match required)', 'Macro-averaged F1 across 10 humanitarian categories for event classification', 'Balanced validation combined score: Score_val = 0.5 * F1_NER + 0.5 * F1_CLS', 'Classification-first deployment policy (prioritizing classification macro-F1 with combined score breaking ties)'], 'ablation_results': {'Row A (BERT-large + Fixed Weights)': {'NER_span_micro_F1': 0.873, 'CLS_macro_F1': 0.736, 'combined_score': 0.805}, 'Row B (RoBERTa-large + Fixed Weights)': {'NER_span_micro_F1': 0.863, 'CLS_macro_F1': 0.749, 'combined_score': 0.806}, 'Row C (RoBERTa-large + Kendall Weighting)': {'NER_span_micro_F1': 0.866, 'CLS_macro_F1': 0.745, 'combined_score': 0.806}, 'Row D (RoBERTa-large + Kendall + Two-Stage / Proposed)': {'NER_span_micro_F1': 0.841, 'CLS_macro_F1': 0.761, 'combined_score': 0.801}}, 'benchmark_comparisons': {'HumAID BERT-base (Single-task)': {'NER_F1': None, 'CLS_F1': '0.700 - 0.730'}, 'HumAID RoBERTa-large (Single-task)': {'NER_F1': None, 'CLS_F1': '0.730 - 0.750'}, 'Proposed Joint RoBERTa-large (Row D)': {'NER_F1': 0.841, 'CLS_F1': 0.761}}}
key_findings: Introduced HUMAID-NER, the first disaster-domain named entity recognition dataset extending HumAID with 60,000 tweets and ~175,000 entity spans across 10 operational entity types (LOCATION, CASUALTY, DISPLACED, REQUEST, RESOURCE, RESCUE, DISASTER_TYPE, ORGANIZATION, PERSON, NUMBER) mapped to 21 BIO classes.; Empirically identified task conflict and gradient asymmetry under fixed-weight joint training, where dense token-level NER supervision (up to 2,688 signals/sample) dominated sentence-level classification (1 signal/sample), causing classification macro-F1 to peak at epoch 3 (0.748) and degrade by 1.4 points to 0.734 by epoch 15 despite monotonic reduction in training loss.; Demonstrated that Kendall homoscedastic uncertainty weighting dynamically balances task losses via learnable log-variance parameters, preventing classification degradation and stabilizing multitask training dynamics.; Found that two-stage layer-freezing training (freezing layers 1–18 in Stage 2) produced the largest classification gain (+1.6 macro-F1 points, reaching 0.761) by reducing active parameters from 355M to 47M and enabling task-head and upper-layer specialization without eroding shared representations.; The proposed joint RoBERTa-large framework achieved 0.841 NER span micro-F1 and 0.761 classification macro-F1 concurrently on the validation split, matching or exceeding single-task RoBERTa-large baselines (0.730–0.750) without incurring classification performance penalties while delivering full entity extraction capabilities.; Demonstrated operational viability via a real-time web dashboard capable of extracting typed entity spans and predicting humanitarian event categories simultaneously in a single forward pass without task-specific inference latency overhead.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Text corpus restricted to English-language disaster tweets sampled from 19 natural disaster events between 2016 and 2019 in the HumAID benchmark.', 'Dataset size delimited to a balanced 60,000-tweet subset across 10 humanitarian categories rather than the complete 77,637 HumAID corpus.', 'Entity taxonomy delimited to 10 operationally motivated humanitarian entity types (21 BIO classes) excluding generic newswire categories.', 'Empirical evaluation delimited to the held-out validation split (8,400 tweets) to intentionally reserve the test set against overfitting.', 'Hardware constraints on TPU v3-8 restricted experimental ablations to single-run point estimates without multi-seed variance analysis.']
limitations_summary: The dataset relies on an automated three-stage hybrid labelling pipeline without human inter-annotator agreement verification; the corpus is restricted to English tweets from 2016–2019 across a 60,000-tweet subset; evaluation reports only validation split results with test set evaluation reserved; ablations are single-run point estimates lacking multi-seed variance analysis due to TPU compute limits; and direct empirical gradient conflict diagnostics were not collected.
limitations_verbatim: Limitations include no human inter-annotator validation of the auto-labelled annotations, English-only coverage (2016–2019), validation-split-only reporting (testset evaluation reserved to prevent overfitting), and single-run point estimates for all ablation results (multi-seed variance analysis was precluded by TPU compute budget and is left for future work).
generalizability_gap: The dataset and joint framework are limited to English-language tweets from 19 natural disaster events (2016–2019), leaving unexamined non-English and multilingual disaster communications, low-resource regional dialects, multimodal crisis streams (paired text and imagery), and non-natural disaster domains such as industrial accidents, armed conflicts, or public health emergencies.
methodological_gap: The auto-labelling pipeline lacks formal human inter-annotator agreement metrics (such as Cohen's or Fleiss' Kappa) to quantify pseudo-label noise; direct gradient diagnostics (such as gradient cosine similarity or conflicting gradient norm tracking across shared layers) were not measured to provide direct mechanistic proof of gradient interference; and the ablation study lacks multi-seed statistical variance bounds.
future_work: Combine PCGrad gradient surgery with Kendall homoscedastic uncertainty weighting to eliminate destructive gradient interference without excessive computational overhead.; Scale the three-stage auto-annotation pipeline to annotate the remaining tweets in the full 77,637-tweet HumAID corpus and new disaster events.; Extend the joint multitask architecture to multilingual crisis tweet analysis using XLM-RoBERTa paired with soft gazetteers.; Conduct direct empirical gradient tracking across encoder layers during multitask training to evaluate gradient conflict dynamics.; Perform multi-seed variance analysis across all model configurations to establish statistical significance bounds.
