title: Improving Large-scale Language Models and Resources for Filipino
authors: Jan Christian Blaise Cruz; Charibeth Cheng
venue: Proceedings of the Thirteenth Language Resources and Evaluation Conference (LREC 2022)
domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Filipino / Tagalog Language Modeling, Low-Resource Languages, Text Classification, Pretraining Corpus Construction
problem_statement: Low-resource languages such as Filipino suffer from a severe scarcity of benchmark datasets, linguistic tools, and large-scale pretrained language models, which impedes NLP research progress. Prior Filipino language models (such as Tagalog BERT and ELECTRA) were pretrained on small, topically narrow corpora like WikiText-TL-39, resulting in sub-optimal downstream performance on complex classification tasks and limiting the capacity of larger transformer architectures.
theoretical_framework: Self-supervised Transformer language modeling and the RoBERTa robust optimization framework (Liu et al., 2019) building upon BERT masked language modeling (Devlin et al., 2018); Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) subword tokenization (Sennrich et al., 2015); memory-efficient optimization via Adafactor (Shazeer and Stern, 2018); and inverted-pyramid discourse entailing structures for natural language inference generation (Cruz et al., 2021).
methodology: The authors construct TLUnified, a large-scale, topically diverse Filipino pretraining corpus, by aggregating and deduplicating diverse Filipino text sources including bilingual bitexts (e.g., bible-uedin, CCAligned, ParaCrawl, TED2020, WikiMatrix, OpenSubtitles), the deduplicated Filipino split of OSCAR, and a 60% subset of the NewsPH news corpus. Raw text is cleaned using five deterministic filters: non-Latin character threshold (>15% non-Latin removed), sentence token length bounds (4 <= N <= 150), consecutive punctuation filtering, average word length ratio bounds (3 <= r <= 18), and HTML/URL artifact removal, followed by deduplication. A 32,000 BPE subword tokenizer with character coverage 1.0 is trained without uncasing. Using TLUnified, the authors pretrain two RoBERTa variants—Base (110M parameters, 12 layers, 768 hidden, 100k steps, lr=6e-4) and Large (330M parameters, 24 layers, 1024 hidden, 300k steps, lr=4e-4)—using Adafactor on 8x NVIDIA Tesla P100 GPUs with dynamic batching up to 8,192 tokens. The models are evaluated by finetuning with Adafactor on three downstream Filipino classification benchmarks: 2016 Election Hate Speech Detection, Dengue Infoveillance multi-label classification (reformulated as 32-class classification), and NewsPH-NLI Medium (generated from the unexposed 40% NewsPH split).
datasets: TLUnified: A large-scale pretraining corpus for Filipino constructed by combining deduplicated Filipino text from bitext corpora (bible-uedin, CCAligned, ELRC 2922, MultiC-CAligned, ParaCrawl, TED2020, WikiMatrix, tico-19, Ubuntu, OpenSubtitles, QED, Tanzil, Tatoeba, GlobalVoices, KDE4, WikiMedia), OSCAR Tagalog split, and 60% of NewsPH; Filipino Hatespeech Dataset: 10,000 Philippine presidential election-related tweets from 2016 annotated for binary hate speech classification (Cabasag et al., 2019); Filipino Dengue Dataset: 4,000 low-resource disease infoveillance tweets annotated across 5 binary health labels, transformed into a 32-class single-label classification task (Livelo and Cheng, 2018); NewsPH-NLI Medium: An entailment benchmark dataset generated from the remaining 40% unseen subset of the NewsPH news corpus to evaluate natural language inference without pretraining data leakage; WikiText-TL-39: Previous small-scale Filipino Wikipedia pretraining corpus used as a historical baseline comparison (Cruz and Cheng, 2019)
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Validation Accuracy', 'Test Accuracy'], 'evaluated_models': ['RoBERTa Base (110M parameters, TLUnified-trained)', 'RoBERTa Large (330M parameters, TLUnified-trained)'], 'baseline_models': ['Tagalog BERT Base (110M parameters, WikiText-TL-39-trained)', 'Tagalog ELECTRA Base (110M parameters, NewsPH-trained)'], 'benchmark_results': {'hatespeech_test_accuracy': {'bert_base': '68.60%', 'electra_base': '68.37%', 'roberta_base': '72.50%', 'roberta_large': '72.67%'}, 'dengue_test_accuracy': {'bert_base': '84.70%', 'electra_base': '83.60%', 'roberta_base': '89.10%', 'roberta_large': '90.00%'}, 'newsph_nli_medium_test_accuracy': {'bert_base': '86.97%', 'electra_base': '87.05%', 'roberta_base': '91.00%', 'roberta_large': '91.09%'}}}
key_findings: RoBERTa models pretrained on TLUnified substantially outperform previous Filipino transformer baselines (Tagalog BERT and ELECTRA) across all three evaluation benchmarks, achieving an average gain of 4.47% test accuracy.; RoBERTa Large achieves the highest test accuracy across all tasks: 72.67% on Hate Speech (+4.07% over BERT Base), 90.00% on Dengue (+5.30% over BERT Base), and 91.09% on NewsPH-NLI Medium (+4.04% over ELECTRA Base).; RoBERTa Base demonstrates strong performance improvements (+3.90% on Hate Speech, +4.40% on Dengue, and +3.95% on NewsPH-NLI Medium over baselines), closely trailing RoBERTa Large.; The performance gap between RoBERTa Base and RoBERTa Large is marginal (+0.17% on Hate Speech, +0.90% on Dengue, and +0.09% on NewsPH-NLI Medium), indicating that while TLUnified improves significantly upon WikiText-TL-39, larger corpora are required to fully saturate and exploit the parameter capacity of large-scale 330M transformer models.; Non-destructive preprocessing preserving capitalization, casing, and adding task-specific tokens ([LINK], [MENTION], [HASHTAG]) with averaged subword embedding initialization maintains vital morphological and syntactic cues in noisy social media text.
scope_and_delimitations: ['The pretraining dataset TLUnified and resulting RoBERTa models focus exclusively on the Filipino (Tagalog) language, excluding other Philippine regional languages.', 'Evaluation is delimited to three specific classification tasks: binary hate speech detection, 32-class dengue infoveillance classification, and natural language inference.', 'Model architecture scope is delimited to masked language modeling via RoBERTa (Base with 110M parameters and Large with 330M parameters), without evaluating autoregressive decoder-only or sequence-to-sequence models.', 'To prevent data contamination and artificial performance inflation, NewsPH-NLI Medium was generated exclusively from a 40% split of NewsPH that was withheld from TLUnified pretraining.', 'Finetuning sequence lengths were truncated to 256 subwords for Base and Large models to reduce memory and training time, as no downstream sentence or sentence pair exceeded 256 subwords.']
limitations_summary: The authors acknowledge that the performance improvement of RoBERTa Large over RoBERTa Base is marginal across the evaluated benchmarks (between +0.09% and +0.90% accuracy). They attribute this bottleneck to pretraining corpus size, noting that although TLUnified is substantially larger and more diverse than WikiText-TL-39, the corpus remains insufficient to fully realize the representational capacity of large 330M-parameter Transformer models.
limitations_verbatim: The difference in performance between the Base and Large RoBERTa variants is marginal in the current benchmarks. Large outperforms Base only by +0.17% for Hatespeech, +0.9% for Dengue, and +0.09% for NewsPH-NLI Medium. We hypothesize that this is due to the size of the pretraining dataset. While the size of TLUnified is much larger than the previous WikiText-TL-39, it may still not be enough to make full use of the capacity of a Large-variant Transformer. We surmise that RoBERTa Large may need to be trained with more data to show significant, non-marginal improvements in performance.
generalizability_gap: TLUnified and the pretrained RoBERTa models cover only standard Filipino/Tagalog text, leaving unexamined the more than 170 other regional Philippine languages (such as Cebuano, Ilocano, Hiligaynon, and Waray) as well as heavy conversational code-switching (Taglish) and generative language modeling capabilities.
methodological_gap: Evaluation was restricted to three sentence- and tweet-level classification tasks, lacking evaluation on generative NLP tasks (such as machine translation, summarization, and question answering) or token-level sequence labeling tasks (such as named entity recognition and part-of-speech tagging). In addition, pretraining data volume constraints prevented RoBERTa Large from demonstrating substantial capacity scaling gains over RoBERTa Base.
future_work: Scaling pretraining data beyond TLUnified to enable large-scale Transformer models to realize their full parameter capacity.; Expanding Filipino language model evaluations to broader downstream tasks, including sequence labeling, question answering, and text generation.; Exploring multilingual and regional pretraining adaptations for other under-resourced Philippine languages.

title: In Defense of the Unitary Scalarization for Deep Multi-Task Learning
authors: Vitaly Kurin; Alessandro De Palma; Ilya Kostrikov; Shimon Whiteson; M. Pawan Kumar
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
domain: Deep Multi-Task Learning, Multi-Objective Optimization, and Computational Efficiency
problem_statement: Investigating whether complex, specialized multi-task optimization (SMTO) algorithms consistently outperform simple unitary linear scalarization (equal weighting) when baselines are properly tuned.
theoretical_framework: Linear Scalarization vs. Specialized Multi-Task Optimization (SMTO), Pareto Optimality, and Regularization Theory
methodology: Rigorous benchmarking comparing unitary scalarization against specialized MTO algorithms (MGDA, GradNorm, PCGrad, CAGrad, IMTL) across computer vision, reinforcement learning, and NLP benchmarks using standardized hyperparameter tuning protocols.
datasets: NYUv2 multi-task vision benchmark; CityScapes autonomous driving dataset; Multi-task reinforcement learning environments (Meta-World, MT10)
evaluation: Per-task performance metrics, relative multi-task transfer, training runtime in wall-clock seconds, and peak GPU memory allocation.
key_findings: Demonstrated that unitary scalarization (equal weighting) combined with standard modern optimization techniques (Adam, learning rate warmup, weight decay) matches or exceeds the performance of complex SMTO methods.; Showed that specialized MTO algorithms introduce massive computational overhead, running 2x to 35x slower than simple scalarization due to multiple backward passes.; Concluded that many SMTO algorithms function primarily as implicit regularizers rather than superior optimization engines.
scope_and_delimitations: Evaluates hard-parameter-sharing architectures across vision and reinforcement learning benchmarks under controlled hyperparameter budgets.
limitations_summary: Acknowledged that scenarios with extreme task gradient scale disparities or severe negative transfer may still benefit from adaptive optimization.
limitations_verbatim: Our experiments focus on benchmarks where tasks are moderately related. In scenarios with extreme task imbalance or severely conflicting gradients, specialized loss weighting may still offer advantages.
generalizability_gap: Does not evaluate low-resource code-switched NLP tasks (such as Taglish disaster triage) or heterogeneous token-versus-sequence loss landscapes.
methodological_gap: Did not decouple intra-task sample gradient variance from inter-task gradient conflict.
future_work: Investigating low-overhead adaptive loss weighting methods that retain the computational efficiency of scalarization while preventing gradient scale dominance.
local_dir: In Defense of the Unitary Scalarization for Deep Multi-Task Learning

title: Independent Component Alignment for Multi-Task Learning
authors: Dmitry Senushkin; Nikolay Patakin; Arseny Kuznetsov; Anton Konushin
venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
domain: Multi-Task Learning — multi-task supervised scene understanding (NYUv2, Cityscapes) and multi-task reinforcement learning (Meta-World MT10)
problem_statement: Direct optimization of an averaged multi-task objective causes optimization instability due to conflicting and dominating gradients, while existing multi-task learning methods converge to arbitrary Pareto-stationary points without mechanisms to enforce user-defined task trade-offs.
theoretical_framework: Linear system stability analysis and singular value decomposition (SVD). The condition number kappa(G) = sigma_max / sigma_min of the gradient matrix serves as a stability criterion that jointly measures gradient conflict and gradient dominance. When kappa(G) = 1, the gradient system is orthogonal with equal singular values, which eliminates destabilizing negative gradient interactions. Aligned-MTL provably guarantees linear convergence to a Pareto-stationary solution corresponding to predefined task weights.
methodology: Aligned-MTL resolves gradient conflicts and gradient dominance by aligning the principal components of the gradient matrix G in task space. The algorithm formulates matrix alignment as an orthogonal Procrustes problem min_{G_hat} ||G - G_hat||_F^2 subject to G_hat^T G_hat = sigma^2 I, where the global scale sigma equals the minimum singular value sigma_min(G) > 0. The method computes the eigenvalue decomposition of the T x T task-space Gram matrix M = G^T G = V Lambda V^T, rescales singular values via transformation matrix B = sqrt(lambda_R) V Sigma^{-1} V^T, and multiplies the transformation matrix by predefined task weights w to obtain cumulative gradient G B w. To reduce computational complexity from O(T) to O(1) in encoder-decoder networks, Aligned-MTL-UB aligns gradients with respect to shared representations Z using a chain-rule upper bound.
datasets: Synthetic 2D two-task benchmark with five initialization points; NYUv2 — indoor scene understanding benchmark with 1,449 RGBD images evaluated on 13-class semantic segmentation, depth estimation, and surface normal prediction; Cityscapes (three-task) — urban scene understanding benchmark evaluated on semantic segmentation, instance segmentation via centroid regression, and disparity estimation; Cityscapes (two-task) — urban scene understanding benchmark evaluated on 7-class semantic segmentation and depth estimation; Meta-World MT10 — multi-task robotic manipulation benchmark comprising 10 distinct manipulation environments
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Synthetic: 2D optimization trajectory plots, cumulative loss landscape, and convergence to Pareto front versus global optimum', 'NYUv2: Mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) and Pixel Accuracy for semantic segmentation; Absolute Error and Relative Error for depth estimation; Mean angle distance, Median angle distance, and percentage within 11.25°, 22.5°, and 30° thresholds for surface normals; average per-task performance drop Delta_m_task (%) and metric-weighted drop Delta_m_metric (%) relative to single-task baselines', 'Cityscapes (three-task): mIoU for semantic segmentation, L1 pixel error for instance segmentation, Mean Squared Error (MSE) for disparity estimation, and Delta_m_task (%)', 'Cityscapes (two-task): mIoU and Pixel Accuracy for semantic segmentation, Absolute Error and Relative Error for depth estimation, and Delta_m_task (%)', 'Meta-World MT10: Mean task success rate and standard error of the mean (SEM) over 10 random seeds'], 'baselines': ['Single-Task Learning (STL baselines)', 'Linear Scalarization / Uniform Baseline', 'Dynamic Weight Average (DWA)', 'Uncertainty Weighting', 'Multiple Gradient Descent Algorithm (MGDA and MGDA-UB)', 'GradNorm', 'GradDrop', 'Projecting Conflicting Gradients (PCGrad)', 'Gradient Vaccine (GradVac)', 'Conflict-Averse Gradient Descent (CAGrad)', 'Impartial Multi-Task Learning (IMTL)', 'Nash-MTL', 'Random Loss Weighting (RLW)', 'Multi-Task Soft Actor-Critic (MTL SAC, MTL SAC + Task Encoder, Multi-Headed SAC, Soft Modularization, CARE)'], 'architectures': ['Multi-Task Attention Network (MTAN with SegNet backbone) for NYUv2 and Cityscapes', 'Pyramid Scene Parsing Network (PSPNet with dilated ResNet backbone) for NYUv2 and Cityscapes', 'Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) multi-layer perceptron architecture for Meta-World MT10']}
key_findings: Aligned-MTL achieves provable linear convergence to a Pareto-stationary solution with predefined task weights by enforcing condition number kappa(G_hat) = 1 through singular value alignment (Theorem 1).; On Cityscapes three-task scene understanding with PSPNet, Aligned-MTL achieves Delta_m = -0.02% and Aligned-MTL-UB achieves Delta_m = -0.35%, outperforming single-task baselines and surpassing CAGrad (1.46%), IMTL (3.10%), Nash-MTL (9.38%), and Uniform weighting (14.30%).; On NYUv2 with MTAN across three random seeds, Aligned-MTL achieves the lowest task-weighted performance drop of Delta_m = -8.40% (and metric-weighted Delta_m = -4.93%), and Aligned-MTL-UB achieves task-weighted Delta_m = -7.83%, outperforming Nash-MTL (-7.56%), IMTL (-4.76%), CAGrad (-4.18%), and Uniform weighting (-1.07%).; On NYUv2 with PSPNet across three random seeds, Aligned-MTL achieves the best task-weighted Delta_m = -1.55%, whereas strong single-task PSPNet baselines cause most competing MTL algorithms to suffer performance drops (Uniform 4.72%, GradNorm 2.18%, CAGrad 0.13%).; On Cityscapes two-task scene understanding with MTAN, Aligned-MTL achieves Delta_m = 5.27% (75.77% mIoU, 0.0133 Absolute Error) and Aligned-MTL-UB achieves Delta_m = 6.37%, outperforming Nash-MTL (6.72%), IMTL (11.04%), CAGrad (11.58%), and Uniform weighting (22.60%).; On the Meta-World MT10 robotic manipulation benchmark, Aligned-MTL achieves a 0.97 ± 0.045 average success rate across 10 random seeds, exceeding Nash-MTL (0.91 ± 0.031), CARE (0.84 ± 0.051), CAGrad (0.83 ± 0.045), Soft Modularization (0.73 ± 0.043), PCGrad (0.72 ± 0.022), and shared MTL SAC (0.49 ± 0.073).; Empirical analysis on Cityscapes confirms that the gradient condition number kappa <= 10 reliably indicates training stability and correlates with superior multi-task convergence, whereas gradient magnitude similarity fails to distinguish balanced optimization from severe gradient dominance.
scope_and_delimitations: ['The authors limit empirical evaluation to multi-task computer vision dense prediction (up to three simultaneous tasks) and simulated robotic manipulation (10 tasks), without evaluating natural language processing or speech domains.', 'The method requires predefined and fixed task weighting vectors (such as uniform weighting w_i = 1/T) and does not perform dynamic adaptive weight scheduling.', 'The exact Aligned-MTL algorithm assumes full linear independence of task gradients and requires T backward passes per optimization iteration.', 'The computationally efficient Aligned-MTL-UB approximation applies theoretically to shared-trunk encoder-decoder architectures, and acts as an empirical heuristic without convergence guarantees for non-encoder-decoder architectures.']
limitations_summary: The primary limitation of exact Aligned-MTL is its computational overhead, which requires T backward passes and scales linearly with the number of tasks. Although the upper-bound approximation (Aligned-MTL-UB) reduces time complexity to O(1) for encoder-decoder architectures, the approximation cannot align the shared representation Jacobian and lacks theoretical convergence guarantees when applied to non-encoder-decoder networks.
limitations_verbatim: The main limitation of Aligned-MTL is its computational optimization cost which scales linearly with the number of tasks. The upper-bound approximation of the Aligned-MTL method can be efficiently applied for encoder-decoder architectures using the same Jacobian over the shared representation. This approximation reduces instability, yet, it does not eliminate it since the Jacobian cannot be aligned.
generalizability_gap: The authors evaluated Aligned-MTL exclusively on multi-task computer vision and simulated robotic control tasks with up to 10 tasks. The authors did not evaluate the approach on natural language processing benchmarks, low-resource code-switched text classification, large language models, or settings with hundreds of heterogeneous tasks.
methodological_gap: Aligned-MTL requires full parameter-level gradient computation across all tasks, which scales linearly with task count; the O(1) upper-bound approximation only aligns gradients with respect to shared representations and cannot align the shared Jacobian directly. Furthermore, the framework relies on fixed task weights and does not incorporate second-order curvature information or dynamic task re-weighting.
future_work: Developing theoretical convergence guarantees for upper-bound gradient alignment on architectures beyond encoder-decoder networks.; Designing methods to align the shared representation Jacobian to eliminate residual optimization instability.; Applying independent component gradient alignment to large-scale natural language processing and multimodal foundation models.; Investigating combinations of principal component gradient alignment with dynamic task weighting and task scheduling strategies.

title: Injecting Imbalance Sensitivity for Multi-Task Learning
authors: Zhipeng Zhou; Liu Liu; Peilin Zhao; Wei Gong
venue: Proceedings of the Thirty-Fourth International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI-2025)
domain: Multi-Task Supervised Learning (Dense Scene Understanding, Facial Attribute Classification) and Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning (Robotic Manipulation)
problem_statement: Multi-task learning optimization methods, particularly gradient manipulation approaches, predominantly focus on resolving gradient conflicts while overlooking the critical issue of gradient imbalance and dominance across tasks, which causes Pareto failures and hinders balanced individual task progress even in the absence of conflicts.
theoretical_framework: Multi-objective optimization and Pareto optimality theory (Pareto dominance, Pareto front, and Pareto stationarity), Lagrangian duality in convex programming under Slater's condition, and gradient dynamics analyzing gradient similarity, imbalance ratios, and conflict-averse properties.
methodology: IMbalance-sensitive Gradient (IMGrad) descent method injects imbalance sensitivity into optimization-based multi-task learning paradigms by imposing projected norm constraints. The framework incorporates a constraint (g_i^T d - ||g_i||) into the dual objective to encourage the projected norms of the combined gradient d across all tasks to surpass individual task gradient norms. By applying Lagrangian duality and interchanging minimum and maximum operators via Slater's condition, IMGrad derives an analytical objective that balances global convergence and Pareto properties. The balancing weight mu is adaptively determined by cos theta, where theta represents the angle between the mean task gradient g_0 and the MGDA minimum norm gradient g^m. The authors also extend this principle to augment Nash-MTL by adaptively weighting its agreement and bargaining terms.
datasets: Cityscapes (urban scene understanding benchmark evaluated on 7-class semantic segmentation and depth estimation); NYUv2 (indoor scene understanding benchmark evaluated on 13-class semantic segmentation, depth estimation, and surface normal prediction); CelebA (large-scale facial attribute dataset with over 200,000 images evaluated across 40 binary attribute classification tasks); Meta-World MT10 (multi-task robotic manipulation reinforcement learning benchmark with 10 distinct manipulation environments); Synthetic two-task toy benchmark (imbalanced two-objective optimization trajectories derived from CAGrad and Nash-MTL settings)
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Delta m% (overall relative multi-task degradation/improvement percentage compared to independent single-task reference oracles)', 'Mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) and Pixel Accuracy (Pix. Acc.) for semantic segmentation on Cityscapes and NYUv2', 'Absolute Error (Abs. Err.) and Relative Error (Rel. Err.) for depth estimation on Cityscapes and NYUv2', 'Mean Angle Error, Median Angle Error, and Percentage of Pixels within 11.25°, 22.5°, and 30° thresholds for surface normal prediction on NYUv2', 'Average classification degradation Delta m% across 40 attribute classification tasks on CelebA', 'Average task success rate and standard error of the mean (SEM) over 10 random seeds on Meta-World MT10 reinforcement learning', 'Statistical imbalance ratios, gradient cosine similarities (cos phi_ij), and individual progress ratios r_i(t) = L_i(t) / L_i(0)'], 'baselines': ['Linear Scalarization (LS / naive mean gradient)', 'Independent single-task learning models', 'Random Loss Weighting (RLW)', 'Dynamic Weight Average (DWA)', 'Multiple Gradient Descent Algorithm (MGDA)', 'Gradient Drop (GradDrop)', 'Projecting Conflicting Gradients (PCGrad)', 'Conflict-Averse Gradient descent (CAGrad)', 'Impartial Multi-Task Learning (IMTL)', 'Nash Multi-Task Learning (Nash-MTL)', 'Momentum-based Correction (MoCo)', 'Fast Adaptive Multitask Optimization (FAMO)', 'Scale Invariant (SI), Uncertainty Weighting (UW), Single-Task SAC, Multi-Task SAC, Multi-Head SAC, Soft Modularization (SM), CARE'], 'architectures': ['Multi-Task Attention Network (MTAN) with SegNet backbone for Cityscapes and NYUv2 scene understanding', '9-layer Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) backbone with task-specific linear classification heads for CelebA', 'Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) multi-layer perceptron architecture for Meta-World MT10 reinforcement learning']}
key_findings: Empirical analysis reveals that gradient imbalance is a more fundamental obstacle in multi-task optimization than gradient conflict, because balanced task gradients converge to global optima despite severe conflicts, whereas imbalanced gradients frequently stall or cause Pareto failures.; Mainstream optimization-based multi-task learning methods (such as PCGrad, CAGrad, and Nash-MTL) experience Pareto failures and imbalanced individual task progress because existing methods lack simultaneous conflict-averse and imbalance-sensitive properties.; On the NYUv2 3-task benchmark, IMGrad achieves a state-of-the-art Delta m% of -4.57% (outperforming Nash-MTL at -4.04% and FAMO at -4.10%), attaining 40.20 mIoU and 66.19% pixel accuracy in segmentation, and 0.52 absolute error in depth estimation.; On the Cityscapes 2-task benchmark, IMGrad attains a Delta m% of 6.61% (substantially improving over CAGrad at 11.58% and outperforming Nash-MTL at 6.82%), with 75.13 mIoU and 0.0128 absolute depth error.; On the CelebA 40-task facial attribute classification benchmark, IMGrad achieves a Delta m% of 1.27%, demonstrating strong scalability across massive task counts and competitive performance alongside FAMO (1.21%).; On the Meta-World MT10 reinforcement learning benchmark, IMGrad improves CAGrad by over 0.10 in success rate, reaching a state-of-the-art success rate of 0.93 ± 0.068 (compared to 0.83 for CAGrad and 0.91 for Nash-MTL).; Ablation and control group experiments demonstrate that selectively gating multi-task optimization based on gradient imbalance ratios yields consistent performance gains across baselines, whereas gating by gradient conflict similarity yields minimal benefit.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Focuses strictly on optimization-based multi-task learning with shared backbone architectures and gradient manipulation algorithms, excluding architecture-based parameter sharing designs.', 'Requires individual per-task gradient evaluations at every training iteration to compute gradient similarities and imbalance ratios.', 'Evaluates empirical performance on standard benchmarks: 2-task and 3-task dense scene understanding (Cityscapes, NYUv2), 40-task image classification (CelebA), and 10-task robotic manipulation (Meta-World MT10).', 'Utilizes the cosine angle cos theta between the average task gradient g_0 and the MGDA minimum norm gradient g^m as the primary operational proxy for quantifying gradient imbalance.']
limitations_summary: The authors acknowledge that IMGrad does not obtain the top metric on every single evaluation benchmark (such as surface normal prediction on NYUv2 or CelebA classification where FAMO slightly outperforms it). Additionally, the method requires per-task backward passes that scale computationally with task count, focuses solely on optimization-based approaches without custom architecture co-design, and did not evaluate augmented Nash-MTL on reinforcement learning benchmarks due to implementation unavailability.
limitations_verbatim: While IMGrad does not achieve the best performance, it consistently ranks among the top methods, underscoring the importance of imbalance sensitivity for learning massive tasks.
generalizability_gap: The authors evaluated IMGrad exclusively on computer vision datasets (NYUv2, Cityscapes, CelebA) and simulated robotic manipulation benchmarks (Meta-World MT10); the authors did not evaluate the method on natural language processing, multilingual or code-switched text corpora, speech processing, large language model multi-task fine-tuning, or physical robotic hardware.
methodological_gap: IMGrad requires computing individual task gradients for all tasks at each training step, incurring linear gradient computation overhead; furthermore, the method relies on a geometric proxy (cos theta between g_0 and g^m) to regulate imbalance sensitivity rather than directly resolving underlying curvature discrepancies across task loss surfaces.
future_work: Extending imbalance-sensitive multi-task gradient descent methods to natural language processing, speech, and multimodal foundation models.; Developing scalable gradient combination algorithms to reduce the per-task gradient computation overhead in massive multi-task settings.; Exploring alternative geometric, statistical, or curvature-based formulations for quantifying task imbalance dynamically during training.; Investigating official implementations and extensions of augmented bargaining-game multi-task frameworks (such as Nash-MTL) in multi-task reinforcement learning environments.
local_dir: Injecting Imbalance Sensitivity for Multi-Task Learning

title: Language Model Tokenizers Introduce Unfairness Between Languages
authors: Aleksandar Petrov; Emanuele La Malfa; Philip H.S. Torr; Adel Bibi
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2023, Datasets and Benchmarks Track)
domain: Natural Language Processing, Subword Tokenization, Multilingual NLP Fairness
problem_statement: Investigates how disparities in the treatment of different languages arise at the subword tokenization stage before a language model is even invoked, leading to severe inflation in sequence lengths across languages.
theoretical_framework: Information-theoretic tokenization efficiency and multilingual tokenization parity; analysis of Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) and WordPiece fertility disparities across Latin and non-Latin scripts.
methodology: Evaluates tokenization lengths, fertility metrics, and character-to-token ratios across multiple commercial and open-source tokenizers (including GPT-2, GPT-4, LLaMA, XLM-R, and mT5) on parallel multilingual corpora spanning typologically diverse languages.
datasets: FLORES-200; OpenSubtitles parallel corpus; Universal Dependencies parallel treebanks
evaluation: Sequence tokenization length ratio relative to English; Fertility (subwords per word / character-to-token ratio); API pricing cost multiplier across languages; Context window saturation rate and generation latency
key_findings: The same text translated into different languages produces drastically different tokenization lengths, exceeding 2x to 7x inflation for low-resource languages and up to 15x in extreme cases.; Subword tokenizers disproportionately segment non-English and low-resource words into character-level fragments, creating a tokenization parity premium.; Over-fragmentation directly inflates downstream inference latency, increases per-query API costs, and prematurely exhausts model context windows for non-English speakers.; Multilingual tokenizers trained without explicit language-balancing constraints still exhibit substantial tokenization length disparities across language families.
scope_and_delimitations: Examines subword and byte-level tokenization algorithms across commercial LLM APIs and pre-trained open multilingual encoders on parallel translated benchmarks.
limitations_summary: The study evaluates tokenization length and pricing fairness across languages but does not train end-to-end downstream models to measure the exact downstream task accuracy trade-offs of vocabulary re-allocation.
limitations_verbatim: While we propose vocabulary balancing, our experiments do not evaluate whether increasing vocabulary allocation for under-represented languages negatively impacts the representation capacity of the core pre-training language.
generalizability_gap: Evaluates parallel sentence translations across standard national languages; untested on informal intra-sentential code-switched microblogs or regional agglutinative dialects such as Taglish.
methodological_gap: Focuses primarily on fertility ratios and cost metrics rather than directly measuring gradient variance or representation dilution in multi-task loss landscapes.
future_work: Developing multilingually fair subword tokenizers with equitable fertility across language families.; Investigating downstream task performance under balanced multilingual tokenization budgets.

title: Leveraging Multi-Task Learning in Code-Switched setting
authors: Mithun Kumar S R; Omkar Pitale; Aruna Malapati
venue: Research Square
domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Code-Switching / Code-Mixing (specifically Hindi-English / Hinglish token classification)
problem_statement: Developing reliable natural language processing models for code-switched text is difficult due to the scarcity of annotated transcriptions and training data. This study investigates whether multi-task learning with shared representations between related token classification tasks (Language Identification and Named Entity Recognition) can leverage auxiliary training signals to improve model generalizability and task performance in code-switched environments.
theoretical_framework: Multi-task learning using hard parameter sharing and homoscedastic uncertainty loss weighting for joint representation learning across related token classification tasks.
methodology: The authors designed a stacked neural architecture consisting of a pre-trained multilingual transformer encoder (mBERT, XLM-RoBERTa base, or XLM-RoBERTa large), a bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network, and shared Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) layers. The shared representations feed into task-specific heads composed of MLP layers with GELU activations and Layer Normalization coupled with Conditional Random Field (CRF) sequence decoders. The framework is trained jointly for Named Entity Recognition (NER) and Language Identification (LID) using an adaptive multi-task loss function weighted by homoscedastic uncertainty.
datasets: LinCE (Linguistic Code-Switching Evaluation) benchmark for Hindi-English (Named Entity Recognition and Language Identification tasks)
evaluation: {'method': "10-fold cross-validation with early stopping, learning rate scheduling, and paired Student's t-test for statistical significance validation.", 'metrics': {'NER_average_F1': {'mBERT': 71.37, 'XLM-RoBERTa_base': 77.41, 'XLM-RoBERTa_large': 82.92}, 'LID_average_F1': {'mBERT': 80.648, 'XLM-RoBERTa_base': 88.154, 'XLM-RoBERTa_large': 88.557}, 'paired_t_test_p_values': {'mBERT': 0.297, 'XLM-RoBERTa_base': 0.392, 'XLM-RoBERTa_large': 1.0}}}
key_findings: Multi-task learning with hard parameter sharing outperforms single-task baselines by providing an implicit data augmentation effect that improves model generalizability in code-switched settings.; Joint training of Named Entity Recognition (NER) and Language Identification (LID) allows the NER task to benefit from representations learned during the LID task, yielding substantial performance gains.; XLM-RoBERTa large achieves the highest average F1 score for both NER (82.92%) and LID (88.557%), substantially outperforming mBERT (71.37% NER, 80.648% LID) and XLM-RoBERTa base (77.41% NER, 88.154% LID).; Adaptive loss weighting based on homoscedastic uncertainty prevents performance degradation across tasks compared to simple loss summation.; Paired Student's t-test analysis confirms that variations across cross-validation splits are not statistically divergent (p > 0.05).
scope_and_delimitations: ['The study restricts its empirical evaluation to two token classification tasks: Named Entity Recognition (NER) and Language Identification (LID).', 'The evaluation focuses exclusively on Hindi-English (Hinglish) code-switched text from the LinCE benchmark.', 'The model backbone comparisons are confined to mBERT, XLM-RoBERTa base, and XLM-RoBERTa large encoders stacked with BiLSTM and CRF layers.', 'Sentence lengths are fixed at a maximum of 64 tokens with a batch size of 32.']
limitations_summary: The authors evaluated the framework exclusively on the LinCE Hindi-English dataset without conducting empirical validations on the broader GLUECoS benchmark or on other language pairs. Additionally, naive loss summation caused performance imbalances across tasks, necessitating uncertainty-weighted loss tuning.
limitations_verbatim: We are yet to experiment on GLUECoS dataset and try out more optimizations in order to achieve much better results than the existing ones.
generalizability_gap: The proposed multi-task architecture has only been evaluated on Hindi-English code-switched text for NER and LID token classification. Its performance and generalizability across other code-switched language pairs (such as Spanish-English, Modern Standard Arabic-Egyptian Arabic, or Nepali-English), other benchmarks like GLUECoS, and higher-level NLP tasks (such as sentiment analysis, question answering, and natural language inference) remain unverified.
methodological_gap: The study limits its architectural design to hard parameter sharing with BiLSTM-CRF sequence classification heads, without examining soft parameter sharing mechanisms, cross-task attention, generative transformer architectures, or the empirical effects of pairing dissimilar tasks.
future_work: Evaluate the multi-task framework on the GLUECoS benchmark dataset.; Implement and test additional optimization strategies to improve downstream task metrics.; Analyze specific task combinations to determine which task pairs optimize shared representations and improve generalizability.; Investigate the effects of implicit data augmentation from multi-task learning when training on similar versus dissimilar tasks.
local_dir: Leveraging Multi-Task Learning in Code-Switched setting

title: LibMTL: A Python Library for Deep Multi-Task Learning
authors: Baijiong Lin; Yu Zhang
venue: Journal of Machine Learning Research (JMLR)
domain: Deep Multi-Task Learning, Computer Vision, and Machine Learning Systems
problem_statement: Most state-of-the-art multi-task learning models are implemented across fragmented codebases with divergent experimental protocols or lack public implementations entirely, which creates barriers to reproducible benchmarking, complicates the development of novel multi-task algorithms, and impedes the practical deployment of multi-task learning systems in real-world applications.
theoretical_framework: Multi-task learning formalization with shared parameters theta and task-specific parameters psi for T tasks under single-input and multi-input settings, structured on an orthogonal decomposition between neural network architecture design and multi-objective loss or gradient balancing optimization strategies.
methodology: LibMTL provides a modular, extensible PyTorch library structured into decoupled functional modules. The library includes LibMTL.config for command-line parameter handling, Dataloader for single-input and multi-input batch loading, LibMTL.model for backbone networks such as ResNet, LibMTL.architecture for 8 multi-task architectures (Hard Parameter Sharing, Cross-stitch Networks, MMoE, MTAN, CGC, PLE, Learning to Branch, and DSelect-k), LibMTL.loss for task loss definitions, LibMTL.weighting for 13 loss-balancing and gradient-balancing optimization strategies (Equal Weighting, GradNorm, Uncertainty Weights, MGDA, Dynamic Weight Average, Geometric Loss Strategy, PCGrad, GradDrop, IMTL, Gradient Vaccine, CAGrad, Nash-MTL, and Random Loss Weighting) supporting exact parameter gradients and representation gradient approximations, LibMTL.metrics for evaluation tracking, LibMTL.Trainer for unified execution, and LibMTL.utils for auxiliary training routines.
datasets: NYUv2 (indoor scene understanding benchmark containing 3 dense prediction tasks: 13-class semantic segmentation, depth estimation, and surface normal prediction)
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) and Pixel Accuracy (PAcc) for semantic segmentation', 'Absolute Error (AErr) and Relative Error (RErr) for depth estimation', 'Mean angle distance, Median angle distance (MED), and percentage of pixels within 11.25°, 22.5°, and 30° error thresholds for surface normal prediction'], 'baselines': ['13 optimization strategies evaluated on the Hard Parameter Sharing architecture: Equal Weighting (EW), GradNorm, Uncertainty Weights (UW), MGDA, Dynamic Weight Average (DWA), Geometric Loss Strategy (GLS), Projecting Conflicting Gradient (PCGrad), GradDrop, Impartial Multi-Task Learning (IMTL), Gradient Vaccine (GradVac), Conflict-Averse Gradient descent (CAGrad), Nash-MTL, and Random Loss Weighting (RLW)', '8 neural network architectures evaluated under the Equal Weighting strategy: Hard Parameter Sharing (HPS), Cross-stitch Networks, Multi-gate Mixture-of-Experts (MMoE), Multi-Task Attention Network (MTAN), Customized Gate Control (CGC), Progressive Layered Extraction (PLE), Learning to Branch (LTB), and DSelect-k', 'Qualitative comparative analysis against existing multi-task learning toolkits including RMTL and MTLV'], 'architectures': ['ResNet backbone feature extractor combined with multi-task parameter sharing heads and task-specific decoders for indoor scene understanding']}
key_findings: LibMTL provides a unified, extensible PyTorch library that supports 13 optimization strategies and 8 deep architectures, and allows flexible combinations across single-input and multi-input multi-task learning paradigms.; On the NYUv2 benchmark using the Hard Parameter Sharing architecture, the Geometric Loss Strategy achieves the highest semantic segmentation performance (54.59 mIoU, 76.06% PAcc) and lowest depth estimation errors (0.3785 AErr, 0.1555 RErr), while CAGrad achieves the lowest surface normal errors (22.47° Mean, 15.71° MED, 37.77% within 11.25°).; On the NYUv2 benchmark using the Equal Weighting strategy, MTAN achieves the highest semantic segmentation performance (54.64 mIoU, 75.99% PAcc) and lowest depth errors (0.3771 AErr, 0.1557 RErr), whereas Progressive Layered Extraction (PLE) and Customized Gate Control (CGC) achieve the lowest surface normal prediction errors (PLE reaches 22.10° Mean, 15.34° MED; CGC reaches 22.14° Mean, 15.33° MED).; The modular design cleanly decouples data loaders, loss functions, metrics, configurations, model backbones, parameter sharing architectures, and gradient weighting strategies, which allows researchers to implement new algorithms or apply existing methods to new applications with minimal code overhead.; Comparative analysis shows that LibMTL provides broader deep neural network support, more contemporary gradient-balancing algorithms, and greater task configuration flexibility than earlier specialized libraries such as RMTL and MTLV.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Implemented specifically for deep multi-task learning using the PyTorch framework.', 'Evaluated benchmark performance exclusively on the NYUv2 indoor scene understanding dataset across 3 dense prediction tasks (semantic segmentation, depth estimation, surface normal prediction) with a ResNet backbone.', 'Restricted empirical benchmark tables to testing individual optimization algorithms on Hard Parameter Sharing and testing individual architectures under Equal Weighting, rather than running full combinatorial matrices across all strategies and architectures.', 'Focused on supervised multi-task learning under single-input and multi-input formulations, excluding reinforcement learning and unsupervised multi-task setups.']
limitations_summary: The authors acknowledge that exact gradient balancing methods demand substantial computation when models contain large numbers of shared parameters or tasks, which requires using representation gradient approximations. Furthermore, the library initially did not include transformer backbones or natural language tokenization models, and empirical benchmark evaluations were restricted to a single computer vision dataset.
limitations_verbatim: Moreover, gradient balancing methods need to calculate the gradients of the task-shared parameters θ for every task, which may be computationally intensive when the number of shared parameters or tasks is large.
generalizability_gap: The empirical benchmark in the paper is restricted to a single indoor RGB-D computer vision dataset (NYUv2); the authors did not evaluate the performance, memory footprint, and scaling properties of the library on large-scale natural language processing corpora, recommender systems, speech processing, tabular data, or multimodal foundation models.
methodological_gap: The benchmark experiments evaluate optimization strategies only on the standard Hard Parameter Sharing architecture and evaluate architectures only under naive Equal Weighting, leaving the empirical interaction effects between advanced architectures (such as MTAN or PLE) and advanced gradient balancing methods (such as CAGrad or Nash-MTL) unexplored; additionally, exact gradient computation methods scale poorly in memory and time when the parameter count or task count increases without feature-level gradient approximations.
future_work: Continuously maintaining and updating the library to incorporate newly proposed multi-task learning architectures and optimization strategies.; Updating the documentation and providing expanded user tutorials for complex multi-task workflows.; Adding multi-task learning application examples and benchmark suites from diverse domains beyond computer vision.; Providing additional neural network backbone models such as Vision Transformers and N-gram language representations.

title: Meta-Pretraining for Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Named Entity Recognition in Low-Resource Philippine Languages
authors: David Demitri Africa; Suchir Salhan; Yuval Weiss; Paula Buttery; Richard Diehl Martinez
venue: Proceedings of the 5th Workshop on Multilingual Representation Learning (MRL 2025)
domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Cross-Lingual Transfer, Low-Resource Languages, Philippine Languages (Tagalog, Cebuano), Named Entity Recognition (NER), Meta-Learning
problem_statement: Named-entity recognition (NER) in low-resource languages is conventionally tackled by finetuning large multilingual language models, which is computationally infeasible in memory- or latency-constrained settings. Furthermore, cross-lingual transfer from high-resource Indo-European models to underrepresented Austronesian languages struggles because morphosyntactic cues, voice alternations, and case particles differ substantially. The authors investigate whether small causal decoder language models can be meta-pretrained using first-order Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) to adapt rapidly and transfer zero-shot to unseen low-resource Philippine languages without any target-language pretraining exposure.
theoretical_framework: First-order Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) framework (Finn et al., 2017); Austronesian typological linguistics contrasting Tagalog's four-way overt voice paradigm and personal case particles (si, ni) with Cebuano's reduced two-way system and discourse-driven marking (Tanangkingsing, 2011; Bautista, 2004; Baklanova, 2019); Subset-Masked Language Modeling Task (SMLMT) framework (Bansal et al., 2020); and Linear-Chain Conditional Random Field (CRF) sequence tagging theory (Lafferty et al., 2001; Ma and Hovy, 2016).
methodology: The authors pretrain LLaMA-style PICO causal decoder Transformer models across four parameter tiers (tiny: 11M, small: 65M, medium: 181M, and large: 570M). Pretraining alternates via a synchronized Bernoulli draw (p = 0.5) between standard autoregressive next-token prediction on pre-tokenized Dolma and a 32-way, 4-shot Subset-Masked LM Task (SMLMT) episodic meta-learning objective using first-order MAML. In each MAML episode, the inner loop updates a lightweight MLP head for 10 SGD steps (learning rate = 1e-3) while the outer loop backpropagates query loss through the backbone with AdamW (peak learning rate = 3e-4, 2,500 warmup steps, cosine decay) over 6,000 total updates. After pretraining, an untrained linear-chain CRF head is attached, and models are finetuned on nine high-resource languages (Danish, English, Croatian, Portuguese, Slovak, Serbian, Swedish, Chinese, and an all-language mixture) under head-only and full-model finetuning regimes. Models are subsequently evaluated zero-shot on Tagalog and Cebuano treebanks. Representation dynamics, learning curves, and token confidences are analyzed across 61 intermediate checkpoints for the 181M medium model finetuned on Slovak.
datasets: Dolma: Pre-tokenized English web and general domain text corpus used for autoregressive pretraining and episodic meta-learning tasks; Universal NER v1 (UNER v1) In-Language Finetuning Treebanks: da_ddt (Danish), en_ewt (English), hr_set (Croatian), pt_bosque (Portuguese), sk_snk (Slovak), sr_set (Serbian), sv_talbanken (Swedish), zh_gsd (Traditional Chinese), zh_gsdsimp (Simplified Chinese); Universal NER v1 (UNER v1) Zero-Shot Target Test Sets: tl_trg (Tagalog TRG), tl_ugnayan (Tagalog Ugnayan), ceb_gja (Cebuano GJA); Parallel Universal Dependencies (PUD) Evaluation Sets: sentence-aligned test sets in German (de_pud), English (en_pud), Portuguese (pt_pud), Russian (ru_pud), Swedish (sv_pud), and Chinese (zh_pud)
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Token-level micro-F1 score', 'Per-entity F1 score (PER, LOC, ORG)', 'Convergence time to 90% final loss (t90)', 'Normalized Area Under the Loss Curve (Loss AUC)', 'Initial learning curve slope', 'Token-level prediction confidence (probability of correct tag)', 'Surprisal delta (change in gold label log-probability)'], 'evaluated_architectures': ['PICO-MAML Tiny (11M parameters, d=96, L=12)', 'PICO-MAML Small (65M parameters, d=384, L=12)', 'PICO-MAML Medium (181M parameters, d=768, L=12)', 'PICO-MAML Large (570M parameters, d=1536, L=12)'], 'baseline_architectures': ['Vanilla PICO Tiny (11M parameters)', 'Vanilla PICO Small (65M parameters)', 'Vanilla PICO Medium (181M parameters)', 'Vanilla PICO Large (570M parameters)']}
key_findings: First-order MAML meta-pretraining improves zero-shot cross-lingual micro-F1 on Tagalog and Cebuano by 2 to 6 percentage points under head-only finetuning and 1 to 3 percentage points under full finetuning across small decoder language models.; The relative benefit of meta-pretraining depends on model capacity: the 11M tiny model shows negligible head-only gains due to capacity limits, whereas models from 65M upward show clear performance lifts, with relative F1 gains peaking at moderate scales and tapering to +6% at 570M.; Meta-pretraining accelerates in-language finetuning convergence, reducing the time to reach 90% of final loss (t90) by up to 8% (approximately 111 steps) in full-model tuning for large and small models without modifying the initial learning slope.; Performance improvements concentrate strongly on Person (PER) entities (F1 of 0.60 to 0.70) while Location (LOC) and Organization (ORG) scores remain near chance in Slovak head-only tuning, resulting from training set entity imbalances (8:1 PER to LOC, 15:1 PER to ORG) and high proportions of single-token names (87.6%).; Meta-pretraining sharpens single-token lexical prototypes and leverages language-specific surface cues, producing earlier and higher zero-shot gains in Tagalog due to overt personal case particles ('si' and 'ni' preceding 11% of PER entities) compared to Cebuano (5% to 6% particle occurrence).; Meta-learning introduces a tradeoff between prototype sharpening and contextual generalization: while MAML increases confidence on common names, it reduces confidence on multi-token or context-dependent locative expressions.
scope_and_delimitations: ['The study is delimited to small decoder-only causal Transformer models ranging from 11M to 570M parameters, excluding encoder-only architectures and large-scale multilingual models.', 'Pretraining compute is delimited to 6,000 outer updates on four NVIDIA A100-80GB GPUs with a fixed Bernoulli objective probability (p = 0.5).', 'Target zero-shot language evaluation is delimited to two Philippine languages, Tagalog and Cebuano, evaluated on Universal NER v1 benchmarks (tl_trg, tl_ugnayan, ceb_gja).', 'Source finetuning languages are delimited to nine high-resource languages and an all-language mixture from Universal Dependencies and Universal NER.', 'Detailed checkpoint dynamics and per-tag qualitative analyses are delimited to a single configuration: the 181M medium model finetuned head-only on Slovak (sk_snk) across a single random seed.']
limitations_summary: The authors acknowledge several study limitations: empirical gains concentrate predominantly on person entities and head-only finetuning; the 6,000-step pretraining budget is short and potentially undertrains larger models; pretraining data is restricted to English Dolma rather than multilingual text; qualitative analyses were conducted on a single medium model configuration, single seed, and a single native speaker with a Manila register; and target evaluations cover only two Austronesian languages (Tagalog and Cebuano), constraining broader typological generalizations across other Philippine and Malayo-Polynesian languages.
limitations_verbatim: The gains are most pronounced for person entities and head-only finetuning, and scale best with larger model capacities. All training runs stop at exactly six thousand outer steps, a horizon that may be too short for the largest model, so the conclusions derived only cover a fraction of the training budget a corporate setup might have. A more diverse and multilingual corpus may alter both quantitative and qualitative conclusions, and varying languages in the meta-task is a natural way to extend this work. Qualitative analysis was conducted on a single configuration and single seed due to cost and GPU constraints. Qualitative analysis was conducted by a native Tagalog speaker with a register typical of Manila, and a wide variety of perspectives would improve the robustness of the analysis. Finally (and most naturally), our focus on only two Austronesian languages controls for certain lexical and syntactic divergences but limits the generality of the typological conclusions; extending to a broader set of Philippine and Malayo-Polynesian languages is a natural next step.
generalizability_gap: The meta-pretraining approach was evaluated only on Tagalog and Cebuano, leaving untested more than 100 other Philippine languages (such as Ilocano, Hiligaynon, Bikol, and Waray) and broader Malayo-Polynesian language families. Furthermore, pretraining used only monolingual English text, leaving open how meta-pretraining behaves when applied to multilingual corpora or noisy code-switched text.
methodological_gap: The meta-pretraining framework demonstrates limited efficacy for multi-token, complex, or highly contextual entity spans (such as locations and organizations), where prototype sharpening suppresses contextual cue recognition. Additionally, all models were trained for a uniform 6,000 steps without full hyperparameter sweeps across seeds or varying Bernoulli objective ratios, and head-only tuning relied on linear CRF heads that cannot update underlying representations to resolve syntactic ambiguities.
future_work: Extending episodic meta-pretraining to multilingual corpora and incorporating diverse language tasks into the meta-learning objective.; Investigating prototype formation dynamics and zero-shot transfer in even lower-resource and typologically distant language settings.; Developing meta-learning objectives capable of capturing multi-token entities, complex syntactic structures, and contextual location and organization boundaries.; Scaling pretraining beyond 6,000 steps to evaluate the full potential of large parameter models under larger compute budgets.; Evaluating the approach across a wider spectrum of Philippine and Malayo-Polynesian languages and diverse dialectal registers.

title: Multi-Task Deep Neural Networks for Natural Language Understanding
authors: Xiaodong Liu; Pengcheng He; Weizhu Chen; Jianfeng Gao
venue: Proceedings of the 57th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL 2019)
domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Natural Language Understanding (NLU), Multi-Task Learning, Domain Adaptation, Pre-trained Language Models
problem_statement: How to combine multi-task learning and unsupervised language model pre-training into a unified neural representation learning architecture that leverages cross-task supervision, provides regularization across tasks, and enables sample-efficient domain adaptation across diverse natural language understanding benchmarks.
theoretical_framework: Multi-task learning principles (Caruana, 1997; Zhang & Yang, 2017) wherein joint representation learning across related tasks provides an inductive bias and regularization effect that alleviates overfitting to specific tasks, combined with bidirectional Transformer language model pre-training (BERT) using masked language modeling and next sentence prediction (Devlin et al., 2018; Vaswani et al., 2017), and multi-step reasoning via Stochastic Answer Networks (Liu et al., 2018a).
methodology: MT-DNN extends BERT by incorporating multi-task learning across shared lower layers and specialized task-specific output layers. The shared layers consist of a lexicon encoder and a multi-layer bidirectional Transformer encoder initialized with pre-trained BERT weights (BERT-Base or BERT-Large). The top layers implement specialized output heads for four distinct NLU task categories: (1) single-sentence classification using softmax logistic regression on the [CLS] embedding; (2) text similarity regression using linear projection on the [CLS] embedding optimized with mean squared error; (3) pairwise text classification using the Stochastic Answer Network (SAN) multi-step reasoning module with stochastic prediction dropout; and (4) relevance ranking (QNLI) formulated as pairwise learning-to-rank using cross-entropy loss over positive and negative candidate answers. The model undergoes a two-stage training process: unsupervised BERT pre-training followed by multi-task mini-batch stochastic gradient descent (SGD with Adamax optimizer) across all training tasks, and optional task-specific fine-tuning or domain adaptation.
datasets: GLUE Benchmark (General Language Understanding Evaluation): CoLA (8.5k train), SST-2 (67k train), MRPC (3.7k train), STS-B (7k train), QQP (364k train), MNLI (393k train), QNLI (108k train), RTE (2.5k train), WNLI (634 train); SNLI (Stanford Natural Language Inference, 549k train / 9.8k dev / 9.8k test); SciTail (Science Textual Entailment, 23.5k train / 1.3k dev / 2.1k test)
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Matthews correlation coefficient (CoLA)', 'Classification Accuracy (SST-2, RTE, WNLI, QNLI, SNLI, SciTail)', 'Accuracy and F1 score (MRPC, QQP)', 'Pearson and Spearman correlation coefficients (STS-B)', 'Matched and mismatched accuracy (MNLI-m/mm)', 'GLUE benchmark macro average score'], 'baselines': ['BiLSTM+ELMo+Attn (Wang et al., 2018)', 'Single-task Pretrain Transformer / GPT (Radford et al., 2018)', 'GPT on STILTs (Phang et al., 2018)', 'BERT-Base and BERT-Large (Devlin et al., 2018)', 'ST-DNN (Single-Task DNN ablation with SAN answer module and pairwise ranking loss without multi-task refinement)', 'MT-DNN without fine-tuning (direct multi-task evaluation)'], 'benchmark_results': {'GLUE_Test_Score': {'MT-DNN': 82.7, 'BERT-Large': 80.5, 'Human_Performance': 87.1}, 'SNLI_Test_Accuracy': {'MT-DNN-Large': 91.6, 'BERT-Large': 91.0, 'GPT': 89.9}, 'SciTail_Test_Accuracy': {'MT-DNN-Large': 95.0, 'BERT-Large': 94.4, 'BERT-Base': 92.0}, 'Domain_Adaptation_SNLI_0.1%_Data': {'MT-DNN': 82.1, 'BERT': 52.5}, 'Domain_Adaptation_SciTail_0.1%_Data': {'MT-DNN': 81.9, 'BERT': 51.2}}}
key_findings: MT-DNN achieves new state-of-the-art results on 10 NLU tasks across three major benchmarks (SNLI, SciTail, and 8 of 9 GLUE tasks), pushing the overall GLUE benchmark score to 82.7% (a 2.2% absolute improvement over BERT-Large).; Multi-task learning provides a strong regularization effect that mitigates task-specific overfitting and yields universal representations that transfer effectively across diverse downstream tasks.; Multi-task learning delivers the most substantial performance gains on tasks with small amounts of in-domain training data (such as RTE and MRPC compared to MNLI and QQP).; Representations learned by MT-DNN enable superior domain adaptation and sample efficiency, achieving 82.1% accuracy on SNLI and 81.9% accuracy on SciTail with only 0.1% of domain training samples, substantially outperforming BERT (52.5% and 51.2% respectively).; Formulating QNLI as a pairwise learning-to-rank task rather than binary classification significantly improves answer ranking accuracy.; Incorporating specialized task architectures like the Stochastic Answer Network (SAN) answer module into the representation framework improves pairwise text classification performance over standard linear classification heads.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Evaluated exclusively on English-language natural language understanding tasks spanning classification, similarity scoring, and ranking, excluding text generation, sequence labeling, multilingual tasks, and multimodal domains.', 'Restricted shared layer initializations to pre-trained BERT-Base and BERT-Large checkpoints with WordPiece tokenization and a maximum sequence length limit of 512 tokens.', 'Delimited domain adaptation experiments to textual entailment benchmarks (SNLI and SciTail) evaluated across discrete subsampling splits (0.1%, 1.0%, 10%, and 100%).', 'Employed hard parameter sharing across lower Transformer layers with task-specific output heads, without investigating soft parameter sharing or dynamic routing mechanisms.']
limitations_summary: MT-DNN underfits unique tasks such as CoLA during multi-task training because isolated task definitions and small sample sizes prevent the model from benefiting from cross-task transfer without dedicated fine-tuning. In addition, MT-DNN does not explicitly model task relatedness or structured linguistic priors, does not surpass majority voting on the problematic WNLI dataset, and lacks verified defense against adversarial perturbations.
limitations_verbatim: Our analysis shows that CoLA is a challenge task with much smaller in-domain data than other tasks, and its task definition and dataset are unique among all GLUE tasks, making it difficult to benefit from the knowledge learned from other tasks. As a result, MTL tends to underfit the CoLA dataset. In such a case, fine-tuning is necessary to boost the performance.
generalizability_gap: The MT-DNN framework was evaluated exclusively on standard English NLU benchmarks (GLUE, SNLI, SciTail) with sequence lengths up to 512 tokens; the authors did not test generalization to non-English languages, cross-lingual transfer settings, low-resource dialects, long-document understanding, conversational dialogue systems, or generative sequence-to-sequence tasks.
methodological_gap: MT-DNN employs uniform mini-batch sampling without dynamic task weighting or formal task covariance modeling to balance gradients and mitigate negative transfer; the hard parameter sharing framework treats all Transformer layers uniformly across tasks without adaptive routing; and the training procedure does not incorporate explicit syntactic or semantic linguistic structures or verify robustness against adversarial perturbations.
future_work: Developing a deeper understanding of model structure sharing in multi-task learning.; Designing more effective training methods that leverage task relatedness among multiple tasks for both multi-task pre-training and fine-tuning.; Incorporating the linguistic structure of text into representation learning in a more explicit and controllable manner.; Verifying and improving the resilience and robustness of MT-DNN against adversarial attacks.

title: Multi-Task Learning Using Uncertainty to Weigh Losses for Scene Geometry and Semantics
authors: Alex Kendall; Yarin Gal; Roberto Cipolla
venue: Proceedings of the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
domain: Computer Vision — monocular scene understanding with joint pixel-wise depth regression, semantic segmentation, and instance segmentation from a single RGB image for real-time robotics
problem_statement: Multi-task deep learning performance is highly sensitive to manual relative weighting of task losses with different scales and units (e.g., meters vs. classification logits), making naive weighted sums w_i L_i expensive to tune by grid search and prohibitive for real-time scene understanding where geometry and semantics must be learned jointly.
theoretical_framework: Probabilistic homoscedastic (task-dependent) uncertainty where observation noise σ captures task noise independent of input; maximizing Gaussian likelihood for regression and scaled softmax (Boltzmann/temperature) likelihood for classification yields principled weighting terms 1/(2σ²) L + log σ that automatically balance losses.
methodology: Derivation of multi-task likelihood factorizing p(y1,…,yK|f^W(x)) = ∏ p(y_k|f^W(x)) and negative log-likelihood. For two regressions: L = 1/(2σ1²)||y1-f||² + 1/(2σ2²)||y2-f||² + log σ1σ2. For classification: scaled softmax p(y=c|f,σ)=Softmax(1/σ² f) giving L ≈ 1/σ² CE + log σ via approximation Σ exp(1/σ² f) ≈ (Σ exp f)^{1/σ²}. Combined regression+classification: L(W,σ1,σ2) ≈ 1/(2σ1²)L1 + 1/σ2² L2 + log σ1 + log σ2, trained by regressing log variance s=log σ² for numerical stability. Architecture uses ResNet101 + ASPP encoder (DeepLabV3, output stride 8) shared across tasks followed by task-specific decoders (3×3 conv 256 + 1×1 output): cross-entropy for semantic segmentation, L1 on instance centroid vectors x̂_n with OPTICS clustering for instance segmentation, and L1 on metric inverse depth (sky set to zero) for depth, averaging losses over labelled pixels per batch.
datasets: CityScapes — 2,975 training and 500 validation stereo images at 2048×1024 (train downsampled to 128×256 and 256×512 for ablations, full resolution for benchmark), with 20-class semantic labels, instance masks for 8 instance classes, disparity from SGM stereo treated as pseudo inverse-depth ground truth (22 cm baseline, fine weather cities), 1,525 test images held out for online server
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Semantic segmentation: mean Intersection over Union (IoU class and category, higher better) and instance-weighted IoU', 'Instance segmentation: mean pixel error between predicted and ground-truth instance centroid vectors [px], and Average Precision AP, AP50%, AP100m, AP50m', 'Depth: mean error [px] and RMS error [px] on inverse depth versus SGM disparity', 'Weight robustness and training dynamics: loss weight trajectories and sensitivity to initialization'], 'baselines': ['Single-task models trained individually for each of the three tasks', 'Unweighted sum with w_i=0.333 each', 'Approximately optimal grid-searched weights (0.89 semantic, 0.01 instance, 0.1 depth on Tiny CityScapes)', 'Pairwise task combinations with uncertainty weighting (2-task) versus all three tasks (3-task)', 'State-of-the-art single-task specialists: Uhrig et al. for semantic+instance, Mask R-CNN, Deep Watershed, R-CNN+MCG for instance only, DeepLabV3, PSPNet, Adelaide for semantic only'], 'architectures': ['ResNet101 + ASPP shared encoder (DeepLabV3) plus task-specific decoders, compared under identical encoder capacity; ablations at 128×256 over 50k iterations, final benchmark at full 1024×2048']}
key_findings: Naive uniform weighting (0.333 each) degrades semantic IoU to 50.1% below single-task 59.4%, while learned uncertainty weighting on all three tasks improves to 63.4% IoU, 3.50 px instance error, and 0.522 mean inverse depth error, outperforming single-task models on all tasks.; Approximate grid-searched optimal weights (62.8% IoU, 0.549 depth error) are still inferior to learned 3-task uncertainty weighting (63.4%, 0.522), because uncertainty weights are dynamic during training (final ratio 43:1:0.16 for semantic:depth:instance) and not limited by search grid resolution, with uncertainty steadily decreasing during training.; Figure 2 demonstrates that at optimal manual weighting the joint model beats separate models, but nearby weightings degrade one task; uncertainty weighting automatically finds that optimum without expensive search and is robust to initialization, converging in a few hundred iterations.; Two-task uncertainty models already beat single tasks (e.g., semantic+depth 62.7% IoU / 0.533 depth versus 59.4% single), and three-task joint learning further improves over any pair, showing complementary regularization: depth cues help segmentation smoothness and vice versa.; On CityScapes test benchmark at full resolution, the single unified model achieves 78.5 class IoU / 57.4 instance-weighted IoU / 89.9 category IoU and performs competitively on instance and depth (77.7 category iIoU, 21.6 AP) while being the first to address all three tasks jointly in real time, reducing computation versus three separate models.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Evaluated exclusively on CityScapes road scenes (German cities, fine weather, same sensor) at 128×256 for ablations and 1024×2048 for benchmark, not on indoor NYU, Mapillary, or non-vision domains.', 'Jointly learned only three tasks with fixed definitions (semantic cross-entropy, instance centroid L1 with OPTICS clustering, inverse depth L1 with sky zero) and not surface normals, optical flow, or other classifications.', 'Compared only uniform, grid-searched, and homoscedastic uncertainty weightings; did not compare to later gradient-based methods (GradNorm, PCGrad, CAGrad) which postdate this work.', 'Assumed homoscedastic (input-independent) uncertainty and factorized likelihood across tasks, ignoring heteroscedastic per-pixel uncertainty and task correlations.']
limitations_summary: Authors acknowledge that multitask weighting may lack a single optimal solution and pose multitask learning as potentially ill-posed without a higher-level objective; they also raise open questions about optimal encoder/decoder split depth and why certain task pairs (semantics+depth) outperform others, without providing those answers.
limitations_verbatim: There are many interesting questions left unanswered. Firstly, our results show that there is usually not a single optimal weighting for all tasks. Therefore, what is the optimal weighting? Is multitask learning is an ill-posed optimisation problem without a single higher-level goal?
generalizability_gap: No evaluation on code-switched, multilingual, or low-resource text, on indoor scenes, or on transformer-based language models; homoscedastic weighting not tested outside geometry+semantics vision tasks or on noisy user-generated data, limiting claims for disaster tweet, code-switch, or NLP multi-task settings surveyed elsewhere in this repository.
methodological_gap: Homoscedastic uncertainty captures only task-dependent constant noise, not input-dependent heteroscedastic noise, task relationships, or gradient conflicts; the softmax temperature scaling relies on approximation Σ exp(1/σ² f) ≈ (Σ exp f)^{1/σ²} which is exact only as σ→1, and instance segmentation relies on separate OPTICS clustering post-processing rather than end-to-end learning, with depth evaluated against noisy SGM pseudo ground truth rather than LiDAR.
future_work: Investigating whether a single optimal weighting exists or whether multitask learning is inherently ill-posed without a higher-level objective.; Determining optimal shared encoder depth and split point into task-specific decoders for balancing shared versus task-specific capacity.; Quantifying task relationships to predict which task combinations are complementary for representation learning.
