title: Multi-Task Learning as Multi-Objective Optimization
authors: Ozan Sener; Vladlen Koltun
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2018)
domain: Multi-Task Deep Learning and Multi-Objective Optimization (Computer Vision)
problem_statement: Multi-task learning (MTL) is inherently a multi-objective optimization problem because tasks often compete and conflict for model capacity. Existing MTL methods commonly minimize a weighted linear combination of per-task losses, which requires expensive grid searches or heuristics and is only theoretically valid when tasks do not compete, failing to model task trade-offs and achieve Pareto optimality in high-dimensional deep networks.
theoretical_framework: Gradient-based multi-objective optimization and Pareto optimality via Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, leveraging the Multiple-Gradient Descent Algorithm (MGDA) and Frank-Wolfe optimization, along with an upper-bound formulation (MGDA-UB) proving that optimizing representations yields Pareto stationary solutions when the representation Jacobian is full-rank.
methodology: The authors formulate multi-task learning as multi-objective optimization to find Pareto optimal solutions. They adapt the Multiple Gradient Descent Algorithm (MGDA) using a Frank-Wolfe optimizer with an exact analytical line search to solve the quadratic min-norm optimization in the convex hull of task gradients. To avoid scaling linearly with task count and gradient dimensions, they propose MGDA-UB (Multiple Gradient Descent Algorithm – Upper Bound) for encoder-decoder architectures, which bounds the shared parameter objective by the norm of representation gradients using the chain rule. MGDA-UB optimizes representation gradients via a single backward pass over shared parameters, provably converging to a Pareto stationary point or a common descent direction assuming the Jacobian of the shared representation is full-rank.
datasets: MultiMNIST (MTL adaptation of MNIST with 60,000 overlaid digit image pairs for top-left and bottom-right classification tasks); CelebA (CelebFaces Attributes dataset with 200,000 face images annotated with 40 binary attribute classification tasks); Cityscapes (urban scene understanding dataset with pixel-level annotations for 19-class semantic segmentation, instance segmentation via center voting, and monocular depth estimation/disparity); ImageNet (used for pretraining the ResNet-50 shared encoder backbone for Cityscapes)
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Classification accuracy (%) on top-left digit (task-L) and bottom-right digit (task-R) for MultiMNIST', 'Mean classification error (%) and attribute-wise binary classification error (%) across 40 facial attributes for CelebA', 'Mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) for semantic segmentation on Cityscapes', 'Mean Squared Error (MSE) of normalized pixel-level center offset regression for instance segmentation on Cityscapes', 'Mean Squared Error (MSE) of disparity estimation for depth estimation on Cityscapes', 'Wall-clock training time (seconds/hours) and GPU computational acceleration factor'], 'baselines': ['Uniform scaling (minimizing a uniformly weighted sum of loss functions)', 'Single-task networks (solving each task independently with dedicated models)', 'Grid search (exhaustive evaluation of static loss weight combinations)', 'Uncertainty weighting (homoscedastic task uncertainty weighting by Kendall et al., 2018)', 'GradNorm (gradient normalization algorithm by Chen et al., 2018)', 'MGDA without approximation (full-parameter multiple gradient descent algorithm)'], 'architectures': ['LeNet-based encoder with two task-specific fully-connected classification heads (MultiMNIST)', 'ResNet-18 shared backbone (without final layer) with 40 task-specific 2048x2 linear heads (CelebA)', 'Fully-convolutional ResNet-50 shared encoder with three task-specific Pyramid Pooling Module (PPM) decoders (Cityscapes)']}
key_findings: Formulating multi-task learning as multi-objective optimization with MGDA enables deep networks to find Pareto optimal solutions that effectively manage task trade-offs when tasks compete for model capacity.; On MultiMNIST, where competing tasks cause static scaling and heuristic weighting (Uncertainty Weighting, GradNorm) to underperform, MGDA-UB achieves digit classification accuracies comparable to dedicated single-task models (96.2% on task-L and 95.3% on task-R).; On the 40-task CelebA benchmark, MGDA-UB outperforms uniform scaling, single-task learning, uncertainty weighting, and GradNorm across the vast majority of attribute classification tasks, achieving the lowest average category error (8.95%).; On Cityscapes scene understanding, joint multi-task learning with MGDA-UB surpasses single-task and heuristic baselines across semantic segmentation (66.60 mIoU), instance segmentation (0.0104 MSE), and disparity estimation (0.0146 MSE).; MGDA-UB eliminates the computational bottleneck of standard MGDA by computing gradients with respect to shared representations via a single backward pass, accelerating training by 40% on Cityscapes (3 tasks) and by a factor of 25 on CelebA (40 tasks).; MGDA-UB achieves equal or slightly superior empirical accuracy compared to full-parameter MGDA because computing gradients in a lower-dimensional representation space reduces SGD gradient estimation variance and improves optimization stability.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Restricts theoretical guarantees and computational acceleration of MGDA-UB specifically to encoder-decoder and shared-trunk deep neural network architectures where task losses depend on a shared intermediate representation.', 'Assumes the Jacobian matrix of the shared representation with respect to shared parameters (dZ/d_theta_sh) is full rank to guarantee equivalence to Pareto stationarity.', 'Focuses on hard parameter sharing setups with gradient-based multi-objective optimization rather than soft parameter sharing or Bayesian prior regularization.', 'Evaluates on computer vision tasks (digit classification, facial attribute prediction, and dense scene understanding) with task counts ranging from 2 to 40.']
limitations_summary: Standard gradient-based multi-objective optimization (MGDA) scales poorly with gradient dimensionality and scales linearly with the number of tasks due to requiring separate backward passes for each task. Although the MGDA-UB approximation mitigates this, it relies on an encoder-decoder structure and assumes the representation Jacobian matrix is full rank.
limitations_verbatim: However, there are two technical problems that hinder the applicability of MGDA on a large scale. (i) The underlying optimization problem does not scale gracefully to high-dimensional gradients, which arise naturally in deep networks. (ii) The algorithm requires explicit computation of gradients per task, which results in linear scaling of the number of backward passes and roughly multiplies the training time by the number of tasks.
generalizability_gap: The proposed method was evaluated exclusively on computer vision benchmarks (MultiMNIST, CelebA, and Cityscapes); the authors did not evaluate the approach on natural language processing, speech recognition, reinforcement learning, cross-modal learning, or large-scale foundation models.
methodological_gap: The MGDA-UB formulation is restricted to shared representation (encoder-decoder) architectures and requires the representation Jacobian to be non-singular (full rank); additionally, the method optimizes for arbitrary Pareto stationary points rather than allowing practitioners to target specific trade-off preferences along the Pareto front.
future_work: Extending gradient-based multi-objective optimization and representation-level bounds to non-vision domains such as natural language processing, speech processing, and multi-agent reinforcement learning.; Developing multi-objective optimization algorithms for complex multi-task architectures beyond encoder-decoder structures, such as branched networks or soft parameter sharing.; Investigating methods to steer multi-objective optimization toward specific desired trade-off regions or target points along the Pareto front.

title: Multi-Task Learning as a Bargaining Game
authors: Aviv Navon; Aviv Shamsian; Idan Achituve; Haggai Maron; Kenji Kawaguchi; Gal Chechik; Ethan Fetaya
venue: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)
domain: Multi-Task Learning across vision (NYUv2, CityScapes), molecular property regression (QM9, 11 tasks), and reinforcement learning (Meta-World MT10)
problem_statement: Multi-task learning by joint training often underperforms single-task models because per-task gradients conflict in direction and magnitude, and existing aggregation heuristics (MGDA, PCGrad, CAGrad) lack a principled axiomatic foundation and may converge to arbitrary Pareto points or be dominated by large-gradient tasks, raising the need for a proportionally fair, scale-invariant gradient combination method.
theoretical_framework: Cooperative bargaining game where each task is a player with linear utility u_i(Δθ)=g_i^T Δθ for update Δθ in ball B centered at 0; Nash Bargaining Solution uniquely satisfies Pareto optimality, symmetry, independence of irrelevant alternatives, and invariance to affine transformations, yielding proportionally fair direction α solving G^T G α = 1/α with G the gradient matrix.
methodology: Nash-MTL: at each step compute task gradients g_i = ∇ℓ_i(θ), form G, solve G^T G α = 1/α (α>0) via sequence of convex surrogates. Define β_i(α)=g_i^T Gα and φ_i(α)=log α_i+log β_i; original concave-constrained problem min Σφ_i s.t. -φ_i≤0 is approximated by convex surrogate min Σ β_i s.t. -φ_i≤0 (often exact), then improved via concave-convex procedure (CCP) adding linearized φ and iterating ≤20 steps (Proposition 3.2 monotonic decrease). Update θ ← θ - η Gα. Practical speedup updates α every T steps instead of every iteration (feature-level gradients were found to degrade performance).
datasets: QM9 — ~130K molecules as graphs with 11 quantum chemical property regression targets, split 110K train / 10K validation / 10K test, targets normalized to zero mean unit variance, trained with message-passing GNN (Gilmer et al.) + set2set pooling for 300 epochs with early stopping on validation Δm; NYUv2 — 1,449 RGB-D indoor images with 13-class semantic segmentation, depth, and surface normal labels, resized for MTAN, evaluated for 200 epochs; CityScapes — 5,000 street-view images at 128×256 (from 2048×1024) for 7-class segmentation and depth, evaluated for 200 epochs; Meta-World MT10 — 10 simulated robotic manipulation tasks (e.g., button press, window open) with Soft Actor-Critic, trained for 2M steps and averaged over 10 seeds
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Per-task metrics: mIoU and Pix Acc for segmentation, Abs/Rel Error for depth, Mean/Median angle distance and within 11.25°/22.5°/30° for normals, mean squared error for QM9 properties, success rate for RL', 'Overall MTL metrics: Mean Rank (MR) across tasks (lower better) and average per-task performance drop Δm % = (1/K) Σ (-1)^{δ_k}(M_{m,k}-M_{b,k})/M_{b,k} versus single-task baseline (STL), where δ_k=1 if higher is better', 'Runtime per episode / per epoch and sensitivity to α-update frequency T'], 'baselines': ['Single-Task Learning (STL) — independent model per task (upper bound)', 'Linear scalarization (LS) — Σ ℓ_k', 'Scale-Invariant (SI) — Σ log ℓ_k (invariant to positive rescaling)', 'Random Loss Weighting (RLW) — normally sampled random weights', 'Dynamic Weight Average (DWA)', 'Uncertainty Weighting (UW, Kendall et al.)', 'Multiple Gradient Descent Algorithm (MGDA, Sener & Koltun)', 'PCGrad (Yu et al.)', 'GradDrop', 'Conflict-Averse Gradient Descent (CAGrad, Liu et al.)', 'Impartial MTL via Gradient (IMTL-G, Liu et al., 2021b) applied at feature level'], 'architectures': ['GNN with message-passing layers + Vinyals pooling for QM9 (from Fey & Lenssen PyTorch Geometric)', 'Multi-Task Attention Network (MTAN) on SegNet for NYUv2 and CityScapes (Adam 1e-4, halved after 100 epochs) with STL SegNet baseline', 'Shared backbone + task-specific heads for MT10 with SAC']}
key_findings: Nash-MTL achieves state-of-the-art overall trade-off: on QM9 MR 2.5 and Δm 62.0% ±1.4 versus next best SI 4.0/77.2% and IMTL-G 4.7/77.2%, with LS 6.8/177.6% and CAGrad 5.7/112.8%; most MTL methods fall behind simple scale-invariant baseline due to varying loss scales, demonstrating Nash-MTL’s affine invariance benefit; per-task results in appendix confirm balanced gains.; On NYUv2 Nash-MTL attains 40.13 mIoU / 65.93 Pix Acc / 0.5261 Abs depth / 25.26 Mean angle with MR 1.55 and Δm -4.04% (improvement over STL), outperforming CAGrad (39.79/26.31, Δm 0.20%, MR 3.77) and IMTL-G (39.35, Δm -0.76%, MR 3.11) and dominating MGDA which collapses to 30.47 mIoU while over-optimizing normals.; On CityScapes (2 tasks) where Nash solution reduces to equally weighted normalized gradients, Nash-MTL gets 75.41 mIoU / 0.0129 Abs Err with MR 1.75 and Δm 6.82%, best overall versus IMTL-G 3.62/11.10%, CAGrad 5.37/11.64%, and SI 8.00/14.11%, showing scale-invariant normalized sum is strong yet still below Nash for >2 tasks.; On MT10 Nash-MTL reaches 0.91 ±0.031 success, the only MTL method matching STL SAC (0.90), ahead of CAGrad 0.83, PCGrad 0.72, CARE (which uses language metadata) 0.84, and Soft Modularization 0.73; visualization shows Nash trajectories are balanced across Pareto front while LS/PCGrad/CAGrad are dominated by large-gradient task.; Update direction analysis on three gradients shows Nash yields most balanced projections onto each task gradient; theoretical analysis proves convergence to Pareto stationary point under linear independence (Assumption 5.1), L-smoothness, and boundedness, and to Pareto optimal if losses convex, with step size µ(t)=min_i 1/(L K α_i(t)); α update every 50–100 steps gives 3.7×–9.8× speedup on QM9 and ~10× on MT10 (≈40.7→7.9) with small degradation (e.g., MT10 0.91→0.87) approaching LS/STL runtime.; Ablation of CCP improvements shows single-step surrogate often suffices; using feature-level instead of shared-parameter gradients dramatically degrades performance, so Nash-MTL keeps shared-parameter gradients and sparsifies α updates for efficiency.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Evaluated on modest task counts (K=2 for CityScapes, 3 for NYUv2, 10 for MT10, 11 for QM9) and not on hundreds of tasks; QM9 targets normalized but still limited to molecular graphs.', 'Used fixed MTAN/SegNet and GNN architectures and fixed training schedules (300 epochs QM9, 200 epochs NYUv2/CityScapes, 2M RL steps) with Adam/SAC hyperparameters, not exhaustive architecture search.', 'Required solving K-dimensional convex problem per α update (20 CCP iterations standard, 1 step for MT10) and assumed gradients linearly independent when not Pareto stationary; did not test on language, code-switched, or noisy low-resource text.', 'Compared at feature-vs-parameter gradient level for speedup and chose parameter-level with infrequent updates; did not evaluate fully asynchronous or distributed MTL.']
limitations_summary: Authors note per-step bargaining solution cost is critical for frequent updates and that feature-level surrogate degrades performance, so they resort to infrequent α updates; implicit limitations include dependence on linear-independence assumption, bounded K, and not handling identical-task degeneracy without additional assumptions.
limitations_verbatim: We note that the computational cost of that approximation is critical because this approximation is executed for each gradient update.
generalizability_gap: Not evaluated on code-switched NLP, disaster tweet, or multilingual language model multi-task settings that dominate this repository’s survey; nor on transformer-based large language models, multi-modal vision-language, or code generation domains.
methodological_gap: Relies on linear utilities and ball B around zero, requiring convex compact payoff set; does not compare to recent second-order or adaptive curvature methods beyond first-order gradients, and CCP approximation lacks exactness guarantee for all α despite monotonic objective decrease.
future_work: Extending Nash bargaining to other cooperative game solutions and to alternative disagreement points beyond zero.; Scaling to many-task MTL via more efficient α solvers and exploring per-layer or per-component bargaining.; Applying Nash-MTL to language, multi-modal, and federated multi-task settings and analyzing task grouping under proportional fairness.

title: Multi-Task Learning in Natural Language Processing: An Overview
authors: Shijie Chen; Yu Zhang; Qiang Yang
venue: Association for Computing Machinery
domain: Natural Language Processing, Multi-Task Learning, Deep Learning, Pre-trained Language Models
problem_statement: Deep neural models and pre-trained language models in natural language processing frequently encounter overfitting, data scarcity, and excessive computational adaptation costs when researchers train the models on isolated downstream tasks.
theoretical_framework: Multi-Task Learning (MTL) principles wherein sharing inductive bias and complementary representations across related tasks improves model generalization and reduces sample complexity compared to isolated single-task learning.
methodology: A comprehensive literature review and taxonomic categorization analyzing multi-task learning across four primary architectural paradigms (parallel, hierarchical, modular, and generative adversarial), multi-task optimization strategies (loss construction, gradient regularization, data sampling, and task scheduling), downstream application areas (auxiliary MTL and joint MTL), and benchmark datasets.
key_findings: Multi-task learning architectures in natural language processing divide systematically into parallel architectures, hierarchical architectures, modular architectures, and generative adversarial architectures.; Modular multi-task learning mechanisms, including parameter-efficient adapters, prefix tuning, and hypernetworks, attain performance comparable to full model fine-tuning while reducing trainable parameter counts and storage requirements.; Optimization techniques such as uncertainty-based sampling, dynamic task scheduling, and gradient regularization prevent catastrophic forgetting and mitigate negative transfer across heterogeneous tasks.; Task relatedness substantially influences multi-task learning outcomes, where auxiliary tasks with high label entropy and balanced distributions provide greater performance gains than unrelated tasks.; Multi-task learning effectively alleviates data scarcity in low-resource languages and specialized domains by transferring shared representations from data-rich auxiliary tasks.
scope_and_delimitations: ['The authors focus specifically on the application of multi-task learning to downstream natural language processing tasks rather than general pre-training objectives.', 'The authors restrict the architectural taxonomy primarily to multi-task models containing task-specific trainable parameters, excluding general instruction tuning without task-specific parameters.', 'The authors examine deep learning approaches and exclude non-neural multi-task learning methods.']
limitations_summary: The authors identify that determining optimal task combinations and establishing a formal understanding of task relatedness remain immature and unresolved challenges in multi-task learning.
limitations_verbatim: Firstly, given multiple NLP tasks, how to find a set of tasks that could take advantage of MTL remains a challenge. Besides improving performance of MTL models, a deeper understanding of task relatedness could also help expanding the application of MTL to more tasks. Though there are some works studying this issue, as discussed in Section 4.4, they are far from mature.
generalizability_gap: Existing research evaluates multi-task learning primarily on high-resource languages and standard benchmark tasks, leaving multi-task transfer in low-resource languages, multimodal environments, and interactive dialogue systems under-explored.
methodological_gap: Current large pre-trained language models predominantly employ basic feature-sharing architectures during training, and existing task selection heuristics lack standardized quantitative metrics and theoretical guarantees across diverse task spaces.
future_work: Developing theoretical and empirical frameworks to quantify task relatedness and systematically select beneficial task combinations.; Incorporating self-supervised and unsupervised learning techniques into multi-task learning to exploit unlabeled data and reduce dependence on human annotations.; Designing advanced multi-task architectures beyond simple feature sharing to improve pre-trained language models.; Extending multi-task learning to complex downstream applications, including dialogue systems and multimodal vision-language tasks.

title: Multitask Learning
authors: Rich Caruana
venue: Machine Learning
domain: Machine Learning, Inductive Transfer, and Neural Network Architectures
problem_statement: Traditional machine learning algorithms train isolated models on individual tasks, discarding domain-specific inductive signals present in related tasks and incurring redundant computation.
theoretical_framework: Inductive Transfer, Representation Learning, and Hard Parameter Sharing
methodology: Parallel joint training of multiple task objectives over a shared hidden representation using backpropagation in neural networks, kernel regression, and k-nearest neighbor algorithms.
datasets: 1D ALVINN autonomous road-following dataset; Medical pneumonia risk prediction database; Synthetic Boolean decision problems
evaluation: Empirical comparison of generalization error, root mean squared error (RMSE), and classification accuracy between isolated single-task learning and shared multi-task learning models.
key_findings: Proved that joint multi-task training over a shared hidden representation provides an inductive bias that improves generalization performance on primary tasks.; Formalized the hard parameter sharing architecture, demonstrating that sharing intermediate hidden representations amortizes computation across multiple tasks.; Identified mechanisms of inductive transfer, including statistical data amplification, feature eavesdropping, representation bias, and attribute selection.
scope_and_delimitations: Focuses on hard parameter sharing in feedforward multi-layer perceptrons, kernel regression, and k-nearest neighbor methods.
limitations_summary: Identified the risk of negative transfer when joint tasks have conflicting gradient directions or unrelated domain signals.
limitations_verbatim: If tasks are not sufficiently related, training them together can cause negative transfer where performance on one or more tasks degrades relative to single-task learning.
generalizability_gap: Evaluated on small-scale MLP and regression architectures; does not investigate modern deep Transformer encoders or multi-task gradient conflict optimization algorithms.
methodological_gap: Used equal loss weighting; did not explore dynamic loss balancing, gradient surgery, or multi-objective Pareto optimization methods.
future_work: Investigation of task relationship discovery algorithms and methods to dynamically mitigate negative transfer in large-scale multi-task architectures.

title: NTKMTL: Mitigating Task Imbalance in Multi-Task Learning from Neural Tangent Kernel Perspective
authors: Xiaohan Qin; Xiaoxing Wang; Ning Liao; Junchi Yan
venue: Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
domain: Multi-task learning across multi-task computer vision dense prediction, molecular property regression, facial attribute classification, and multi-task reinforcement learning.
problem_statement: Task imbalance in multi-task learning causes certain tasks to dominate shared parameter updates while other tasks suffer from insufficient optimization due to differing convergence speeds and loss dynamics.
theoretical_framework: Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) theory and spectral analysis of gradient flow ordinary differential equations, which model convergence speeds of individual tasks through the eigenvalues of an extended multi-task NTK matrix.
methodology: NTKMTL constructs an extended Neural Tangent Kernel matrix across tasks and normalizes task loss weights inversely proportional to the square root of the maximum eigenvalue of each task-specific NTK matrix scaled by the average maximum eigenvalue; NTKMTL-SR accelerates computation by calculating the NTK matrix over shared representations rather than full network parameters.
datasets: NYUv2 (indoor scene understanding benchmark with 3 dense prediction tasks: 13-class semantic segmentation, depth estimation, and surface normal prediction; 795 train / 654 test images); Cityscapes (urban scene understanding benchmark with 2 dense prediction tasks: 7-class semantic segmentation and depth estimation; downsampled to 128×256); CelebA (large-scale facial attribute dataset with over 200,000 images evaluated across 40 binary attribute classification tasks); QM9 (quantum chemistry molecular property regression benchmark containing over 130,000 organic molecules as graphs with 11 property prediction tasks); Meta-World MT10 (multi-task reinforcement learning benchmark comprising 10 robotic manipulation environments evaluated with Soft Actor-Critic)
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Mean Rank (MR)', 'Average per-task performance drop relative to single-task learning baseline (Δm%)', 'Semantic segmentation mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) and pixel accuracy', 'Depth estimation absolute error and relative error', 'Surface normal mean error, median error, and percentage within angular thresholds (11.25°, 22.5°, 30°)', 'Mean Absolute Error (MAE) across 11 quantum chemical regression properties', 'Multi-attribute classification accuracy across 40 facial attributes', 'Success rate across 10 robotic manipulation tasks'], 'baselines': ['Single-task learning (STL)', 'Linear Scalarization (LS)', 'Scale-Invariant (SI)', 'Dynamic Weight Average (DWA)', 'Uncertainty Weighting (UW)', 'Multi-Gradient Descent Algorithm (MGDA)', 'Random Loss Weighting (RLW)', 'PCGrad', 'GradDrop', 'CAGrad', 'IMTL-G', 'Nash-MTL', 'MoCo', 'Aligned-MTL', 'SDMGrad', 'DB-MTL', 'STCH', 'FAMO', 'FairGrad', 'GO4Align', 'Multi-task SAC (MTL SAC)', 'Multi-task SAC with Task Encoder (MTL SAC + TE)', 'Multi-headed SAC (MH SAC)'], 'architectures': ['SegNet-based Multi-Task Attention Network (MTAN) for NYUv2 and Cityscapes', '9-layer Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) with task-specific linear heads for CelebA', 'Message Passing Neural Network (MPNN) with Set2Set pooling for QM9', 'Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) multi-layer perceptron policy network for Meta-World MT10']}
key_findings: The convergence speed of each task in multi-task learning is governed by the eigenvalues of its task-specific Neural Tangent Kernel matrix, leading to spectral bias where tasks with larger eigenvalues dominate training.; Weighting tasks inversely proportional to the square root of their maximum NTK eigenvalue balances convergence speeds across tasks and mitigates task imbalance.; NTKMTL achieves state-of-the-art performance on the NYUv2 dense prediction benchmark with a mean rank of 4.33 and a relative performance drop of -6.99%, outperforming single-task learning across all three tasks.; On Cityscapes, NTKMTL achieves balanced performance across semantic segmentation and depth estimation, securing the lowest relative performance drop of 1.92%.; On the CelebA 40-task benchmark, NTKMTL achieves an overall improvement over single-task learning (Δm% of -0.77%), outperforming all previous multi-task baselines.; NTKMTL-SR uses shared representations to achieve training speeds comparable to loss-oriented linear scalarization while attaining state-of-the-art results on the QM9 11-task regression benchmark (mean rank 4.00, Δm% 30.7%).; The authors identified that prior QM9 multi-task benchmarks suffered from premature learning rate decay in the shared codebase; re-evaluating baselines under adjusted scheduler parameters significantly improved convergence across all methods.; NTKMTL generalizes effectively to multi-task reinforcement learning on the Meta-World MT10 benchmark, achieving a 0.96 success rate.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Evaluated on supervised multi-task learning (2 to 40 tasks) and multi-task reinforcement learning (10 tasks).', 'Focuses optimization weight derivations primarily on the diagonal task-specific blocks of the extended NTK matrix.', 'NTKMTL uses mini-batch size n=1 for shared parameter calculations, while NTKMTL-SR uses mini-batch size n=4 on shared representations.', 'Model architectures are restricted to SegNet-based MTAN for dense vision, 9-layer CNN for facial classification, MPNN for molecular regression, and SAC for robotic RL.', 'All computational benchmarks were executed on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU.']
limitations_summary: The task weight design focuses strictly on the diagonal task-specific blocks of the extended NTK matrix rather than modeling cross-task interactions or synergies represented in the off-diagonal blocks; full NTKMTL incurs computational overhead requiring gradient computation across mini-batches, while its fast shared-representation variant (NTKMTL-SR) is challenging to apply in environments such as reinforcement learning where models do not cleanly separate into shared backbones and task-specific heads.
limitations_verbatim:
In this work, we proposed the extended NTK Ke for MTL as a tool for more comprehensive analysis of training dynamics across tasks. The weight design of our current method mainly focuses on the analysis of the task-specific NTK matrices Kii. The full structure

of the extended NTK matrix Ke offers further analytical opportunities. For example, analyzing the off-diagonal Kij blocks could reveal novel insights into task interactions or guide the development of task grouping strategies. These potential avenues are left for future investigation.
generalizability_gap: The authors did not evaluate the method on natural language processing tasks, large language models, multi-modal foundation models, or non-stationary online environments.
methodological_gap: The weight calculation considers only the maximum eigenvalue of each task-specific NTK block rather than the full eigenvalue spectrum or off-diagonal task-interaction blocks, requires computing gradients across multiple mini-batches for full NTKMTL, and assumes a separable shared-representation architecture that limits NTKMTL-SR in policy networks.
future_work: Analyzing the off-diagonal blocks Kij of the extended NTK matrix to model inter-task interactions.; Developing task grouping and task clustering strategies based on the full structure of the extended NTK matrix.; Extending shared representation approximations to policy architectures in multi-task reinforcement learning.

title: Low-supervision urgency detection and transfer in short crisis messages
authors: Mayank Kejriwal; Peilin Zhou
venue: Proceedings of the 2019 IEEE/ACM International Conference on Advances in Social Networks Analysis and Mining (ASONAM 2019)
domain: Crisis Informatics, Disaster Response, Social Media NLP (Twitter), Low-Supervision Machine Learning, Transfer Learning
problem_statement: How to semi-automatically detect urgency in short crisis messages on social media with minimal supervision when only a small labeled dataset and an unlabeled background corpus exist, and how to effectively transfer urgency knowledge across disparate crisis events in immediate post-disaster scenarios where no target background corpus is available.
theoretical_framework: Multi-source feature ensembling combining domain-specific heuristic keyword indicators, local unsupervised subword-aware representations (fastText skip-gram), and generalized out-of-domain embeddings (pre-trained Wikipedia skip-gram); instance-based transfer learning via target up-sampling to mitigate domain shift and concept drift across heterogeneous disaster domains.
methodology: A minimally supervised urgency classification pipeline evaluating two operational crisis settings: (1) Single-crisis low-supervision setting: Tweets undergo preprocessing (tokenization, stripping '@' mentions, 'RT' prefixes, special suffixes, non-alphanumeric characters, and converting to lowercase), followed by extracting an 11-dimensional manual feature vector (10 domain-specific keyword presence indicators: hit, help, kill, injure, strand, miss, urgent, die, need, food, plus 1 numeric digit presence indicator), training local fastText skip-gram word and sentence embeddings on the in-domain unlabeled background corpus, and extracting 300-dimensional pre-trained Wikipedia fastText embeddings. Three separate Linear Regression models are trained on each respective feature set and combined into a weighted ensemble calibrated on a held-out validation set. (2) Cross-crisis transfer learning setting (Algorithm 1): For a new target crisis lacking a background corpus, local fastText embeddings are trained on the auxiliary source crisis corpus, target manual features are extracted, and the small labeled target dataset is up-sampled by a factor of 6x before mixing with labeled source data to train three Linear Regression models whose predictions are combined via unweighted score averaging.
datasets: Nepal Dataset - Tweets collected in the aftermath of the 2015 Nepal earthquake (Gorkha earthquake) via the DARPA LORELEI program, comprising a balanced labeled subset of 400 tweets (curated via iterative active learning) and an unlabeled background corpus; Kerala Dataset - Tweets collected in the aftermath of the 2018 Kerala floods in South India, comprising an imbalanced labeled subset of 400 tweets (curated via active learning) and a large unlabeled background corpus; Macedonia Dataset - Information-dense dataset from a live-action disaster simulation in Macedonia in late 2018 via the DARPA LORELEI program, consisting of 205 messages all labeled as urgent or non-urgent without an unlabeled background corpus
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Accuracy', 'Precision', 'Recall', 'F-Measure (harmonic mean of precision and recall)', "One-sided Student's paired t-test across 10 experimental trials against the Local baseline"], 'rq1_low_supervision_results': {'nepal_f_measure': '69.44% (significant at p < 0.01 over Local baseline)', 'kerala_f_measure': 'Demonstrates statistically significant improvements over individual feature representations on imbalanced data'}, 'rq2_transfer_learning_results': {'transfer_configurations': ['Nepal (source) -> Macedonia (target)', 'Kerala (source) -> Macedonia (target)', 'Nepal (source) -> Kerala (target)', 'Kerala (source) -> Nepal (target)'], 'observations': 'Transfer methods outperform target-only Local baselines across almost all metrics; target up-sampling (6x) improves transfer robustness; source-target instance mixing achieves a 2.0% to 2.7% F-Measure improvement over up-sampling alone in two configurations'}}
key_findings: Combining manual keyword features, local unsupervised fastText embeddings, and pre-trained Wikipedia embeddings in a linear regression ensemble significantly outperforms individual feature representations and local baselines for low-supervision urgency detection (achieving 69.44% F-Measure on the Nepal dataset at 99% statistical significance).; Local background embeddings substantially improve recall and accuracy, whereas manual keyword heuristics elevate precision, confirming that multi-source feature ensembling effectively balances precision-recall trade-offs in short crisis message classification.; Pre-trained Wikipedia embeddings act as an effective free regularizer that stabilizes model performance and enhances generalization without requiring additional labeled or domain-specific unlabeled data.; In immediate post-disaster settings lacking target background corpora, transferring word embeddings from an auxiliary source disaster combined with 6x target up-sampling consistently exceeds target-only local baselines.; Cross-crisis transfer learning achieves lower overall performance than single-crisis training with target background corpora (for example, Nepal F-Measure decreases from over 69% in single-crisis training to 62.5% when transferring from Kerala) due to domain shift and disaster-specific vocabulary variations.; Mixing labeled source and target instances provides diminishing performance gains (2.0% to 2.7% F-Measure improvement over target up-sampling alone in two out of four transfer configurations).
scope_and_delimitations: ['Restricted crisis communications exclusively to English-language short messages and tweets across three disaster events (2015 Nepal earthquake, 2018 Kerala floods, and 2018 Macedonia disaster simulation).', 'Delimited classification objective strictly to binary urgency detection (urgent versus non-urgent).', 'Delimited classification architectures to Linear Regression models over static manual keyword indicators and fastText sentence embeddings, excluding deep transformer neural networks.', 'Delimited target labeled data acquisition in transfer learning scenarios to a maximum of 400 actively sampled instances without an in-domain target background corpus.']
limitations_summary: The transfer learning methodology yields diminishing returns when combining source and target labeled data, providing only modest F-Measure improvements (2.0% to 2.7%) over target up-sampling alone in two of four transfer settings. Additionally, cross-crisis transfer performance remains consistently lower than single-crisis models trained on in-domain background corpora because of domain shift and vocabulary divergences across distinct disaster types. The system also relies on manually engineered keyword indicators that introduce noise and shallow fastText embeddings that lack deep contextual token modeling.
limitations_verbatim: Our approach shows a slight improvement over the upsampling baseline on two of the four scenarios (Tables V and VII) by 2-2.7% on the F-Measure metric, which shows the diminishing returns from mixing source and target labeled training data. Further improving performance by high margins will require a radically new approach left for future work.
generalizability_gap: The framework is evaluated exclusively on English-language short messages from three specific emergency scenarios (earthquake, flood, and disaster simulation); generalizability to other disaster categories (such as biological epidemics or armed conflicts), non-English languages, multilingual code-switched text, and social platforms beyond Twitter remains unexamined.
methodological_gap: The architecture relies on static keyword heuristics and shallow fastText embeddings evaluated with Linear Regression classifiers rather than deep contextual transformer models; the transfer learning mechanism employs simple instance up-sampling without domain adaptation objectives, adversarial feature alignment, or uncertainty calibration to handle severe class prior and lexical distribution shifts across crises.
future_work: Expanding the manual feature space with broader domain-specific crisis lexicons and syntactic features.; Utilizing more sophisticated local embedding architectures with systematic hyperparameter optimization for learning rates and vector dimensionality.; Developing deep learning transfer architectures with informative priors to leverage auxiliary source crisis domains on irregular social media text.; Investigating advanced domain adaptation techniques to bridge substantial lexical and contextual shifts between disparate disaster events.

title: Recent Neural Methods on Slot Filling and Intent Classification for Task-Oriented Dialogue Systems: A Survey
authors: Samuel Louvan; Bernardo Magnini
venue: Proceedings of the 28th International Conference on Computational Linguistics (COLING 2020)
domain: Task-Oriented Dialogue Systems, Spoken Language Understanding (SLU), Natural Language Understanding (NLU), Intent Classification, Slot Filling, Transfer Learning, Cross-Domain and Multilingual Dialogue Processing
problem_statement: How neural network architectures have evolved to address natural language understanding in task-oriented dialogue systems, specifically focusing on slot filling as token-level sequence tagging and intent classification as utterance-level classification, categorizing independent, joint, and transfer learning models, and identifying unresolved challenges in domain scaling and evaluation complexity.
theoretical_framework: Semantic frame parsing theory (Tur and De Mori, 2011; Wang et al., 2005) structuring user utterances into dialogue act intents and slot-value attributes; token-level sequence labeling via recurrent networks and Conditional Random Fields (Mesnil et al., 2013; Raymond and Riccardi, 2007); multi-task learning synergy between intent detection and slot tagging (Caruana, 1997); and contextual transfer learning via pre-trained Transformer language models (Devlin et al., 2019).
methodology: A systematic taxonomy and comparative analysis structuring neural approaches for slot filling (SF) and intent classification (IC) across three paradigms: (1) Independent models training SF and IC separately using RNNs (Elman, Jordan, LSTM, BiLSTM), CNNs, and Recurrent CRFs with lexical, named entity, and syntactic embeddings; (2) Joint models exploiting mutual task benefits simultaneously via parameter/state sharing (shared Bi-GRU/Bi-LSTM encoders, bi-models, token-level intent guidance, BERT fine-tuning) and slot-intent gating mechanisms; and (3) Transfer learning models for domain scaling via data-driven approaches (multi-task learning, pre-training and fine-tuning), model-driven approaches (reusable slot expert models with attention), and zero-shot architectures (slot descriptions and exemplar values).
datasets: ATIS (Airline Travel Information System) - English single-turn benchmark (~5,000 utterances, 18 intents, 83 slots) and multilingual adaptations (Hindi, Turkish, Indonesian, MultiATIS++ for Spanish, Portuguese, German, French, Chinese, Japanese); SNIPS-NLU - Crowdsourced single-turn digital assistant benchmark in English (13,084 train / 700 dev / 700 test, 7 intents, 39 slots) and Italian (5,742 train / 700 dev / 700 test, 7 intents, 39 slots); MEDIA - French hotel reservation dialogue corpus (12,908 train / 1,259 dev / 3,005 test sentences, 68 slot labels); Facebook Multilingual - Single-turn task-oriented dialogue dataset covering English (30,521 train / 4,181 dev / 8,621 test), Thai (3,617 train / 1,983 dev / 3,043 test), and Spanish (2,156 train / 1,235 dev / 1,692 test) across 12 intents and 11 slots in weather, alarm, and reminder domains; MIT Corpus - English crowdsourced queries for Restaurant domain (6,128 train / 1,532 dev / 1,521 test, 8 slots) and Movie domain (7,820 train / 1,955 dev / 2,443 test, 12 slots); Multi-turn and hierarchical benchmarks surveyed: RESTAURANT-8K, Taskmaster-1 and 2, Frames, Schema-Guided Dialogue (SGD / DTSC-8), TOP, MTOP

key_findings: Joint models simultaneously optimizing slot filling and intent classification outperform independent single-task pipeline models while requiring fewer parameters and mitigating cascading error propagation.; Fine-tuning pre-trained contextual Transformer models (BERT) combined with intent gating mechanisms achieves state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks (98.75% slot F1 and 99.76% intent accuracy on ATIS; 98.78% slot F1 and 98.96% intent accuracy on SNIPS).; Incorporating broader contextual representations via bidirectional encoding, self-attention, and sentence-level global representations consistently improves sequence tagging accuracy.; Integrating external semantic features such as named entity recognition labels yields substantial performance gains for slot filling compared to syntactic part-of-speech features.; For domain scaling with limited target data, multi-task learning and pre-training/fine-tuning provide effective transfer, whereas model-driven expert architectures and zero-shot slot description models enable scaling without retraining the entire model or requiring target-domain annotations.; Standard single-turn benchmark datasets (ATIS and SNIPS) have reached saturation under standard train/dev/test splits, which demonstrates that high benchmark scores reflect solved datasets rather than solved natural language understanding.

limitations_summary: Current slot filling and intent classification models are predominantly evaluated on overused, simplistic, single-turn benchmark datasets (such as ATIS and SNIPS) where performance has saturated without demonstrating true natural language understanding. Furthermore, existing models struggle with data efficiency, cross-domain and cross-lingual transfer, real-world noisy live traffic, complex multi-intent utterances, and fine-grained error interpretability beyond aggregate F1 scores.
limitations_verbatim: Based on the results in Table [2](#page-4-1) and [3,](#page-6-0) it is evident that neural models have achieved outstanding performance on ATIS and SNIPS, showing that it is relatively easy for neural models to capture patterns that recognize slots and intents. ATIS, in particular, is already overused for SF and IC evaluations and recent analysis [\(Bechet and Raymond, 2018](#page-10-12) ´ ; [Niu and Penn, 2019\)](#page-13-9) have shown that the dataset is relatively simple and the room for performance improvement is tiny. A similar trend in performance can be noted for other datasets, such as SNIPS, and it is likely that performance improvement can be quickly saturated. However, it does not mean these models have solved SF and IC, or NLU problems in general, rather that the model has merely solved the datasets. Nevertheless, there are still a number of issues in SF and IC that need further investigation:
generalizability_gap: Existing research predominantly evaluates models on clean, single-turn English datasets with fixed domain boundaries; models remain insufficiently tested on non-English languages, low-resource cross-lingual scenarios, real-world live traffic with diverse or irrelevant user utterances, complex multi-turn dialogues, and multi-intent or multi-sentence conversational turns.
methodological_gap: Standard evaluation frameworks rely exclusively on aggregate exact-match F1 and accuracy metrics that fail to reveal specific behavioral differences between models; zero-shot slot prediction architectures suffer from prediction overlaps and computational inefficiency across large slot vocabularies; discriminative models dominate over sample-efficient generative models; and data augmentation techniques struggle to generate diverse synthetic utterances that faithfully preserve semantic intent.
future_work: Designing portable and data-efficient models that generalize across new domains and languages in few-shot and zero-shot settings.; Developing semi-supervised learning and data selection methods to leverage unlabeled, noisy live user traffic data from commercial digital assistants.; Exploring generative models and semantic-preserving data augmentation techniques for data-scarce dialogue understanding scenarios.; Evaluating slot filling and intent classification models on complex, multi-intent, hierarchical, and multi-turn dialogue corpora (such as SGD, Taskmaster, TOP, and MTOP).; Conducting fine-grained error analyses to understand qualitative behavioral differences among neural architectures beyond aggregate F1 metrics.

title: Recon: Reducing Conflicting Gradients from the Root for Multi-Task Learning
authors: Guangyuan Shi; Qimai Li; Wenlong Zhang; Jiaxin Chen; Xiao-Ming Wu
venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2023)
domain: Multi-Task Learning — Multi-Task Computer Vision (Multi-Fashion+MNIST, CelebA, CityScapes, NYUv2, and PASCAL-Context)
problem_statement: Multi-task learning frequently suffers from negative transfer and optimization difficulties caused by conflicting gradients across tasks; existing gradient manipulation methods alter gradients after computation but fail to prevent the occurrence of conflicting gradients in shared parameters.
theoretical_framework: First-order Taylor expansion and layer-wise gradient conflict analysis in multi-task optimization; Theorem 4.1 proves that when task gradients satisfy the cosine projection condition cos(φ_ij^(k)) ||g_i^(k)|| < ||g_j^(k)|| across selected conflict layers, an update under Recon achieves strictly lower multi-task loss than an update under the standard shared architecture for sufficiently small learning rates.
methodology: Recon (Removing Layer-wise Conflicting Gradients) addresses task conflicts at the architectural level. In the search phase, the network is trained for initial iterations (e.g., the first 25% of training epochs) using joint training or gradient manipulation while computing layer-wise S-conflict scores s^(k) (the frequency with which pairwise cosine similarities between task gradients fall below severity threshold S). In the modification phase, the top-K shared layers exhibiting the highest conflict scores are turned into task-specific layers, and the modified network architecture is retrained from scratch.
datasets: Multi-Fashion+MNIST (two-task image classification benchmark combining FashionMNIST and MNIST items); CityScapes (urban scene understanding benchmark evaluated on 7-class semantic segmentation and depth estimation); NYUv2 (indoor scene understanding benchmark evaluated on 13-class semantic segmentation, depth estimation, and surface normal prediction); PASCAL-Context (multi-task dense visual perception benchmark evaluated on semantic segmentation, human parts segmentation, saliency estimation, surface normal estimation, and edge detection); CelebA (large-scale facial attribute benchmark containing 40 binary classification tasks)

Sener & Koltun, 2018)', 'Projecting Conflicting Gradients (PCGrad; Yu et al., 2020)', 'Gradient Sign Dropout (GradDrop; Chen et al., 2020)', 'Conflict-Averse Gradient Descent (CAGrad; Liu et al., 2021a)', 'RotoGrad (Javaloy & Valera, 2022)', 'Branched Multi-Task Architecture Search (BMTAS; Bruggemann et al., 2020)', 'Cross-Stitch Networks (Misra et al., 2016)', 'Multi-gate Mixture-of-Experts (MMoE; Ma et al., 2018)', 'Random Layer Selection (RSL) and Random Parameter Selection (RSP) ablation baselines', 'First K layers (FSK) and Last K layers (LSK) selection baselines'], 'architectures': ['ResNet18 backbone for Multi-Fashion+MNIST and CelebA', 'SegNet encoder-decoder architecture with split convolutional decoders for CityScapes', 'Multi-Task Attention Network (MTAN) with SegNet backbone for NYUv2', 'MobileNetV2 with Reduced ASPP (R-ASPP) backbone pre-trained on ImageNet for PASCAL-Context', 'SegNet backbone for NYUv2 cross-architecture transfer experiments', 'MTAN backbone for CityScapes cross-architecture transfer experiments']}
key_findings: Recon consistently improves the multi-task learning performance of all evaluated base models, including joint training, gradient manipulation methods (MGDA, PCGrad, GradDrop, CAGrad, RotoGrad), and branched architecture search methods (BMTAS, MMoE), across all 5 benchmark datasets.; Modifying a small proportion of shared parameters into task-specific parameters yields substantial performance gains; Recon converts only 1.42% of parameters on Multi-Fashion+MNIST, 1.46% on CelebA, 12.77% on CityScapes, 0.26% on NYUv2, and 9.80% on PASCAL-Context, with overall model size increasing by only 0.52% to 57.25%.; Recon reduces severe conflicting gradients (cos φ_ij ∈ (−0.01, −1.0]) in remaining shared parameters by 67% to 79% on Multi-Fashion+MNIST, and over 50% across CityScapes, NYUv2, and PASCAL-Context, whereas existing gradient manipulation methods only slightly decrease or sometimes increase gradient conflicts.; Recon combined with gradient manipulation methods (such as CAGrad w/ Recon) achieves superior performance compared to branched architecture search methods (BMTAS) while utilizing substantially fewer parameters.; Identified conflict layers are highly stable across training stages (early 25% versus later iterations), across different multi-task optimization algorithms, and transfer effectively across datasets sharing the same backbone architecture (e.g., 100% layer overlap between Multi-Fashion+MNIST and CelebA on ResNet18; 95% layer overlap between NYUv2 and CityScapes on SegNet).; Ablation experiments confirm that targeted selection of top conflict layers is essential: random layer selection (RSL), random parameter selection (RSP), first-K layer selection (FSK), and last-K layer selection (LSK) all incur significant performance drops relative to Recon.; Theorem 4.1 mathematically proves that under the cosine projection condition, a single gradient update under Recon achieves strictly lower multi-task loss than an update under the fully shared network.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Evaluates multi-task convolutional architectures (ResNet18, SegNet, MTAN, MobileNetV2) exclusively across visual image classification and dense visual perception datasets.', 'Requires a two-stage training workflow: an initial search phase (e.g., the first 25% of training epochs) to compute pairwise layer-wise conflict scores, followed by training the modified network from scratch.', 'Requires tuning two discrete hyperparameters per architecture: the conflict severity threshold S ∈ (−1, 0] and the number of converted task-specific layers K.', 'Focuses on hard parameter sharing architectures converted via layer duplication rather than soft modular routing or dynamic weight generation.']
limitations_summary: The authors acknowledge that Recon is much slower than joint training during the conflict score computation phase when the number of tasks is large because computing pairwise cosine similarities of task gradients scales quadratically with the task count; additionally, the approach requires two hyperparameters (conflict severity S and number of selected layers K) which are sensitive to tune, and computing conflict scores during early iterations exhibits slight noise compared to later iterations.
limitations_verbatim: The results in Fig. [11](#page-19-0) show that Recon is as fast as other gradient manipulation methods such as CAGrad [\(Liu et al., 2021a\)](#page-10-5) and Graddrop [\(Chen et al., 2020\)](#page-9-3), but much slower than joint-training especially when the number of tasks is large, which is natural since Recon needs to compute pariwise cosine similarity of task gradients. However, since Recon only needs to search for the conflict layers once for a given network architecture, as discussed above, the running time is not a problem.
generalizability_gap: Recon was evaluated exclusively on computer vision classification and dense prediction tasks with convolutional backbones; the authors did not test the method on natural language processing tasks, transformer architectures, code-switched text, reinforcement learning domains, or multi-modal settings.
methodological_gap: Recon relies on discrete layer-level duplication rather than soft parameter sharing, fine-grained sub-layer modularization, or automated continuous architecture search; furthermore, pairwise conflict score computation scales quadratically with the number of tasks O(T^2), which introduces computational overhead for large task sets.
future_work: Extending layer-wise gradient conflict analysis to broader network families including Transformer-based architectures and recurrent models.; Applying Recon to non-vision modalities such as natural language processing, speech recognition, and multi-task reinforcement learning.; Developing adaptive or automated selection mechanisms for hyperparameters K (number of conflict layers) and S (conflict severity threshold) to eliminate manual tuning.; Investigating hybrid architectures combining layer-wise conflict isolation with dynamic routing or soft parameter sharing.

title: Reporting Score Distributions Makes a Difference: Performance Study of LSTM-networks for Sequence Tagging
authors: Nils Reimers; Iryna Gurevych
venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)
domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Deep Learning for Sequence Tagging
problem_statement: Reporting a single performance score is insufficient and misleading when comparing non-deterministic deep learning models, because random seed variation across weight initialization, data shuffling, and dropout masks causes statistically significant performance fluctuations that alter perceived state-of-the-art rankings.
theoretical_framework: Non-convex optimization landscape and generalization dynamics of deep neural networks, focusing on the distinction between sharp and flat local minima in parameter weight-space under stochastic initialization and non-deterministic training dynamics.
methodology: The authors conducted an extensive empirical study evaluating over 50,000 BiLSTM network configurations across five sequence tagging tasks (POS tagging, Chunking, Named Entity Recognition, Entity Recognition, and Event Detection). The study evaluated random seed sensitivity by re-running two state-of-the-art NER systems (Ma and Hovy 86 times, Lample et al. 41 times) and analyzing 1,830 paired seed configurations across all five tasks using Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Brown-Forsythe tests. The authors then evaluated hyperparameter stability and sensitivity across 10 architectural choices (pre-trained word embeddings, character representations, optimizers, gradient clipping/normalization, tagging schemes, dropout configurations, output classifiers, stacked BiLSTM layers, recurrent units, and mini-batch sizes) to identify configurations that achieve superior performance with minimal score variance.
datasets: Penn Treebank (WSJ section reduced to the first 500 training sentences for POS tagging); CoNLL 2000 shared task dataset (Chunking); CoNLL 2003 shared task dataset (Named Entity Recognition); ACE 2005 dataset (Entity Recognition); TempEval-3 Task B dataset (Event Detection)

BoW, 2014)', 'Levy and Goldberg Dependency-based (Le. Dep., 2014)', 'GloVe 100-dimensional (GloVe1, Pennington et al., 2014)', 'GloVe 300-dimensional (GloVe2, Pennington et al., 2014)', 'GloVe Common Crawl (GloVe3, Pennington et al., 2014)', 'Komninos and Manandhar Dependency-based (Komn., 2016)', 'FastText Subword Embeddings (Bojanowski et al., 2016)'], 'character_representations': ['CNN character representation (Ma and Hovy, 2016)', 'BiLSTM character representation (Lample et al., 2016)', 'No character representation'], 'optimizers': ['Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD)', 'Adagrad', 'Adadelta', 'RMSProp', 'Adam', 'Nadam'], 'gradient_strategies': ['Gradient clipping (thresholds 1, 3, 5, 10)', 'Gradient normalization (threshold 1)', 'No gradient clipping/normalization'], 'tagging_schemes': ['BIO', 'IOBES'], 'dropout_configurations': ['No dropout', 'Naive dropout', 'Variational dropout (applied to output units, recurrent units, or both)'], 'classifiers': ['Softmax classifier', 'Linear-chain Conditional Random Field (CRF) classifier'], 'network_depth_and_units': ['1, 2, and 3 stacked BiLSTM layers', '25, 50, 75, 100, 125, and 150 recurrent units per layer'], 'mini_batch_sizes': [1, 8, 16, 32, 64]}}
key_findings: The sequence of random numbers has a statistically significant impact on test performance (up to 1.01% F1 variation on CoNLL 2003 NER and up to 8.23% F1 on ACE 2005 Entities), demonstrating that comparing single performance scores is unreliable for non-deterministic neural networks.; Re-running published NER models over multiple seeds demonstrated that Lample et al. achieved a statistically significantly superior score distribution and lower variance compared to Ma and Hovy, reversing conclusions drawn from single reported scores.; Development set performance exhibits a weak Spearman rank correlation (rho = 0.229) with test set performance, indicating that selecting the single best checkpoint on development data does not guarantee optimal generalization or prevent convergence to poor local minima on unseen test data.; Linear-chain CRF output classifiers outperformed Softmax classifiers across 4 out of 5 tasks (achieving 27% lower standard deviation on NER) and reduced sensitivity to network depth, whereas Softmax required deeper stacked BiLSTM layers.; Nadam and Adam optimizers demonstrated the fastest convergence, highest median performance, and roughly 35% lower score standard deviation compared to Adagrad, Adadelta, and SGD, which frequently failed to converge.; Pre-trained word embeddings had a substantial impact across all tasks (e.g., Komninos and Manandhar embeddings outperformed GloVe2 by 4.97% accuracy on small-sample POS tagging).; Variational dropout applied to both recurrent and output dimensions consistently outperformed naive dropout and no-dropout configurations across 83.5% of evaluated setups while yielding the lowest performance variance.; Gradient normalization with a threshold of 1 significantly improved performance over unnormalized gradients and element-wise gradient clipping across all benchmark tasks.; Differences between CNN-based and BiLSTM-based character representations were statistically insignificant across all five tasks when other architectural parameters were held constant.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Focused exclusively on English linguistic sequence tagging benchmarks (POS tagging, Chunking, NER, Entity Recognition, Event Detection) using bidirectional LSTM architectures.', 'Deliberately reduced the Penn Treebank POS training set from over 38,000 sentences to the first 500 sentences to avoid performance saturation and detect architectural differences.', 'Evaluated pre-trained word embedding artifacts released by original authors rather than controlling the underlying corpora, vocabulary sizes, or training token counts.', 'Evaluated optimizers using the default hyperparameter configurations recommended in their respective original publications rather than tuning learning rates separately for each optimizer.']
limitations_summary: The authors acknowledge that their evaluation of word embeddings was restricted to pre-trained vector artifacts generated from non-comparable corpora and preprocessing pipelines, preventing conclusions about the algorithmic superiority of embedding methods. Additionally, the study evaluated optimizers using default hyperparameter settings rather than tuning learning rates exhaustively, and the empirical scope was restricted to English BiLSTM sequence tagging.
limitations_verbatim: Note we only evaluated the pre-trained embeddings provided by different authors, but not the underlying algorithms to generate these embeddings. The quality of word embeddings depends on many factors, including the size, the quality, and the preprocessing of the data corpus. As the corpora are not comparable, our results do not allow concluding that one approach is superior for generating word embeddings.
generalizability_gap: The empirical study evaluated only English-language sequence tagging benchmarks using bidirectional LSTM architectures; the findings were not evaluated on morphologically rich or low-resource languages, non-sequential NLP tasks (such as machine translation or text classification), or Transformer-based foundation architectures.
methodological_gap: The study evaluated pre-trained word embeddings directly without standardizing training corpora or tokenization across algorithms, evaluated optimizers using fixed default hyperparameters without per-optimizer learning rate search, and relied on empirical score distributions without proving theoretical bounds on local minima convergence.
future_work: Investigate whether specific architectural components (such as optimizers and variational dropout) are intrinsically less sensitive to hyperparameters or specifically avoid converging to bad local minima caused by random seed variation.

title: Resolving Token-Space Gradient Conflicts: Token Space Manipulation for Transformer-Based Multi-Task Learning
authors: Wooseong Jeong; Kuk-Jin Yoon
venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:2507.07485
domain: Multi-task dense computer vision prediction across indoor scene understanding, geometric surface parsing, and semantic segmentation benchmarks (NYUD-v2, PASCAL-Context, and Taskonomy).
problem_statement: Multi-task learning with pre-trained vision transformers encounters negative transfer when conflicting gradients emerge across different task objectives. Previous dynamic architectures address gradient conflicts by directly converting shared transformer parameters into task-specific parameters, but that strategy incurs severe parameter inefficiency, excessive computational overhead, and high risk of overfitting. Furthermore, existing transformer multi-task architectures rely on rigid module designs with fixed capacity, preventing dynamic allocation of shared and task-specific representations across different network depths.
theoretical_framework: The authors analyze token representations through Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) on the uncentered covariance matrix of shared transformer tokens, partitioning the token space into an orthogonal range space (representing capabilities acquired during pre-training) and a null space (representing unspanned feature directions). Task-specific token gradients are projected onto both subspaces using orthogonal projection operators. Propositions 1 and 2 prove that applying channel-wise affine token modulators in the range space and introducing learnable task-specific tokens in the null space reduce gradient conflicts and alleviate multi-task loss increases.
methodology: The Dynamic Token Modulation and Expansion for Multi-Task Learning (DTME-MTL) framework detects and resolves gradient conflicts within the token space of transformer architectures. Early in the training process, the framework computes the uncentered covariance of shared tokens and applies SVD to separate the range and null spaces using a variance ratio threshold r. When task gradients conflict in the range space, the framework inserts channel-wise affine token modulators (W ⊙ T + b) to rotate and scale shared tokens. When task gradients conflict in the null space, the framework inserts learnable task-specific tokens concatenated with shared tokens before transformer self-attention blocks. These adaptations are selectively applied to the top 25% to 50% most conflicted layers, and the complete network is fine-tuned without freezing the backbone.
datasets: NYUD-v2 — Indoor RGB-D dataset evaluating 4 dense prediction tasks: depth estimation, semantic segmentation, surface normal prediction, and edge detection.; PASCAL-Context — In-the-wild scene understanding dataset evaluating 5 dense prediction tasks: semantic segmentation, human parts estimation, saliency estimation, surface normal prediction, and edge detection.; Taskonomy — Large-scale indoor scene dataset evaluating 11 dense prediction tasks: Depth Euclidean, Depth Zbuffer, Edge Texture, Keypoints 2D, Keypoints 3D, Surface Normal, Principal Curvature, Reshading, Segment Unsupervised 2D, and Segment Unsupervised 2.5D.; ImageNet-22K — Large-scale image classification dataset utilized for pre-training the Vision Transformer backbone encoders (ViT-T, ViT-S, ViT-B, ViT-L).
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) for semantic segmentation, human parts estimation, and saliency estimation', 'Mean angular distance (degrees) between predicted and ground-truth normal vectors for surface normal prediction', 'Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) for depth estimation and principal curvature', 'Optimal-dataset-scale F-measure (odsF) for edge detection', 'L1 distance for remaining Taskonomy dense prediction tasks', 'Average multi-task relative performance metric (Δm %) measuring per-task gain or drop relative to single-task baselines', 'Parameter increase percentage (#Param ↑ %)', 'Computational execution time (minutes) for SVD and conflict computation, and inference latency overhead percentage'], 'baselines': ['Baseline (ST) — Single-task learning upper baseline with dedicated models per task', 'Baseline (MT) — Multi-task baseline with shared ViT backbone and 3×3 Conv-BN-ReLU task-specific decoders', 'Dynamic architecture baseline — Recon (layer-wise parameter-level conflict resolution)', 'Multi-task optimization methods — Gradient Descent (GD), GradDrop, MGDA, PCGrad, CAGrad, IMTL, Nash-MTL, Aligned-MTL, Uncertainty Weighting (UW), Dynamic Weight Average (DWA), and FAMO', 'State-of-the-art transformer MTL architectures — InvPT and TaskPrompter', 'Parameter-efficient adaptation baseline — LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation)'], 'architectures': ['Vision Transformer (ViT) backbones: ViT-Tiny (ViT-T), ViT-Small (ViT-S), ViT-Base (ViT-B), and ViT-Large (ViT-L) pre-trained on ImageNet-22K', 'Task-specific decoders: single-layer 3×3 Conv-BN-ReLU prediction heads', 'Multi-task prompting architectures: InvPT and TaskPrompter integrated with DTME-MTL modules']}
key_findings: DTME-MTL consistently outperforms the multi-task baseline across NYUD-v2 and PASCAL-Context benchmarks while requiring only a 0.2% to 0.3% parameter increase, achieving performance comparable to single-task models without complex architectural modules.; On the 11-task Taskonomy benchmark using ViT-B, DTME-MTL achieves the highest average multi-task improvement of 4.67% with only a 0.118% parameter increase, outperforming previous multi-task optimization methods including CAGrad, Nash-MTL, FAMO, and PCGrad.; DTME-MTL integrates directly with state-of-the-art transformer MTL architectures, improving InvPT and TaskPrompter performance on NYUD-v2 and PASCAL-Context with minimal parameter additions of 0.048% and 0.046% respectively.; Token Modulation (TM) and Token Expansion (TE) resolve distinct conflict mechanisms: TM resolves range-space conflicts while TE resolves null-space conflicts, and swapping the assignment of TM and TE across conflict spaces causes substantial performance degradation.; Selecting layers based on gradient conflict severity outperforms random layer selection and reverse-order selection, with expanding 25% to 50% of the most conflicted layers yielding optimal performance gains.; Overexpansion beyond 50% of transformer layers degrades performance because adding task-specific tokens and modulators to low-conflict layers induces overfitting.; Performing SVD early during training produces better task performance than late-stage expansion because early expansion leverages the pre-trained feature structure.; Training the expanded network without freezing the pre-trained backbone parameters significantly outperforms training with frozen backbones, enabling the model to dynamically partition the token space.; Resolving gradient conflicts in token space avoids the severe overfitting observed in parameter-level expansion methods such as Recon, while enabling parallel multi-task inference with only a 13.4% latency overhead on ViT-B compared to the linear latency scaling of LoRA.
scope_and_delimitations: ['The empirical evaluation is focused on dense visual prediction tasks on NYUD-v2, PASCAL-Context, and Taskonomy benchmarks using pre-trained Vision Transformer backbones (ViT-T, ViT-S, ViT-B, ViT-L).', 'The number of task-specific expanded tokens is statically set to six learnable tokens per layer rather than being dynamically adapted per task or per input sample.', 'The SVD computation and gradient conflict analysis are executed once at an early training stage rather than being recomputed iteratively at every optimization step.', 'Token modulation and expansion are selectively restricted to the top 25% to 50% most conflicted transformer layers rather than applied across all transformer layers.', 'The study focuses on transfer learning from pre-trained backbones and does not evaluate training vision transformers from random initialization.']
limitations_summary: The authors acknowledge that expanding beyond 50% of transformer layers degrades multi-task performance because indiscriminate expansion into low-conflict layers causes overfitting. In addition, the method relies on statically allocating a fixed number of six task tokens per layer and requires manual selection of the layer expansion ratio rather than dynamic per-step adaptation.
limitations_verbatim: Performance improves as more high-conflict layers are expanded, but begins to degrade when expansion exceeds 50%, especially when low-conflict layers are included. This suggests that overexpansion can be detrimental. Table [2](#page-6-1) further confirms that using a moderate expansion ratio (50%) avoids overfitting, whereas Fig. [6](#page-13-0) highlights that indiscriminate expansion into less conflicting layers harms performance. These findings underscore the importance of both the *extent* and *location* of TM+TE application.
generalizability_gap: The authors do not evaluate the framework on natural language processing benchmarks, code-switched language understanding, speech processing, reinforcement learning, or multi-modal vision-language foundation models. Furthermore, the experiments examine up to 11 visual tasks, leaving performance on massive multi-task setups with dozens or hundreds of tasks unverified.
methodological_gap: The framework relies on static allocation of six task-specific tokens per layer and computes SVD only once early in training, rather than dynamically adjusting the token count or updating token subspaces iteratively. Additionally, selecting the optimal expansion ratio and activation threshold requires empirical tuning, and the framework lacks an automated routing mechanism to allocate token capacity dynamically during optimization.
