title: Sentiment Analysis of Typhoon Related Tweets using Standard and Bidirectional Recurrent Neural Networks
authors: Joseph Marvin R. Imperial; Jeyrome A. Orosco; Shiela Mae O. Mazo; Lany L. Maceda
venue: arXiv
domain: Crisis informatics, disaster response, and social media NLP (Twitter) in the Philippines during Typhoon Yolanda (Haiyan), focusing on English and Filipino sentiment classification.
problem_statement: Identifying and analyzing the underlying sentiments expressed in tweets posted by Filipino citizens before, during, and after Typhoon Yolanda (Haiyan) to understand social involvement, public empathy, and disaster-related communication patterns using standard and bidirectional recurrent neural networks.
theoretical_framework: Supervised sequential modeling and sentiment analysis using recurrent neural architectures (standard RNN with truncated BPTT and bidirectional RNN with full BPTT) operating over continuous Word2Vec vector space word embeddings.
methodology: A supervised sentiment classification pipeline comprising data collection via Twitter search for disaster hashtags (#YolandaPH, #BangonPH, #BangonPilipinas) between November 2013 and January 2014 (92,040 raw tweets), text preprocessing (deduplication, removal of usernames, URLs, retweets, emojis, stopwords, infrequent words, short words, and special characters leaving 39,867 tweets), continuous word representation using Word2Vec embeddings, balanced manual ground-truth annotation of 3,900 tweets across three classes (positive, negative, neutral; 1,300 per class), an 80/20 train/test split, hyperparameter tuning across batch sizes (64, 128), dropout rates (0.0, 0.5), and backpropagation through time configurations (truncated BPTT vs. full BPTT) for both standard and bidirectional RNNs on fine-grained and binary classification tasks, followed by corpus-wide inference on the remaining 35,967 unlabeled tweets.
datasets: 39,867 preprocessed Typhoon Yolanda tweets collected between November 1, 2013, and January 31, 2014, filtered from an initial corpus of 92,040 tweets gathered using the hashtags #YolandaPH, #BangonPH, and #BangonPilipinas; A manually annotated ground-truth benchmark of 3,900 balanced tweets (1,300 positive, 1,300 negative, and 1,300 neutral) split into an 80% training set (3,120 tweets) and a 20% test set (780 tweets); 35,967 unannotated disaster tweets classified during corpus-level sentiment distribution inference
evaluation: {'fine_grained_classification': {'classes': ['positive', 'negative', 'neutral'], 'best_model': 'Standard RNN', 'best_hyperparameters': {'batch_size': 64, 'dropout': 0.5, 'bptt_type': 'truncated BPTT (tBPTT, value=50)', 'learning_rate': '1.80E'}, 'best_accuracy': 0.8179, 'best_f1_score': 0.8176, 'bidirectional_rnn_best_accuracy': 0.8141, 'bidirectional_rnn_best_f1_score': 0.8135}, 'binary_classification': {'classes': ['positive', 'negative'], 'best_model': 'Bidirectional RNN', 'best_hyperparameters': {'batch_size': 64, 'dropout': 0.0, 'bptt_type': 'Full BPTT', 'learning_rate': '1.80E'}, 'best_accuracy': 0.8769, 'best_f1_score': 0.876, 'standard_rnn_best_accuracy': 0.8712, 'standard_rnn_best_f1_score': 0.8699}, 'corpus_inference_distribution': {'total_inferred_tweets': 35967, 'positive_sentiment_count': 18395, 'positive_sentiment_percentage': 0.511, 'neutral_sentiment_count': 10441, 'neutral_sentiment_percentage': 0.29, 'negative_sentiment_count': 7131, 'negative_sentiment_percentage': 0.198}}
key_findings: The standard RNN model configured with a batch size of 64, dropout rate of 0.5, and truncated BPTT achieved the highest accuracy of 81.79% and F1 score of 0.8176 for fine-grained 3-class sentiment classification.; The bidirectional RNN model configured with a batch size of 64, no dropout, and full BPTT achieved the highest accuracy of 87.69% and F1 score of 0.8760 for binary sentiment classification.; A batch size of 64 consistently outperformed a batch size of 128 across all tested model configurations, yielding accuracies above 80% across all evaluated runs.; Error analysis indicated that inaccuracies in both binary and fine-grained classification were predominantly caused by false negative misclassifications (accounting for 11.9% to 14% of errors).; Corpus-wide inference over 35,967 unannotated tweets using the best fine-grained model revealed that 51.1% of tweets were positive (prayers, hope, support, and gratitude), 29.0% were neutral (news reports, relief operation announcements, and citizen observations), and 19.8% were negative (sadness, despair, and grief for victims along with criticism of government relief mismanagement).
scope_and_delimitations: ['Restricted tweet collection to a specific historical time window between November 1, 2013, and January 31, 2014, corresponding to Typhoon Yolanda (Haiyan).', 'Delimited data harvesting exclusively to three hashtags: #YolandaPH, #BangonPH, and #BangonPilipinas.', 'Delimited manual sentiment annotation to a balanced sample of 3,900 tweets (1,300 positive, 1,300 negative, 1,300 neutral) with an 80/20 train/test partition.', 'Constrained neural architectures to vanilla standard RNNs and bidirectional RNNs with Word2Vec word embeddings, excluding gated architectures (LSTM, GRU) and transformer models.', 'Delimited sentiment labels to three discrete categories (positive, negative, neutral) without fine-grained emotion sub-categorization (e.g., fear, gratitude, anger).']
limitations_summary: The classification models exhibited persistent false negative misclassifications accounting for 11.9% to 14% of errors across binary and fine-grained tasks, and the study evaluated only basic standard and bidirectional RNN configurations without exploring multi-layer architectures or gated recurrent units.
limitations_verbatim: In the error analysis of binary classification, the cause of the 14% and 12% inaccuracy for standard and bidirectional models respectively is based on false negative misclassifications. Same case with the fine-grained classification, wherein 12% and 11.9% for standard and bidirectional models respectively were misclassified by the models as false negative. The error similarity is expected since the same dataset is used for both type of classifications. Moreover, it can be deduced that the complexity of finer-grained classification would result to slightly lower accuracy than binary classification since the datasets are being compared to three classes.
generalizability_gap: The dataset and evaluation are restricted to a single catastrophic event (Typhoon Yolanda) in the Philippines during late 2013 and early 2014 using three specific hashtags; generalizability to other disaster categories (e.g., earthquakes, floods, volcanic eruptions), other typhoon events, diverse regional Philippine languages beyond English and Tagalog (e.g., Waray, Cebuano, Hiligaynon), and other social media platforms remains unproven.
methodological_gap: The study utilized basic standard and bidirectional RNN models with Word2Vec embeddings rather than evaluating gated recurrent networks (LSTM, GRU), attention mechanisms, or pretrained contextual transformer architectures (e.g., BERT, RoBERTa). The evaluation was conducted on a single fixed 80/20 train/test split without k-fold cross-validation, out-of-domain robustness testing, or incorporation of multimodal and temporal social media metadata.
future_work: Experimenting with different combinations and configurations of neural network layers in the hidden layer.; Exploring new architectures of Recurrent Neural Networks (such as LSTMs and GRUs) to improve classification performance on disaster-related text.

title: Smarter, Better, Faster, Longer: A Modern Bidirectional Encoder for Fast, Memory Efficient, and Long Context Finetuning and Inference
authors: Benjamin Warner; Antoine Chaffin; Benjamin Clavié; Orion Weller; Oskar Hallström; Said Taghadouini; Alexis Gallagher; Raja Biswas; Faisal Ladhak; Tom Aarsen; Nathan Cooper; Griffin Adams; Jeremy Howard; Iacopo Poli
venue: Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL 2025)
domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Bidirectional Encoder Transformers, Information Retrieval (IR), Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR), Multi-Vector Retrieval (ColBERT), Long-Context Understanding, Source Code Retrieval, Hardware-Aware Deep Learning
problem_statement: Encoder-only transformer architectures such as BERT and RoBERTa remain essential for non-generative downstream natural language processing applications including semantic search, passage retrieval, classification, reranking, and safety routing. However, existing encoder models have seen limited architectural modernization since their introduction. Practitioners face key bottlenecks including context windows limited to 512 tokens, inefficient subword tokenizers lacking programming language syntax, quadratic attention scaling, padding token compute overhead, hardware-agnostic layer dimensions, and training corpora that lack recent data or code.
theoretical_framework: Modern bidirectional transformer architectures (Vaswani et al., 2017; Devlin et al., 2019); Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) for context extension (Su et al., 2024); alternating sliding-window local attention and global attention (Beltagy et al., 2020; Gemma Team et al., 2024); Gated Linear Units (GeGLU) activation theory (Shazeer, 2020); hardware-aware deep-and-narrow network scaling and GPU tensor core tile/wave alignment theory (Anthony et al., 2024; Tay et al., 2022); Masked Language Modeling (MLM) with 30% masking rate (Wettig et al., 2023); and Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD) trapezoidal learning rate scheduling with StableAdamW optimization (Wortsman et al., 2023).
methodology: The authors developed ModernBERT in two configurations: ModernBERT-base (149 million parameters across 22 layers, hidden size 768, intermediate GLU dimension 2,304) and ModernBERT-large (395 million parameters across 28 layers, hidden size 1,024, intermediate GLU dimension 5,248). The architecture incorporates modern design optimizations: removal of bias terms across linear layers and LayerNorms (retaining bias solely in the final decoder projection), post-embedding LayerNorm with pre-normalization, GeGLU activation, RoPE positional embeddings, alternating attention (every third layer applies global attention with RoPE theta=160,000, while intermediate layers apply 128-token local sliding window attention with RoPE theta=10,000), FlashAttention (combining FlashAttention-3 for global attention and FlashAttention-2 for local attention), full-model unpadding before the embedding layer with dynamic greedy sequence packing (>99% token efficiency), and torch.compile module compilation. Pretraining was conducted on 2 trillion tokens of primarily English web data, code, and scientific literature with a 50,368-vocabulary BPE tokenizer (modified OLMo). Pretraining used StableAdamW with Adafactor-style update clipping, trapezoidal learning rate scheduling with 1 - sqrt decay, batch size warmup schedules, Megatron random initialization for base, and Phi-style center-tiling weight initialization with Gopher scaling for large. Native context length was extended from 1,024 to 8,192 tokens during the final 300 billion tokens by elevating global RoPE theta to 160,000 and upsampling high-quality sources. The models were evaluated across GLUE (NLU classification), BEIR (single-vector DPR and multi-vector ColBERT retrieval), MLDR (long-context retrieval in-domain and out-of-domain), CodeSearchNet and StackOverflow-QA (code retrieval), and synthetic variable/fixed-length benchmarks on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 for memory and throughput efficiency.
datasets: Pretraining Corpus: 2 trillion tokens comprising English web crawl data, source code repositories, and scientific papers; GLUE (General Language Understanding Evaluation): 8 NLU classification subsets (MNLI, QNLI, QQP, RTE, SST-2, MRPC, CoLA, STS-B); MS-MARCO: 1.25M passage retrieval training samples with mined hard negatives (for DPR) and 810k samples with BGE-M3 distillation scores (for ColBERT via PyLate); BEIR (Benchmarking Information Retrieval): 15 zero-shot evaluation datasets (TREC-COVID, NFCorpus, SciFact, FiQA, Touche-2020, DBPedia, SCIDOCS, Climate-FEVER, CQADupStack, Quora, FEVER, Robust04, Signal-1M, TREC-NEWS, BioASQ); MLDR (Multi-Lingual Dense Retrieval): English subset of over 200,000 long documents evaluated under zero-shot out-of-domain and fine-tuned in-domain settings; CodeSearchNet: Code-to-text retrieval benchmark across 6 programming languages evaluated via the CoIR framework; StackOverflow-QA: Hybrid code-and-text long-context question answering retrieval benchmark evaluated via the CoIR framework; Synthetic Efficiency Benchmark: 4 sets of 8,192 documents (fixed 512 tokens, fixed 8,192 tokens, variable short mean 256 tokens, variable long mean 4,096 tokens)
evaluation: {'metrics': ['GLUE average dev score and per-task accuracy/F1/Spearman correlation', 'BEIR nDCG@10 (single-vector DPR and multi-vector ColBERT)', 'MLDR nDCG@10 (out-of-domain and in-domain)', 'CoIR / CodeSearchNet Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR@10)', 'StackOverflow-QA nDCG@10', 'Throughput (thousands of tokens per second on NVIDIA RTX 4090)', 'Max batch size (memory efficiency / VRAM utilization)'], 'benchmark_results': {'glue_dev_average': {'modernbert_base': 89.15, 'modernbert_large': 89.91, 'deberta_v3_base': 88.75, 'deberta_v3_large': 90.02, 'bert_base': 83.27, 'roberta_base': 86.43}, 'beir_ndcg_at_10': {'single_vector_dpr': {'modernbert_base': 47.92, 'modernbert_large': 49.33, 'gte_en_mlm_base': 47.78, 'gte_en_mlm_large': 48.71}, 'multi_vector_colbert': {'modernbert_base': 50.81, 'modernbert_large': 51.52, 'gte_en_mlm_base': 49.7, 'gte_en_mlm_large': 49.99}}, 'mldr_long_context_ndcg_at_10': {'single_vector_out_of_domain': {'modernbert_base': 45.47, 'modernbert_large': 46.52, 'gte_en_mlm_base': 53.64, 'gte_en_mlm_large': 56.4}, 'single_vector_in_domain': {'modernbert_base': 61.12, 'modernbert_large': 64.91, 'gte_en_mlm_base': 61.42, 'gte_en_mlm_large': 65.05}, 'multi_vector_out_of_domain': {'modernbert_base': 59.95, 'modernbert_large': 65.65, 'gte_en_mlm_base': 50.86, 'gte_en_mlm_large': 53.6}}, 'code_retrieval': {'codesearchnet_mrr_at_10': {'modernbert_base': 72.84, 'modernbert_large': 75.39}, 'stackoverflow_qa_ndcg_at_10': {'modernbert_base': 71.05, 'modernbert_large': 72.63}}, 'inference_efficiency_tokens_per_sec': {'fixed_512': {'modernbert_base': 167578, 'modernbert_large': 69828}, 'fixed_8192': {'modernbert_base': 125950, 'modernbert_large': 46801, 'gte_en_mlm_base': 47507, 'gte_en_mlm_large': 16532}}}}
key_findings: ModernBERT-base (149M parameters) and ModernBERT-large (395M parameters) establish state-of-the-art results across natural language understanding, text retrieval, long-context retrieval, and code retrieval benchmarks.; ModernBERT-base is the first Masked Language Modeling (MLM)-trained encoder to surpass DeBERTaV3-base on GLUE (89.15 versus 88.75 average score), showing that MLM with modern architectural design matches or exceeds Replaced Token Detection (RTD).; ModernBERT-large achieves an 89.91 average score on GLUE with 395M parameters, nearly matching DeBERTaV3-large (90.02 with 435M parameters) while processing sequence tokens at twice the throughput.; On the BEIR benchmark, ModernBERT surpasses all existing encoders in both single-vector Dense Passage Retrieval (base: 47.92, large: 49.33 nDCG@10) and multi-vector ColBERT settings (base: 50.81, large: 51.52 nDCG@10).; In long-context multi-vector ColBERT retrieval on MLDR, long-context encoders gain over 40 nDCG@10 points over short-context baselines without long-context fine-tuning, with ModernBERT outperforming all competing models by over 9 nDCG@10 points.; On code retrieval tasks (CodeSearchNet and StackOverflow-QA), ModernBERT outperforms all competing encoders due to pretraining on code repositories and employing a code-aware BPE tokenizer with 50,368 tokens.; Hardware-aware deep-and-narrow architecture design, full-model unpadding, and alternating local-global attention enable ModernBERT to process 8,192-token inputs 2.65x to 3.0x faster than competing long-context encoders while supporting up to 2x larger batch sizes on an NVIDIA RTX 4090.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Model architecture scope is delimited to bidirectional encoder-only transformer models in base (22 layers, 149M parameters) and large (28 layers, 395M parameters) configurations.', 'Pretraining data is delimited to 2 trillion tokens of primarily English-language text, source code repositories, and scientific literature.', 'Maximum native context sequence length is delimited to 8,192 tokens.', 'Architectural constraints omit bias terms in linear layers and LayerNorms (retaining bias only in the final decoder projection) and restrict sliding window local attention to 128 tokens.', 'Hardware design optimizations target a specific basket of GPUs (NVIDIA T4, A10, L4, RTX 3090, RTX 4090, A100, H100), with priority given to inference deployment over training-cluster-specific wave quantization.']
limitations_summary: The authors acknowledge several explicit limitations: the model family focuses exclusively on the English language and source code, rendering it not directly applicable to non-English and low-resource languages; pretraining representations inherit societal and web data biases; masked language modeling retains a minor residual capability to suggest harmful token replacements; pretraining relied solely on the Masked Language Modeling objective rather than hybrid MLM and Replaced Token Detection (RTD); parameter scaling beyond 395 million parameters was left unexplored; and out-of-domain zero-shot long-context dense retrieval trails specialized retrieval models unless fine-tuned in-domain.
limitations_verbatim:
Language This study focuses exclusively on the English language, and trains on a very large number of tokens. As such, a major limitation of our work is that it is not directly applicable to other languages, and potentially even less-so to lower resources languages. Exploration of modernizing encoder models in multilingual [\(Zhang et al.,](#page-14-5) [2024\)](#page-14-5) and monolingual but non-English [\(Antoun et al.,](#page-9-12) [2024\)](#page-9-12) settings is a promising avenue.

Biases Our model is trained largely on web data, as a result, all of its representations are subject to the biases present in such data.

Harmful Content Generation The MLM objective gives the model some ability to generate text by suggesting a given token to replace the [MASK] token [\(Samuel,](#page-13-15) [2024\)](#page-13-15), which could result in the generation of harmful content. However, Modern-BERT is not, primarily, a generative model, and as such, has not been trained to and therefore cannot generate longer sequences of text. As a result, it is considerably less likely to be at risk of generating harmful content of any kind.

MLM-only objective Given the strong results of DeBERTav3 on classification tasks but weak ones on retrieval, it seems that a training leveraging both MLM and RTD might be better suited to achieve best results on classification. Extending our work to RTD is thus a promising line of research.

Scaling Besides the architectural modifications, a key aspect of our studies is data scaling. However, other scaling axes, notably in terms of model parameters are left unexplored.
generalizability_gap: ModernBERT was pretrained exclusively on English-language corpora and programming code, leaving multilingual representation, cross-lingual transfer, and non-English low-resource language understanding completely unaddressed. In addition, parameter scaling behavior beyond 395M parameters remains unexamined.
methodological_gap: The pretraining framework relies solely on the Masked Language Modeling (MLM) objective rather than incorporating Replaced Token Detection (RTD); zero-shot out-of-domain single-vector dense passage retrieval on long contexts exhibits performance degradation without task-adapted fine-tuning; parallel attention and softcapping techniques were omitted due to downstream performance degradation or compatibility constraints; and hardware throughput optimizations were evaluated exclusively on NVIDIA GPU architectures.
future_work: Extending ModernBERT architecture and pretraining recipes to multilingual settings and non-English monolingual domains, with special attention to low-resource languages.; Investigating hybrid pretraining objectives that combine Masked Language Modeling (MLM) with Replaced Token Detection (RTD) to enhance downstream classification accuracy.; Exploring model parameter scaling axes beyond 395M parameters to evaluate whether deep-and-narrow encoder scaling laws continue to hold at larger capacities.; Analyzing the theoretical and empirical synergy between alternating local-global attention and multi-vector ColBERT retrieval over extended context windows.; Developing improved long-context pretraining and adaptation recipes to elevate zero-shot out-of-domain single-vector dense passage retrieval performance.

title: Statistical Comparisons of Classifiers over Multiple Data Sets
authors: Janez Demšar
venue: Journal of Machine Learning Research
domain: Machine Learning Evaluation and Applied Statistics
problem_statement: Comparing the performance of machine learning classifiers across multiple benchmark datasets is a fundamental task in empirical machine learning research, yet researchers frequently apply inappropriate parametric tests such as paired t-tests or uncorrected all-pairs comparisons whose statistical assumptions are severely violated.
theoretical_framework: Non-parametric statistical hypothesis testing, ranking-based comparison procedures (Wilcoxon signed-ranks test, Friedman test with Iman-Davenport correction), and family-wise error rate control methodologies (Bonferroni-Dunn, Holm, Hochberg, Hommel) under non-normal score distributions and incommensurable measurement scales.
methodology: The author theoretically reviews parametric and non-parametric statistical procedures and empirically analyzes their behavior across 40 real-world benchmark classification datasets from the UCI repository. The analysis evaluates two-classifier comparison methods (paired t-test on absolute differences, paired t-test on relative differences, Wilcoxon signed-ranks test, and sign test) and multiple-classifier comparison methods (repeated-measures ANOVA with Tukey and Dunnett post-hoc tests, Friedman test with Nemenyi, Bonferroni-Dunn, Holm step-down, Hochberg step-up, and Hommel post-hoc procedures). The empirical framework simulates researcher selection bias using a logistic sampling function across 1,000 resamples of 10 datasets, evaluates statistical power (rejection frequencies and mean p-values) and replicability (outcome-based R(e) and variance-based R(p)), and introduces Critical Difference (CD) diagrams for visual ranking representation.
datasets: 40 UCI Machine Learning Repository benchmark datasets (adult, balance-scale, bands, breast cancer (haberman), breast cancer (lju), breast cancer (wisc), car evaluation, contraceptive method choice, credit screening, dermatology, ecoli, glass identification, hayesroth, hepatitis, housing, imports-85, ionosphere, iris, liver disorders, lung cancer, lymphography, mushrooms, pima indians diabetes, post-operative, primary tumor, promoters, rheumatism, servo, shuttle landing, soybean, spambase, spect, spectf, teaching assistant evaluation, tic tac toe, titanic, voting, waveform, wine recognition, yeast)
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Mean p-value across 1,000 experiment repetitions', 'Null-hypothesis rejection frequency at alpha = 0.05', 'Bouckaert outcome-based replicability R(e)', 'Variance-based replicability R(p)', 'Classification accuracy (10-fold cross-validation)', 'Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC, 5-fold cross-validation)'], 'evaluated_statistical_tests': ['Paired t-test on absolute differences', 'Paired t-test on relative differences', 'Sign test (counts of wins, ties, losses)', 'Wilcoxon signed-ranks test', 'Repeated-measures ANOVA (with Tukey and Dunnett post-hoc tests)', 'Friedman test (with Iman-Davenport F_F correction)', 'Nemenyi post-hoc test (all-to-all comparisons)', 'Bonferroni-Dunn post-hoc test (comparison with control)', 'Holm step-down procedure', 'Hochberg step-up procedure', 'Hommel procedure'], 'evaluated_learning_algorithms': ['C4.5 decision tree (with default and tuned m / cf hyperparameters)', 'Orange decision tree learner', 'Naive Bayes with LOESS continuous probability modeling', 'Naive Bayes with Fayyad-Irani discretization', 'k-Nearest Neighbors (k=10 with Gaussian kernel weighting)']}
key_findings: Non-parametric tests (Wilcoxon signed-ranks test for two classifiers and Friedman test with post-hoc tests for multiple classifiers) should be preferred over parametric tests (paired t-test and repeated-measures ANOVA) for comparing classifiers over multiple datasets.; Parametric tests rely on assumptions of normal distribution and sphericity/homogeneity of variance, which are routinely violated by classifier performance metrics across diverse benchmark datasets.; The Wilcoxon signed-ranks test achieves higher statistical power (lower average p-values and higher null-hypothesis rejection rates) and superior variance-based replicability R(p) compared to paired t-tests across 40 UCI benchmark datasets.; The Iman-Davenport F_F statistic resolves the severe conservatism of the standard Friedman chi-squared statistic.; When comparing multiple algorithms against a single control classifier, post-hoc procedures such as Bonferroni-Dunn, Holm, and Hochberg provide substantially greater statistical power than all-to-all Nemenyi comparisons by evaluating only k-1 hypotheses instead of k(k-1)/2 hypotheses.; Critical Difference (CD) diagrams effectively summarize average classifier ranks and statistically significant pairwise differences in a compact graphical format.; Filtering comparisons to count only statistically significant wins and losses degrades test reliability by establishing an arbitrary p < 0.05 threshold.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Delimited to evaluating classifier comparison methods across multiple independent datasets rather than assessing within-dataset variance or cross-validation fold dependencies.', 'Treated dataset scores as reliable point estimates without modeling the covariance or variance of individual training-test splits.', 'Restricted empirical simulations to 40 classification benchmark datasets from the UCI repository with discrete class attributes.', 'Simulated algorithm performance differences by varying dataset selection probabilities via a logistic bias function k over 1,000 resamples of 10 datasets.']
limitations_summary: The author acknowledges that the empirical simulation did not measure Type I and Type II error rates because defining ground-truth hypotheses would require synthetic datasets with predetermined distributions, which would undermine evaluating whether real-world data conforms to test assumptions. Additionally, the non-parametric framework cannot incorporate cross-validation fold variance due to overlapping training samples, and post-hoc tests may occasionally fail to pinpoint significant pairs despite omnibus Friedman significance.
limitations_verbatim: In the empirical study we provided no analysis of Type 1/Type 2 error rates. The main reason for this is that the correct result—rejection or non-rejection of the null-hypothesis—is not well defined and depends upon the kind of difference between the algorithms we intend to measure. Besides, conducting the experiments in which we knew the true hypotheses would require artificial data sets and classifiers with the prescribed probabilities and distributions of errors. For this we would need to make some assumptions about the real-world distributions; these assumptions are, however, exactly what we were testing in the first place.
generalizability_gap: The empirical simulations evaluated only 40 discrete-target classification datasets from the UCI repository and classical learners (decision trees, Naive Bayes, kNN); the study did not empirically test regression algorithms, unsupervised models, structured output predictors, or modern deep learning architectures across large-scale heterogeneous benchmarks.
methodological_gap: The proposed non-parametric framework cannot model within-dataset sample variance or repeated cross-validation fold covariance because training data overlaps across folds, and omnibus Friedman significance does not guarantee that post-hoc tests will have sufficient statistical power to identify specific differing pairs.
local_dir: Statistical Comparisons of Classifiers over Multiple Data Sets

title: TASKWEB: Selecting Better Source Tasks for Multi-task NLP
authors: Joongwon Kim; Akari Asai; Gabriel Ilharco; Hannaneh Hajishirzi
venue: Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2023)
domain: Multi-Task Natural Language Processing (NLP), Transfer Learning, Task Selection, Pairwise Task Transferability, Parameter-Efficient Tuning, Zero-Shot Generalization (English)
problem_statement: While joint multi-task training can improve general language model performance, it remains unclear how NLP tasks are interrelated and how to systematically select optimal source tasks to assist learning a new, unseen target task with few labeled examples without incurring massive computational costs.
theoretical_framework: Cross-task transfer learning theory; non-commutativity and empirical transitivity of task transferability; graph path-based task affinity estimation; parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT).
methodology: The authors introduce TASKWEB and TASKSHOP: (1) TASKWEB is a large-scale empirical benchmark comprising approximately 25,000 pairwise task transfer experiments across 22 diverse NLP tasks, evaluating 3 model architectures (encoder-decoder T5-small/base/large, decoder-only GPT-2 medium, encoder-only RoBERTa-base) and 3 adaptation settings (full fine-tuning, Adapter-tuning, BitFit) across 8 random seeds; (2) Mathematical analysis of task transfer properties discovers that transferability is non-commutative (A -> B does not imply B -> A) but exhibits strong transitivity for positive transfers (high A -> B and B -> C implies high A -> C); (3) TASKSHOP is a novel task selection algorithm that predicts directional transfer to an unseen target task (having <= 32 examples) by searching over pivot paths (s -> p -> t) combining known TASKWEB scores with lightweight text similarity methods (Retrieval-of-Experts or LLM-similarity) interpolated with direct estimation; (4) Multi-task selection evaluates fine-tuning T5-3B on small curated subsets (kn examples, e.g., top-5 tasks with 2,000 examples each = 10,000 examples) against target-agnostic massive multi-task baselines (T0-3B, T5-3B + all 21 tasks = 42,000 examples) across 11 target tasks in zero-shot settings.
datasets: 22 NLP Tasks in TASKWEB: Natural Questions, SQuAD 2.0, HotpotQA, CommonsenseQA, SocialIQA, CosmosQA, MultiRC, BoolQ, WiC, WSC (Winograd), COPA, HellaSwag, PIQA, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, OpenBookQA, MNLI, QNLI, RTE, QQP, MRPC, SST-2.; Target Evaluation Tasks: ANLI (R1, R2, R3), Story Cloze, COPA, HellaSwag, RTE, Winogrande, CB, WSC, and other zero-shot NLU benchmarks evaluated across prompt templates via PromptSource.
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG) for overall source task ranking quality', 'Regret@k (Regret@5) measuring performance gap between predicted top-k and oracle top-k source tasks', 'Average Percentage Change (PC) and Positive Transfer Proportion (PM) across 8 random seeds for pairwise transferability', 'Zero-shot accuracy across 11 target tasks and multiple prompt templates for multi-task fine-tuning'], 'results': ['TASKSHOP with Retrieval-of-Experts (TASKSHOP-RoE) achieves highest NDCG and lowest Regret@5, improving overall ranking by 10% and top-k precision by 38% over baseline selection methods.', 'Models trained on small multi-task subsets (10,000 examples across top-5 source tasks chosen by TASKSHOP) outperform T0-3B by 14.7% and T5-3B + all tasks (42,000 examples) by 4.3% in zero-shot target accuracy.', 'Using oracle top-5 source tasks from TASKWEB further improves target accuracy, whereas training on bottom-5 (unhelpful) tasks causes severe accuracy degradation (decreasing by 3.4 points on average).']}
key_findings: Pairwise task transfer is directional and predominantly non-commutative (only 97 of 210 pairs exhibit commutativity), meaning transferability from task A to B does not imply equal transfer from B to A.; Positive task transfers display strong transitivity: when intermediate transfers (source -> pivot and pivot -> target) exceed higher transferability thresholds, the probability of positive source -> target transfer increases up to 97%.; Curated small multi-task training sets (top 3 to 5 source tasks, 10k examples total) consistently outperform massive target-agnostic multi-task training sets (21 tasks, 42k examples or T0-3B's millions of examples) on zero-shot generalization.; Pairwise transfer dynamics are more consistent across different model sizes and adaptation methods within the same architectural family (e.g., T5 variants) than across distinct model families (T5 vs. GPT-2 vs. RoBERTa).; Including negative or unhelpful source tasks in a multi-task training mixture actively degrades target performance, demonstrating that negative transfer can counteract the benefits of multi-task scaling.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Delimited to 22 English-language NLP tasks covering classification, multiple-choice QA, and extractive QA, explicitly excluding generative long-form QA, summarization, dialogue, and domain-specific corpora (legal, medical).', 'Restricted to English monolingual benchmarks without evaluating multilingual or cross-lingual transfer.', 'Multi-task fine-tuning experiments evaluate models up to 3 billion parameters (T5-3B), without testing multi-billion emergent parameter scales (>10B+).', 'Training data construction relies on uniform random sampling of 2,000 examples per selected source task without exploring dynamic data weighting or temperature-based task scheduling.']
limitations_summary: The authors identify four principal limitations: (1) TASKWEB covers 22 English classification and multiple-choice tasks, excluding long-form generative tasks (summarization, long-form QA), domain-specific tasks (legal, medical), and multilingual datasets; (2) adding new tasks or architectures requires substantial pairwise computational investment (|T| or |M| × |T| fine-tuning runs); (3) experiments are restricted to models up to 3 billion parameters (T5-3B), meaning findings may not transfer directly to much larger models with emergent properties; and (4) multi-task fine-tuning utilizes uniform sampling of 2,000 examples per selected task rather than dynamic, proportional, or instruction-mixture sampling strategies.
limitations_verbatim:
Our work contains several limitations. First, our set of tasks does not constitute the entirety of NLP tasks. While we use 22 NLP tasks that are representative enough to cover various types of reasoning, we do not include long-form tasks (e.g., summarization, LFQA) or domain-specific tasks (e.g., law, medicine) to facilitate experiments across various model architectures such as encoder-only models. In order to add entirely new forms of task to TASKWEB, one would have to compute pairwise transfer scores between the new task and other tasks in TASKWEB. If the model is known beforehand, this would require ∥T∥ iterations of fine-tuning with 1,000 examples where T is the set of tasks in TASKWEB. On the other hand, if the model is not known beforehand, this would require ∥M∥ × ∥T∥ iterations where M is the set of models used in TASKWEB.

Moreover, our datasets are in English and we do not incorporate multilinguality in our experiments. Second, our work focuses on models with at most three billion parameters. Our finding may not be directly applicable to models with orders of magnitude more parameters considering factors such as emergence [\(Wei et al.,](#page-12-6) [2022b\)](#page-12-6), which can be explored in future work. Third, we perform our multi-task finetuning experiments by uniformly sampling 2,000 examples from each source task following the style of [Wang et al.](#page-12-0) [\(2022b\)](#page-12-0). Therefore, different behavior may arise when other sampling strategies are used. Finally, recent work shows the effectiveness of using diverse instruction-output pairs which do not necessarily have clear boundaries as our tasks do [\(Ouyang et al.,](#page-11-8) [2022;](#page-11-8) [Wang](#page-12-7)

[et al.,](#page-12-7) [2022a,](#page-12-7) [2023\)](#page-12-8). Recently, [Wang et al.](#page-12-8) [2023](#page-12-8) report that large language models finetuned on specific instruction datasets perform better on related target tasks, which is closely related to our findings. Future work could extend our approach to setups without clear boundaries between tasks and explore ways to perform target-specific instruction tuning. Considering these limitations, we encourage the NLP community to contribute to quantifying the transferabilities between different language tasks.
generalizability_gap: The benchmark and task selection framework are evaluated only on English-language classification, multiple-choice, and extractive QA benchmarks on models up to 3B parameters. Transferability and selection dynamics remain untested on multilingual and low-resource settings, generative long-form text, multi-turn conversational tasks, code generation, and 10B+ large language models.
methodological_gap: TASKSHOP relies on static pairwise transfer matrices and lightweight prompt text embeddings (RoE/LLM-similarity) without modeling higher-order task interactions or negative gradient interference among selected source tasks during joint multi-task training; furthermore, multi-task dataset mixtures use uniform example sampling (2k per task) rather than learned task weighting or temperature-scaled sampling.
future_work: Extending TASKWEB to broader task paradigms including generative long-form QA, summarization, and domain-specific benchmarks.; Incorporating multilinguality and cross-lingual task transfer relationships into the pairwise matrix.; Investigating task selection and transferability dynamics in large language models exceeding 10 billion parameters with emergent abilities.; Applying task selection principles to instruction-tuning datasets lacking explicit task boundaries to enable target-specific instruction mixture optimization.

title: Taskonomy: Disentangling Task Transfer Learning
authors: Amir R. Zamir; Alexander Sax; William Shen; Leonidas Guibas; Jitendra Malik; Silvio Savarese
venue: IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
domain: Computer Vision, Transfer Learning, Visual Task Space Modeling (26 2D, 2.5D, 3D, and semantic indoor scene tasks)
problem_statement: Visual tasks are commonly solved in isolation via fully supervised learning, ignoring structural redundancies and quantifiable transfer dependencies across tasks, which leads to massive labeled data requirements and computational inefficiency.
theoretical_framework: Computational task space taxonomy modeling; transfer learning representations as sufficient statistics in feedforward neural networks; Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) for normalized pairwise task affinity matrix construction; Binary Integer Programming (BIP) optimization for global transfer policy selection under a fixed supervision budget.
methodology: The authors propose a four-step computational framework to map the structure of visual task space across 26 visual tasks: (1) Train fully supervised task-specific feedforward convolutional networks (ResNet-50 without pooling) for each task; (2) Train small, shallow transfer networks (2 convolutional layers) between representations in latent space across first-order and higher-order task combinations; (3) Normalize transfer performance into a pairwise task affinity matrix using ordinal win-rate comparisons and the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP); (4) Solve a Binary Integer Programming (BIP) problem to discover the globally optimal supervision policy that minimizes target task error given a limited supervision budget (maximum number of source tasks trained from scratch). The discovered structure is validated on novel out-of-dictionary tasks and external benchmarks (ImageNet and MIT Places).
datasets: Taskonomy Dataset: 4 million high-resolution indoor images with ground truth across 26 vision tasks, captured from about 600 buildings. The experimental subset uses 120,000 training, 16,000 validation, and 17,000 testing images across non-overlapping buildings.; ImageNet (used for external benchmark correlation validation on object classification).; MIT Places (used for external benchmark correlation validation on scene classification).
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Win Rate (%): proportion of test set images where a proposed model beats a baseline', 'Gain: win rate against a network trained from scratch using the same limited training data as transfer networks', 'Quality: win rate against a fully supervised network trained with 120k images (gold standard)', "Spearman's Rho: rank correlation across external benchmark rankings"], 'baselines': ['Random Network Baseline (Gaussian representation readout)', 'Statistically informed average guess baseline', 'Training from scratch with limited data (16k images)', 'Fully supervised task-specific networks (gold standard, 120k images)', 'Self-supervised representation baselines: Video/Motion (Wang & Gupta, 2015), Colorization (Zhang et al., 2016), Jigsaw Puzzles (Noroozi & Favaro, 2016), Generic 3D Representation (Zamir et al., 2016), and Egomotion (Agrawal et al., 2015)', 'ImageNet FC7 off-the-shelf feature transfer', 'Random feasible transfer policies']}
key_findings: Discovered a strong, non-trivial computational structure among 26 visual tasks, enabling solving all tasks with significantly reduced supervision (supervision budget substantially lower than total task count).; Taxonomy-suggested transfer policies consistently outperform state-of-the-art self-supervised representations and off-the-shelf ImageNet features on novel tasks, approaching fully supervised performance with only a fraction of the data.; Transfer relationships are frequently asymmetric and counter-intuitive; for instance, transferring surface normals to depth estimation is computationally more effective than transferring depth to surface normals, contrary to analytical expectations.; Higher-order transfers (combining features from multiple source tasks, such as surface normals and occlusion edges) provide synergistic gains for targets like reshading and point matching.; The discovered task structure generalizes to external image distributions, exhibiting high rank correlation on MIT Places (Spearman's rho = 0.857) and ImageNet (Spearman's rho = 0.823).; The taxonomy remains remarkably stable across variations in network architecture (ResNet-50 vs. others), dataset size (up to 16x transfer data variance), and data splits.
scope_and_delimitations: ['The empirical investigation is delimited to indoor scene perception across 26 predefined visual tasks (2D, 2.5D, 3D, and semantic).', 'The function class is restricted to convolutional neural networks (ResNet-50 encoder with identical shallow 2-layer transfer decoders).', 'Supervision policy discovery is optimized under fixed, discrete task budgets (ranging from 1 to 26 source tasks) evaluated on 16k transfer examples.']
limitations_summary: The computational taxonomy is fundamentally conditioned on neural network representations and specific indoor scene datasets; task definitions rely on human-defined visual heuristics rather than unsupervised latent subtasks; mapping a continuous task space via a discrete dictionary lacks theoretical regularity guarantees; and the static one-pass framework cannot dynamically update as new tasks arrive sequentially in lifelong learning environments.
limitations_verbatim:
*Model Dependence:* We used a computational approach and adopted neural networks as our function class. Though we validated the stability of the findings w.r.t various architectures and datasets, it should be noted that the findings are in principle model and data specific.

*Compositionality:* We performed the modeling via a set of common human-defined visual tasks. It is natural to consider a further compositional approach in which such common tasks are viewed as *observed samples* which are composed of computationally found latent subtasks.

*Space Regularity:* We performed modeling of a dense space via a sampled dictionary. Though we showed a good tolerance w.r.t. to the choice of dictionary and transferring to out-of-dictionary tasks, this outcome holds upon a proper sampling of the space as a function of its regularity. More formal studies on properties of the computed space is required for this to be provably guaranteed for a general case.

*Lifelong Learning*: We performed the modeling in one go. In many cases, e.g. lifelong learning, the system is evolving and the number of mastered tasks constantly increase. Such scenarios require augmentation of the structure with expansion mechanisms based on new beliefs.
generalizability_gap: The empirical task taxonomy is restricted to static 2D/3D indoor visual environments and convolutional architectures, leaving unexamined task transfer structures in non-visual domains (e.g., natural language processing, speech, audio), outdoor environments, dynamic temporal sequences, and transformer-based architectures.
methodological_gap: The framework models transfer relationships through feedforward transfer functions in a fixed latent space rather than simultaneous bidirectional multi-task learning or dynamic gradient balancing, and task affinity is derived through ordinal pairwise comparisons rather than optimization-level gradient conflict analysis.
future_work: Developing compositional task space formulations where tasks are decomposed into computationally discovered latent subtasks.; Formulating mathematical analyses and theoretical guarantees on task space regularity and completeness.; Extending the taxonomy framework to dynamic lifelong learning systems where task dictionaries expand incrementally over time.; Investigating the relationship between transfer learning task structure and simultaneous multi-task parameter sharing.
local_dir: Taskonomy - Disentangling Task Transfer Learning

title: The Decades Progress on Code-Switching Research in NLP: A Systematic Survey on Trends and Challenges
authors: Genta Indra Winata; Alham Fikri Aji; Zheng-Xin Yong; Thamar Solorio
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2023
domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Speech Processing, Code-Switching (CSW), Multilingual Language Modeling, Computational Linguistics
problem_statement: A systematic investigation into decades of code-switching (CSW) research in natural language and speech processing to understand historical progress from linguistic theories to pre-trained neural language models, identify task and language coverage imbalances, evaluate dataset accessibility and attrition issues, and conceptualize open research challenges and future directions.
theoretical_framework: Grammatical and linguistic constraint theories of bilingual code-switching, including Poplack's Equivalence Constraint (1980), Myers-Scotton's Matrix-Embedded Language Framework (MLF) (1997, 2005), and Belazi et al.'s Functional Head Constraint (1994), alongside cognitive theories of multilingual competence and cross-lingual representation alignment.
methodology: Systematic literature survey and manual multi-annotator taxonomy coding analyzing over 400 papers published in the ACL Anthology (crawled up to October 2022) and ISCA proceedings using 14 code-switching search keywords. Three annotators categorized publications across language varieties (bilingual, trilingual, 4+; regional groups), publication venues, paper contribution genres, dataset sources/modalities, computational methodologies (rule-based/linguistic constraints, statistical methods, neural sequence models, pre-trained language models), and text/speech downstream tasks.
key_findings: The vast majority of code-switching NLP research is bilingual with English as one of the pair (particularly South Asian languages like Hindi, Tamil, Malayalam, as well as Spanish and Chinese), while non-English pairs, Middle Eastern languages, and multilingual switching (trilingual or 4+) remain substantially under-represented.; Language identification and sentiment analysis dominate ACL text-based code-switching research, whereas ASR and TTS dominate ISCA speech processing publications, demonstrating ongoing fragmentation between the speech and text processing research communities.; Social media text and recorded conversational speech constitute the primary data sources, but over 60% of surveyed corpora are private/closed, and social media datasets suffer from significant data attrition due to URL-only sharing policies and deleted posts.; The methodological paradigm has shifted from rule-based linguistic constraints (Poplack's equivalence constraint, MLF, functional head constraint) and statistical models (CRF, SVM, HMM) to neural sequence architectures (RNN/LSTM) and pre-trained multilingual language models (mBERT, XLM-R).; While pre-trained multilingual language models enable end-to-end task performance without manual linguistic rules, they lack interpretability regarding failure modes and face catastrophic forgetting/language attrition when fine-tuned on mixed-language inputs.
scope_and_delimitations: ['The survey systematically indexes academic literature on code-switching published in open proceedings of the ACL Anthology (up to October 2022) and ISCA conferences, supplemented by curated public research repositories.', 'The scope covers both written natural language processing and spoken speech processing modalities across token-level, sequence-level, and generative tasks.', 'The analysis excludes papers published after October 2022 and excludes fine-grained categorization of code-switching types (such as intra-sentential versus inter-sentential switching) due to lack of reporting in source literature.', 'The survey is non-empirical and synthesizes findings and statistics across literature without running new experimental benchmarks or retraining models.']
limitations_summary: The quantitative review is delimited to publications indexed in the ACL Anthology and ISCA proceedings (excluding broader journals and post-October 2022 literature), and does not categorize fine-grained linguistic switching types (such as intra-sentential vs. inter-sentential switching) because many surveyed papers omit these structural details.
limitations_verbatim: The numbers in this survey are limited to papers published in the ACL Anthology and ISCA Proceedings. However, we also included papers as related work from other resources if they are publicly available and accessible. In addition, the category in the survey does not include the code-switching type (i.e., intra-sentential, inter-sentential, etc.) since some papers do not provide such information.
generalizability_gap: Code-switching research and resources are heavily skewed toward a few high-resource bilingual pairs involving English (Hindi-English, Spanish-English, Chinese-English). Geographic varieties, regional dialects, underrepresented indigenous languages, non-English mixed pairs, and complex multilingual interactions (trilingual and 4+ languages) remain severely understudied and lack generalizable models.
methodological_gap: Pre-trained multilingual models lack interpretability in code-switched contexts, suffer from catastrophic forgetting and cross-lingual representation degradation, and remain under-evaluated for scaling laws and compute-performance trade-offs. Furthermore, evaluation methods for generative code-switched text rely heavily on subjective human evaluation, lacking automated metrics that reliably align with human judgments of fidelity, style mimicry, and discourse naturalness.
future_work: Broadening language scope to under-represented code-switching styles, regional dialects, and non-English/multilingual (>2 languages) language combinations.; Developing open, accessible, and ecologically valid written code-switched corpora that avoid data attrition issues associated with social media APIs.; Investigating model scaling laws, compute-performance trade-offs, and zero-shot/few-shot prompt and instruction tuning with large multilingual foundation models on code-switched tasks.; Integrating code-switching evaluation into standardized cross-lingual benchmarks (e.g., XTREME-R, XGLUE) to assess model robustness and continual learning against catastrophic forgetting.; Creating complex reasoning and comprehension benchmarks for code-switched text, including natural language inference, coreference resolution, and question answering.; Developing code-switching conversational dialogue agents and generative models with automated evaluation metrics aligned with human judgments of quality, style, and naturalness.
local_dir: The Decades Progress on Code-Switching Research in NLP - A Systematic Survey on Trends and Challenges

title: Towards Impartial Multi-task Learning
authors: Liyang Liu; Yi Li; Zheng Kuang; Jing-Hao Xue; Yimin Chen; Wenming Yang; Qingmin Liao; Wayne Zhang
venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2021)
domain: Multi-Task Optimization, Deep Learning, Computer Vision
problem_statement: Investigates the partial training issue in multi-task learning where naively training all tasks simultaneously leads to specific tasks dominating the shared representations due to disparate loss scales and gradient magnitudes.
theoretical_framework: Multi-objective gradient projection and loss scale invariance; angle bisector formulation for task-shared parameter gradient balancing.
methodology: Proposes Impartial Multi-Task Learning (IMTL), combining IMTL-G (gradient balance) and IMTL-L (loss balance). IMTL-G optimizes scaling factors via a closed-form solution so that aggregated gradients have equal projections onto individual task gradients (finding the geometric angle bisector). IMTL-L dynamically balances loss scales across tasks using learnable parameters without distributional assumptions.
datasets: Cityscapes; NYUv2; CelebA
evaluation: Semantic segmentation mIoU; Instance segmentation L1 error; Disparity / depth estimation L1 error; Surface normal cosine similarity; Multi-attribute classification accuracy; Training runtime in seconds per iteration
key_findings: IMTL-G provides a closed-form gradient balance solution ensuring equal projections onto raw task gradients, avoiding majority task bias (unlike GradNorm, MGDA, and PCGrad).; Gradient balance on shared parameters and loss balance on task-specific parameters are complementary; combining them achieves superior multi-task performance over single-task and equal weighting baselines.; IMTL is scale-invariant and maintains consistent convergence even when individual task losses are manually rescaled by orders of magnitude.; Computing gradients with respect to shared feature representations rather than full model parameters reduces computational overhead from T backward passes to 1 backward pass after loss weighting.
scope_and_delimitations: Evaluates hard-parameter-sharing neural network architectures on multi-task computer vision benchmarks (Cityscapes, NYUv2, CelebA) across semantic segmentation, depth estimation, surface normal estimation, and attribute classification.
limitations_summary: Impartial fairness weighting assumes equal priority among all tasks and may be suboptimal when specific tasks are of primary operational importance and require preferential weighting.
limitations_verbatim: Taking fairness among tasks as a proxy is not always beneficial, especially when one of the tasks is more important than others. In this case we may deliberately down-weight certain tasks to better aid the most concerned one.
generalizability_gap: Evaluated exclusively on vision benchmarks (Cityscapes, NYUv2, CelebA); untested on natural language processing, low-resource languages, or code-switched multi-task triage text.
methodological_gap: Gradient balance computation assumes linear projection on shared feature activations, which may introduce approximation error relative to full parameter-level backpropagation in non-vision architectures.
future_work: Extending impartial multi-task learning to task grouping and dynamic neural architecture search.; Evaluating IMTL on non-vision modalities including natural language understanding and speech processing.
local_dir: Towards Impartial Multi-task Learning

title: Transformer-based Multi-task Learning for Disaster Tweet Categorisation
authors: Congcong Wang; Paul Nulty; David Lillis
venue: Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Information Systems for Crisis Response and Management (ISCRAM 2021)
domain: Crisis Informatics, Disaster Response, Social Media Natural Language Processing (Twitter/X Disaster Tweet Classification and Prioritization), Multi-Task Learning
problem_statement: Manual identification of actionable disaster messages during crises is unfeasible due to explosive message volumes on social media. Emergency response operators require real-time categorization of crisis-related tweets by requested information types and accurate message prioritization to establish situational awareness, but single-task models and traditional classifiers struggle with cross-task dependencies, severe class imbalance, and diverse disaster contexts.
theoretical_framework: Multi-task learning parameter-sharing theory (Zhang and Yang, 2017) positing that joint optimization across related downstream tasks regularizes representation learning, mitigates overfitting, and transfers inductive knowledge through a shared transformer encoder backbone; Situational Awareness (SA) framework in crisis response (Endsley, 2017; Vieweg et al., 2010).
methodology: Proposed a transformer-based multi-task learning (MTL) framework combining multi-label Information Type Categorisation (ITC) across 25 categories and continuous Priority Estimation (PE) into a unified architecture. The framework shares an upstream transformer encoder (evaluating BERT_base, DistilBERT_base, ELECTRA_base, and ALBERT_base_v2) and adds two task-specific projection heads: a linear multi-label projection layer with sigmoid activation for ITC, and a linear regression projection layer for PE mapping categorical priority levels (Critical: 1.0, High: 0.75, Medium: 0.5, Low: 0.25) to continuous scores in [0, 1]. The joint model optimizes a composite loss combining binary cross-entropy for ITC and Mean Squared Error for PE with equal loss weighting (alpha = 0.5). To enhance generalization across heterogeneous encoders, introduced an ensemble technique combining disparate MTL models using a Union strategy for information type predictions and a Highest strategy for priority level predictions.

key_findings: Multi-task learning with a shared BERT encoder backbone outperforms single-task learning baselines (both BERT STL and Logistic Regression STL), yielding superior ranking (NDCG 0.5101 vs. 0.4393) and alerting worth (AW-HC -0.2689 vs. -0.4057) while eliminating the operational requirement of training separate models for separate tasks.; Parameter-efficient transformer variants (DistilBERT at 66M parameters and ALBERT at 11M parameters) achieve competitive disaster tweet classification performance relative to full-sized encoders (BERT and ELECTRA at 110M parameters), demonstrating operational viability on resource-constrained hardware.; Combining diverse multi-task transformer models into an ensemble yields substantial performance gains, elevating the overall harmonic mean score (HarM) from 0.2609 (single BERT MTL) to 0.3141 (EnsembleD) and achieving state-of-the-art results across benchmark metrics.; Ensemble fusion ablations demonstrate that combining predictions via a Union strategy for information types and a Highest strategy for priority levels produces optimal performance across ranking, alerting worth, and categorization metrics.; The proposed multi-task framework and ensemble method achieved state-of-the-art performance when evaluated against participating systems in the TREC Incident Streams (TREC-IS 2020A) benchmark track across both 25-class (Task 1) and 12-class (Task 2) evaluations.; Qualitative error analysis indicates that misclassifications often arise from missing ground truth annotations, ambiguous multi-perspective interpretations (first-party versus third-party reporting), complex geographic entity disambiguation, and human assessor subjectivity.
scope_and_delimitations: ['The experimental evaluation is delimited to English-language disaster tweets from the TREC-IS 2018–2020A benchmark dataset covering 42 crisis events.', 'Input representations are delimited strictly to raw text sequences with a maximum length of 128 WordPiece tokens, excluding linked web articles, images, and author metadata.', 'Architectural exploration is delimited to four pre-trained uncased base-scale transformer encoders (BERT_base, DistilBERT_base, ELECTRA_base, ALBERT_base_v2) using hard parameter sharing across two downstream heads.', 'Multi-task optimization is delimited to an equal fixed loss weighting parameter (alpha = 0.5) combining binary cross-entropy and mean squared error.', 'Ensemble aggregation is delimited to heuristic rule-based fusion strategies (Union/Intersection and Highest/Average/Lowest) rather than learned stacking classifiers.']
limitations_summary: The proposed approach is limited to processing raw textual tweet content without incorporating linked external web pages or multimodal imagery; the multi-task formulation is restricted to two downstream tasks evaluated on a single benchmark corpus; computational efficiency and real-time processing throughput during high-volume crisis surges have not been empirically evaluated; and evaluation relies on human assessor annotations that contain subjective inconsistencies and errors.
limitations_verbatim: Regarding the eectiveness, there is still much room to improve. We oer our approach as a baseline for future work on this problem. Our approach is currently limited to using the raw text of tweets. Per McCreadie et al. [2020,](#page-0-17) linked content such as the web pages, or images posted along with the tweets are likely to improve performance. Hence, future work will incorporate this linked information into our current approach. In addition, since our current approach only focuses on two tasks from a single corpus, we plan to extend our approach to support more tasks from multiple corpora. Although eectiveness is an essential performance measurement for an emergency response system, another aspect to which the same importance should be given is eciency. When employing an emergency response system in a real-world situation, the speed of message handling is crucial because social media message quantities are usually enormous during a crisis. Our approach has not yet been examined regarding its eciency, which also requires further exploration.
generalizability_gap: The empirical evaluation is restricted to English-language Twitter posts across 42 disaster events in the TREC-IS benchmark, leaving unexamined performance on non-English crisis communications, code-switched microblogging streams, alternative messaging platforms (such as Facebook, Reddit, or Telegram), and multimodal disaster data streams containing synchronized imagery and geolocation coordinates.
methodological_gap: The multi-task training setup uses a static, uniform loss weight parameter (alpha = 0.5) without exploring dynamic multi-task gradient balancing algorithms (such as GradNorm or PCGrad) to mitigate gradient conflict; the model ensemble relies on static heuristic aggregation rules rather than learned meta-classifiers; and the architecture lacks integration with geographical knowledge graphs or gazetteers to resolve localized place name ambiguities.
future_work: Incorporating linked external content, including web pages and images posted alongside disaster tweets, into multimodal representation learning.; Extending the multi-task learning framework to support additional crisis informatics tasks across multiple diverse corpora.; Evaluating computational efficiency, inference latency, and high-throughput deployment architectures for real-time crisis message handling.; Integrating external knowledge maps, gazetteers, and geographical ontologies to disambiguate localized location references and enrich spatial context awareness.

title: TweetTaglish: A Dataset for Investigating Tagalog-English Code-Switching
authors: Megan Herrera; Ankit Aich; Natalie Parde
venue: Proceedings of the Thirteenth Language Resources and Evaluation Conference (LREC 2022)
domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Tagalog-English Code-Switching (Taglish), Social Media (Twitter), Low-Resource Languages
problem_statement: Tagalog and Tagalog-English code-switching (Taglish) are under-represented in natural language processing research and practice, lacking large-scale annotated datasets, linguistic analysis, and standardized benchmarks for computational modeling and language distribution identification.
theoretical_framework: Sociolinguistic theories of code-switching, including Goulet's (1968) six CS motivations, Bautista's (2004) framework on communicative efficiency and proficiency/deficiency drivers, Hamers and Blanc's (2000) and Poplack's (1980) three-way CS typology (inter-sentential, extra-sentential, intra-sentential), and Flores's (2020) empirical identification of Tagalog-English linguistic markers (bound morphemes, enclitics).
methodology: Multilingual keyword harvesting on Twitter using six Tagalog CS-indicative linguistic features (magko-, di ba, talaga, ano yung, para sa, parang) across English and Filipino query settings to gather 21,150 tweets; preprocessing involving case normalization, stopword removal, and stripping of usernames, hashtags, emojis, punctuation, non-Roman text, and URLs; dictionary-based token-level language identification using PyEnchant for English, a scraped Tagalog lexicon, and rule-based morphological parsing for Tagalog verb conjugations; multi-label tweet-level language proportion assignment (percentages of English, Tagalog, and Other tokens); dataset validation via proof-of-concept regression modeling using 50-dimensional Filipino Word2Vec embeddings and six regressors (Mean baseline, OLS Linear, SVR, SGD, Bayesian Ridge, MLP) under an 80/20 train/test split.
datasets: TweetTaglish: 21,150 Tagalog-English code-switched and unilingual tweets collected from Twitter with word-level and tweet-level English, Tagalog, and Other language distribution annotations; Pretrained 50-dimensional Filipino Word2Vec embeddings trained on Philippine social media data (Marges, 2019)
evaluation: {'metrics': ['R² (Coefficient of Determination)', 'RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error)', "Cohen's Kappa (Inter-Annotator Agreement)"], 'inter_annotator_agreement': {'instance_level': 'κ = 0.70 (substantial agreement on 20 sample tweets)', 'word_level': 'κ = 0.15 (slight agreement due to Spanish cognates and morphological blending)'}, 'benchmark_results': {'MLP (Best)': {'English': {'R2': 0.909, 'RMSE': 0.057}, 'Tagalog': {'R2': 0.883, 'RMSE': 0.068}, 'Other': {'R2': 0.797, 'RMSE': 0.068}}, 'SVR': {'English': {'R2': 0.898, 'RMSE': 0.061}, 'Tagalog': {'R2': 0.854, 'RMSE': 0.076}, 'Other': {'R2': 0.699, 'RMSE': 0.083}}, 'Linear': {'English': {'R2': 0.861, 'RMSE': 0.071}, 'Tagalog': {'R2': 0.7, 'RMSE': 0.109}, 'Other': {'R2': 0.375, 'RMSE': 0.119}}, 'Ridge': {'English': {'R2': 0.861, 'RMSE': 0.071}, 'Tagalog': {'R2': 0.7, 'RMSE': 0.109}, 'Other': {'R2': 0.374, 'RMSE': 0.119}}, 'SGD': {'English': {'R2': 0.848, 'RMSE': 0.074}, 'Tagalog': {'R2': 0.688, 'RMSE': 0.112}, 'Other': {'R2': 0.333, 'RMSE': 0.123}}, 'Mean_Baseline': {'English': {'R2': -0.0, 'RMSE': 0.19}, 'Tagalog': {'R2': -6.32, 'RMSE': 0.2}, 'Other': {'R2': -0.0, 'RMSE': 0.151}}}}
key_findings: Constructed TweetTaglish, a novel dataset containing 21,150 Tagalog-English code-switched and unilingual tweets with token-level and tweet-level language distribution annotations.; Validated dataset learnability through regression benchmarking, where all models substantially outperformed the Mean baseline, and the MLP regressor achieved the highest performance (English: R² = 0.909, RMSE = 0.057; Tagalog: R² = 0.883, RMSE = 0.068; Other: R² = 0.797, RMSE = 0.068).; Observed that regression models predicted English language distributions most accurately, while encountering the greatest difficulty predicting the 'Other' category.; Determined the overall corpus language distribution per tweet to average 55.2% Tagalog, 19.4% English, and 24.5% Other.; N-gram frequency analysis computationally validated the efficacy of Flores (2020) Tagalog linguistic features for harvesting Taglish text at scale, revealing high frequencies of personal pronouns ('ko', 'ako') characteristic of informal social media discourse.; Validation of dictionary-based annotation against a human speaker yielded substantial agreement at the instance level (κ = 0.70), though word-level agreement was lower (κ = 0.15) due to cross-lingual cognates and affixation.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Restricted to Tagalog-English code-switched text gathered from Twitter without geographic or user-specific constraints.', 'Data collection relies on six specific linguistic query terms (magko-, di ba, talaga, ano yung, para sa, parang) rather than comprehensive lexicon search.', 'Empirical evaluation is delimited to tweet-level language proportion regression rather than token-level sequence labeling, dependency parsing, or code-switching point detection.', 'Feature representation is limited to static 50-dimensional Word2Vec embeddings rather than contextualized multilingual transformer architectures.']
limitations_summary: The keyword search strategy and dictionary-based language identification introduced noise from cross-lingual cognates (particularly Spanish words like 'para' misidentified as Tagalog), contributing to low word-level inter-annotator agreement (κ = 0.15). Additionally, regression models exhibited lower accuracy on the 'Other' category containing slang, misspellings, and hybrid morphological combinations.
limitations_verbatim: One minor observation was that our current keyword search strategy allowed for the inclusion of text from some other non-English languages with similar phrases (e.g., Spanish, due to cognates such as para). This could be addressed in future iterations of data collection using more advanced regular expressions and text preprocessing techniques.
generalizability_gap: The dataset is limited to Twitter and Tagalog-English code-switching, leaving unaddressed other Philippine regional languages (e.g., Cebuano, Ilocano, Hiligaynon), formal or spoken discourse modalities, other social media platforms, and non-Tagalog code-switching pairs.
methodological_gap: Dictionary lookup paired with simple rule-based morphological parsing fails to robustly handle intra-word code-switching (Tagalog bound morphemes on English stems such as 'nakakatouch') and cross-lingual homographs/cognates; evaluations rely on static token-averaged 50-dimensional Word2Vec embeddings without comparing against contextualized multilingual language models.
future_work: Experiment with more advanced NLP approaches to effectively process code-switching in everyday text and learn better representations for low-resource languages, including Taglish.; Employ advanced regular expressions and text preprocessing techniques to filter out non-target language text and cross-lingual cognates during data collection.; Explore more complex downstream code-switching tasks, such as word-level language identification, syntactic/dependency parsing, and code-switching point detection.
