title: Twitter as a Lifeline: Human-annotated Twitter Corpora for NLP of Crisis-related Messages
authors: Muhammad Imran; Prasenjit Mitra; Carlos Castillo
venue: Proceedings of the Tenth International Conference on Language Resources and Evaluation (LREC 2016)
domain: Crisis informatics, disaster response management, and social media text processing on Twitter.
problem_statement: During sudden-onset disaster crises, affected individuals publish time-critical situational information on microblogging platforms, but processing noisy, brief, and informal messages is hindered by the scarcity of standardized human-annotated crisis corpora, domain-specific distributed word representations, and lexical normalization resources for out-of-vocabulary variations.
theoretical_framework: Situational awareness theory in emergency management, humanitarian information taxonomies aligned with the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (UN OCHA), and Bayesian probability modeling for single-edit spelling correction and lexical normalization.
methodology: The authors collected over 52 million crisis-related tweets across 19 natural and human-induced disasters (2013–2015) using the Artificial Intelligence for Disaster Response (AIDR) platform. They annotated approximately 50,000 tweets via Stand-By Task Force (SBTF) volunteers on MicroMappers and paid workers on CrowdFlower across nine UN OCHA humanitarian categories using a three-annotator consensus protocol. To support natural language processing on informal crisis text, the authors trained 300-dimensional continuous bag-of-words (CBOW) word2vec embeddings on the full 52-million tweet corpus. In addition, the authors implemented a lexical normalization pipeline for out-of-vocabulary (OOV) terms combining dictionary lookups (SCOWL, MaxMind World Cities), a Bayesian single-edit language model, and crowdsourced human verification. Finally, they evaluated multiclass classification using Naive Bayes, Random Forest, and Support Vector Machines with unigram and bigram features and Information Gain feature selection under 10-fold cross-validation.
datasets: CrisisNLP 19 Crises Dataset: Over 52 million Twitter messages collected via the AIDR platform across 19 disaster events (2013–2015) with ~50,000 human-annotated tweets categorized across UN OCHA humanitarian classes; Crisis Word2Vec Embeddings: 300-dimensional continuous bag-of-words (CBOW) distributed word representations trained on 52 million crisis tweets; Crisis Normalized Lexical Resources: Human-annotated dataset of out-of-vocabulary (OOV) slang, abbreviations, misspellings, phonetic substitutions, and joined words normalized via crowdsourcing and language modeling; SCOWL (Spell Checker Oriented Word Lists) Aspell English Dictionary (349,554 words); MaxMind Free World Cities Database (3,173,959 cities); British National Corpus (BNC) and Wiktionary word frequency lists
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC)', '10-Fold Cross-Validation'], 'results_summary': "Evaluated Naive Bayes (NB), Random Forest (RF), and Support Vector Machines (SVM) across 8 disaster datasets. Classifiers achieved AUC scores >= 0.80 for most humanitarian categories, whereas the rare 'missing, trapped, or found people' class exhibited lower performance due to severe class imbalance."}
key_findings: Human-annotated crisis microblog corpora from 19 diverse disaster events enable effective supervised multiclass classification across UN OCHA humanitarian categories, achieving Area Under ROC Curve (AUC) scores exceeding 0.80 for most classes across Naive Bayes, Random Forest, and Support Vector Machines.; Severe class imbalance noticeably degrades classifier performance on sparse categories, particularly the 'missing, trapped, or found people' category, which had the smallest proportion of labeled examples across datasets.; Continuous word2vec embeddings trained on 52 million domain-specific crisis tweets provide rich distributed semantic representations tailored to informal disaster communications.; Out-of-vocabulary (OOV) lexical noise in crisis tweets spans five distinct categories: typos/misspellings, single-word abbreviations/slang, multi-word abbreviations/slang, phonetic substitutions, and joined words without spaces.; A hybrid normalization pipeline combining dictionary lookups, single-edit Bayesian language modeling, and crowdsourcing effectively detects and normalizes out-of-vocabulary terms in social media crisis communications.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Restricted data collection to Twitter messages gathered via the AIDR streaming API across 19 specific disaster events occurring between 2013 and 2015.', 'Delimited open distribution to full text for fewer than 50,000 annotated tweets and tweet IDs for the remaining unannotated corpus in compliance with Twitter developer data redistribution policies.', 'Restricted supervised classification benchmarking to 8 disaster datasets using traditional machine learning algorithms (Naive Bayes, Random Forest, Support Vector Machines) with n-gram features and Lovins stemming.', 'Constrained automated candidate spelling correction to a single edit-distance threshold, delegating multi-edit candidates and complex OOV categories to crowdsourced human annotators.']
limitations_summary: The authors acknowledge that the collected crisis datasets exhibit severe class imbalance across categories, particularly for rare classes such as missing or trapped individuals, which impedes learning performance. Additionally, standard geographical dictionaries lack complete coverage of local towns and cities in non-Western disaster zones (such as Nepal), and automated spelling correction is restricted to single edit-distance candidates.
limitations_verbatim: After the first round of annotations, we found that some categories are small in terms of number of labels thus showing high class-imbalance. A dataset is said to be *imbalanced* if at least one of the classes has significantly fewer annotated instances than the others. The class imbalance problem has been known to hinder the learning performance of classification algorithms. In this case, we performed another round of annotations for datasets that have high class imbalance using the paid crowdsourcing platform CrowdFlower.
generalizability_gap: The dataset and evaluation focus primarily on Twitter messages from 19 specific disaster events between 2013 and 2015, with classification experiments evaluated on 8 events. While multilingual tweets exist in the raw stream, the lexical normalization pipeline and evaluated models focus on English text, leaving low-resource non-English languages, dialectal variations without external gazetteers, and alternative social media platforms unaddressed.
methodological_gap: The classification experiments rely on classical shallow learning algorithms (Naive Bayes, Random Forest, Support Vector Machines) with bag-of-words features rather than modern contextualized deep learning architectures. Furthermore, the automated spell-correction mechanism is limited to single edit-distance changes, and Twitter redistribution policies limit full-text publication to 50,000 tweets.
future_work: Developing advanced computational NLP methods and situational awareness tools on top of the published corpora and word embeddings.; Expanding normalized lexical resources to cover additional languages, regional dialects, and localized geographical entities.; Investigating deep learning architectures and transfer learning mechanisms for real-time crisis message classification.

title: When is Multi-task Learning Beneficial for Low-Resource Noisy Code-switched User-generated Algerian Texts?
authors: Wafia Adouane; Jean-Philippe Bernardy
venue: Workshop on Computational Approaches to Linguistic Code-Switching (CALCS)
domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Low-Resource Colloquial Languages, Code-Switching (specifically Algerian Arabic / ALG user-generated social media text with Berber, French, English, and Modern Standard Arabic)
problem_statement: Scarcity of annotated morpho-syntactic and semantic training data poses substantial challenges for natural language processing in low-resource, non-standardized, code-switched languages. The authors investigate the specific conditions under which multi-task learning with shared representations is beneficial or detrimental for noisy user-generated Algerian Arabic across sequence tagging, sequence-to-sequence, and text classification tasks.
theoretical_framework: Multi-task representation learning theory (Caruana, 1997), which posits that joint learning of complementary tasks induces shared generalizable representations, contextualized within sociolinguistic frameworks of multilingual code-switching and diglossia in North Africa.
methodology: The authors implement an end-to-end multi-task neural network consisting of shared convolutional encoders and task-specific decoders. The token-level encoder uses two CNN layers (100 features, filter size 5, dropout 0.2, max pooling) mapping characters to token representations. The sequence-level encoder applies two CNN layers (200 and 100 features, filter size 3, dropout 0.05) to output sentence representations. Task heads include: (1) CSD sequence-tagging dense softmax layer across 9 classes, (2) NER sequence-tagging dense softmax layer across 6 classes with IOB tagging, (3) SPELL sequence-to-sequence 1-layer LSTM decoder (100 units, dropout 0.1) followed by a dense layer, and (4) SA classification dense softmax layer across 4 sentiment classes. Models are trained using the Adam optimizer (batch size 64, gradient clipping norm 5) by alternating tasks per full epoch. Empirical experiments evaluate pairwise task combinations, task ordering (3-task and 4-task permutations), word context effects (token-level vs. sequence-level SPELL), SPELL training dataset sizing (10k, 50k, 100k, full), and data augmentation (combining token and sequence inputs).
datasets: Code-Switch Detection (CSD) Dataset: 10,590 user-generated texts (223,541 tokens) annotated token-level across 9 classes (ALG, MSA, FRC, BOR, NER, DIG, SND, ENG, BER) (Adouane & Dobnik, 2017).; Spelling Normalisation and Correction (SPELL) Dataset: Parallel corpus of 185,219 samples (50,456 words, 26,199 types) for non-standardized orthographic normalization (Adouane et al., 2019).; Sentiment Analysis (SA) Dataset: 36,120 user-generated comments annotated for 4 sentiment classes (POS, NEG, NEU, MIX) (Adouane et al., 2020).; Named Entity Recognition (NER) Dataset: Newly compiled corpus of 46,710 user-generated comments (17,133 entity mentions) annotated with OntoNotes 5.0 IOB labels across 6 classes (PER, LOC, PRO, ORG, COM, OTH) and non-entity (OOO).
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Accuracy (%)', 'Macro F-score', 'Micro F-score (per-class convergence analysis)'], 'baseline_vs_pairwise_results': {'CSD': {'single_task': {'accuracy': 96.8, 'macro_f1': 64.54}, 'CSD_plus_NER': {'accuracy': 97.2, 'macro_f1': 71.29}, 'CSD_plus_SPELL': {'accuracy': 96.32, 'macro_f1': 62.27}, 'CSD_plus_SA': {'accuracy': 94.3, 'macro_f1': 34.61}}, 'SPELL': {'single_task': {'accuracy': 93.49}, 'SPELL_plus_NER': {'accuracy': 93.71}, 'SPELL_plus_CSD': {'accuracy': 93.6}, 'SPELL_plus_SA': {'accuracy': 93.2}}, 'SA': {'single_task': {'accuracy': 61.23, 'macro_f1': 54.08}, 'SA_plus_CSD': {'accuracy': 61.35, 'macro_f1': 53.31}, 'SA_plus_SPELL': {'accuracy': 60.74, 'macro_f1': 51.5}, 'SA_plus_NER': {'accuracy': 59.82, 'macro_f1': 53.46}}, 'NER': {'single_task': {'accuracy': 99.8, 'macro_f1': 49.68}, 'NER_plus_CSD': {'accuracy': 99.82, 'macro_f1': 48.65}, 'NER_plus_SPELL': {'accuracy': 99.78, 'macro_f1': 42.05}, 'NER_plus_SA': {'accuracy': 99.74, 'macro_f1': 34.6}}}}
key_findings: Multi-task learning is not universally beneficial for low-resource code-switched text; benefits depend heavily on task compatibility, task order, dataset size, and data noise.; Jointly training CSD and NER provides mutual performance improvements, elevating CSD accuracy to 97.20% and macro F1 to 71.29% while improving minority classes such as English tokens and Named Entity mentions.; Joint training with SPELL or SA degrades performance on CSD and NER due to severe orthographic sparsity and noise present in user-generated spelling and sentiment datasets.; Multi-task learning accelerates learning speed in the first 1 to 7 epochs, but performance often plateaus or degrades over extended training compared to single-task baselines.; Task execution order strongly influences early training dynamics in 3-task and 4-task configurations, with NER+CSD+SPELL+SA and SPELL+CSD+NER+SA optimizing SPELL performance.; Sentence-level word context is essential for sequence-to-sequence spelling correction; omitting context reduces both SPELL accuracy and multi-task transfer effectiveness.; Increasing auxiliary dataset size for SPELL yields diminishing returns in multi-task configurations; transfer gains peak at 10k samples for SA/NER and 100k samples for CSD rather than scaling monotonically with data size.; Data augmentation (combining token-level and sequence-level inputs for SPELL) improves single-task SPELL accuracy but offers negligible gain at convergence in multi-task settings.
scope_and_delimitations: ['The study focuses exclusively on Algerian Arabic (ALG) user-generated text from social media platforms, characterized by multilingual code-switching and unstandardized orthography.', 'The experimental evaluation is restricted to four specific tasks: Code-Switch Detection, Named Entity Recognition, Spelling Normalisation/Correction, and Sentiment Analysis.', 'The neural architecture relies on convolutional character and token encoders with LSTM/dense decoders, without utilizing large pre-trained multilingual transformers.', 'Evaluation is capped at 50 epochs for pairwise experiments and 20 epochs for 3-task and 4-task configurations.']
limitations_summary: The authors identify that multi-task learning improvements are frequently transient and confined to initial training epochs before degrading due to dataset noise and sparsity. Furthermore, substantial class and dataset size imbalances exist, and multi-task efficacy remains highly sensitive to task selection and task ordering.
limitations_verbatim: Other tasks benefit from jointly learning them with some other tasks but the gain is only during the first few epochs, especially for tasks with little training data (CSD, NER and SA comparably to SPELL). Training for more epochs degraded their performance compared to learning them separately which is likely caused by the noisiness and sparsity of the data. This means that it is hard to say whether multi-tasking is useful or not without mentioning several factors such as the tasks themselves, their order, the size of their datasets.
generalizability_gap: The empirical findings are established specifically on Algerian Arabic code-switched social media text. The generalizability of these multi-task dynamics to other low-resource dialectal Arabic varieties, non-Arabic code-switched language pairs, formal linguistic domains, or standardized text remains unverified.
methodological_gap: The framework utilizes a fixed CNN-based encoder architecture with alternating whole-epoch training, omitting exploration of dynamic loss-balancing strategies (e.g., GradNorm, uncertainty weighting), soft parameter sharing mechanisms, or pretrained transformer backbones.
future_work: Examine noise and sparsity hypotheses using sequential transfer learning, such as applying SPELL normalization across all datasets prior to downstream task training.; Explore curriculum learning strategies on both tasks and individual classes by introducing tasks and classes in increasing order of difficulty.; Investigate advanced multi-task loss balancing and optimization techniques to prevent negative transfer during extended training.

title: Which Tasks Should Be Learned Together in Multi-task Learning?
authors: Trevor Standley; Amir Zamir; Dawn Chen; Leonidas Guibas; Jitendra Malik; Silvio Savarese
venue: Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)
domain: Computer Vision, Deep Multi-Task Learning, Task Compatibility and Task Grouping under Inference Time Constraints
problem_statement: In multi-task learning, jointly training all tasks in a single neural network frequently causes negative transfer due to gradient interference and competing task objectives, resulting in accuracy inferior to standalone single-task models; identifying which tasks cooperate or compete to determine optimal task-to-network groupings under inference time budgets remains an open computational challenge.
theoretical_framework: Hard parameter sharing multi-task learning; task cooperation versus task competition dynamics; negative transfer in deep neural representations; combinatorial optimization (Branch-and-Bound reduction from Set Cover) for optimal task subset assignment under computational budgets.
methodology: The authors develop a computational framework to determine optimal task groupings for multi-task learning under inference time budgets: (1) Formulate task grouping as minimizing total loss over a task set T subject to combined inference time cost <= b; (2) Exhaustively train candidate networks across all 2^|T| - 1 possible task subsets (evaluating 36 candidate architectures across full-size and half-size encoders); (3) Solve the NP-hard network selection problem via branch-and-bound optimization; (4) Propose two time-saving approximation strategies: Early Stopping Approximation (ESA), which predicts final performance using validation loss after 20% training (yielding ~20x speedup), and Higher Order Approximation (HOA), which estimates performance on 3+ tasks by linearly averaging first-order pairwise task performances (~45% speedup). Evaluated across four controlled experimental settings varying network capacity (standard vs. high-capacity Xception), dataset size (full vs. 5% subset / 200k examples), and task distributions (Task Set 1: semantic segmentation, depth, normals, keypoints, edges; Task Set 2: autoencoding, normals, occlusion edges, reshading, principal curvature).
datasets: Taskonomy Dataset: Subset of indoor scene images evaluated across four experimental settings. Standard training uses 4 million images across non-overlapping buildings; Setting 3 uses a reduced subset of 199,498 training images (420 images from each training building).; Task Set 1: Semantic Segmentation, Surface Normal Prediction, Depth Estimation, Keypoint Detection, 2D Edge Detection.; Task Set 2: Autoencoder, Surface Normal Prediction, Occlusion Edges, Reshading, Principal Curvature.
evaluation: {'metrics': ['Total Multi-Task Loss under inference time budget (Single Network Time, SNT, evaluated from 1 SNT to 5 SNT in 0.5 SNT increments)', 'Pairwise Multi-Task Affinity (% relative performance gain or drop relative to standalone training)', 'Pearson correlation (r) across training settings and against transfer affinities', 'Qualitative visual prediction comparisons'], 'baselines': ['Single-Task Networks (independent dedicated networks per task evaluated at full and half capacity)', 'All-in-One Multi-Task Network (single shared network training all tasks simultaneously)', 'MGDA / Pareto Multi-Objective Optimization (Sener & Koltun, 2018)', 'GradNorm (Chen et al., 2018b)', 'Random Task Grouping (average of 1 million valid random task assignments)', 'Pessimal Task Grouping (worst-case feasible task assignment)']}
key_findings: Training all tasks in a single large multi-task network is often suboptimal; assigning compatible cooperating tasks to a few smaller networks consistently outperforms both all-in-one MTL and isolated single-task models across all computational budgets.; Multi-task task affinities do not correlate with transfer learning task affinities (e.g., Pearson r = -0.12 with Taskonomy), demonstrating that transfer relationships cannot predict joint multi-task training compatibility.; Multi-task affinities are highly sensitive to network capacity and dataset size; tasks that compete under low capacity or low data often cooperate effectively when encoder capacity is increased.; More functionally similar tasks do not necessarily train well together (e.g., depth and surface normals show low multi-task affinity despite strong geometric relatedness).; Adding an auxiliary task (such as Surface Normals) can improve performance on primary outputs even when the auxiliary task itself suffers performance degradation, functioning as beneficial loss guidance.; The Higher Order Approximation (HOA) accurately estimates higher-order task combinations from pairwise networks, achieving performance close to the exact combinatorial optimum while saving 45% training computation.
scope_and_delimitations: ['Empirical evaluation is delimited to indoor computer vision tasks on the Taskonomy benchmark across 5-task dictionaries.', 'Architectures are delimited to convolutional encoder-decoder backbones (standard convolutional networks and Xception) using hard parameter sharing.', 'Multi-task training uses uniform loss weighting by default, with comparative baselines delimited to GradNorm and Sener & Koltun (2018) without testing recent gradient surgery methods (PCGrad, CAGrad).']
limitations_summary: Multi-task affinities are not invariant and depend heavily on network capacity, dataset volume, and training hyperparameters; the combinatorial search over candidate networks requires substantial training computation that scales exponentially without approximations; and Early Stopping Approximation is constrained by adaptive learning rate schedules.
limitations_verbatim: However, because we had five tasks, more than half of the candidate set was fully trained for this approximation. The Early Stopping Approximation was usually competitive, but the solutions tended to be worse than optimal. In principle, one could stop after training on more of the data, likely resulting in better results. We could not test ESA with other data amounts because our adaptive learning rates resulted in networks that were no longer comparable after being trained on more data.
generalizability_gap: The task grouping framework was evaluated exclusively on static computer vision dense prediction tasks in indoor environments; task compatibility dynamics and grouping behavior remain untested on natural language processing tasks, code-switched text, audio, or mixed-granularity sequence labeling and classification architectures.
methodological_gap: The framework assumes uniform task loss weighting during candidate network training and does not integrate modern gradient surgery algorithms (such as PCGrad, CAGrad, or Nash-MTL) to arbitrate gradient conflicts within task groups; additionally, the approach does not consider soft parameter sharing or modular routing.
future_work: Integrating candidate networks trained with diverse architectures, adaptive loss weighting, and dynamic gradient balancing algorithms into the grouping search.; Exploring ensemble predictions when multiple networks in a solution solve the same task.; Extending task compatibility estimation to large task sets using scalable graph-based clustering or task embedding techniques.
